sources.why: Applies psychological principles (Fitts's Law, Hick's Law, Jakob's Law) to practical UX and interface design decisions.

sources.why: Explains cognitive and perceptual psychology principles underlying effective UI design guidelines and standards.

sources.why: Establishes microinteractions (trigger, rules, feedback, loops) as essential detail pattern for delight and usability in interface design.

sources.title: Inclusive Components: Cards
sources.why: Accessible pattern for card components with semantic HTML, ARIA guidance, and responsive considerations.

sources.title: Inclusive Components: Data Tables
sources.why: Accessible approach to data table design with header markup, scope attributes, and keyboard navigation.

claims.rule: Mark column headers with <th> and scope="col" so screen readers announce the column when navigating table cells.
claims.quote: If I use my screen reader to navigate to a row cell, it will read out the header under which it sits, letting me know which column I am currently in.

claims.rule: Use scope="row" on row headers to clarify that a header labels cells to its right, not below.
claims.quote: Unless you state it explicitly, it isn't clear whether a header labels cells below it or to its right. That's where the scope attribute comes in.

sources.title: Inclusive Components: Notifications
sources.why: Pattern for accessible toast/notification components using ARIA live regions and semantic markup.

sources.title: Inclusive Components: Content Slider
sources.why: Accessible carousel/slider pattern respecting keyboard navigation and screen reader announcement.

claims.rule: Show affordance that content is slidable: use a focus style and ensure the rightmost item is partially cut off.
claims.quote: There are already a couple of things that tell the user this is a slidable region: the focus style, and the fact that the right-most image is usually cut off, suggesting there is more to see.

sources.title: Inclusive Components: Collapsible Sections
sources.why: Pattern for accessible disclosure/accordion components with proper ARIA attributes and keyboard support.

claims.rule: Hide collapsed content with the hidden attribute so it is not focusable by keyboard users.
claims.quote: Another advantage is that keyboard users do not have to step through all of the focusable elements on the page to get to where they want to go: Hidden content is not focusable.

sources.title: Inclusive Components: Tabbed Interfaces
sources.why: Accessible tab component pattern with keyboard navigation (arrow keys), ARIA roles, and semantic structure.

claims.rule: Do not use tabbed interfaces for site-wide navigation; tabs expect within-page behavior, not page navigation.
claims.quote: It is for the same reason that a tabbed design should not be employed for site-wide navigation. At the very least, when a user selects a "tab" they would not expect to be navigated to an entirely new page!

claims.rule: Use semantic HTML (table of contents + same-page links) before adding ARIA tab semantics.
claims.quote: For my money, an embryonic tabbed interface is just a table of content with same-page links pointing at different sections of the page.

sources.title: Inclusive Components: Theme Switcher
sources.why: Accessible dark mode toggle pattern respecting user preferences (prefers-color-scheme) and persistence.

claims.rule: Implement dark mode by augmenting existing styles, not loading separate stylesheets.
claims.quote: The most efficient course of action is not to provide a completely alternative stylesheet, but to augment the existing styles directly, as tersely as possible.

sources.title: Inclusive Components: Tooltips & Toggletips
sources.why: Accessible tooltip pattern with keyboard interaction, proper ARIA, and visual/non-visual considerations.

claims.rule: Use aria-labelledby for primary tooltip labels and aria-describedby for supplementary tooltips.
claims.quote: A notifications control with a tooltip reading "Notifications" treats the tooltip as a primary label. Alternatively, a tooltip that reads "View notifications and manage settings" is supplementary.

claims.rule: Make tooltips visible on keyboard focus, not only on hover, so keyboard users can access them.
claims.quote: The tooltip text is available on focus, just as it would be on hover for sighted users.

sources.title: Inclusive Components: Todo List
sources.why: Accessible interactive list with checkboxes, form semantics, and keyboard support patterns.

claims.rule: Hide delete buttons on hover and show them permanently, or provide keyboard access; do not hide functionality from keyboard users.
claims.quote: Most notably, the delete functionality only appears on hover, making it an entirely inaccessible feature by keyboard.

sources.title: Every Layout: The Stack
sources.why: Algorithmic layout primitive for vertical stacking with consistent spacing, eliminating media queries.

claims.rule: Style spacing context, not individual elements; use adjacent sibling combinator to inject margin only between elements.
claims.quote: margin is really a property of the relationship between two proximate elements

claims.rule: Base vertical spacing on body text line-height to align spacing rhythm with typographic rhythm.
claims.quote: The vertical spacing of your design should be based on your standard line-height because text dominates most pages

claims.rule: Use CSS custom properties for exception-based spacing overrides within layout contexts.
claims.quote: you can create per-element exceptions within a single Stack context (i.e. at the same nesting level)

sources.title: Every Layout: The Box
sources.why: Fundamental container pattern with consistent padding and constraints for reusable layout primitives.

sources.title: Every Layout: The Center
sources.why: Horizontally-centered container pattern with max-width constraint and intrinsic sizing principles.

sources.title: Every Layout: The Cluster
sources.why: Layout pattern for flexible grouping of variable-width child elements with consistent gap and wrapping.

sources.title: Every Layout: The Sidebar
sources.why: Two-column layout that flips to single-column on smaller viewports without media queries using flex-basis.

claims.rule: Use content-aware media queries, not device-based breakpoints, to reconfigure layout when content requires it.
claims.quote: It's important we use content rather than device based @media queries. That is, we should intervene anywhere the content needs reconfiguration

sources.title: Every Layout: The Switcher
sources.why: Adaptive layout that switches from horizontal to vertical orientation based on intrinsic sizing constraints.

claims.rule: Use flex-basis to suggest ideal element width rather than width to enforce fixed dimensions regardless of context.
claims.quote: flex-basis: 20rem is more nuanced. It tells the browser to consider 20rem as an ideal or target width

claims.rule: Think intrinsically about element dimensions and let the browser generate breakpoints based on available space, not viewport width.
claims.quote: Instead of manually pairing the column count to the viewport width, I'm telling the browser to generate the columns based on my desired column width

sources.title: Every Layout: The Cover
sources.why: Centering layout with header/footer and flexible center content, useful for full-height page layouts.

sources.title: Every Layout: The Grid
sources.why: Auto-flow CSS Grid pattern for equal-sized multi-column layouts that adapt to viewport without breakpoints.

sources.title: Every Layout: The Frame
sources.why: Decorative border container pattern maintaining aspect ratio and consistent internal padding.

sources.title: Every Layout: The Reel
sources.why: Horizontal scrollable carousel pattern with consistent spacing and intrinsic sizing.

sources.title: Every Layout: The Imposter
sources.why: Overlay positioning pattern for centered content that sits above or replaces normal document flow.

sources.title: Every Layout: The Icon
sources.why: Layout pattern for icon-plus-text combinations with consistent spacing and alignment.

sources.title: Every Layout: The Container
sources.why: Max-width wrapper pattern for constraining and horizontally-centering content with safe margins.

sources.title: Ben Shneiderman
sources.why: Eight foundational heuristics for interface design: consistency, shortcuts, feedback, closure, error handling, reversal, control, and memory.

claims.rule: Use consistent sequences, terminology, colors, layout, fonts, and capitalization throughout interfaces.
claims.quote: Consistent sequences of actions should be required in similar situations; identical terminology should be used in prompts, menus, and help screens; and consistent color, layout, capitalization, fonts, and so on, should be employed throughout.

claims.rule: Design interfaces to serve users across novice-to-expert ranges, ages, disabilities, and international contexts.
claims.quote: Recognize the needs of diverse users and design for plasticity, facilitating transformation of content. Novice to expert differences, age ranges, disabilities, international variations, and technological diversity each enrich the spectrum of requirements that guides design.

claims.rule: Provide interface feedback for every user action, scaled to the significance of that action.
claims.quote: For every user action, there should be an interface feedback. For frequent and minor actions, the response can be modest, whereas for infrequent and major actions, the response should be more substantial.

claims.rule: Organize action sequences into grouped tasks with a clear beginning, middle, and end plus completion feedback.
claims.quote: Sequences of actions should be organized into groups with a beginning, middle, and end. Informative feedback at the completion of a group of actions gives users the satisfaction of accomplishment, a sense of relief, a signal to drop contingency plans from their minds, and an indicator to prepare for the next group of actions.

sources.title: Dieter Rams: Ten Principles for Good Design
sources.why: Ten design principles emphasizing innovation, utility, honesty, longevity, and restraint as path to good design.

sources.title: Bruce Tognazzini's First Principles of Interaction Design
sources.why: 19 principles of interaction design covering aesthetics, anticipation, autonomy, consistency, control, and efficiency.

claims.rule: Ensure visual design improvements do not harm productivity, learnability, or satisfaction through user testing.
claims.quote: User test after aesthetic changes have been made, benchmarking, where applicable, the new design against the old. Ensure that learnability, satisfaction, and productivity have been improved or at least have stayed the same.

sources.why: First commercial interface guidelines establishing principles for Lisa and Macintosh design that became standards.

sources.org: Jeff Johnson, Teresa Roberts, William Verplank, David Smith, Charles Irby, Marian Beard, Kevin Mackey
sources.why: Retrospective of first commercial graphical user interface system establishing desktop metaphor and pointing device interaction.

sources.title: Laws of UX: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
sources.why: Users perceive aesthetically pleasing design as more usable, even when it functions identically to less attractive alternatives.

claims.rule: Apply aesthetically pleasing design; it creates positive perception and increases perceived usability.
claims.quote: An aesthetically pleasing design creates a positive response in people's brains and leads them to believe the design actually works better.

claims.rule: Beware: attractive design can mask usability problems and prevent issues from being discovered in testing.
claims.quote: Visually pleasing design can mask usability problems and prevent issues from being discovered during usability testing.

sources.title: Laws of UX: Choice Overload
sources.why: Excessive choices increase cognitive load and decision paralysis; limit options to three to five core alternatives.

claims.rule: Limit visible options to avoid overwhelming users and degrading decision quality.
claims.quote: Too many options hurts users' decision-making ability.

claims.rule: Enable side-by-side comparison when users must choose between related options or pricing tiers.
claims.quote: avoid choice overload by enabling side-by-side comparison of related items and options that require a decision

claims.rule: Prioritize featured content and add search or filtering tools to narrow choices upfront.
claims.quote: prioritizing the content that's shown to them at any given moment (e.g. featured product), providing tools for narrowing down choices up front (e.g. search and filtering)

sources.title: Laws of UX: Chunking
sources.why: Breaking information into smaller, meaningful chunks reduces cognitive load and improves memory retention.

claims.rule: Group content into visually distinct chunks with clear hierarchy so users scan and process faster.
claims.quote: Structuring content into visually distinct groups with a clear hierarchy enables designers to align information with how people evaluate and process digital content.

claims.rule: Use separate visual rules and distinctive modules to show content relationships and underlying structure.
claims.quote: grouping content into distinctive modules, applying rules to separate content, and providing hierarchy

sources.title: Laws of UX: Cognitive Bias
sources.why: Users interpret information in ways that confirm existing beliefs and filter out contradictory information.

sources.title: Laws of UX: Cognitive Load
sources.why: Working memory capacity is limited; design should minimize cognitive demands through simplification and clarity.

claims.rule: Reduce intrinsic cognitive load by helping users absorb information and track goals without extra effort.
claims.quote: Intrinsic cognitive load refers to the effort required by users to carry around information relevant to their goal, absorb new information and keep track of their goals.

claims.rule: Remove distracting and unnecessary design elements that consume mental resources without aiding comprehension.
claims.quote: Extraneous cognitive load refers to the mental processing that takes up resources but doesn't help users understand the content

sources.title: Laws of UX: Doherty Threshold
sources.why: Systems responding within 400 milliseconds feel responsive; faster responses increase perceived productivity.

claims.rule: Provide system feedback within 400 milliseconds to maintain user attention and productivity.
claims.quote: Provide system feedback within 400 ms in order to keep users' attention and increase productivity.

claims.rule: Use animation to engage users visually during loading or background processing.
claims.quote: Animation is one way to visually engage people while loading or processing is happening in the background.

claims.rule: Show progress bars to make wait times tolerable, regardless of their measured accuracy.
claims.quote: Progress bars help make wait times tolerable, regardless of their accuracy.

claims.rule: Add intentional delay to increase perceived value and user trust, even if the process runs faster.
claims.quote: Purposefully adding a delay to a process can actually increase its perceived value and instill a sense of trust

sources.title: Laws of UX: Fitts's Law
sources.why: Target acquisition time depends on distance and size; make important buttons larger or place at screen edges.

claims.rule: Make touch targets large enough for accurate selection and easy acquisition.
claims.quote: Touch targets should be large enough for users to accurately select them.

claims.rule: Space touch targets far apart to prevent accidental selection of adjacent controls.
claims.quote: Touch targets should have ample spacing between them.

claims.rule: Place task-related buttons close to users' focus area to minimize distance and interaction time.
claims.quote: the distance between a user's task/attention area and the task-related button should be kept as short as possible

sources.title: Laws of UX: Flow
sources.why: Users achieve flow state when challenge level matches skill level; design tasks with appropriate difficulty progression.

claims.rule: Balance task difficulty with user skill level to sustain focused engagement and prevent frustration or boredom.
claims.quote: Flow occurs when there is a balance between the difficulty of a task with the level of skill at the given task.

claims.rule: Provide immediate feedback so users know what action was performed and what has been accomplished.
claims.quote: Design for flow by providing the necessary feedback so that the user know what action has been done and what has been accomplished.

claims.rule: Remove unnecessary friction and surface content and features for discovery to maintain user engagement.
claims.quote: Optimize for efficiency and system responsiveness by removing any unnecessary friction, and making content and features available for discovery to avoid disengagement with the interface.

sources.title: Laws of UX: Goal-Gradient Effect
sources.why: Users are motivated to increase effort as they approach a goal; show progress and celebrate milestones.

claims.rule: Show clear progress indication to motivate users toward task completion.
claims.quote: Provide a clear indication of progress in order to motivate users to complete tasks.

claims.rule: Provide artificial progress markers to sustain motivation and task completion rates.
claims.quote: Providing artificial progress towards a goal will help to ensure users are more likely to have the motivation to complete that task.

sources.title: Laws of UX: Hick's Law
sources.why: Decision time increases logarithmically with number of options; progressively reveal advanced options.

claims.rule: Minimize choices at critical decision points to reduce decision time and enable faster response.
claims.quote: Minimize choices when response times are critical to decrease decision time.

claims.rule: Break complex tasks into smaller sequential steps to reduce cognitive load.
claims.quote: Break complex tasks into smaller steps in order to decrease cognitive load.

claims.rule: Highlight recommended options to prevent user overwhelm when multiple choices exist.
claims.quote: Avoid overwhelming users by highlighting recommended options.

claims.rule: Introduce features progressively during onboarding to minimize cognitive load for new users.
claims.quote: Use progressive onboarding to minimize cognitive load for new users.

sources.title: Laws of UX: Jakob's Law
sources.why: Users prefer interfaces that work like sites they already know; follow established conventions and patterns.

claims.rule: Align interface patterns with familiar mental models users have formed from other products.
claims.quote: By leveraging existing mental models, we can create superior user experiences in which the users can focus on their tasks rather than on learning new models.

claims.rule: Allow users to preview and revert to familiar designs when introducing significant changes.
claims.quote: When making changes, minimize discord by empowering users to continue using a familiar version for a limited time.

sources.title: Laws of UX: Law of Common Region
sources.why: Elements placed within a shared bounded region are perceived as related and grouped together.

claims.rule: Use borders or backgrounds to define clear boundaries that group related elements together.
claims.quote: Common region creates a clear structure and helps users quickly and effectively understand the relationship between elements and sections.

sources.title: Laws of UX: Law of Proximity
sources.why: Objects placed close together are perceived as related; use spacing to establish visual groupings.

claims.rule: Position related elements close together to establish perceived relationships and shared functionality.
claims.quote: Proximity helps to establish a relationship with nearby objects. Elements in close proximity are perceived to share similar functionality or traits.

sources.title: Laws of UX: Law of Prägnanz
sources.why: People perceive complex visual forms as simple, regular, symmetrical shapes; simplify design to leverage this.

claims.rule: Prevent visual overwhelm by organizing information into simple, ordered patterns.
claims.quote: The human eye likes to find simplicity and order in complex shapes because it prevents us from becoming overwhelmed with information

sources.title: Laws of UX: Law of Similarity
sources.why: Elements sharing visual properties are perceived as related; use consistent styling for related items.

claims.rule: Use color, shape, size, and orientation to signal that elements share meaning or function.
claims.quote: Color, shape, and size, orientation and movement can signal that elements belong to the same group and likely share a common meaning or functionality

claims.rule: Differentiate links and navigation visually from normal text to avoid ambiguity.
claims.quote: Ensure that links and navigation systems are visually differentiated from normal text elements

claims.rule: Perceive separated elements as a group when they share visual properties like color or shape.
claims.quote: The human eye tends to perceive similar elements as a complete picture, shape, or group, even if those elements are separated

sources.title: Laws of UX: Law of Uniform Connectedness
sources.why: Elements connected by visual properties like color or shape are perceived as more related than separate elements.

claims.rule: Connect related functions visually via colors, lines, frames, or shapes to show relationships.
claims.quote: Group functions of a similar nature so they are visually connected via colors, lines, frames, or other shapes

claims.rule: Use tangible connectors like lines or arrows between elements to establish visual relationships.
claims.quote: you can use a tangible connecting reference (line, arrow, etc) from one element to the next to also create a visual connection

sources.title: Laws of UX: Mental Model
sources.why: Users form mental models of systems based on experience; design interfaces aligned with how users think.

claims.rule: Match product design to users' existing mental models to enable knowledge transfer.
claims.quote: Match designs to the users' mental models to improve their experience. This enables them to easily transfer their knowledge from one product or experience to another

claims.rule: Use familiar patterns and conventions in e-commerce to conform to user expectations.
claims.quote: e-commerce websites, which use consistent patterns and conventions such product cards, virtual carts and checkout flows in order to conform to users' expectations

claims.rule: Conduct user research to align your design with users' mental models of how systems work.
claims.quote: The task of shrinking the gap between our own mental models and those of the users is one of the biggest challenges we face, and to achieve this goal we use a variety of user research methods

sources.title: Laws of UX: Miller's Law
sources.why: Average person can hold 7±2 chunks in working memory; organize information into meaningful groups.

claims.rule: Chunk content into smaller units to help users process, understand, and memorize information.
claims.quote: Organize content into smaller chunks to help users process, understand, and memorize easily

claims.rule: Account for working memory limits that vary by individual knowledge and situational context.
claims.quote: short-term memory capacity will vary per individual, based on their prior knowledge and situational context

sources.title: Laws of UX: Occam's Razor
sources.why: Simpler explanations are usually better; remove unnecessary elements and complexity from design.

claims.rule: Remove elements that don't compromise function to reduce overall complexity.
claims.quote: Analyze each element and remove as many as possible, without compromising the overall function

claims.rule: Avoid complexity at the outset rather than trying to reduce it later.
claims.quote: The best method for reducing complexity is to avoid it in the first place

sources.title: Laws of UX: Paradox of the Active User
sources.why: Users rarely read documentation; design interfaces that are self-discoverable without extensive learning.

claims.rule: Provide contextual guidance throughout the product, not upfront documentation, so users can learn while accomplishing immediate tasks.
claims.quote: Make guidance accessible throughout the product experience and design it to fit within the context of use

sources.title: Laws of UX: Pareto Principle
sources.why: 80% of effects come from 20% of causes; focus design effort on the most impactful features.

claims.rule: Prioritize design effort on the 20% of features and flows that deliver 80% of user value and impact.
claims.quote: Focus the majority of effort on the areas that will bring the largest benefits to the most users

sources.title: Laws of UX: Parkinson's Law
sources.why: Work expands to fill allotted time; set clear deadlines and time constraints in user interactions.

claims.rule: Set and display expected task duration to prevent users from expanding effort to fill available time.
claims.quote: Limit the time it takes to complete a task to what users expect it'll take

claims.rule: Use autofill and pre-populated fields in forms to reduce actual task completion time below user expectations.
claims.quote: Leverage features such as autofill to save the user time when providing critical information within forms

sources.title: Laws of UX: Peak-End Rule
sources.why: Users judge experiences by their peak and end moments; design memorable emotional moments in key transitions.

claims.rule: Design the most intense moments and the final moments of a user journey to create lasting positive impressions.
claims.quote: Pay close attention to the most intense points and the final moments (the "end") of the user journey

claims.rule: Soften negative experiences with character, illustration, animation, or humor to prevent lasting negative impressions.
claims.quote: infusing a touch of brand character through illustration, subtle animation, and humor, the tool defuses what could potentially be a stressful moment

sources.title: Laws of UX: Postel's Law
sources.why: Be conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept; gracefully handle user input and errors.

claims.rule: Accept variable and non-standard user input, translating it to meet your system's requirements while providing clear feedback.
claims.quote: Accept variable input from users, translating that input to meet your requirements, defining boundaries for input, and providing clear feedback

claims.rule: Anticipate diverse user capabilities and access patterns, building resilience into design through flexible and tolerant interfaces.
claims.quote: Be empathetic to, flexible about, and tolerant of any of the various actions the user could take or any input they might provide

sources.title: Laws of UX: Selective Attention
sources.why: Users filter information to focus on relevant tasks; highlight important elements and reduce distractions.

claims.rule: Avoid styling content to resemble ads or placing it near ads, as users consciously ignore banner-like information.
claims.quote: Users have learned to ignore content that resembles ads, is close to ads, or appears in locations traditionally dedicated to ads

claims.rule: Guide user attention to relevant information and actions by reducing visual clutter and distracting competing changes.
claims.quote: Designers must guide users' attention, prevent them from being overwhelmed or distracted, and help them find relevant information or action

claims.rule: Analyze designs for simultaneous competing visual changes that divert attention; avoid triggering change blindness.
claims.quote: Avoid this by analyzing your design for any competing changes that may happen at the same time and that may divert attention from each other

sources.title: Laws of UX: Serial Position Effect
sources.why: Users remember first and last items in sequences better; place key actions at beginning or end.

claims.rule: Place key actions on the far left and right of navigation elements to increase memorization.
claims.quote: Positioning key actions on the far left and right within elements such as navigation can increase memorization.

claims.rule: Place least important items in the middle of lists because they are stored less in working and long-term memory.
claims.quote: Placing the least important items in the middle of lists can be helpful because these items tend to be stored less frequently in long-term and working memory.

sources.title: Laws of UX: Tesler's Law
sources.why: Complexity cannot be eliminated; move it from users to designers through thoughtful interface design.

claims.rule: Shift core complexity from the user to the system during design and development.
claims.quote: All processes have a core of complexity that cannot be designed away and therefore must be assumed by either the system or the user.

claims.rule: Make guidance accessible and contextual so new users can find help regardless of their path.
claims.quote: Make guidance accessible and fit within the context of use so that it can help these active new users, no matter what path they choose to take (e.g., tooltips with helpful information).

sources.title: Laws of UX: Von Restorff Effect
sources.why: Visually distinct elements are more memorable and attention-grabbing; use contrast to highlight key items.

claims.rule: Make important information or key actions visually distinctive.
claims.quote: Make important information or key actions visually distinctive.

claims.rule: Use restraint when emphasizing visual elements to prevent them competing and appearing as ads.
claims.quote: Use restraint when placing emphasis on visual elements to avoid them competing with one another and to ensure salient items don't get mistakenly identified as ads.

claims.rule: Do not rely exclusively on color to communicate contrast to users with color vision deficiency.
claims.quote: Don't exclude those with a color vision deficiency or low vision by relying exclusively on color to communicate contrast.

claims.rule: Carefully consider users with motion sensitivity when using motion to communicate contrast.
claims.quote: Carefully consider users with motion sensitivity when using motion to communicate contrast.

sources.title: Laws of UX: Working Memory
sources.why: Working memory is temporary and limited in capacity; reduce cognitive load through progressive disclosure.

claims.rule: Display only necessary and relevant information since working memory holds 4-7 chunks for 20-30 seconds.
claims.quote: Working memory is limited to 4-7 chunks of information at any given moment with each chunk fades after 20-30 seconds.

claims.rule: Support recognition over recall by visually differentiating visited links and providing breadcrumbs.
claims.quote: We can support recognition over recall by making it clear what information has already been viewed (e.g. visually differentiating visited links and providing breadcrumbs links).

sources.title: Laws of UX: Zeigarnik Effect
sources.why: Incomplete tasks are remembered better than completed ones; show progress and incomplete states to maintain engagement.

claims.rule: Provide clear signifiers of additional content to invite discovery.
claims.quote: Invite content discovery by providing clear signifiers of additional content.

claims.rule: Provide artificial progress toward a goal to motivate users to complete tasks.
claims.quote: Providing artificial progress towards a goal will help to ensure users are more likely to have the motivation to complete that task.

claims.rule: Provide clear progress indication to motivate users to complete tasks.
claims.quote: Provide a clear indication of progress in order to motivate users to complete tasks.

sources.title: Jakob Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
sources.why: Foundational 10 heuristics for evaluating interface usability: system visibility, real-world language, control, standards, error prevention.

claims.rule: Keep users informed of system status through appropriate feedback within reasonable time.
claims.quote: The design should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within a reasonable amount of time.

claims.rule: Present feedback to the user as quickly as possible, ideally immediately.
claims.quote: Present feedback to the user as quickly as possible (ideally, immediately).

claims.rule: Use words and concepts familiar to users rather than internal jargon.
claims.quote: The design should speak the users' language. Use words, phrases, and concepts familiar to the user, rather than internal jargon.

claims.rule: Follow real-world conventions and present information in natural, logical order.
claims.quote: Follow real-world conventions, making information appear in a natural and logical order.

claims.rule: Make controls follow real-world conventions for natural mapping to ease learning.
claims.quote: When a design's controls follow real-world conventions and correspond to desired outcomes (called natural mapping ), it's easier for users to learn and remember how the interface works.

claims.rule: Provide a clearly marked emergency exit to leave unwanted actions without extended process.
claims.quote: Users often perform actions by mistake. They need a clearly marked "emergency exit" to leave the unwanted action without having to go through an extended process.

claims.rule: Support Undo and Redo to give users control and confidence.
claims.quote: Support Undo and Redo .

claims.rule: Follow platform and industry conventions to meet user expectations.
claims.quote: Users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations, or actions mean the same thing. Follow platform and industry conventions.

claims.rule: Maintain internal consistency across a product and external consistency with industry standards.
claims.quote: Improve learnability by maintaining both types of consistency: internal and external.

claims.rule: Prevent errors by eliminating error-prone conditions or confirming actions before commit.
claims.quote: Good error messages are important, but the best designs carefully prevent problems from occurring in the first place. Either eliminate error-prone conditions, or check for them and present users with a confirmation option before they commit to the action.

claims.rule: Avoid slips by providing helpful constraints and good defaults.
claims.quote: Avoid slips by providing helpful constraints and good defaults .

sources.title: Refactoring UI: 7 Practical Tips for Cheating at Design
sources.why: Practical design tips for developers including use of constraint, consistency, depth, and hierarchical variation.

sources.title: Shape language: Duolingo's art style
sources.why: Defines core shape-based approach to illustration and visual design: rounded rectangle, circle, rounded triangle create rhythm.

claims.rule: Use the fewest details needed to make illustrations instantly recognizable at a glance.
claims.quote: using the fewest details needed to get the point across. Not enough details, and learners might be confused. Too many, and shapes could be less readable at a glance

claims.rule: Frame artwork with white negative space so each illustration enhances the app experience and never interrupts it.
claims.quote: framed with white negative space and constructed of clever, clearly recognizable details so each illustration enhances our learners' app experience, and never interrupts it

claims.rule: Use exaggeration and humor in visual design to reduce learner intimidation and encourage daily practice.
claims.quote: When the visuals are playful, the intimidation falls away, and learners actually look forward to coming back to practice every day

claims.rule: Rotate lines and angles in artwork to direct the eye toward UI elements or text that needs attention.
claims.quote: To draw attention to UI or text on the screen, we rotate lines and angles in the artwork to direct the eye

sources.title: Elevating craft: How we refreshed our core tabs
sources.why: Documents tab redesign focusing on consistency, typography hierarchy, spacing, and framework for balanced design decisions.

claims.rule: Balance consistency with purpose; avoid consistency patterns that lack function or occupy space without signaling value.
claims.quote: using artwork in every tab header is consistent, but it can also feel forced, especially if it occupies significant space without signaling anything useful

claims.rule: Balance simplicity with clarity; remove elements strategically but retain what users need to understand the interface.
claims.quote: Simplicity is good but not at the expense of clarity. Good design means knowing what to remove and what to keep

claims.rule: Use tiered header sizes based on each tab's purpose while keeping titles consistently positioned across tabs.
claims.quote: we created tiered sizes based on each tab's purpose while keeping the titles consistently positioned

sources.title: Four Principles for the Future of Design
sources.why: Evolves Microsoft design principles to: Natural on every platform, Built for focus, One for all, Unmistakably Microsoft.

claims.rule: Design layouts that adapt to different screen sizes and are aware of the platform to make experiences feel natural.
claims.quote: A layout that adapts to different screen sizes and is aware of the platform it's on makes an experience feel natural

claims.rule: Reduce visual clutter and noise to keep people centered, calm, and confident in their work.
claims.quote: Less visual clutter and noise keeps people centered, calm, and confident

claims.rule: Include people with diverse abilities and perspectives early in design to generate better solutions and help people feel they belong.
claims.quote: Including and learning from a variety of people with a range of abilities and perspectives earlier in the design process makes for better solutions

claims.rule: Focus design energy on signature experiences that connect products together and give them a distinctively recognizable feel.
claims.quote: We focus our energy on signature experiences that connect our products together and give them a distinctively Microsoft feel

sources.title: Output isn't design
sources.why: Addresses misconception that design is output; explores design as product judgment and structure.

claims.rule: Design visually by moving things around and testing relationships; the act of doing builds clarity instead of assuming it.
claims.quote: Working visually keeps me close to the problem and is slow enough gives me time to think while I work. Moving things around, testing relationships, and refining structure is not separate from the thinking

sources.title: Styling Linear for the future with StyleX
sources.why: Documents design system migration with automation and clearer boundaries for design and engineering.

claims.rule: Keep styles colocated with components for developer clarity, not separated into distant files.
claims.quote: Styles stay colocated with components, the API is small, and style resolution is deterministic

claims.rule: Define styling foundations—variables, constants, and shared primitives—before scaling a large migration.
claims.quote: Before the codemod could do useful work, we had to define the StyleX variables, constants, and shared primitives

claims.rule: Give coding agents narrow scopes, codemods, examples, validation scripts, and checklists to succeed in large migrations.
claims.quote: Agents work better when they have a narrow scope, a codemod runner, examples, validation scripts, and a clear checklist

sources.title: A calmer interface for a product in motion
sources.why: Details interface refresh focused on balance, reducing visual clutter while maintaining information density.

claims.rule: Make navigation and supporting elements visually recede so the main content area—where users work—takes precedence.
claims.quote: The navigation sidebar used to appear bright enough that it remained visually prominent even after a user had reached their destination. In the updated interface, it's a few notches dimmer, allowing the main content area—where users work—to take precedence

claims.rule: Reduce icon usage, scale down their sizes, and remove unnecessary visual treatments like colored backgrounds.
claims.quote: The refresh reduces icon usage, scales their sizes down, and removes unnecessary visual treatments like colored team icon backgrounds

claims.rule: Round separator edges and soften contrast to provide structure without visual clutter.
claims.quote: By rounding out their edges and softening the contrast, the polished interface gives users structure on the page without cluttering their view

claims.rule: Shift default color palettes toward warmer grays that feel crisp without high saturation to avoid a muddy appearance.
claims.quote: The old palette was a cool, blue-ish hue, and the aim was to inch toward a warmer gray that still feels crisp, but less saturated

sources.title: Invisible Details of Interaction Design
sources.why: Essay on micro-interactions, animations, and tactile feedback that make software feel alive.

claims.rule: Design gestures to mirror real-world physics and interruptibility, not require waiting for animations.
claims.quote: Great interactions are modeled after properties from the real world, like interruptibility. This sounds silly because obviously flipping a page in a book is interruptible. But imagine if it were an animation that you had to wait for.

claims.rule: Teach core gestures early so users unlock control of many interface parts through metaphor reuse.
claims.quote: Great interaction design rewards learning by reusing metaphors. You can use most touch interfaces with just two gestures: tapping and swiping.

claims.rule: Use horizontal swiping to navigate pages because humans have intuitively flipped through books for millennia.
claims.quote: Why does swiping horizontally navigate between pages? Because that's how we've intuitively interfaced with books for thousands of years.

sources.title: Human Interface Guidelines
sources.why: Comprehensive design system across iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS covering Clarity, Deference, Depth.

sources.title: How Meta product designers are shaping the future of social connection
sources.why: Perspectives from Meta product designers on designing for billions at scale.

sources.title: Writing the metaverse
sources.why: Meta's approach to content design in immersive environments.

claims.rule: Maintain consistent terminology and content standards across all products so users understand how to navigate your entire ecosystem.
claims.quote: One of the most important results of this collaboration–in regard to terminology and content standards–is excellent UX writing and our ability to communicate across the entire world. We work hard to drive alignment, create robust standards and be consistent so that people can understand how to navigate our products as part of an entire ecosystem.

sources.title: Figma's new icon
sources.why: Documents icon design evolution for Figma's product.

claims.rule: Build complex designs from a small set of carefully selected basic elements—points, lines, and shapes—used efficiently together.
claims.quote: Every design begins with same basic elements — points, lines, and shapes. Similarly, even the most complex designs can be reduced to these indispensable pieces. It's our belief that a great design is one where these pieces are used efficiently together.

claims.rule: Encourage discovery through structured experimentation and play to solve old problems with new solutions.
claims.quote: The second concept that underpinned our new icon was 'encouraging play.' We believe the way to discover new solutions to old problems is through (sometimes very structured) experimentation and play.

claims.rule: Design with vectors and modular systems so designs adapt to any screen size or environment instead of breaking in wrong contexts.
claims.quote: An example of this is designing with vectors rather then pixels. If you can create a design that is made up of a ruleset, it can adapt to any environment. If you design with a fixed set of pixels, they're bound to break down in the wrong context.

sources.title: Figma on Figma: How we built figma.com's design system
sources.why: Figma applies design system principles to its own website and design tooling.

claims.rule: Standardize repeated elements (typography sizes, spacing, colors) into one style instead of maintaining multiple near-identical versions.
claims.quote: We also looked for elements that were similar, but not exactly the same, and agreed on one style. So, instead of 12 different sizes for headings, we established an H1-H3, body copy, and technical copy styles.

claims.rule: Update design system components once in a central location so changes propagate across all pages without hunting through code.
claims.quote: Additionally, when we want to make a universal change to an atom or molecule, we can do it once in Contentful, rather than getting a developer to hunt through every page to make dozens of updates directly.

claims.rule: Break out of the design system for exceptional focal points (like homepage hero animations) that don't repeat elsewhere.
claims.quote: There are also times when we break out of the system. For example, we wanted to capture a visitor's attention right away on our homepage, so we opted for larger, centered headline that is animated. There are no other sections like this on our site and therefore this is not part of our design system.

sources.title: Material Design
sources.why: Comprehensive design language with principles for adaptive, material-based interfaces and responsive interactions.

sources.title: Intercom's Product Principles
sources.why: Connected modular systems, opinionated by default, follow fundamentals, make it feel personal.

sources.title: How to Get the Most Out of Shopify's Design System Polaris
sources.why: Introduces Polaris design system principles, voice and tone, developer resources, pre-made components.

claims.rule: Use consistent color purposefully throughout your interface to guide merchant attention and understanding.
claims.quote: Color is used purposefully in our interface redesign

claims.rule: Design type hierarchy and scale so merchants can easily find the information they need.
claims.quote: clear do and don't examples for page layouts, designed to help merchants easily find the information they're looking for

claims.rule: Match your interface language tone to merchant needs and emotions in each context.
claims.quote: tone should change in order to respond to merchant needs and emotions

claims.rule: Normalize all interaction patterns—keyboard, mouse, and callback events—into a single simple interface.
claims.quote: normalize all the ways those events could occur (including keyboard events), and give you a simple interface for responding to them

claims.rule: Build experiences that feel designed by the same team across all touchpoints and partners.
claims.quote: Polaris helps everyone in building experiences that look and feel like they were designed by the same team

sources.title: IBM Design Language
sources.why: Three principles: Carefully Considered, Uniquely Unified, Expertly Executed. Guides IBM's brand expression.

sources.title: Carbon Design System
sources.why: Open source design system with components, patterns, working code, and design tools.

sources.title: Lightning Design System
sources.why: Four principles: Clarity, Efficiency, Consistency, Beauty. CSS framework for Lightning Experience.

sources.title: Atlassian Design System
sources.why: Three values (foundational, harmonious, empowering) guide design system for team collaboration software.

claims.rule: Use a unified design language across all apps so teams feel the experience is cohesive and familiar.
claims.quote: Across all collections, every app feels cohesive and familiar, empowering teams through one design language.

claims.rule: Design AI experiences to be clear and useful as part of modern teamwork tools.
claims.quote: Designing for teams today means making clear, useful AI experiences.

sources.title: Design Principles Library
sources.why: Curated collection of 1660+ design principles from 230+ organizations. Resource for exploring how principles guide decisions.

sources.title: Google Design Principles
sources.why: Ten principles: useful, fast, simple, engaging, innovative, universal, profitable, beautiful, trustworthy, personable.

sources.title: Apple Design Principles
sources.why: Design principles guiding Apple's product development and user experience across platforms.

sources.title: Facebook Design Principles
sources.why: Design principles from Facebook guiding product design and brand expression.

sources.title: Guiding Principles of Uber
sources.why: Act responsibly, Put design at center, Say we not me - from 77 Things primer for Uber Design.

claims.rule: Guide users clearly through required steps without making them figure things out alone.
claims.quote: Guide users clearly through what they need to do. Provide direction without requiring them to figure things out themselves.

claims.rule: Respect the user's primary task and never demand attention at moments when they cannot focus.
claims.quote: Respect the user's primary task—in this case, driving safely. Don't demand attention at dangerous moments.

claims.rule: Show only information relevant to the current moment; display and hide it based on need.
claims.quote: Show only what's relevant right now. Information should appear when needed and disappear when it's not.

sources.title: Figma Design Principles
sources.why: Nine principles: Powerful, Precise, Systematic, Predictable, Biased toward Simplicity, Natural, Responsible, Detail-oriented, Respectful.

claims.rule: Keep simple interactions simple; make complex tasks possible without adding unnecessary complexity.
claims.quote: Keep the simple things simple, and make the complex things possible.

claims.rule: Base interface patterns on how humans naturally think, not on computer architecture or implementation.
claims.quote: Our solutions should be based on the way humans think, rather than how computers work.

claims.rule: Respect user attention as precious; avoid interrupting them with unnecessary notifications or dialogs.
claims.quote: The attention of our users is precious and we should guard them from unnecessary interruptions.

claims.rule: Introduce new patterns and features mindfully, building on existing user trust and mental models.
claims.quote: When we introduce a new pattern, we do so mindfully.

sources.title: Airbnb Design Language System

claims.rule: Limit options to prevent user overwhelm when presenting choices in an interface.
claims.quote: The tendency for people to get overwhelmed when they are presented with a large number of options

claims.rule: Group related information together to reduce cognitive load and aid comprehension.
claims.quote: A process by which individual pieces of an information set are broken down and then grouped together in a meaningful whole

claims.rule: Respond to user input within 400ms to maintain productivity and interaction flow.
claims.quote: Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace (<400ms) that ensures that neither has to wait on the other

claims.rule: Position targets large and close together to reduce selection time per Fitts's Law.
claims.quote: The time to acquire a target is a function of the distance to and size of the target

claims.rule: Reduce decision time by decreasing the number and complexity of choices available.
claims.quote: The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices

claims.rule: Maintain consistency with familiar patterns users encounter on other established sites.
claims.quote: Users spend most of their time on other sites. This means that users prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know

claims.rule: Group elements with clear visual boundaries to help users perceive them as related.
claims.quote: Elements tend to be perceived into groups if they are sharing an area with a clearly defined boundary

claims.rule: Place related elements near each other to help users perceive them as grouped.
claims.quote: Objects that are near, or proximate to each other, tend to be grouped together

claims.rule: Simplify ambiguous designs into the simplest form to reduce cognitive effort required.
claims.quote: People will perceive and interpret ambiguous or complex images as the simplest form possible, because it is the interpretation that requires the least cognitive effort

claims.rule: Use visual similarity to help users perceive related elements as a complete group.
claims.quote: The human eye tends to perceive similar elements as a complete picture, shape, or group, even if those elements are separated

claims.rule: Connect related elements visually to signal their relationship more strongly.
claims.quote: Elements that are visually connected are perceived as more related than elements with no connection

claims.rule: Limit working memory load to seven items plus or minus two when presenting lists.
claims.quote: The average person can only keep 7 (plus or minus 2) items in their working memory

claims.rule: Choose the simplest solution among competing design approaches that achieve equal results.
claims.quote: Among competing hypotheses that predict equally well, the one with the fewest assumptions should be selected

claims.rule: Design without assumption users will read documentation; make interfaces self-explanatory.
claims.quote: Users never read manuals but start using the software immediately

claims.rule: Focus on the peak moment and conclusion of an experience; users judge these most heavily.
claims.quote: People judge an experience largely based on how they felt at its peak and at its end, rather than the total sum or average of every moment

claims.rule: Accept flexible user input while sending consistent, well-formed responses.
claims.quote: Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send

claims.rule: Design apps to work for people with disabilities, expanding reach and sparking creative innovation.

claims.rule: Support multiple interaction types so users can interact with your app using different senses and abilities.
claims.quote: Find out how to make your apps more inclusive by supporting multiple types of interaction, providing customization, and adopting accessibility APIs.

claims.rule: Recognize that disability emerges from gaps between abilities and environmental design; close these gaps.
claims.quote: When there's a difference between what a person can actually do and what society expects, that is where disability is really born.

claims.rule: Let users customize text size, colors, fonts, and layout density so they can tailor the interface to their individual needs.

claims.quote: adopt the Accessibility APIs so that people who use accessibility features can also use your app. Adopting Accessibility APIs will help you close the rest of the inclusion gap

claims.rule: Identify and track inclusion gaps—where user abilities don't match environmental design—as technical debt to close iteratively.
claims.quote: Think of this as inclusion tech debt, or just inclusion debt for short. This is normal. Inclusion is a journey, it's not a one-time thing

claims.rule: Use optical sizes for fonts: smaller text needs wider letter-spacing and sturdier thin strokes for legibility.
claims.quote: When type becomes smaller, letters tend to need more space between them, so that they eye can more easily tell them apart.

claims.rule: Apply tracking (letter-spacing) consistently with optical size changes to prevent abrupt spacing shifts at size transitions.
claims.quote: With no tracking, the difference in native spacing between SF Text and Display would have been an issue when we switched from one font to the other at 20 points.

claims.rule: Use the tracking API instead of kerning to tighten truncated strings and preserve ligatures for consistent word rhythm.
claims.quote: with a kerning API, that ligature remains and breaks the rhythm of the word. On the other hand, with the tracking API, we take of de-assembling that ligature for you

claims.rule: Design windows with glass material to provide contrast with the world and give people awareness of their surroundings.
claims.quote: The glass material provides contrast with the world, gives people more awareness of their surroundings, and adapts to different lighting conditions.

claims.rule: Ensure windows always turn to face the user when moved to keep interfaces easy to read and use.
claims.quote: Notice how they always turn to face someone when moving. This keeps interfaces easy to read and easy to use.

claims.rule: Keep your app interface in a single window; multiple windows can quickly become overwhelming for users to manage.
claims.quote: Ideally, keep your app's interface in a single window. Multiple windows can quickly become a lot for people to manage.

claims.rule: Use points to specify interface element sizes so they scale correctly as windows move closer or farther from the user.
claims.quote: as people move windows, they scale larger as they move away and scale smaller as they move closer to them. This keeps interfaces legible and usable.

claims.rule: Place primary content in the center of the field of view and spread secondary content horizontally to match landscape perception.
claims.quote: It's easiest to see things in the center, so place the most important content there. And the field of view is wide, so use landscape layouts.

claims.rule: Study the Human Interface Guidelines alongside design resources to understand when and why to use each component.
claims.quote: looking at the Apple Human Interface Guidelines in tandem with the design resources is really, really beneficial because we have so much information about where and when and why to use different components

sources.title: Design for iPhone Duo
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Move controls to the side of the outer display to maximize vertical space for content.
claims.quote: Buttons and controls that normally sit at the top and bottom move to the right side of the display in order to maximize vertical space and to make them easier to reach

claims.rule: Shift text and images away from the center fold when device is partially folded to ensure readability.
claims.quote: When that happens, content automatically moves away from the center region. Text and images shift away from the curve so they are easier to read.

claims.rule: Use layout margins and horizontal safe area insets instead of fixed widths or breakpoints for responsive design.
claims.quote: Build your layouts with layout margins and horizontal safe area insets. If you're already using these tools, you're off to a great start.

claims.rule: Design apps to be freely resizable rather than tied to specific screen sizes or poses.
claims.quote: design your app to be freely resizable and you'll be in good shape

claims.rule: Do not tie app functionality to specific device poses; ensure all controls exist in every pose.
claims.quote: You don't want to tie functionality to a specific pose.

claims.rule: Position controls on the side edge of folding device displays to maximize vertical space for content.
claims.quote: controls that normally sit at the top and bottom move to the right side of the display in order to maximize vertical space

claims.rule: Preserve all controls and functionality across every device pose rather than tying features to specific fold states.
claims.quote: You don't want to tie functionality to a specific pose. So controls move to the side for most of those layouts.

claims.rule: Offset content from the right edge when controls occupy vertical space to prevent blocking interactive elements.
claims.quote: on iPhone Duo, most content needs an offset so it isn't hidden behind the controls

sources.title: Strike a pose with adaptive layouts on iPhone Duo
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use displacement patterns to keep important content visible and reachable when device folds.
claims.quote: displacement, which adjusts the frame of the existing elements based on the available space, keeping important content visible, reachable, and unobstructed even when the device is partially folded

claims.rule: Move related elements together to preserve their visual relationship during displacement.
claims.quote: When elements work together, move them together to preserve their relationship. And remember to be mindful of excessive movement.

claims.rule: Do not displace continuous scrolling content like articles, feeds, and lists.
claims.quote: Continuous scrolling content like articles, feeds, documents, and lists don't displace. These experiences already adapt through scrolling, so moving them between the available regions can interrupt continuity.

claims.rule: Use displacement patterns to move elements away from the fold while preserving their visual relationships and contextual meaning.
claims.quote: displacement, which adjusts the frame of the existing elements based on the available space, keeping important content visible, reachable, and unobstructed

claims.rule: Avoid displacing continuous scrolling content like articles and feeds; let scrolling handle fold adaptation naturally.
claims.quote: Continuous scrolling content like articles, feeds, documents, and lists don't displace

sources.title: Raise the bar with iPhone Duo
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Move navigation, toolbar, and tab bar controls to the side on iPhone Duo's outer display to preserve vertical space.
claims.quote: To make the most out of that width and preserve vertical space for content, controls that normally sit at the top and bottom, move to the side, where they're also easier to reach.

claims.rule: Rebuild apps against the latest iOS SDK to opt into vertical bar layout on iPhone Duo.
claims.quote: To opt your app into the new bar behavior, there are a few things you'll need to do. First, rebuild your app against the latest SDKs.

claims.rule: Use standard navigation containers like NavigationStack or TabView instead of custom bars.
claims.quote: Next, make sure you're using the bars provided by navigation containers like TabView or NavigationStack.

claims.rule: Order toolbar items vertically with primary navigation at top, followed by prominent actions.
claims.quote: When displayed vertically, items retain a clear top-to-bottom hierarchy. Start by auditing your existing toolbar configuration, making sure that controls follow the recommended order. Reserve the top for primary navigation controls, like back or close, followed by prominent actions, such as done.

claims.rule: Prefer symbol-only items in vertical bars to conserve space.
claims.quote: Prefer symbol-only items

claims.rule: Prefer symbol-only items in vertical bars to conserve space; provide both icon and title in your code so the system can choose the right representation.
claims.quote: Typically, your app specifies two pieces of data on your toolbar content, an icon and a title. Depending on the context and what's specified on the item, the system then chooses what representation to show.

claims.rule: Use axisBehavior API to keep related items on the same axis; set horizontalOnly for items that transition between symbol and text, verticalPreferred for custom views that support vertical layout.
claims.quote: Related items should stay on the same axis. One common instance is an item that transitions between a symbol and a text, like this edit button in Clock. That item shouldn't be placed in a vertical bar, even though the symbol could theoretically be displayed vertically.

claims.rule: In multi-display or tall narrow layouts, move secondary navigation to the side edge and preserve vertical space for content.
claims.quote: To make the most out of that width and preserve vertical space for content, controls that normally sit at the top and bottom, move to the side

claims.rule: Use system navigation containers (NavigationStack, TabView, UINavigationController) instead of custom bars to opt into responsive layout behavior.
claims.quote: make sure you're using the bars provided by navigation containers like TabView or NavigationStack

claims.rule: In vertical bars, order items top-to-bottom: primary navigation (back/close) first, then prominent actions (done), then remaining items.
claims.quote: Reserve the top for primary navigation controls, like back or close, followed by prominent actions, such as done

claims.rule: Always provide both icon and title for toolbar items; let the system choose symbol-only or text+icon based on available space.
claims.quote: Typically, your app specifies two pieces of data on your toolbar content, an icon and a title. Depending on the context and what's specified on the item, the system then chooses what representation to show

claims.rule: Replace text+icon pairs with symbol+badge patterns to reduce vertical bar width and preserve space for more actions.
claims.quote: rather than keeping the count inline, I can use a badge on the inbox to turn an item that displays both text and a symbol into a symbol-only item

claims.rule: Prioritize which items stay visible longest in overflow: use visibilityPriority(high) for frequently-used actions and status indicators.
claims.quote: Frequently used actions like Compose in Mail or New Note in Notes should be amongst the last to move into overflow. Likewise, controls that convey important status, such as items with badges, should remain visible for longer

sources.title: Prepare your app for iPhone Duo
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use size classes instead of interface orientation to make layout decisions.
claims.quote: Avoid checking interface orientation for layout decisions. Use size classes instead.

claims.rule: Avoid referencing the main screen; use environment, trait collection, or scene bounds instead.
claims.quote: avoid referencing the main screen in your code. It's ambiguous and will be deprecated in a future release. If possible, don't use screen references at all. Instead, use more local concepts like the environment, trait collection, or the scene's bounds.

claims.rule: Use Concentricity APIs to ensure UI fits perfectly in corners on curved displays.
claims.quote: To make sure your UI fits the corners of the screen perfectly, use Concentricity APIs introduced in iOS 26. They're updated to work with the screen shapes on iPhone Duo.

claims.rule: Build apps with flexible layouts that adapt across a continuum of sizes instead of assuming fixed dimensions.
claims.quote: The best app layouts are adaptive across a continuum of devices. They avoid making assumptions about display sizes or device capabilities based on user interface idioms.

sources.title: Meet Apple Watch Series 7
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Enlarge UI components on Apple Watch Series 7 to make full use of the expanded content area.
claims.quote: We enlarged UI components to make full use of the additional space for enhanced usability.

claims.rule: Use large titles in watchOS to improve glanceability and establish clearer hierarchy.
claims.quote: We brought large titles into watchOS this year to make apps more glanceable, offer a better sense of place, and establish clearer hierarchy within apps.

claims.rule: Apply scenePadding modifier only to text content that would distort or be clipped by edges.
claims.quote: Try to preserve using the .scenePadding modifier only for text content that would distort or be clipped by the edges of the display.

claims.rule: Use color strategically for wayfinding, hierarchy, and app identity on watch interfaces.
claims.quote: Color is meant to help with wayfinding, information hierarchy, and signal the personality of your app.

claims.rule: Craft button shapes to harmonize with the device's curved display; derive pinned button shapes from the hardware curvature rather than using simple pill shapes.
claims.quote: I'll do that again. The change is subtle, but deriving the shape of the button from the shape of the display itself makes it so that these buttons that are pinned to the bottom of the screen and will harmonize with the hardware of the watch.

sources.title: Designing for Apple Watch Series 4
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Account for all watch display dimensions when designing layouts; ensure apps deliver same information and actions across all screen sizes.
claims.quote: Your app should deliver the same information and actions to the user, regardless of screen size.

claims.rule: Extend graphic elements and button backgrounds nearly edge-to-edge, respecting one-pixel margins on watch displays.
claims.quote: Graphic elements and button backgrounds should extend beyond these margins and run nearly edge to edge, up to the one pixel margin that runs by default on either side.

claims.rule: Use scroll clear areas at top and bottom to ensure text and buttons are fully visible when users complete scrolling actions on watches.
claims.quote: To account for the corners in scroll views, there are clear areas at the top and bottom of the content area. These are known as scroll clear areas, and they ensure that text and buttons are nudged fully into view when the user completes a scrolling action.

claims.rule: Recompile apps for watchOS 5 to allow full use of new Series 4 display dimensions and create immersive experiences.
claims.quote: Recompiling your app for watchOS 5 will allow your app to occupy the full width and height of the new display. As long as you've implemented your WatchKit elements relative to their containers rather than at fixed widths, your app will expand to fill the additional screen space on Series 4 watches, and this will feel much more immersive and engaging to your users.

claims.rule: Scale PDF graphics automatically across watch sizes using 2x scale factor and Automatic property; this reduces file production effort.
claims.quote: prepare your graphics with a scale factor of 2 and save them as PDFs, you can create a single file for usage across all four watch sizes

claims.rule: Set Digital Crown haptic feedback to align UI events with tactile detents so users perceive consistent interaction feedback.
claims.quote: if your app coordinates events in the UI with Digital Crown rotation, you'll want to make sure that those UI events line up with these new haptic effects

claims.rule: Use Dynamic Type default categories matching watch case size: Small for 38mm, Large for 40–42mm, XLarge for 44mm.
claims.quote: different default content categories that correspond to the watch case size. Small is the default category for 38mm, Large for 40mm and 42mm, and XLarge for 44mm

sources.title: Designing for Subscription Success
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Present subscription offers at moments when users show interest in gated features or content.
claims.quote: Another way to be visible would be to present your subscription when a person has shown interest in a feature or piece of content that you offer through your subscription.

claims.rule: Minimize clicks in subscription flows; three clicks achieves 61% conversion, nine clicks drops to 7%.
claims.quote: A subscription flow with three clicks led to a 61 percent conversion rate, and a subscription flow with four clicks led to a 48 percent conversion rate. However, nine clicks... the conversation rate drops significantly to seven percent.

claims.rule: Ask for signup before requesting personalization, favoriting, or additional personal details in subscription flows.
claims.quote: Focus people on singing up first. Personalization, favoriting, and requesting additional personal details can all wait until after someone has signed up.

claims.rule: Make subscription offers glanceable; include value proposition, call to action, login option, restore purchase, clear terms, pricing, and multiple tiers in one view.
claims.quote: Strive to be glanceable; in one view and in just a few seconds, people should be able to clearly understand what your subscription offer is and how to sign up.

claims.rule: Present subscription offers immediately when users attempt to access a gated feature, not as a pop-up ad.
claims.quote: present your subscription when a person has shown interest in a feature or piece of content that you offer through your subscription

claims.rule: Limit subscription signup flow to three clicks maximum to achieve 61% conversion; nine clicks drops conversion to 7%.
claims.quote: A subscription flow with three clicks led to a 61 percent conversion rate, and a subscription flow with four clicks led to a 48 percent conversion rate. However, nine clicks... the conversation rate drops significantly to seven percent

claims.rule: Ask for signup before requesting personalization, favoriting, or additional personal details in subscription flows.
claims.quote: Focus people on singing up first. Personalization, favoriting, and requesting additional personal details can all wait until after someone has signed up

sources.title: Designing for iPhone X
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use PDFs for image assets on high-density displays to reduce app size and ensure resolution independence.
claims.quote: When producing and delivering image assets, we recommend using PDFs because they're resolution-independent and may significantly reduce the size of your app.

claims.rule: Use layout margins to provide consistent content margins across apps and align content with controls like navigation bar buttons.
claims.quote: Layout margins provide consistent content margins across apps and help you to align content to other controls like navigation bar buttons.

claims.rule: Fill the entire display with app content; avoid placing black bars at top or bottom as this makes apps feel small and inconsistent.
claims.quote: Your app or game should always fill the display that it runs on. Placing black bars at the top or bottom of the screen makes your app feel small, cramped, and inconsistent with other apps on iPhone X.

claims.rule: Consider different aspect ratios when designing background graphics for devices with varying screen proportions.
claims.quote: When designing background graphics, or rendering background scenes, keep in mind that iPhone X's display has a different aspect ratio than a 4.7 inch display.

claims.rule: Use Safe Area layout guide to inset content from iPhone X sensor housing, rounded corners, and home indicator in both orientations.
claims.quote: The Safe Area layout guide helps avoid underlapping system UI elements when positioning content and controls

sources.title: Explore prompt design & safety for on-device foundation models
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Break down complex reasoning tasks into simpler steps when using smaller on-device language models.
claims.quote: If you're not getting good results with a system model for a complex reasoning task, try breaking down your task prompt into simpler steps.

claims.rule: Avoid using on-device language models for calculations; use non-AI code instead for math-related tasks.
claims.quote: For math-related tasks, you're gonna wanna avoid asking this small model to act as a calculator. Non-AI code is much more reliable for math.

claims.rule: Provide verified information in prompts when generating facts; thoroughly fact-check model outputs for new prompts.
claims.quote: If you do want to generate facts, consider providing the model with verified information written into your prompt. And thoroughly fact check model outputs for any new prompts you write.

claims.rule: Use guided generation to control what the model generates, whether strings, numbers, arrays, or custom data structures.
claims.quote: With the Foundation Models Framework, Guided generation gives you control over what the model should generate, whether that be strings, numbers, arrays, or a custom data structure that you define.

claims.rule: Instruct the on-device model to handle negative or harmful user input in an empathetic and constructive way.
claims.quote: I'm appending a sentence to tell the model to respond to negative prompts in an empathetic and wholesome way.

claims.rule: Collect prompts covering all major use cases and safety-triggering scenarios, then automate end-to-end testing or use another LLM to grade responses at scale.
claims.quote: Remember to collect prompts to cover all major use cases of your app, and you will also need to collect prompts that may trigger safety issues.

claims.rule: When a safety error occurs in a user-initiated feature, provide UI feedback explaining the app cannot process the request and offer alternative actions.
claims.quote: For a user-initiative feature, especially one that has someone wait, remember to provide appropriate UI feedback to explain that the app cannot process the request. It can be a simple alert, or you can use this opportunity to provide alternative actions for people to choose from.

claims.rule: Use less than five examples when prompting on-device LLMs; write them directly into the prompt without external references.
claims.quote: You can boost your task performance by giving the model less than five examples of the kinds of outputs you want, and just write those directly into your prompt.

sources.title: What’s new in visionOS 26
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Present momentary information like alerts, sheets, menus, and popovers inside and on top of volumes so they break through content and remain visible.
claims.quote: Momentary information like alerts, sheets, menus, and popovers are frequently used in apps and are an essential part of its user experience. In visionOS 26, presenting this transient content inside and on top of volumes becomes possible. In spatial experiences where 3D content can overlap user interfaces, key elements like presentations will break through the content to remain visible.

claims.rule: Configure dynamic bounds restrictions to allow app content to peek outside its bounds and blend seamlessly with the real world.
claims.quote: Now by configuring dynamic bounds restrictions, your apps can blend even more seamlessly with the real world by rendering outside your app's bounds. You can apply this effect to your apps by adding a simple view modifier, specifying how much you want your content to peek outside its bounds.

claims.rule: Allow objects to rotate intuitively with the user's hand as if they were holding the real thing to create natural interaction.
claims.quote: Interacting with virtual objects should feel natural, mimicking the real world. Now, objects can rotate intuitively with the user's hand as if they were holding the real thing.

sources.title: Make a big impact with small writing changes
