sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

sources.title: What’s new in iPad app design
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Arrange important toolbar items in the trailing section to remain visible across window sizes.
claims.quote: Arrange important toolbar items in the trailing section to avoid overflow in smaller window sizes.

claims.rule: Group related toolbar actions to keep them together and prevent toolbar overflow.
claims.quote: Use groups to keep related actions together in the toolbar or the overflow menu.

claims.rule: Use horizontal submenus on iPad for quick in-place selection when screen space allows.
claims.quote: on iPadOS 16, submenus open horizontally when they have space available. This makes them much faster, especially with a pointer.

sources.title: Meet the Presenter: Design App Shortcuts
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

sources.title: Design App Shortcuts
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Choose features for shortcuts that are self-contained and can be completed outside the app without opening it.
claims.quote: A great App Shortcut is one that actually doesn't require your app in focus at all. You're looking for a lightweight task that can be completed via Siri or via search in its entirety.

claims.rule: Name app shortcuts with brief, memorable phrases that clearly communicate function and include the app name naturally.
claims.quote: The first important thing to remember when you're crafting that hero phrase is to keep it brief. You want your app shortcut phrase to be easy to remember and to clearly communicate its function.

claims.rule: Limit app shortcuts to two to five high-quality shortcuts per app; maximum ten.
claims.quote: in most cases, the key features of your app can be captured in two to five high-quality app shortcuts, and we strongly recommend keeping your set as focused as possible

claims.rule: Use dynamic parameters only for finite, predictable lists of five or fewer items.
claims.quote: you can only have one dynamic parameter in your phrase, and it can only be used to select from a finite list

claims.rule: Use parameter confirmation to present an assumed value and ask for confirmation rather than forcing users to choose.
claims.quote: try to make a meaningful assumption and present it as an option for people to confirm. This is called a Parameter Confirmation

claims.rule: Use intent confirmation only for consequential actions: financial, destructive, or high-risk.
claims.quote: only use this step for consequential actions, be it a financial transaction, a destructive action like deleting content, or an action that may just feel high risk

claims.rule: Use custom snippets for self-contained actions; use live activities for continuous access needs like timers.
claims.quote: If you're not sure which one to use, think about whether people would benefit from continuous access to this information, such as transit progress for a food order or a timer counting down. If so, use a Live Activity

sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

sources.title: What's new in SF Symbols 4
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use Palette rendering mode with two or more contrasting colors to give symbol elements prominence and allow customization to environment color palettes.
claims.quote: Palette uses two or more contrasting colors to give elements of a symbol more prominence and versatility, allowing for the symbols to be customized to integrate with the color palette of the environment.

claims.rule: Use Automatic rendering mode for symbols; it selects the preferred rendering mode that best highlights each symbol's unique characteristics.
claims.quote: Symbols now feature a preferred rendering mode, which can vary between symbols. And we call this behavior Automatic Rendering. When selected, it provides the preferred rendering mode configuration for each symbol without having to specify it manually

claims.rule: Use Variable Color to represent sequential states or strength levels in symbols, not to create depth.
claims.quote: Variable Color is not meant to create depth; instead, it's meant to highlight a sequence of steps or stages that the symbol can represent

sources.title: Apple Design Awards
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

sources.title: Make a great SharePlay experience
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design SharePlay activities to bring people together through shared experiences beyond text or video alone.
claims.quote: some of the most meaningful moments people have together are about more than just sharing a conversation. When we're together, we connect most by sharing experiences.

claims.rule: Show participant initials or names when others interact with shared content to reinforce presence and context.
claims.quote: the app shows the initials of who drew it, and this makes for a much more intuitive experience for the entire group. It also helps reinforce the feeling of presence

claims.rule: Provide easy access to status bar controls during immersive experiences; use a simple, discoverable gesture to redisplay hidden UI.
claims.quote: it is important to remember that the pill in the status bar gives people access to important controls. So, let people redisplay a hidden status bar using a simple, discoverable gesture

claims.rule: Support Picture in Picture for coordinated media so users maintain presence with the group while multitasking or switching apps.
claims.quote: remember to support Picture in Picture for coordinated media experiences. This will allow everyone to continue watching with their friends, maintaining a sense of presence

claims.rule: Use shared playback controls without restrictions on who can interact; everyone should feel able to control shared experiences equally.
claims.quote: it's critical that we don't put any limitations on who can interact with these controls. We want to create an engaging experience where everyone feels like they're able to walk up and control that same music player

claims.rule: Include descriptive metadata (title, subtitle, image, web URL) for group activities so invitees know what to expect before joining.
claims.quote: It's important that this information is descriptive so that Ryan and Adam know what to expect when they join the SharePlay session. So be sure to implement the metadata property for your group activity with meaningful information

sources.title: Design for Collaboration with Messages
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use the system share sheet to help users begin collaboration in a familiar, consistent way.
claims.quote: The system share sheet gives people an easy way to begin a collaboration. It will help make collaboration in your app more consistent and familiar.

claims.rule: Place the share button in toolbars where people can easily access it.
claims.quote: Put the button in a place where people can easily access. Toolbars are a good candidate.

claims.rule: Write concise copy for permission settings to avoid truncation and aid quick decision-making.
claims.quote: You need to provide a descriptive copy of default settings your app supports. To avoid truncation, be as concise as possible.

claims.rule: Keep permission settings screens simple so users can easily skim options and decide quickly.
claims.quote: keep the structure of choices simple so people can easily skim the options and make quick decisions.

claims.rule: Place the collaboration button next to the share button where it stands out and draws attention as a primary feature.
claims.quote: This collaboration button is one of the most important UI elements of the entire collaboration experience. Find a place where it can stand out and draw people's attention. It's best to place the collaboration button right next to the share button

claims.rule: Consolidate multiple collaboration notifications in Messages into a single banner to avoid cluttering the conversation.
claims.quote: To not clutter conversation with too many banners, Messages will consolidate those banners into one. When people tap on the view button in this banner, Messages will show all the updates in one place

claims.rule: Keep the collaboration popover middle section glanceable; avoid overloading with too much information or too many buttons.
claims.quote: Try not to overload this collaboration popover with too much information or too many buttons. Keep it glanceable

sources.title: Writing for interfaces
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Order screen information by importance; place the most critical message at the top.
claims.quote: think about the most important thing someone needs to know at that moment. That's the purpose of your screen.

claims.rule: Make headers and buttons clear because people do not read screens linearly.
claims.quote: people don't always read the text on screen in order, so make sure your headers and buttons are clear.

claims.rule: Anticipate the next action or question users will have and provide information or prompts in sequence to guide them.
claims.quote: When writing for apps, you always have to ask, 'What comes next?' Anticipating the next action or question someone's going to have will help you know what to say

claims.rule: Write button labels that describe the specific action, not generic terms like Yes or No, so users understand the choice without additional context.
claims.quote: it's always best to be specific about the action the buttons are going to take. On this alert, if you only read the button labels, you would still understand what you were choosing

claims.rule: Use simple, plain language avoiding idioms and culturally specific phrases that may not translate or be universally understood.
claims.quote: It's best to use simple, plain language, as idioms and humor can be misunderstood or not translate, and some phrases have meanings that exclude people

claims.rule: Consider context outside the app—whether users are at rest, moving, occupied with other tasks—and adjust text verbosity accordingly.
claims.quote: When someone uses your app, are they likely to be at home in a quiet space, or traveling at busy airport? Are they occupied with something else, like driving or cooking, or can they give your app their full attention?

claims.rule: Position on-screen instructions where users are already looking, not in arbitrary locations, to reduce cognitive load during focused tasks.
claims.quote: An on-screen arrow guides you with instructions, to 'Move continuously when taking a Panorama.' The words appear right below the arrow because that's where you're looking

sources.title: Explore navigation design for iOS
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use familiar navigation patterns so users focus on content rather than learning how to navigate.
claims.quote: Familiar navigation patterns can help people easily explore the information within your app — and save them from unnecessary confusion.

claims.rule: Organize app functionality into balanced, focused sections rather than cramming features into one tab.
claims.quote: It's much easier to understand an app's functionality when it's well organized and clearly communicated.

claims.rule: Distribute functionality evenly across tabs instead of loading the first tab heavily.
claims.quote: Try to create balance in your interface by distributing functionality throughout your tabs.

claims.rule: Keep tab bar persistent at bottom of screen so users can toggle between top-level content areas without losing context.
claims.quote: Persistent access to the tab bar gives someone the ability to toggle between different levels of your information hierarchy while maintaining context in each.

claims.rule: Never force a user to switch tabs automatically; let them choose when to navigate between tabs.
claims.quote: Never force someone to change tabs automatically.

claims.rule: Use clear, concise, self-evident tab labels that tell a story about app functionality without requiring users to see content first.
claims.quote: Notice how the tabs hint at functionality. They tell a story about what the app can do just by displaying concise labels.

claims.rule: Present modals from bottom of screen to cover tab bar and reinforce focus on a single task.
claims.quote: When using modals on iOS, always present them from the bottom of the screen. A modal interrupts information hierarchy. It comes from the bottom of the screen to cover your tab bar.

sources.title: Design for Arabic
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: For Arabic layouts, reverse entire layout directionality so content flows from right to left to match reading behavior.
claims.quote: If this phrase exists in a layout, the entire layout flows from top to bottom, right to left, to match the reading behavior and direction of the language.

claims.rule: Invert carousel and animation interactions in right-to-left layouts to match the inverted UI direction.
claims.quote: Both, the interaction and the animation of this component are inverted to match the UI direction.

claims.rule: Increase Arabic font size by 10% when paired with uppercase Latin to compensate for optical size difference.
claims.quote: you may want to increase the Arabic font size by 10%. This subtle difference would also help with legibility especially when upper case is used in smaller point sizes.

claims.rule: Increase vertical spacing in UI when using vocalization marks and diacritics in Arabic to prevent text clipping.
claims.quote: If your app would include an intense use of vocalization marks, make sure to have more vertical spacing in the UI to avoid clipping.

sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

sources.title: Design app experiences with charts
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Accompany every chart with text describing its contents; if isolated, the description should be informative.
claims.quote: A chart should be accompanied by text that describes the chart contents. If read in isolation, it should be informative.

claims.rule: Use charts to direct attention to the most important information, not to visualize everything possible.
claims.quote: Charts are a strong signal. They direct attention to the information you want them to understand.

claims.rule: Use bar charts for comparing values across categories to enable easier relative size comparison.
claims.quote: By making the bars horizontal, I can accentuate the difference between this chart and the recent sales chart.

claims.rule: Use distinct colors or visual styles when displaying multiple chart types to signal differences in data.
claims.quote: Giving each of these charts a distinct color helps. Now it is easier to notice that these charts are unique.

claims.rule: Preserve chart values and context when linking static preview charts to expanded detailed versions.
claims.quote: When you create a link between two versions of the same chart, that progression should maintain continuity by preserving values, context and state.

sources.title: Design an effective chart
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design charts with focused intent on a few key insights, not every possible insight in the data.
claims.quote: An effective chart focuses on a few key pieces of information. Design charts with intention.

claims.rule: Use bar marks over point or line marks when data has gaps or zeros, as bars reveal absence without distraction.
claims.quote: Here, zeros are visible without creating a distraction. This chart is also intuitive to read: more white means more sales. Since sales are cumulative, the visual weight of all the bars corresponds directly to the number of sales made in the last 30 days.

claims.rule: Test chart designs with real, messy data early; clean synthetic data masks interpretation problems.
claims.quote: It's important to test your designs with real data early. While point marks are a great at revealing some insights, such as identifying outliers or clusters in data, our needs call for something else.

claims.rule: For chart axes with no natural maximum, use dynamic ranges to let data fill available vertical space.
claims.quote: There is no limit to how many pancakes the food trucks will sell. So let's use a dynamic range to automatically adapt the upper bound of our vertical axis to our data.

claims.rule: Fix the lower axis bound to zero for bar charts to keep bar heights proportional to their values.
claims.quote: We still fix the lower bound to 0. Doing so is generally a good idea when using bar marks as it keeps the heights of the bars meaningful.

claims.rule: Use approximately four horizontal grid lines; adjust density based on context and space to balance readability.
claims.quote: For our chart's context and intended use, it's more effective to use around four horizontal grid lines and adjust as the range of the axis changes.

claims.rule: Use intuitive values like multiples of 20 or 7-day intervals for axis labels to aid mental math.
claims.quote: Note that as we place these grid lines and labels, we use intuitive values to make the chart approachable– in this case, multiples of 20. In the same way, it's intuitive for people to read time in steps of seven days, which gives us five grid lines for a 30-day period.

claims.rule: Use chart titles as headings to provide context; omit axis labels if title clarifies meaning.
claims.quote: By using 'Pancakes sold' as a heading for the chart, the chart's meaning is front and center.

claims.rule: Summarize the main takeaway in a title, not just the metric: include a concrete value or interpretation.
claims.quote: Let's bring out a main take-away for our chart by rewriting our chart title to say 'Total Sales: 1,234 Pancakes'. This description grounds our chart with a concrete value and summarizes the most critical information.

claims.rule: Order VoiceOver data labels: context (date) first, then value, to help users locate specific points.
claims.quote: We also order the contextualizing data value, in this case, the date, to come first. This ordering makes it easier to quickly look for a specific value.

sources.title: Adopt Variable Color in SF Symbols
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Round percentage thresholds to whole numbers to avoid rounding errors in symbol appearance.
claims.quote: Thresholds between layers are rounded to the nearest percentage point, and we don't activate the next layer until you're one full percentage point above that rounded value.

sources.title: Meet the Presenter: Design app experiences with charts
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

sources.title: Qualities of great AR experiences
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Involve physical space meaningfully in AR experiences so they respond to and affect the user's immediate surroundings.
claims.quote: AR is at its most delightful when it affects and responds to what's immediately around you, involving physical space in a meaningful way.

claims.rule: Use AR to enable people to visualize and try on objects in 3D before making decisions or purchases.
claims.quote: With AR, you can build features that help people try on things in a way that's virtual yet realistic enough for someone to make a confident purchasing decision.

claims.rule: Keep AR experiences lightweight with minimal UI when the interaction is device movement and information is temporary.
claims.quote: The experience feels lightweight because there's very little UI, the interaction is based on device movement, and the measurement information disappears after you've seen it.

claims.rule: Keep AR experiences under two minutes to prevent user fatigue and manage battery and thermal impact.
claims.quote: craft experiences that last no more than a minute or two. This is for the ergonomic reasons I mentioned earlier, but also because AR is a resource-intensive superpower that has a big impact on battery and thermals.

claims.rule: Use screen space overlay for text and buttons rather than placing them in 3D world to preserve legibility in AR.
claims.quote: It's best to place text and interactive elements like buttons here in screen space, rather than in the 3D world of the camera to preserve legibility.

claims.rule: Provide real-time audio and haptic feedback as users move devices in AR to signal actions outside their view.
claims.quote: Try to provide real-time feedback with visual effects and sound as people move, so that even if the action is taking place out of view, people can still connect with the experience.

claims.rule: Design AR buttons for one-handed thumb use with high contrast, oversized icons at arm's length.
claims.quote: Use oversized buttons with high-contrast icons that are easy to tap one-handed with a thumb.

claims.rule: Use realistic shadows and lighting in AR to help virtual objects feel grounded in the scene.
claims.quote: The quality of lighting and shadows in your experiences can have a huge impact on people's feeling that things are really there, even when an object isn't very realistic.

sources.title: Meet the expanded San Francisco font family
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use width styles—Condensed, Compressed, or Expanded—to accommodate space constraints and stylistic needs in UI design.
claims.quote: adding a Width axis was the natural evolution of SF: Joining the Regular Width we have three more styles: Condensed, narrow and space-efficient; Compressed, the most compact style currently available in SF; and last but not least, on the other end of the spectrum, Expanded.

claims.rule: Match font weight and width choices to typographic hierarchy intent: neutral styles for balance, extreme proportions for emphasis and attention.
claims.quote: you can expect the styles that gravitate towards the center of the stylistic map of SF to have a more neutral voice, while the styles around the perimeter of the map, which feature more extreme Weight and Width proportions, to be more expressive, have a stronger voice, attributes that can be useful if you want to draw people's attention towards a certain area of the UI or strengthen a typographic hierarchy.

claims.rule: Use Compressed width style only for single lines or display headlines; avoid for extended reading passages.
claims.quote: the Compressed style, while still functional for small single lines, might be too tight for longer passages of text, like you see here. So always consider legibility when opting for a non-Regular Width.

claims.rule: Pair extreme weight and width proportions for expressive display styles; center styles for neutral voice.
claims.quote: the styles that gravitate towards the center of the stylistic map of SF to have a more neutral voice, while the styles around the perimeter of the map, which feature more extreme Weight and Width proportions, to be more expressive, have a stronger voice

claims.rule: Use Condensed width to fit more text per line in narrow columns without sacrificing readability.
claims.quote: the Width styles can help control longer passages of text, providing the ability to fit more characters per line, achieving a more ideal and comfortable reading experience for narrow columns.

sources.title: Apple Design Awards (ASL)
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

sources.title: Meet the Presenter: Writing for interfaces
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

sources.title: Tap into virtual and physical game controllers
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Display button glyphs that match the specific controller type the player is holding, so UI looks correct across different controller families.
claims.quote: Consider this hint to use a button to display your inventory. On an MFi or Xbox controller, we should show the Y button. On a PlayStation controller, we instead want to show a triangle.

claims.rule: Abstract input hardware through a common API to write input code once without worrying about controller remapping or hardware differences.
claims.quote: By abstracting input hardware through the common API, the game controller framework lets you write your input code once without having to worry about how input may have been remapped or the differences among specific controllers, keyboards, or pointing devices.

claims.rule: Show the correct button glyph for the controller the player is holding, even after they remap buttons in system settings.
claims.quote: we actually want to show the X glyph when a developer asks for the glyph associated with the A action

claims.rule: Use positional button locations instead of button names for new and young players who may not recognize button labels.
claims.quote: Some players, especially new and young players, may more quickly recognize the location you're showing them and they don't have to glance down to try to read the button names

claims.rule: Apply adaptive trigger resistance dynamically based on player action intensity to emulate physical sensations like rope tension.
claims.quote: By dynamically applying a varying resistance to the trigger based on what the player is doing, you can emulate the feeling of pulling a bow string or a slingshot that's under tension

claims.rule: Turn off adaptive trigger effects when no longer needed to prevent unexpected haptic feedback.
claims.quote: just like I remind my kids to turn out the lights when they leave a room, you need to make sure you turn off the adaptive trigger effect when you're done

sources.title: Out of this world... on to Mars
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

sources.title: Create custom symbols
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use optical margins in symbol templates to ensure symbols align correctly with one another when displayed in lists and table views.
claims.quote: margins for making sure symbols are optically centered with one another when used in lists and table views

claims.rule: Design symbols with multiple weights to match text styling and adapt to features such as accessibility bold on iOS.
claims.quote: Multiple weights to match text and adjust to features such as accessibility bold on iOS

claims.rule: Provide three weight-matched scales in custom symbols to adjust symbol appearance across different UI contexts and element sizes.
claims.quote: three weight-matched scales to adjust to the context of different UI elements

claims.rule: Preserve the number and order of paths across all design variants when supporting multicolor or hierarchical rendering modes.
claims.quote: Preserving the number of paths across all design variants is a requirement if you want to produce a symbol with multicolor or hierarchical data

claims.rule: Convert live strokes to paths in symbol designs to enable colors and hierarchy groups to be applied later.
claims.quote: Avoid using live strokes in the final design. Instead, make sure to convert any strokes to paths so that the resulting shapes can take on colors or hierarchy groups

claims.rule: Use system-provided colors in multicolor symbols so they adapt to light mode, dark mode, high contrast, and vibrancy contexts automatically.
claims.quote: It's recommended to use system-provided colors whenever possible, as they will adapt to changes in the system's appearance to look great in light mode, dark mode, high contrast modes, and different vibrancy contexts

sources.title: SF Symbols in SwiftUI
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use Label views to pair icons with text, as they adapt their layout to context automatically.
claims.quote: A Label is a combination of a title with an icon, which is most often a symbol. The great thing about a label is that it's a general description of this pairing and will adapt its behavior to the context where it's shown.

claims.rule: Localize custom symbol names in Localizable.strings files so SwiftUI uses them automatically for accessibility.
claims.quote: A great way to improve that is to provide a localization for the image's name in a Localizable.strings file. SwiftUI will automatically use this localizable string for the accessibility label of this image anywhere it's used.

claims.rule: Use text styles like body or caption with symbols so both text and symbols scale with dynamic type.
claims.quote: If you use a text style, like body or caption, then the text and symbol will scale with dynamic type, and if you choose a fixed size, then they stay constant.

claims.rule: Use the symbolVariant modifier on view hierarchies to apply variants like fill or outline across nested components.
claims.quote: This modifier sets the specified variant in the environment, so it's great to use on a whole view hierarchy, like we're doing here.

sources.title: Design great actions for Shortcuts, Siri, and Suggestions
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design actions that complete tasks fully without opening the app unless necessary; use follow-up questions instead.
claims.quote: Your action should perform the task completely, and you should avoid opening your app into the foreground, unless it's necessary for your use case. Where possible, you should ask follow-up questions instead of opening the app.

claims.rule: Donate actions to the system so Siri learns usage patterns and suggests them in Suggestions, Search, and Lock screen.
claims.quote: If you donate actions to the system, Siri will automatically learn how people use your app and will suggest your actions at the right time, in the Suggestions widget, in Search, and on the Lock screen.

claims.rule: Show previews before destructive or permanent actions complete, and different previews after completion.
claims.quote: For actions that are permanent, like deletion or ordering, you should strongly consider showing a different snippet before the action is completed as compared to the one that is shown after it's completed.

sources.title: What’s new in SF Symbols
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use outlined symbols in toolbars, navigation bars, and lists where symbols appear alongside text.
claims.quote: An outlined, or default variant, of a symbol is great for Toolbars, Navigation Bars, Lists and other places in the UI where symbols are presented alongside text or where symbols need to display a uniform appearance.

claims.rule: Use symbols to reduce visual complexity and communicate quickly, as they are largely language-independent.
claims.quote: They are the simplest form of communication between the user and a product and serve as little pieces of a puzzle that aid in usability and intuitive navigation. They also make interfaces faster to use, helping us navigate quickly, as most symbols are language-independent.

claims.rule: Use filled symbols in swipe actions and tab bars to indicate selection and emphasize active state with accent color.
claims.quote: A filled symbol in swipe actions and iOS tab bars give a consistent appearance and level of emphasis, giving better control in areas that indicate selection when defined with an accent color.

claims.rule: Apply hierarchical rendering (single color with varying opacity) to emphasize symbol differences when displaying multiple related symbols.
claims.quote: When multiple symbols that share common shapes are presented alongside one another, this rendering mode emphasizes the differences between them, intending to make the symbols more legible and recognizable.

sources.title: Accessibility by design: An Apple Watch for everyone
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design high-contrast text on dark backgrounds early, as it benefits low-vision users and the general population.
claims.quote: Apple developed this product, and the primary focus was to be able to read the time, and so the contrast with the black background with the legible letters was very important. Well, it turns out that was also important for low-vision users, and it's great for the person who needs that accessibility, but it also turns out to be useful for everyone else.

claims.rule: Provide voice output alongside visual features so blind or low-vision users access content equivalent to sighted users.
claims.quote: When it was introduced, I think it really surprised everybody, especially because it even had some really neat little features like Mickey's tapping his foot, but to a low-vision or blind audience, if I touched the watch, all I would get is a description, or maybe, perhaps, the time spoken by the same text-to-speech I hear everywhere else on the watch face, and that's just not good enough.

claims.rule: Enable interaction through gestures using minimal muscle effort: pinch, double pinch, clench, double clench for complete device access.
claims.quote: pinch, double pinch, clench, and double clench for complete access to the Apple Watch

claims.rule: Combine hardware sensors (accelerometer, gyroscope, heart-rate) with machine learning to detect subtle muscle movements for gesture recognition.
claims.quote: combine the accelerometer, the gyroscope, and some of those health sensors that detect heart rate, and use that to detect subtle muscle movements in your arm

claims.rule: Vary feedback frequency based on accessibility mode: increase repetition (laughs) when VoiceOver is on; decrease when off.
claims.quote: When VoiceOver is on, Mickey laughs more often. When VoiceOver is not on, Mickey doesn't laugh quite as much

sources.title: Design for Safari 15
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use the theme-color meta tag to align the browser tab bar with your site's design, extending content to window edges.
claims.quote: To provide your choice for the toolbar color, put it in the HTML head using a meta tag with name="theme-color," and use the content attribute to specify the color.

claims.rule: Set separate theme-color values for light and dark modes using media attributes on meta tags.
claims.quote: You can support both Light and Dark Mode by setting two colors. Yes, now you can add media attributes to meta tags. In this case, media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" in the first meta tag and "(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" in the second.

claims.rule: Put fallback theme-color declarations first, not last, so browsers without media attribute support use the first declaration.
claims.quote: In browsers that do support name="theme-color" but don't yet support using the media attribute on meta tags, those browsers will use the first theme-color declaration and ignore the rest. So put your fallback first, not last, the way you do in CSS.

claims.rule: Use CSS environment variables (safe-area-inset-top, -right, -bottom, -left) to dynamically position content clear of notches and tab bars.
claims.quote: env(safe-area-inset-bottom) is a measurement of however many pixels it is from the safe area to the bottom of the viewport

claims.rule: Apply viewport-fit=cover in meta viewport to extend content to screen edges; use environment variables to prevent data loss in safe areas.
claims.quote: I can signal to Safari that I want the browser to extend the content to the left and right edges by changing the meta viewport tag to viewport-fit=cover

claims.rule: Place tab bar at bottom of iOS screen, within thumb reach for one-handed use; minimize it on scroll to preserve content space.
claims.quote: we've moved the tab bar to the bottom of the screen. This puts it directly under the user's thumb, making it easier for them to reach, especially if they're using their phone one-handed

claims.rule: Declare fallback theme-color first, then dark-mode variant; browsers without media-attribute support use the first declaration.
claims.quote: put your fallback first, not last, the way you do in CSS

claims.rule: Use page title in browser tab to surface content, not site name; place content first to aid tab identification in multi-tab sessions.
claims.quote: put the content title first. That way, if someone has your site open in multiple tabs, it's easier to tell which tab is which

claims.rule: Provide transparent-background favicon to maintain clarity and appearance in high-resolution devices and Safari tab bar.
claims.quote: A favicon with a transparent background can look especially great

claims.rule: Use Flexbox or CSS Grid to create layouts where content below a tab bar hugs the bar as it expands; content above stays fixed.
claims.quote: the chat area is the area that resizes when the tab bar is expanded. Everything above it stays the same size, while everything below it hugs the tab bar. This is because we're using Flexbox layout

sources.title: Discoverable design
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Prioritize features by importance and make essential ones immediately visible on the main screen.
claims.quote: The essential parts of your app should be immediately visible to people. It's okay for the non-essential parts to require some navigation to reach.

claims.rule: Avoid hamburger menus for primary navigation; use visible alternatives like tab bars so users see available sections.
claims.quote: When we tested our interface in the hands of people and found out that, when the hamburger menu is closed, people don't know what's inside. The three lines don't convey anything about the features inside. So, instead, we decided to go with a tab bar navigation system, which appears at the bottom of an app and lets people quickly switch between different sections.

claims.rule: Limit tab bar buttons to avoid reducing tappable area and increasing visual complexity that obscures features.
claims.quote: What if all the features are equally important, and I have to cram them all into one space with six tab buttons? But too many tabs reduces the tappable area of each tab and increases the complexity of your app, which can make it harder for people to locate information.

claims.rule: Use familiar words and visual symbols to provide recognizable cues that guide people through your interface.
claims.quote: Second, use words and symbols people are familiar with to provide visual cues.

claims.rule: Hint at gestural interactions rather than hiding them entirely, so people discover and learn gestures naturally.
claims.quote: Third, use gestures for fluid navigation, but hint at gestures.

claims.rule: Prioritize and display essential features immediately visible on the main screen; hide non-critical features behind navigation.
claims.quote: The essential parts of your app should be immediately visible to people. It's okay for the non-essential parts to require some navigation to reach

claims.rule: Avoid hamburger menus for primary navigation; use visible tab bars or alternatives so users see available sections at a glance.
claims.quote: when the hamburger menu is closed, people don't know what's inside. The three lines don't convey anything about the features inside

claims.rule: Limit tab bar buttons to 3–5; exceeding this reduces tappable area, increases visual complexity, and obscures features.
claims.quote: too many tabs reduces the tappable area of each tab and increases the complexity of your app, which can make it harder for people to locate information

claims.rule: Add text labels to icons to clarify ambiguous actions; camera icon can mean photo, scan document, or scan QR code without context.
claims.quote: Even the camera icon that we are familiar with could have many possible uses, such as taking a picture, scanning a document or a QR code. When we add text labeling the button "New," we clarify this button is for capturing toast to add a new recipe

claims.rule: Guide search entry by showing example inputs (ingredients, places, friends) to overcome blank-page paralysis and discoverability.
claims.quote: we decided to provide examples of possible types of input, such as searching by ingredients, places, or friends. In this way, people can quickly discover different methods for how to search

claims.rule: Use standard platform gestures (tap, swipe, long press, pinch, rotate); custom gestures mimic real-world interactions or remain invisible shortcuts.
claims.quote: use the accepted gesture for the platform. If you're inventing a new gesture, try to mimic real-life interactions

claims.rule: Organize content into categories matching user behavior and real-world context, not just available data; group by restaurants, friends, preferences.
claims.quote: organize the content of your app into categories that fits people's motivation and natural behavior

claims.rule: Visually separate content categories with header titles and spacing; grouping reduces overwhelm and clarifies existing divisions.
claims.quote: By grouping the categories into different logical sections, separated by a header title, it feels immediately more understandable. People can easily ignore one category and explore deeper in one specific section

claims.rule: Invite explicit user feedback on content (like, hide, flag); clear invitations increase feedback rate and feed recommendation engines useful training data.
claims.quote: If you clearly invite people to provide feedback, they are more likely to give feedback. This will feed the recommendation engine's useful data that will reinforce relevant items and discoverability of the content

sources.title: Accessibility by design: An Apple Watch for everyone (ASL)
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Start accessibility work by understanding a product's core mission and primary use case.
claims.quote: What is the product supposed to do? What is its core mission of what this is gonna bring value for?

claims.rule: Test gesture-based interactions with users who have low muscle tone to ensure the gestures require minimal energy.
claims.quote: we needed the gesture that would expend the least amount of energy, and we started with just this pinch gesture

claims.rule: Use machine learning on sensor data to detect subtle muscle movements, enabling gesture control for users with limited mobility.
claims.quote: combine the accelerometer, the gyroscope, and some of those health sensors that detect heart rate, and use that to detect subtle muscle movements

sources.title: WWDC21 Apple Design Awards (ASL)
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Measure and test motion sensitivity in apps and games; provide reduced-motion modes for users with motion sensitivities.
claims.quote: Turning on reduced motion in a game so people with motion sensitivities can still have fun and experience the game fully.

claims.rule: Present accessibility controls and warnings upfront so users discover them before encountering barriers.
claims.quote: This app has got some really great visual warnings about potential sensory and cognitive needs. It's also very good at presenting those controls and those warnings upfront.

claims.rule: Present accessibility controls and visual warnings upfront so users discover them before encountering barriers.
claims.quote: very good at presenting those controls and those warnings upfront

claims.rule: Offer text customization settings including contrast, line spacing, and word spacing to support users with low vision or dyslexia.
claims.quote: increase contrast or decrease contrast, space out lines, words, and highlight certain phrases

sources.title: Design for spatial interaction
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Remove layers of abstraction by letting users interact directly with physical surroundings via device proximity.
claims.quote: These human-scale interactions -- the ones that happen between devices nearby -- have the ability to remove layers of abstraction and allow users to interact more directly with their surroundings.

claims.rule: Design onscreen elements to animate in direct proportion to physical user movement, creating a clear cause-and-effect relationship.
claims.quote: look for opportunities for the onscreen elements to animate in a way that feels related to your physical movements

claims.rule: Use haptic feedback instead of sound when the target is close; haptics communicate distance and proximity more effectively at arm's reach.
claims.quote: the arrow defers to a form of feedback that we find much more effective at this small scale. The design transforms to highlight haptic feedback

claims.rule: Use multiple feedback modes that are salient enough to be clearly understood; no single feedback mode should dominate or compete with the primary task.
claims.quote: Make sure your design uses more than one mode of feedback, and that each one is salient enough to be clearly understood

sources.title: Design for Group Activities
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Identify activities in your app that people naturally want to do together; design for group-first sharing.
claims.quote: All these examples are things people love to do together. You should look for activities in your app to bring people together, encourage conversation, collaboration, or just enjoyment.

claims.rule: Restrict visibility of sensitive data during screen sharing by default; exclude secure entry fields automatically.
claims.quote: By default, everything is shared except for secure entry fields. You can use UIKit API to further restrict the visibility of this information on iOS during screen sharing sessions.

claims.rule: Automate joining shared activities; minimize required interactions before launching the experience.
claims.quote: automate as much as you can and minimize unneeded upfront interaction before getting into the activity

claims.rule: Use activity previews with title, subtitle, and thumbnail to provide context about shared content.
claims.quote: Use it like a rich link, with a title, subtitle, and thumbnail to describe the experience everyone is enjoying

claims.rule: Question every interaction and delay non-essential sign-ups or purchases in group activities.
claims.quote: question every interaction and see if it's really necessary to get to the content and, if possible, delay or automate those interactions

sources.title: The process of inclusive design
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: View your app through multiple axes of diversity including ability, language, culture, class, and connectivity.
claims.quote: Diversity axes can include class; culture; ethnicity; language; education; political, philosophical and religious beliefs; race; gender; sexual orientation; age; abilities; disabilities; whether you are right- or left-handed; body measurements like height; and also environmental conditions like location, internet connectivity, or access to technology devices.

claims.rule: Empower diverse teams to voice ideas; accessible solutions often emerge from diverse perspectives.
claims.quote: In truth, having an empowered diverse team means your app or game can be inclusive. We all share the responsibility to build an inclusive environment that enables inclusive actions.

claims.rule: Use constraints as tools to narrow the problem space and drive creative solutions.
claims.quote: Constraints help your process by helping you make the first few early decisions. This allows you to put most of your energy into creating new solutions in a narrow problem space.

claims.rule: Design for extremes of ability and context, not just average users, across multiple diversity axes.
claims.quote: think concretely about the extremes of how people will use the app or game, not just the average person

claims.rule: Use constraints as creative tools to narrow problem scope and drive innovative solutions.
claims.quote: Constraints help your process by helping you make the first few early decisions. This allows you to put most of your energy into creating new solutions in a narrow problem space

claims.rule: Integrate accessibility and internationalization planning from the start of development, not at the end.
claims.quote: start planning for accessibility and internationalization at the beginning of development

claims.rule: Center perspectives at intersections of multiple diversity axes when designing inclusive features.
claims.quote: focusing in on intersections of diversity axes is one way to not only be innovative, but respectful

sources.title: Explore the SF Symbols 3 app
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use system symbols that automatically localize for different languages and text directions.
claims.quote: The symbol I grabbed for my rule book earlier automatically appears with a character in the user's native script. It even adjusts the direction that the book opens to account for differences between left-to-right and right-to-left languages.

claims.rule: Check platform and OS version compatibility of symbols before using them in shipped code.
claims.quote: The information inspector that the name person.fill.badge.plus has been available in monochrome since SF Symbols version 2.0, which corresponds to iOS 14; that's too new for me.

claims.rule: Use SF symbols with no localization suffix to let the system automatically adapt for the user's language and text direction.
claims.quote: in general, you'll want to use the symbol name with no localization suffix and let the system choose the proper representation for your user's preferred language

sources.title: The practice of inclusive design
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Show diverse people and activities in app screenshots and marketing to help users from different backgrounds feel included.
claims.quote: The way you describe your app or game, its name, video trailer, and even the screenshots you select tell a story about whom it was built for

claims.rule: Use inclusive language and imagery that reflects diverse backgrounds, cultures, languages, and abilities throughout your interface and content.
claims.quote: An inclusive app or game is not only usable by different people, but also welcomes people from diverse backgrounds and perspectives.

claims.rule: Let people customize names, avatars, and profile details to represent themselves authentically in your app.
claims.quote: It's also how you let folks identify themselves. This can be through the names, profile details, avatars, or characters that people can customize

claims.rule: Use gender-neutral language and pronouns; avoid binary gender references in copy and default avatars.
claims.quote: instead of using the binary pronouns "he" or "she" in your copy, you can replace this language with the gender-neutral pronoun "they" instead

claims.rule: Design interface functionality to support diverse family structures instead of assuming fixed roles; let users define relationships.
claims.quote: instead of assuming there are fixed family roles, I can label each profile something neutral, like "family member." And instead of assuming how many people make up a family

sources.title: Practice audio haptic design
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Ensure haptic feedback clearly corresponds to its visual cause so users understand what triggered the sensation.
claims.quote: For feedback to be useful, it must be obvious what caused it. It's about making the source or the cause of the feedback clear and obvious.

claims.rule: Reserve haptics and audio feedback for significant moments and actions; avoid overusing them or they become overwhelming.
claims.quote: Don't add feedback just because you can. It can quickly become overwhelming and unpleasant. Reserve haptics and audio for significant moments

sources.title: Design great App Clips
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Make App Clips lightweight by including only essential functionality needed for the immediate task.
claims.quote: App Clips are lightweight versions of apps. They offer some of an app's functionality and they offer it when and where people need it.

claims.rule: Craft App Clip card subtitles to explain what the App Clip does; assume users have no prior knowledge of your brand.
claims.quote: they might not know what your name means. They're gonna need an explanation of what it is that your App Clip is there to do, and that's what you can put in the subtitle

claims.rule: Use photographs or custom graphics for App Clip card headers; avoid screenshots and dense text as they are hard to read in small spaces.
claims.quote: You should never use screenshots or fill it up with lots of text since both of those can be really hard to read in the small space available

claims.rule: Launch App Clips into the specific feature or context the user needs; skip unnecessary navigation steps when context is already clear.
claims.quote: Etsy would launch right into the part of their App Clip for the product being shown in Safari below. That saves people from having to navigate back to that product

claims.rule: Use Apple Pay and Sign in with Apple in App Clips to reduce friction and enable seamless authentication and payment.
claims.quote: Consider using technologies like Apple Pay and Sign in with Apple for a more seamless experience

sources.title: Design with iOS pickers, menus and actions
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use menus instead of action sheets on iPad and large screens to avoid heavy background dimming and better preserve context.
claims.quote: Upon appearing, they dimmed the background, which causes a heavy transition, especially on larger screens like an iPad.

claims.rule: Position menus near where users tap to minimize finger movement and improve speed of selection.
claims.quote: To start, the menu appears right next to where you tapped, and that requires far less movement of your finger to select an action.

claims.rule: Use menus to organize secondary or less critical actions and reduce visual clutter in your interface.
claims.quote: A simple more button in a view is a great way to show a menu of actions. These actions are often not important enough to be prominently displayed

claims.rule: Dismiss menus by tapping outside them; do not require a dedicated cancel button.
claims.quote: At any given time, I can tap outside the menu to dismiss it. This will hide the menu and take me back with no changes applied. It is therefore not needed to add an additional option to your menu to cancel.

claims.rule: Position menu items smaller and more concise than action sheet items while keeping them easily tappable.
claims.quote: The items in the menu are smaller and more concise, but still easily tappable, and they support multiple lines for longer strings.

claims.rule: Use menus with checkmarks to show the currently selected item in selection-based interactions.
claims.quote: Menus used for selection receive check marks next to the items that are selected.

claims.rule: Do not hide all primary actions in a menu; keep frequently used actions prominently displayed.
claims.quote: Hiding all actions in a menu is definitely not an approach we encourage. It hides primary actions behind an additional tap, and it doesn't give you a good understanding of what this view can do for you.

sources.title: Design for intelligence: Apps, evolved
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design intelligence as an adaptive, evolving platform convention that changes with user behavior, not static like icons.
claims.quote: Unlike other forms of design, intelligence isn't a static glyph or icon like the 'share' button. It's alive. It manifests itself by adapting to how the system, the platform, conforms to how people use their devices.

claims.rule: Help users accomplish their core job; view intelligence as a design practice that enables familiar patterns.
claims.quote: What's the core job of a designer? It's to help people accomplish something. And one of the key ways a designer enables this is by leveraging the familiar.

sources.title: Design for intelligence: Meet people where they are
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Provide the right value at the right time to help users accomplish their goals and develop lasting habits with your app.
claims.quote: Learn how you can provide the right kind of value at the right time to help them in their everyday tasks

sources.title: Design for Game Center
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Place the Game Center access point on your game's main menu where possible.
claims.quote: Whenever possible, display your access point at your game's main menu.

claims.rule: Position the access point in the top left corner of the screen if feasible.
claims.quote: However, we'd recommend placing it at top left, if possible.

claims.rule: Reserve safe areas around the access point to prevent game UI overlap.
claims.quote: You'll just want to make sure none of your game's UI encroaches upon the area the access point takes at its maximum size.

claims.rule: Keep achievement titles and descriptions under 30 characters for reliable display across devices.
claims.quote: try to keep your text under 30 characters to guarantee it will work well across devices

claims.rule: Keep leaderboard titles under 30 characters to prevent truncation across all devices and accessibility settings.
claims.quote: keeping your leaderboard titles under 30 characters to guarantee that it will work well across all devices and accessibility settings

claims.rule: Display unique, eye-catching artwork for each leaderboard to improve player differentiation.
claims.quote: Ensure that you use different artwork for each leaderboard so that players can differentiate between them

claims.rule: Use opaque circular achievement images centered, as system automatically crops to circle.
claims.quote: provide an opaque image for each achievement. The system automatically crops the image into a circle, so make sure any primary content is centered

sources.title: Make your app visually accessible
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Never rely on color alone to convey meaning; add shapes or icons.
claims.quote: using color only to create emphasis can get lost. There are extra steps you can take to achieve good design, and I'll give you a hint: It's shapes.

claims.rule: Provide alternate button appearance when button shapes accessibility setting is enabled.
claims.quote: If you can't fit button shapes in your default design, you should provide an alternate appearance for people with this setting enabled.

claims.rule: Update color tint or provide alternate assets when Increase Contrast accessibility setting is enabled.
claims.quote: You'll need update the tint color or provide alternate assets for high-contrast appearances

claims.rule: Suppress parallax and motion effects when Reduce Motion accessibility setting is enabled.
claims.quote: If you are using dramatic or frequent animations in your app, check is-Reduce-Motion-Enabled on UIAccessibility before performing them

claims.rule: Make text wrap and avoid truncation as content size increases; use full display width available.
claims.quote: You should avoid truncating text as the content size increases so that the user doesn't miss out on anything. Instead, wrap labels and use all of the available display width

sources.title: Design for intelligence: Make friends with "The System"
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Define key repeatable actions in your app using the Intents framework.
claims.quote: Ultimately, you, as developers and designers, just need to ask yourself, what are the important actions that people want to perform with your app?

claims.rule: Define key repeatable user actions as intents with their necessary parameters before implementing features.
claims.quote: determine what are the key and repeatable things that people want to accomplish. You can define these actions using what we call intents

sources.title: Evaluate and optimize voice interaction for your app
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Ensure Siri dialogue sounds natural with your app's actual data.
claims.quote: you should still make sure that the dialogue sounds good with your data in it, both from a sentence structure perspective and a text-to-speech perspective.

claims.rule: Use questions in voice dialogue to signal you expect an answer and need information to continue.
claims.quote: Questions are a great conversational marker. They let people know you're expecting an answer, so be sure to use them when people need to provide information to continue.

sources.title: Design for the iPadOS pointer
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use adaptive precision to adjust pointer behavior to match interface element size.
claims.quote: dynamically adjusting the precision of the pointer to match the precision of the interface is called, Adaptive Precision.

claims.rule: Ensure the pointer highlights controls without obscuring them.
claims.quote: the pointer highlights the element rather than obscuring it.

claims.rule: Match pointer precision to interface precision; reduce pointer precision for low-precision controls like buttons.
claims.quote: This concept of dynamically adjusting the precision of the pointer to match the precision of the interface is called, Adaptive Precision.

sources.title: App accessibility for Switch Control
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Group navigation items logically to reduce wait time for Switch Control users.
claims.quote: the efficiency and grouping of these navigation items is key for Switch Control users, as poor grouping can lead to large wait times to arrive at the item of interest.

claims.rule: Make destructive actions error-tolerant for users with limited motor control.
claims.quote: If there's an option to delete all data or log out, one accidental tap could have quite destructive consequences for a Switch Control user, so error tolerance is very important.

claims.rule: Require confirmation for destructive or high-consequence actions, especially for users with motor impairments.
claims.quote: Make sure you confirm any destructive behaviors or high-consequence behaviors in your applications. This is especially important for Switch Control users who may be more likely to mistap an item.

sources.title: Design great widgets
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Surface the most useful and timely information people return to your app for, prioritizing personal, informational, and contextual content.
claims.quote: Three useful principles we've found to focus on when thinking about ideas is to look for things that are personal, informational and contextual.

claims.rule: Show glanceable details and key information at a glance without requiring users to open the app to find it.
claims.quote: Glanceable details like the start time and event location save people a potential step in opening the app to find this information.

claims.rule: Adapt widget content based on context and time of day, showing relevant information before users need to search for it.
claims.quote: Context helps surface the right information at the right moment and allows for a better experience that at its best feels like it's magically predicting someone's needs and next steps.

claims.rule: Limit small widgets to maximum four pieces of information to avoid overcrowding.
claims.quote: We recommend only including a max of four pieces of information in the small widget size.

claims.rule: Use 16-point layout margins for all widget sizes to maintain consistent spacing with adjacent widgets.
claims.quote: follow the default sixteen point layout margins across all sizes to make sure the content in your widget feels consistent when it's place next to other widgets

claims.rule: Use 11-point margins for layouts with graphical shapes like circles and inset platters to maintain tighter alignment.
claims.quote: For layouts with graphical shapes like circles and inset platters use tighter eleven point margins across all sizes

claims.rule: Deep-link small widgets to relevant content with a single tap target; medium and large widgets support multiple tap targets.
claims.quote: The small widget supports a single tap target. Tapping it should deep link to the content that's on the widget.

sources.title: SF Symbols 2
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Vertically center symbols with text cap height and weight-match them so they appear consistent despite scaling differences.
claims.quote: When symbols appear next to text they are vertically centered with a cap height, still there are other typography guidelines we need to consider.

claims.rule: Compensate symbol weight when scaling to maintain optical consistency; small scales appear lighter and large scales bolder without adjustment.
claims.quote: Small symbols are approximately 20 percent smaller than the medium scale and large symbols are about 30 percent larger than the medium scale. But as we can see, only scaling the symbol will make them appear to have different weights.

claims.rule: Apply weight compensation when scaling symbols to maintain consistent stroke thickness across small, medium, and large scales.
claims.quote: we make some weight compensations which allow us to maintain the same stroke thickness making the symbols look weight matched not only between the scales but also with text

claims.rule: Never specify fixed frames for symbols; instead use text styles and point sizes so symbols resize with Dynamic Type.
claims.quote: Symbols are not designed to be constrained in frames with a specific size. It's the typographic nature of symbols that really makes it easy to spec, as if they were text.

claims.rule: Use center alignment for symbols rather than aspect fit or scale to fit to maintain optical balance.
claims.quote: make sure to use center alignments rather than aspect fit or scale to fit. And check your content gravity is set to centered

sources.title: Design for location privacy
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Prioritize user control by allowing people to share approximate location and function without requiring precise location data.
claims.quote: First, when designing for location privacy, prioritize user control. Give everyone control over the location data that they share and respect their preferences.

claims.rule: Use clear writing at critical decision points to explain what data your app requests and what value it provides to users.
claims.quote: Clear language, especially at important decision points, like here on first app launch, explains what data our app asks for and what value it provides.

claims.rule: Show status of shared location data persistently but reduce prominence after initial interaction to balance transparency without distraction.
claims.quote: When people first launch Maps, that status appears larger and stronger in visual treatment. This reminds them of past decisions and gives them direct access to control of the setting. Once people show interest and interact elsewhere in the app, the visual treatment reduces in prominence.

claims.rule: Remove nonessential UI that requires precise location data when users share only approximate location instead.
claims.quote: remove nonessential UI that requires precise data

claims.rule: Show location-sharing status prominently on first launch, then reduce visual prominence after user interaction to balance transparency without distraction.
claims.quote: status appears larger and stronger in visual treatment. This reminds them of past decisions and gives them direct access to control of the setting. Once people show interest and interact elsewhere in the app, the visual treatment reduces in prominence.

sources.title: What's new in watchOS design
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Keep watchOS apps lightweight and limit lengthy interactions; display all essential information at a glance without scrolling.
claims.quote: When designing your Watch app, keep in mind that Watch apps should be lightweight. Like in this example from the Sleep Cycle app, limit lengthy interactions and be choosy when it comes to functionality. Ideally you can get all the information from your Watch app at a glance.

claims.rule: Make secondary actions discoverable and visible directly in the app instead of hiding them in gesture-based contextual menus.
claims.quote: Secondly, relevant actions should always be visible in the app. And thirdly, eliminate gesture-based contextual menus without removing functionality.

claims.rule: Use sort and filter options at the top of lists to help users narrow down long lists and find relevant information in the moment.
claims.quote: A long scrolling list can become much easier to use, and more personal, if you have the ability to sort and filter to just the information relevant to you in the moment.

claims.rule: Use a More button (ellipsis in circular container) for secondary actions in glanceable, non-scrolling views.
claims.quote: So, we've added another button in the bottom right with the ellipsis glyph in the app's key color that can present these actions. This is known as a More button.

claims.rule: Place action buttons at the bottom of detail views, applying only to the content above them.
claims.quote: Action buttons at the bottom of a detail view may be the most discoverable and intuitive way to show actions in your app.

claims.rule: Use the toolbar button API sparingly, only in scrolling views for essential actions not primary to the view.
claims.quote: Only use it in a scrolling view. Scrolling is what makes this button discoverable. And use it judiciously, only for actions that are essential to the functioning of your app, but may not be the primary action for the view.

sources.title: Design for intelligence: Discover new opportunities
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Integrate your app with system intelligence entry points like Shortcuts, sharing suggestions, and Siri to extend beyond the home screen.
claims.quote: Your app can participate in intelligence by integrating with the system, which allows the system to see your app as much more than a monolithic container.

claims.rule: Apps sharing suggestions experience 100% increase in sharing when users engage with first suggestion.
claims.quote: when a user engages on their first Sharing Suggestion for your app, they will, on average, share twice as much as they did before through your app.

claims.rule: Integrate Siri Event Suggestions for actions like check-in; airlines saw 82% of check-ins come through this.
claims.quote: Some airlines shared with us that they saw 82% of notification check-ins come from their Siri Event Suggestion check-in action.

claims.rule: Expose app actions through system entry points; third-party apps appear five times daily via these channels.
claims.quote: Some third-party apps are seen, on average, five times every day on the lock screen, in Sharing, in Search, and other entry points throughout the system.

sources.title: Adopt the new look of macOS
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use NSSearchToolbarItem to collapse search into a button when window space is constrained.
claims.quote: When the window is large enough, the full search field is shown as normal, but when the window is compressed down, the search field is collapsed down into a button.

claims.rule: Apply inset style to table views for improved readability: add horizontal and vertical padding around selections.
claims.quote: The inset style applies some extra horizontal padding around your cell views and vertical padding around the top and bottom rows.

sources.title: Build for the iPadOS pointer
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Make pointer effects adapt shape to the control type being hovered.
claims.quote: a fluid adaptive pointer that morphs into controls when hovering over them to adapt its accuracy and provide a clear indication that you're about to interact with them

claims.rule: Change pointer shape contextually: beam for text, arrows for drag targets, standard elsewhere.
claims.quote: When hovering over text, for example, the pointer changes into a beam and snaps to lines to make interacting with text easier

claims.rule: Prioritize high-level APIs over low-level for pointer; they offer polished, consistent behavior.
claims.quote: Start with the higher-level APIs. They'll offer you the most polished experience with tuned behaviors and visuals that are consistent with similar UI in the rest of the system

claims.rule: Constrain pointer movement along axes to guide users toward target rows or columns, creating magnetic alignment.
claims.quote: constrain the pointer's movement on the vertical axis. If we're using the guide, return the crosshair with the constrainedAxes set to "vertical."

claims.rule: Extend pointer region padding beyond control bounds so pointer snaps to targets before reaching their visual edges.
claims.quote: providing expanded padding around views to amplify the pointer's magnetism and make it easier to interact with important elements

claims.rule: Coordinate pointer region transitions seamlessly across adjacent controls by providing contiguous regions without gaps.
claims.quote: providing the interaction with contiguous pointer regions. When coordinating multiple pointer regions or styles, it often makes sense to take your interaction up to a higher level in the view hierarchy

sources.title: Designed for iPad
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Use sidebar navigation on iPad to show both content and navigation on one screen.
claims.quote: instead of empty space, it fills the display with the content that you want to see, your photos, as well as your navigation controls on the left

claims.rule: Avoid full-screen transitions on iPad; update parts of screen instead to use large display efficiently.
claims.quote: Flatten your app's navigation. Avoid big full-screen transitions in favor of updating part of the screen at a time

claims.rule: Show navigation alongside content simultaneously on iPad instead of in overlays or modals to maintain context during interaction.
claims.quote: showing content along with your navigation also helps in other ways too. For example, if you want to switch between different parts of your photo library, to your albums or to all of your photos, it's now just a single tap away.

claims.rule: Avoid modal overlays on iPad; instead keep controls at the same level as content so users see results and context simultaneously.
claims.quote: see if you have any modal sheets or popovers, and see if those modal sheets and popovers are giving people useful context or if they're blocking other parts of your app. See if it would work better if your controls are at the same level, rather than an overlays.

sources.title: Designing iPad Apps for Mac
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Support Auto Layout fully so iPad app layouts adapt to arbitrary Mac window resizing.
claims.quote: By fully supporting Auto Layout in your iPad app, your interface will be resizable on Mac

claims.rule: Move controls from iPad bottom edge to Mac toolbar to prevent them from being hidden below the dock.
claims.quote: If your iPad app has any actions that are located along the bottom edge of the screen, doing the same thing in a Mac window can be very problematic. Mac windows are draggable. The bottom edge of Mac windows might be dragged out of you, or below the dock.

claims.rule: Avoid small text styles like caption and footnote on Mac; bump up text size to remain legible after 77% scaling.
claims.quote: Using some of the smallest size like footnote, caption one, caption two, can make text that's difficult to read on Mac. Even the Mac size mini is often too small. So, just -- you may find that you need to bump up text a little bit to keep it legible on Mac.

sources.title: Apple Design Awards
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

sources.title: Visual Design and Accessibility
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Make all text dynamic if possible; text that can grow should grow with user's font size setting.
claims.quote: First, you make as much of your text dynamic as possible. If the text can grow, it should grow

claims.rule: Scale glyphs and icons alongside text to maintain visual balance as text size grows.
claims.quote: you should scale glyphs that appear next to text so that your UI continues to look balanced

claims.rule: Never auto-play video without checking the user's motion auto-play setting; respect accessibility preferences for motion.
claims.quote: Auto-play video previews starts as enabled by default, but you can turn it off at any time. And, additionally, we've made this public API.

claims.rule: Do not use color alone to convey meaning; add additional visual indicators like shapes, symbols, or text for users with color-vision deficiency.
claims.quote: any place in my app where I use color as the only way of conveying information, I should now add some additional indicator. For example, a shape.

sources.title: What's New in iOS Design
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: All apps should support Dark Mode; users expect it when device is set to Dark Mode.
claims.quote: In general, all of your apps should support Dark Mode. When the people using your app have set their device to be in Dark Mode, they'll expect your app to change as well

claims.rule: All apps must support Dark Mode; users expect it when their device is set to Dark Mode.
claims.quote: In general, all of your apps should support Dark Mode. When the people using your app have set their device to be in Dark Mode, they'll expect your app to change as well.

claims.rule: Use semantic colors from the system palette instead of hardcoded color values to support both Light and Dark modes automatically.
claims.quote: instead of maintaining two separate lists of colors for Light and Dark Modes, you can apply semantic colors from the system palette to UI elements and their appearance will automatically adapt

claims.rule: Achieve a contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1 or higher for tint colors between Light and Dark modes using a color contrast calculator.
