claims.quote: aim for a contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1 or higher. Strong color contrast improves the accessibility and usability of your apps.

claims.rule: Use vibrancy rather than solid colors over system materials to maintain contrast and legibility regardless of background context.
claims.quote: With system materials, it's typically best to use vibrancy rather than solid colors. Because depending on the background context, solid colors can get really muddy and can lead to some serious legibility issues.

claims.rule: Allow users to dismiss card-style modal sheets by swiping down anywhere on screen; implement swipe-to-dismiss as the primary dismissal method.
claims.quote: Card-style modal sheets can be dismissed by swiping down anywhere on the screen. And that dismiss gesture is often going to be easier than tapping a button in the navigation bar.

claims.rule: Use navigation bars without background or shadow by default to allow titles to connect seamlessly with content, fading in the background and shadow when content scrolls underneath.
claims.quote: By default, they're now drawn for large titles without the background and shadow. This allows the title to connect seamlessly with the content that it's labeling. When content scrolls underneath the navigation bar, the background and shadow will fade back in.

sources.title: Introducing SF Symbols
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design symbols to sit on the same baseline as adjacent text, with invisible margins that ensure proper alignment.
claims.quote: When symbols appear next to text, they all sit nicely on the same baseline.

claims.rule: Specify symbols using typographic points like text, not screen dimensions, to ensure proper rendering at all sizes.
claims.quote: They're specified in typographic points, like text.

claims.rule: Design symbol weights to maintain detail and visibility across the full weight range from ultra-light to black.
claims.quote: Every weight has been drawn manually, and special consideration went into each design. Thinner weights have a distinctive, beautiful elegance, while the heavier ones strive to maintain detail and visibility.

sources.title: Mastering the Living Room With tvOS
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Present content immediately upon app launch with live, playing material to engage users and reduce friction.
claims.quote: Apple TV has purposefully migrated its designs towards a content first experience. And all that really means is something's on, something's playing. When you launch into the application, it's alive.

claims.rule: Avoid forcing sound and video on launch; allow users to invoke audio after content appears.
claims.quote: it's important to note here that that trailer, we don't force sound on the viewer in this instance. Too much sound and video when you first launch into something, it can be destructive.

claims.rule: Eliminate latency and remove overstimulation by minimizing animations, icons, images, and text styles that compete for attention.
claims.quote: By using too many animations, icons, images and text styles, it competes for somebody's attention. And we don't want somebody be-- to be in that competitive mindset. We want them to be focused and relaxed.

claims.rule: Keep 5 to 10 items maximum in carousel-style content discovery to avoid noise and cognitive overload.
claims.quote: Too many items in the Top Shelf just adds noise and clutter. So we think a good number to keep in mind is somewhere between 5 and 10.

claims.rule: Deliver carousel images at 1920 by 1080 points filling the entire frame for full-screen content display.
claims.quote: Content in the Top Shelf Carousel is full screen. So your images should be 1920 by 1080 points and they should draw in the entire frame of that content.

sources.title: Designing Audio-Haptic Experiences
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Synchronize haptic feedback with on-screen animations to create causality: make the relationship between user action and sensory response obvious.
claims.quote: Causality is about, for feedback to be useful; it must be obvious what caused it.

claims.rule: Match haptic and audio feedback to the physical properties of what users interact with, as they would expect from real-world objects.
claims.quote: Now, when designing sounds for your experiences, think about what would it feel and sound like, if what you interact with would be a physical object.

claims.rule: Match haptic sharpness and intensity to the physical properties and velocity of on-screen objects and actions.
claims.quote: We choose a transient event with high sharpness. We also modulate the intensity to match the velocity of the bounce.

sources.title: What’s New in iOS and macOS Design
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

sources.title: Expanding the Sensory Experience with Core Haptics
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Synchronize haptic sensations from the Taptic Engine with audio output to create combined audio-haptic experiences.
claims.quote: The haptic sensations from the taptic engine are synchronized to the sounds coming from the speaker, and the result is what we call an audio haptic experience.

claims.rule: Use continuous haptic experiences for sustained feedback and transient haptics for momentary impacts, strikes, or taps.
claims.quote: So, we can play these continuous experiences. We can also have something that's more shorter and compact. It's a single cycle, and we call this experience a transient. It's much more momentary, and it feels like an impact or a strike or a tap.

claims.rule: Use transient haptics for momentary impacts; use continuous haptics for sustained feedback lasting over time.
claims.quote: We can play these continuous experiences. We can also have something that's more shorter and compact. It's a single cycle, and we call this experience a transient.

claims.rule: Design audio-haptic feedback to match the visual animation's energy, pace, and emotional tone.
claims.quote: Think about the pace, the energy level, and the different quality that you're trying to convey in your app. Design feedback that tell the consistent and unified story.

claims.rule: Add audio and haptic feedback only to the most significant interactions; remove feedback that doesn't enhance value or communicate importance.
claims.quote: Utility is about adding audio and haptic feedback only when you can provide clear value and benefit to your app experience. Use moderation. Don't add sound and haptics just because you can.

sources.title: Introducing Core Haptics
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

sources.title: Designing Award Winning Apps and Games
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Question basic assumptions about feature design from the start; convert problems into opportunities.
claims.quote: question assumptions from the start. Ask questions. Ask, "Why are we doing it this way?"

claims.rule: Remove obstacles to getting started; focus on effortless entry to core functionality.
claims.quote: focused on removing obstacles to getting started with each of your drills and workouts

sources.title: Designing Great Shortcuts
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design shortcuts for frequently repeated, valuable actions that work by voice without visual browsing.
claims.quote: a great use for shortcuts will be something that is valuable, or interesting to repeat. Doable with your voice by not relying on visuals or tapping.

claims.rule: Place Add to Siri buttons selectively near high-intent actions, not on every menu item.
claims.quote: Don't do this, where you put an Add to Siri button on every item on your main menu

claims.rule: Keep suggested voice command phrases to three or fewer words, using proper nouns or verb-object patterns only.
claims.quote: keep it short, at around three or fewer words. Try limiting it to a proper noun, or just a verb and an object.

claims.rule: Test voice dialog repeatedly before shipping; discard dialog that becomes irritating after ten repetitions.
claims.quote: Listen to Siri speak your dialog. How does your dialog feel to you after the third time hearing it? What about the 10th?

claims.rule: Avoid first-person pronouns in voice dialog because users may misattribute agency to Siri rather than the app.
claims.quote: Avoid using first-person pronouns, since Siri isn't performing the action, your app is.

claims.rule: Present option lists upfront with phrased prompts using which-questions to minimize disambiguation steps in voice flows.
claims.quote: You can minimize disambiguation prompts, which add another step to your conversation, by presenting an option list up front.

claims.rule: Provide pronunciation hints for voice options to avoid verbosity, reading only differentiating details aloud.
claims.quote: you can separately specify how Siri reads your options out loud, by providing pronunciation hits that you can add to each option.

sources.title: Designing Great ML Experiences
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Collect training data intentionally to reflect the experience you want, not just the world as it exists; optimize for customers you want, not those you have.
claims.quote: You shouldn't reflect the world as it is. You should reflect a better world, that world that you want it to be.

claims.rule: Categorize and analyze ML model failures by scenario; some need better models, others need design or non-ML solutions.
claims.quote: Group failure cases into categories and scenarios. This will help you understand how important each scenario is. Decide if it's best handled by a non-ML approach

claims.rule: Treat metrics as proxies for abstract values like customer happiness; evolve them when they diverge from actual user experience.
claims.quote: Metrics provide numbers, a sense of scientific accuracy, and it's easy to get caught up in numbers and improving them but we ultimately care about abstract concepts.

sources.title: Building Great Shortcuts
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Keep shortcut parameter summaries short, verb-first, and exclude app name; show optional parameters under Show More.
claims.quote: Summaries should read like a sentence and start with a verb. There's no need to write the name of your app in the summary

claims.rule: Prefill suggested shortcut invocation phrases with a short, speakable, memorable phrase.
claims.quote: Try to keep this phrase short and descriptive about the kind of action that the user just did. And because the user will be able to say this to Siri, it should also be easy to speak and remember.

claims.rule: Present Add to Siri immediately after the user performs an action they are likely to repeat.
claims.quote: this is a great time to present an Add to Siri button because the user just performed an action that they're very likely to repeat

sources.title: Great Developer Habits
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

sources.title: Designing Fluid Interfaces
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design direct, responsive gesture interactions that feel like an extension of the user's mind and body.
claims.quote: when the tool feels like an extension of your mind. An extension of your mind.

claims.rule: Detect pause in finger motion by measuring acceleration, not velocity thresholds or timers.
claims.quote: We look at your finger's acceleration. It turns out there's a huge spike in the acceleration of your finger when you pause.

sources.title: Intentional Design
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Remove UI elements that don't serve the immediate task; let people focus on essential actions.
claims.quote: They remove the UI and allow people to focus on what they need, which is to find something, to ask a question, to get their bearings.

claims.rule: Design apps for the context where they will actually be used, accounting for users' physical and mental state.
claims.quote: They considered the context really well, the context that this will be used in. They took into account where and when people would pull out their phone and launch their app.

claims.rule: Make apps feel simple and natural so users perceive them as an extension of what they already know.
claims.quote: When an app feels simple users perceive it as natural, an extension of what they know. It feels like it arises from their experience and it flows naturally from what they expect.

sources.title: The Life of a Button
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design feedback for three interaction phases: before (anticipation), during (response), and after (completion).
claims.quote: We can think of these phases in terms of a physical button. Before I have pressed the button it's just hanging out there. During my interaction with that button it's being pressed in. And finally after I've pressed that button my finger is lifting off of it and it's returning to its original state.

claims.rule: Use both telling (text and icons) and showing (visual, audio, haptic changes) to communicate feedback.
claims.quote: The first is that you can tell people, you can literally put text on screen explaining what's going on or design icons that explain things. The second is that you can show people, you can allow people to experience the results of their action more like the real world through visual, audio or even haptic change over time.

claims.rule: Animate button state changes instantly or very quickly to feel responsive; slow fades make interactions feel unresponsive.
claims.quote: if we are going to animate it do it very quickly

claims.rule: Allow users to drag a finger outside a button to cancel activation before release; this makes interactions feel undecided and fluid.
claims.quote: I can actually drag my finger outside of the button to begin canceling it. This is something that's actually very important for all sorts of fluid interactions because it's what makes a fluid interaction undecided.

claims.rule: Make the hit area of small controls larger than the visual size to aid interaction, especially for fingers.
claims.quote: the hit area of this button might not be what you expect, if you look closely at the circle maybe I'm not quite touching it. But perhaps the hit area is actually a little bit larger than the visual size, this is particularly important for very small controls

sources.title: Designing Notifications
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Make notifications beautiful, helpful, actionable, and respectful of people's time and attention.
claims.quote: Thoughtfully designed notifications are a powerful way to communicate timely information to people that they will find valuable and useful. Learn how you can design notifications people want to receive by making them beautiful, helpful, actionable, and respectful of their valuable time and attention.

claims.rule: Offer quiet notifications that go to notification center without lock screen, sound, or haptic interruption.
claims.quote: At the top, the first option is to deliver quietly. And these quiet notifications will be send directly into your notification center without interruption. It did not appear on the lock screen. It did not play a sound or haptic, or present as banners.

claims.rule: Use rich notifications to provide context and information so users understand without launching the app.
claims.quote: Rich notifications are a great way to provide more context and information around each notification. That way you can see one, understand what it's for and get the extra information that you need to take action. And it all happens right in line. You don't need to launch into the app and lose the context of what you're doing.

claims.rule: Make every notification serve a specific purpose with real, meaningful information; never use notifications just to drive app launches.
claims.quote: Everything you said in a notification has got to be meaningful. Every notification should provide a specific purpose. Each notification should have a specific message to communicate or a task to complete. Notifications are not just a reason to get people to launch into your app.

sources.title: Presenting Design Work
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Clarify your presentation objectives and the bigger picture before diving into details and minutia.
claims.quote: Try not to dive in to details and minutia before you clarify the bigger picture.

claims.rule: Show how you have integrated audience feedback into designs to demonstrate you are listening and responding.
claims.quote: Integrate their feedback. Let them know how it affected your designs. Show that you're listening and responding.

sources.title: Get Started with Display P3
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Tag all design assets with the correct color profile to enable accurate color management across devices.
claims.quote: As a designer makes sure to tag your assets properly to allow for color management to accurately display your colors.

claims.rule: Use 16-bit color depth with Display P3 to reduce banding in gradients compared to 8-bit sRGB.
claims.quote: When working with the Display P3 color profile you have the opportunity to also use a larger color depth. 16 bit per channel instead of the usual 8. That allows you to represent more colors within the wide gamut, which is especially useful for gradients.

claims.rule: Work on a wide gamut display when creating Display P3 assets to maintain full control over colors.
claims.quote: Make sure to work on a wide gamut display that supports Display P3 like the MacBook Pro of the Touch Bar, the iMac Retina, or the LG5K Display.

claims.rule: Use PNG format with Save As in Photoshop to embed color profiles and maintain color depth in exported assets.
claims.quote: It is key then to use Save As and PNG as your format because this is the only way at the moment to both imbed a color profile and maintain the color depth without -- in the exported asset.

claims.rule: Use 16-bit color depth instead of 8-bit when creating Display P3 assets to reduce visible banding in gradients.
claims.quote: 16 bit per channel instead of the usual 8. That allows you to represent more colors within the wide gamut, which is especially useful for gradients.

claims.rule: Save Display P3 assets as PNG using Save As in Photoshop to embed color profiles and maintain color depth.
claims.quote: it is key then to use Save As and PNG as your format because this is the only way at the moment to both imbed a color profile and maintain the color depth

claims.rule: Use Convert to Profile rather than Assign to Profile when converting existing assets to Display P3 to preserve design intent.
claims.quote: Do not use Assign to Profile as that will take your existing colors and stretch those out into the new color space changing your design

claims.rule: Apply Display P3 selectively to apps with vibrant imagery, nature scenes, or products where color accuracy matters, not to calm desaturated designs.
claims.quote: Display P3 works great in some cases, in others it's just not the right choice. For example, if your app is designed with a calm, de-saturated color scheme, it doesn't use a lot of imagery, display P3 might not be the right choice

sources.title: Express Yourself!
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design iMessage apps to be playful and personal, allowing users to express themselves in unique and colorful ways.
claims.quote: Using Stickers is playful, and personal. There are so many different types of ways to send Stickers, expressing yourself in unique and colorful ways is fun.

claims.rule: Enable core financial transactions in iMessage without leaving the conversation using Apple Pay.
claims.quote: Apple Pay allows you to perform financial transactions without leaving messages. It is super convenient.

claims.rule: Design collaborative apps in iMessage to require and enable participation from both parties to create engagement.
claims.quote: Games and polling rely on both parties to participate, to make the most of the app experience.

claims.rule: Design iMessage apps to feature only core communication-focused features, not replicate the entire main app experience.
claims.quote: Tumblr, Dunkin Donuts and Tinder do not set out to put their entire apps into messages, and thankfully they didn't. They integrated only features that were focused on communication.

claims.rule: Enable users to create and customize content within iMessage apps to increase engagement and discovery of new use cases.
claims.quote: Handcrafted messages are fun to send and receive. Find ways to let your users create and customize the experience. You may find that there are ways to use your app that you never even imagined.

sources.title: Designing for a Global Audience
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Help users understand content and locate key information by using clear headings and titles.
claims.quote: Help your users orient themselves with headings and titles. Make sure that the important information from your instructions is conveyed and that commonly used terms are clear.

claims.rule: Provide context clues for informal language so users can understand meaning even if unfamiliar.
claims.quote: If you do, do a quick check to make sure that it's not offensive and be sure to offer contextual clues so that even if a user isn't totally sure what you mean they can still figure it out.

claims.rule: Use simple glyphs and silhouettes in icons rather than detailed depictions to avoid excluding users.
claims.quote: When depicting people keep in mind that more detailed icons may exclude some of your users, but that simpler glyphs like this silhouette are much more general and maybe a better choice.

claims.rule: Choose terms that translate similarly across languages to improve multilingual clarity; for example use photo rather than picture.
claims.quote: When terms can be used more or less interchangeably in your app's primary language is there one choice that's very similar to other languages. For example, picture and photo are more or less the same in English, but look at the difference in these other languages. Photo is the clear winner for multilingual clarity.

sources.title: Rich Notifications
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Send notifications only when your app has important information, never to boost traffic or engagement.
claims.quote: We should send notifications only when they're relevant. Don't spam. Don't send them to boost traffic or engagement, but only when your app has some important information to share.

claims.rule: Make notifications self-contained packages of information allowing users to complete specific tasks without launching the app.
claims.quote: Don't think of notifications as just a hook into your app. You know, they should be a self-contained package of information that allows you to complete a specific task.

claims.rule: Provide contextually relevant additional information in the expanded view of a notification.
claims.quote: And here is where you should provide some additional context, some additional information around your notification.

claims.rule: Use custom UI, typography, and visualizations in notification long looks to match your app's design language.
claims.quote: if you have custom UI, custom typography, elements that make your app unique, you should add them here

claims.rule: Update notification content in real time when displaying live data like maps, stock prices, or social feeds.
claims.quote: you can update the content of a Long Look in real time. So any case where you're using a map, that is a nice example.

claims.rule: Include 1–3 relevant quick action buttons in notifications to let users complete tasks without launching the app.
claims.quote: at the bottom of the notification there can be some optional Quick Actions. So if it relates to the notification, add some relevant buttons.

sources.title: 60-Second Prototyping
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Test interactive prototypes in realistic contexts on the target device, not in abstract settings.
claims.quote: It is also very important to show your prototypes in context, on the device they're meant for, in a somewhat realistic situation. You can't test things in a vacuum.

claims.rule: Test prototypes on the target device in realistic contexts, not in abstract or vacuum settings.
claims.quote: show your prototypes in context, on the device they're meant for, in a somewhat realistic situation. You can't test things in a vacuum.

claims.rule: Gather feedback on prototypes without defending, arguing, or dismissing user observations and suggestions.
claims.quote: Don't argue, defend, or dismiss the feedback you get.

sources.title: Design Tips for Great Games
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design the first screen to immerse players in the game style before showing functional text or requirements.
claims.quote: No matter what you need to say first, whether it is Accept Terms, or Headsets Recommended, design the first screen to fit within the style of your game. That way, they're immersed immediately.

claims.rule: Entertain or educate during loading to make wait times feel shorter and more valuable.
claims.quote: During Loading, make it fun by educating or entertaining; then, Loading won't see to take as long.

claims.rule: Show progress bars instead of activity indicators to communicate what is happening and how long it will take.
claims.quote: Always favor progress bars over activity indicators because they do a much better job communicating what's happening and how long it will take.

claims.rule: Make the main call to action most dominant in your menu UI, especially in busy interfaces with news and stores.
claims.quote: Make sure that the main call to action to play, start, battle, or begin a new game is the most dominant in your Main Menu UI.

claims.rule: Place controls in consistent, predictable locations throughout your game interface to improve usability.
claims.quote: Consistency improves usability because it helps people mentally map your interface. It's much easier to play and navigate when controls are in predictable locations.

claims.rule: Include three visual states for all buttons and controls: normal, pressed, and disabled to prevent confusion.
claims.quote: In your interface, for clarity, it's important always to include three visual states for buttons and controls because a lack of visual feedback can confuse players. Be sure to use a Normal state to show people that something's tappable. Use a Press state when something has been tapped. And finally, use a Disabled state for control that's not currently active or enabled.

claims.rule: Use disabled state rather than hiding controls, so players understand location and future availability.
claims.quote: Many developers struggle if they should remove or hide a control if it cannot be activated, but if you do that, when it does pop back it could be really confusing to players, especially if this happens during gameplay. So, for a much better user experience, use a Disabled state. This lets people know the control's location and action that will be possible

claims.rule: Place a dominant call-to-action button (Play, Start, Battle) most prominently in busy main menu UIs with news, tournaments, and stores.
claims.quote: game Main Menus have become increasingly busy with news, tournaments, stores, and more. And these can all be on your interface, but make sure that the main call to action to play, start, battle, or begin a new game is the most dominant in your Main Menu UI.

claims.rule: Keep tutorial directions short, simple, and single-action; avoid repeating directions to respect player intelligence.
claims.quote: keep directions short and simple to be effective. So, whether you teach with a character or through in-game instructional text, a single clear direction is going to be the most effective. And please, don't repeat directions.

claims.rule: Avoid bouncing arrows and floating hand tutorials; use animation or learn-by-play instead for more effective and immersive teaching.
claims.quote: One of the least effective ways to teach is with a bouncing arrow. It's not effective because people just end up playing tap the pointing arrow game and not learning. And the same goes for the floating hand.

claims.rule: Ensure all interactive elements meet a minimum 44×44 point tap target size on iOS to prevent user frustration.
claims.quote: make sure that everything that's interactive on your game's interface meets the minimum tap targets on iOS which is 44 by 44 points.

sources.title: How to Pick a Custom Font
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Increase letter spacing as point size decreases to maintain comfortable reading experiences at smaller sizes.
claims.quote: For optical reasons, reading stays comfortable if the space between letters increases as the point size decreases. Adobe Caslon Pro has looser spacing and this contributes to a nicer reading experience at smaller size.

claims.rule: Create typographic contrast through size, weight, or style to guide attention and establish hierarchy in layouts.
claims.quote: The key element is typographic contrast. Whether I did it through size, weight, or style.

sources.title: Communication Between Designers and Engineers
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Establish shared terminology with your team and clients to eliminate confusion and build credibility.
claims.quote: Using the same terminology. This saves time, eliminates confusion, and increases credibility with your team and clients.

claims.rule: Create a single source of truth for approved design deliverables accessible to the entire team.
claims.quote: What if you and your team or client could agree before hand a single place where all of the approved deliverables can be accessed. This would ensure that everyone knows where to go to check out the necessary assets.

claims.rule: Show prototypes and implementations to stakeholders rather than explaining designs with static mockups.
claims.quote: Show and tell. Or rather show more than tell. Designers can be guilty of throwing static mockups inspects over to engineers, especially in a time crunch.

claims.rule: Show working prototypes or videos to stakeholders instead of static mockups to communicate intent and spark conversations about constraints.
claims.quote: More often than not, demonstrating with a video or a small interactive prototype can be extremely valuable in communicating the intent or better yet, sparking a conversation on constraints, possible solutions, and next steps.

sources.title: Writing Great Alerts
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Make alert titles and actions understandable without reading message details; design so users grasp the situation at a glance.
claims.quote: If people scan the title and the actions, ideally, they should be able to understand what is going on without paying too much attention to the message details.

claims.rule: Structure alerts to answer three questions: what happened, why users see this, and how to proceed based on the information.
claims.quote: A good alert answers three key questions. What happened? Why people are seeing this? And how this should proceed based on the information they've received.

sources.title: Love at First Launch
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design interfaces to be intuitive and self-explanatory; minimize or eliminate upfront instruction and onboarding tutorials.
claims.quote: You should strive to design your interfaces to be as intuitive and as easy to understand as possible. Ideally no upfront instruction is needed at all.

claims.rule: Lead with content first to demonstrate app value; show features and benefits before asking for commitments or permissions.
claims.quote: Always lead with great content. Show off what makes your app great right off the bat and let people dig in.

claims.rule: Request permissions on an as-needed basis in context; immediately show the benefit when asking for access to user data.
claims.quote: The app requests permissions on a need to know basis. So you retain a sense of control over both the experience and your private data.

claims.rule: Teach app mechanics through interactive experiences rather than static onboarding; embed learning into the early gameplay or task flow.
claims.quote: If your app requires a bit of upfront education, it's going to be a lot more compelling if it's interactive and gives people that sense of jumping right in.

sources.title: Size Classes and Core Components
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Limit text styles to two or three per screen to create clear hierarchy while maintaining visual consistency.
claims.quote: In most cases, we recommend using two to three of these text styles per screen.

claims.rule: Apply readability margins on larger screens to restrict line length; allow text size to adjust based on Dynamic Type settings without compromising layout.
claims.quote: If you're using Dynamic Type with readability margins, then people using your app will have a much more comfortable reading experience.

claims.rule: Reuse standard UIKit elements (TableViews, navigation, tab bars) across iOS device sizes to maintain consistency and inherit accessibility features automatically.
claims.quote: We have a bunch of standard UI elements that you can use in your app that will automatically adapt on all screen sizes.

sources.title: Designing Glyphs
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design glyphs with high simplification, conceptual universality, and quick readability to communicate function or purpose clearly.
claims.quote: Effective glyphs have some key characteristics. They're highly simplified in form. They're conceptually universal, and they're quickly readable in context as to their function or purpose.

claims.rule: Use optical balance and scaling to adjust glyphs of different shapes, accounting for surface area differences to appear equal in visual weight.
claims.quote: Because the elliptical shape of messages and the narrow shape of phone have less surface area, we can use scale to achieve this optical balance.

claims.rule: Normalize line weight across all glyphs in a set; consistent stroke width creates visual cohesion and prevents glyphs from appearing emphasized unevenly.
claims.quote: Because they don't share a consistent line weight, some look more emphasized than others, and this can be confusing, and they just don't family well.

claims.rule: Apply optical positioning adjustments to asymmetrical glyphs; mathematically centered art may need pixel adjustments to appear visually balanced.
claims.quote: Notice, that art is perfectly centered within that space, but optically, it just, it just looks off. So, if we nudge that over a few pixels to the right, we achieve a much more balanced result.

sources.title: App Icon Design
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Keep app icons simple and clear with no clutter; design for quick, easy recognition at multiple sizes.
claims.quote: The second, simplicity; your design should be simple and clear, no clutter or over complicate it. If your icon is designed well, it should be quick and easy to read.

claims.rule: Maintain icon lineage across versions; refine identity deliberately over time rather than changing icons with each app update.
claims.quote: And lineage, make changes to your icon meaningful and deliberate. Don't change your app icon every single time that you update your app. Refine your identity over time.

claims.rule: Ensure visual consistency across platforms by using the same metaphor and design in both iOS and Mac versions of an app.
claims.quote: The visual connection here is really important because it tells users that they can expect at consistent experience across platforms.

claims.rule: Test app icons at multiple sizes, in folders, and next to other icons to ensure clarity and recognizability at small scales.
claims.quote: examine on the Home screen, in a folder, and if your app has settings, the settings app

sources.title: Essential Design Principles
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Design interfaces to provide safety, predictability, clarity, achievement, and beauty to meet users' fundamental human needs.
claims.quote: We have the need for safety and predictability. We have a need for knowledge, for meaning, and understanding. We have a need to accomplish tasks, to achieve our personal and professional goals. And we have the need to experience beauty and joy.

claims.rule: Use design principles as foundations for decisions, not just techniques; they express universal truths about perception and behavior.
claims.quote: Design principles don't tell us how to do specific things in our design, they tell us why we should do those things. They serve as the foundation upon which great designs are built.

claims.rule: Help users understand where they are, where they can go, and how to exit by answering these questions on every screen.
claims.quote: every screen in your app should answer all of these questions, or else people will feel lost

claims.rule: Provide immediate, clear, and understandable feedback for all user actions to build confidence and prevent errors.
claims.quote: feedback that cars provide must be clear, immediate, and understandable

claims.rule: Surface critical status information at higher levels of hierarchy to avoid forcing users to navigate deeper.
claims.quote: surface key status information at higher levels whenever possible

sources.title: Designing Sound
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Create notification sounds that clearly convey their message without requiring users to look at the screen.
claims.quote: if your app relies on notifications, it makes a lot of sense to think about creating your own notification sound

claims.rule: Design notification sounds to be easily recognizable so users instantly know which app sent them.
claims.quote: This sound is easily recognizable. When you hear this, you know it's coming from Dark Sky.

claims.rule: Use sound to help users understand interactions better and give devices a voice to communicate with them.
claims.quote: It helps us understand interactions better. And it gives our devices a voice so they can tell us things, they can talk back to us.

claims.rule: Make notification sounds unobtrusive and repeatable by testing them over a week to ensure they do not become annoying with frequent use.
claims.quote: If after a week you still like the sound, it's probably a pretty good one

claims.rule: Synchronize sound design with haptics and animation to create a cohesive multisensory experience that reinforces user perception.
claims.quote: combining sounds and haptics the right way and synchronizing them precisely, we can come up with this great multisensory experience

sources.title: Iterative UI Design
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Answer core design questions before implementation: what are you making, who is it for, and does it work.
claims.quote: Questions like, what are we making? Who is it for? Does it actually work? And did we get it right?

claims.rule: Define your app by identifying features that matter most to users and serve your own goals.
claims.quote: take all the things you can imagine your app could do. Identify the features that matter most to the people who will use your app

claims.rule: Identify which features matter most to users and your goals before designing; exclude features that don't serve either.
claims.quote: Identify the features that matter most to the people who will use your app, and the features that serve your own goals for the app itself, in order to determine what your app should do.

sources.title: Designing for Apple Watch
sources.why: Apple design-team session from the WWDC design track.

claims.rule: Send notifications sparingly and only when urgent or deeply relevant to avoid users disabling them.
claims.quote: Carefully consider how frequently you send notifications to people. They will get annoyed if you send notifications too often.

claims.rule: Use location and time context to determine notification relevance and improve user experience.
claims.quote: The two main contextual factors that are used to determine relevancy are location and time.

claims.rule: Complement apps with Apple Watch notifications that are valuable and useful, not interruptive.
claims.quote: the notifications that you send to people should contain valuable and useful information. People should actually feel thankful for the notifications that you send to them.

claims.rule: Learn user preferences implicitly from their behavior and interactions, not only explicit settings.
claims.quote: By observing and responding to people's interactions or behaviors, your app can make subtle but significant adjustments to better accommodate the preferences of the people who use it.

claims.rule: Use menus for contextual actions and view preferences, not critical-path actions needed to progress.

claims.rule: Avoid transparency in graphics unless compositing requires it; alpha channels increase file size.

claims.quote: Do you know how to do this one particular thing that we have prototyped? Is it easy to do that thing? And in general, how can we make this better?

claims.quote: you should not start prototyping from just a single idea. You want to explore and understand the whole space in order to figure out the best direction

claims.rule: When testing prototypes with users, ask three questions: whether they understand how to perform the key interaction, whether it feels easy, and how they would improve it.
claims.quote: we want to ask them three questions as we're showing them. Do you know how to do this one particular thing that we have prototyped? Is it easy to do that thing? And in general, how can we make this better?

claims.rule: Zoom to the actual device size while prototyping to verify that text, images, and touch targets remain readable and tappable at real scale.

claims.rule: Arrange elements along smooth, continuing lines rather than ragged ones to signal they belong together.

claims.rule: Group filters and navigation elements close together; place view-specific filters near the views they control.
claims.quote: Group global filters and navigation elements together. If a filter only applies to a single view, put it close to that view so the user understands that the two are related.

claims.rule: Maintain consistent button styling across the dashboard so users recognize similar function.
claims.quote: If your first button contains a white background with a blue stroke, maintain that style across all your buttons so the user recognizes that they have a similar function.

sources.title: What is the Data Ink Ratio?
sources.why: Explains Tufte's data-ink ratio principle: maximizing meaningful data representation while minimizing decorative elements
sources.found_via: dashboard clutter visual noise reduction data ink

claims.rule: Eliminate gridlines and unnecessary borders that do not contribute to viewer understanding of data.
claims.quote: Eliminate gridlines and unnecessary borders that do not contribute to the viewer's understanding. Gridlines actually distract the viewer's attention from the actual data.

claims.rule: Incorporate labels directly into visualizations instead of using separate legends when possible.
claims.quote: Avoid unnecessary legends by incorporating labels directly into the visualization. For example, instead of an axis on a bar chart, we can have the values at the end of the bars.

claims.rule: Reserve tooltips for specific, detailed information rather than displaying it on the main chart.
claims.quote: For more specific information that you want to include in the chart, leave them to tooltips.

claims.rule: Minimize background colors and shading to focus attention on the data itself.
claims.quote: Minimize the use of background colors and shading to focus attention on the data.

claims.rule: Avoid 3D effects in charts because they are difficult to understand and ineffective at conveying information.
claims.quote: Be cautious with 3D effects, as these can be quite difficult for the average viewer to understand and are often not the best at conveying information.

sources.title: Monitoring Dashboard Design: Creating Effective Visualizations for Operations Teams
sources.why: Design patterns for real-time operational dashboards: update frequency, latency, interaction design, and rendering optimization
sources.found_via: real-time monitoring dashboard design patterns update frequency

claims.rule: Prioritize primary metrics with most prominent visual treatment because they directly impact user experience or business outcomes.
claims.quote: Primary metrics get the most prominent visual treatment because they directly impact user experience or business outcomes. System availability, response times, and error rates typically deserve top-level placement because they indicate immediate problems.

claims.rule: Use color intentionally and consistently; red for problems, green for normal, yellow for warnings.
claims.quote: Color usage should be intentional and consistent throughout your dashboards. Red universally indicates problems, green suggests normal operation, and yellow warns of potential issues.

claims.rule: Avoid using color as the only way to convey information to prevent accessibility issues.
claims.quote: Avoid using color as the only way to convey information, as this creates accessibility issues.

claims.rule: Use line charts for trends over time, bar charts to compare quantities, and heat maps to show patterns across dimensions.
claims.quote: Chart type selection affects how quickly people can extract insights from data. Line charts work well for trends over time, bar charts compare quantities effectively, and heat maps show patterns across multiple dimensions.

claims.rule: Use white space and layout organization strategically to help viewers focus on important information.
claims.quote: White space and layout organization help viewers focus on important information. Cluttered dashboards overwhelm users and hide critical information in visual noise.

claims.rule: Provide baseline comparisons to help viewers understand whether current metric values are normal or problematic.
claims.quote: Baseline comparisons help viewers understand whether current values are normal or problematic. Showing current CPU usage as 85% is less helpful than showing it's 40% higher than typical for this time of day.

claims.rule: Use visual indicators or color changes to clearly mark when metrics enter warning or critical states.
claims.quote: Threshold indicators clearly mark when metrics enter warning or critical states. Visual indicators like color changes or icons should make it obvious when values cross important thresholds.

claims.rule: Provide drill-down capabilities to allow viewers to access detail without cluttering the main dashboard view.
claims.quote: Drill-down capabilities allow viewers to get more detail without cluttering the main view. Dashboard hierarchies let users start with high-level overviews and dive deeper into specific areas that need attention.

claims.rule: Design executive dashboards to emphasize business metrics and trends rather than technical details.
claims.quote: Business metric emphasis shows how technical performance affects business outcomes. Revenue impact, customer satisfaction scores, and SLA compliance matter more to executives than server CPU usage.

claims.rule: Include performance correlation displays to help technical teams understand relationships between different metrics.
claims.quote: Performance correlation displays help technical teams understand relationships between different metrics. Memory usage correlated with response times or database performance linked to application errors help with root cause analysis.

claims.rule: Update critical metrics every 10-30 seconds to catch problems quickly without overwhelming viewers.
claims.quote: Critical metric streaming should update frequently enough to catch problems quickly but not so frequently that it overwhelms viewers. Error rates and availability metrics might update every 10-30 seconds, while CPU trends might update every minute.

claims.rule: Batch non-critical metrics to update less frequently and reduce system load and visual noise.
claims.quote: Non-critical metric batching reduces system load and visual noise. Historical trends, capacity metrics, and other non-urgent information can update less frequently without affecting operational effectiveness.

claims.rule: Implement automatic reconnection for WebSocket connections so users don't need to manually refresh dashboards.
claims.quote: Connection reliability mechanisms handle network interruptions and ensure dashboards reconnect automatically. Users shouldn't need to refresh dashboards manually when temporary connectivity issues occur.

claims.rule: Use color-blind friendly palettes so status indicators remain distinguishable for people with color blindness.
claims.quote: Color-blind friendly palettes use colors that remain distinguishable for people with different types of color blindness. Tools like ColorBrewer help choose accessible color schemes for data visualization.

claims.rule: Combine color with shapes, patterns, or text to convey status information accessibly.
claims.quote: Multiple visual indicators combine color with shapes, patterns, or text to convey status information. Icons, text labels, and visual patterns ensure information remains accessible regardless of color perception.

claims.rule: Ensure high contrast ratios between text and background colors for readability.
claims.quote: Contrast optimization ensures text remains readable against background colors. High contrast ratios help users with various visual impairments read dashboard information clearly.

claims.rule: Use semantic HTML and proper heading hierarchies so screen readers can navigate dashboards effectively.
claims.quote: Semantic HTML structure provides screen readers with the information they need to navigate dashboards effectively. Proper heading hierarchies, labels, and landmarks help assistive technologies understand dashboard organization.

claims.rule: Provide alt text descriptions for visualizations since screen readers cannot interpret graphs directly.
claims.quote: Alt text for visualizations describes chart content in text form. Screen readers can't interpret graphs directly, so alternative text descriptions provide equivalent information for users who can't see visual elements.

claims.rule: Support keyboard navigation with proper tab ordering so users who cannot use mice can interact with dashboards.
claims.quote: Keyboard navigation support ensures that users who can't use mice can still navigate and interact with dashboard elements. Proper tab ordering and keyboard shortcuts improve accessibility.

claims.rule: Adapt responsive layouts to remain usable on different screen sizes with appropriate information prioritization.
claims.quote: Responsive layout adaptation ensures dashboards remain usable on different screen sizes. Mobile-friendly designs prioritize the most important information and organize it appropriately for smaller screens.

claims.rule: Size and space touch-friendly interface elements appropriately for finger-based navigation.
claims.quote: Touch-friendly interface elements accommodate finger-based navigation rather than precise mouse cursors. Buttons and interactive elements need appropriate sizing and spacing for touch interaction.

sources.title: Dashboard Design Patterns
sources.why: Interactive website documenting 42 design patterns from systematic dashboard analysis, supporting dashboard design exploration and development

claims.rule: Curate and simplify large complex datasets to provide overview of most important information at a glance.
claims.quote: Dashboards offer a curated lens through which people view large and complex data sets at a glance. They combine visual representations and other graphical embellishments to provide layers of abstraction and simplification for numerous related data points, so that dashboard viewers get an overview of the most important or relevant information, in a time efficient way.

claims.rule: Ensure grouped sparklines have comparable start and end points and the same number of data points.

claims.rule: Keep titles and supporting text brief to provide context without overwhelming the visualization.
claims.quote: Good titles and supporting text can be invaluable for providing context, but keep them as brief as possible.

claims.rule: Include a data source citation to increase graphic credibility and allow deeper investigation.
claims.quote: Providing a data source makes your graphic more reputable. It also allows those who are interested to dig deeper.

claims.rule: Always enable row hover state to help users visually scan columns.
claims.quote: The data table's row hover state should always be enabled as it can help the user visually scan the columns of data in a row even if the row is not interactive.

claims.rule: Keep column titles to one or two words; wrap to two lines then truncate, showing full text in tooltip.
claims.quote: Column titles should stick to one or two words that describe the data in that column. In cases where a column title is too long, wrap the text to two lines and then truncate the rest of the text.

claims.rule: Match toolbar height to data table row height for visual alignment and consistency.
claims.quote: The toolbar height should always match the row height of the data table to maintain visual alignment and consistency.

claims.rule: Use skeleton states instead of spinners for tables with expected load time.
claims.quote: If extra load time is expected to display information, use skeleton states instead of spinners.

claims.rule: Use zebra stripe alternating row colors to aid horizontal scanning.

claims.rule: Persist overflow menu icons by default; only hide on hover if visual clutter is a priority.
claims.quote: By default, the overflow menu icons are persistent on each row. Having the overflow menus always visible signals to the user actions can be taken on the table rows.

claims.rule: Disable single action icons and overflow menus when batch mode is active.

claims.rule: Use medium (40px) row height as default; adjust for density or readability needs.
claims.quote: Use as the default and most commonly used size. Use when no specific density or spacing requirements exist.

claims.rule: Avoid exclamation points in welcome messages; keep tone calm and welcoming to reduce user anxiety.
claims.quote: Keep in mind that the user might be a bit nervous, so avoid exclamation points or other writing mechanics that make your tone sound excited.

claims.rule: Empower users by stating what they can do, not what the product enables them to do.

claims.rule: Use icons with semantic color: gray for neutral states, red for errors, green for success.

claims.rule: Use sentence case for capitalization; capitalize only the first letter and proper nouns.

claims.rule: Avoid using 'please' in empty states; it sounds overly formal and is unnecessary.

claims.rule: Keep filter dropdown open as user selects multiple checkbox values.

claims.rule: Pair key metrics with context charts showing current, recent, and historical data to help users interpret performance instantly.

claims.quote: The goal of a color key — also called a color legend — is to help your reader figure out as quickly as possible what the colored elements in your visualization mean.

claims.rule: Use direct labels instead of color keys when possible to reduce cognitive load.
claims.quote: Your readers won't know what a color indicates if you don't explain it to them. But that explanation doesn't need to happen in the form of a key. You might be able to use direct labels instead

claims.rule: Arrange color key items in a grid layout when the key has many items or long labels to improve scannability.
claims.quote: If your key has lots of items, or you need a lot of letters to describe them, it can become overwhelming. If this is the case, consider using a grid layout — it's easier to skim and looks tidier.

claims.rule: Show form (line thickness, dashes, patterns, strokes) alongside color in legends to help readers match visual elements.
claims.quote: If your colored elements have different forms (thick lines, thin lines, dashed lines, rectangles…), then showing these forms in the color key is an excellent way to help readers quickly find them in the chart.

sources.title: Colors for data visualization style guides – Datawrapper Blog
sources.why: Lisa Charlotte Muth: building organizational color palettes with principles for consistency and accessibility.

claims.rule: Create a fixed color palette for data visualizations to build brand trust and consistency.
claims.quote: Consistent colors will help to build a brand and hence more trust. Readers will know they can trust a chart — no matter where it appears — when it looks like it comes from you.

claims.rule: Start with 3-10 colors for a basic data visualization palette using brand or website colors.
claims.quote: Choose 3-10 different colors. These can be your logo color(s), or colors from your website

claims.rule: Organize color palette order and primary colors to reduce designer decisions and speed up chart creation.
claims.quote: Keeping the order of colours in the palette consistent helps non-designers create basic charts in a fast-paced environment without having to spend time on yet another design decision

claims.rule: Define primary colors explicitly; most organizations complete 90% of simple charts with only a few core hues.
claims.quote: We find we can get 90% of our simple charts done with this simple palette.

claims.rule: Use few hues with multiple shades for brand recognition; designers recognize this style instantly after one exposure.
claims.quote: Brand recognition through these colors is crazy high. It's basically through the roof. You can't do better.

sources.title: How to find & create good color palettes – Datawrapper Blog
sources.why: Lisa Charlotte Muth: tools, approaches, and principles for finding and extending color palettes.

claims.rule: Avoid color meanings that conflict with topic; use mixed or desaturated colors when unsure of cultural associations.
claims.quote: Be appropriate for the topic and evoke the right associations — or none at all. You might want to avoid intense reds ('Danger!'), grass green ('Good')

sources.title: What questions should you ask when creating charts? – Datawrapper Blog
sources.why: Lisa Charlotte Muth: framework for designing charts with intention and clarity.

sources.title: In defense of simple charts – Datawrapper Blog
sources.why: Lisa Charlotte Muth: arguing for simplicity and clarity over complexity in visualization design.

claims.rule: Vary chart types within a story to maintain reader attention and show data more accurately than repeating one type.
claims.quote: Repetitive chart types, even when they're nicely designed, don't attract readers' attention

claims.rule: Prioritize chart content relevance over novelty; interesting data in simple formats outperforms complex visualizations with dull data.
claims.quote: Simple charts are not boring when they show interesting data

sources.why: Stephen Few: 13-page foundational guide on color theory applied to data displays. Relative perception, contrast, and effective color use.

sources.title: Color and Visualization Perception Research – Danielle Albers Szafir
sources.why: Szafir's empirical studies on color perception in visualization design: mark types, sizes, and color difference perception.

sources.why: Comprehensive scientific foundation: color, organization, space, motion, texture. 160+ design guidelines based on vision science.

sources.why: Foundational mathematical theory of graphics: variables, algebra, geometry, aesthetics, statistics, scales, coordinates.

sources.why: Constraint-based visualization design knowledge formalization: learned weights from experiments, Answer Set Programming implementation.

sources.why: Emil Kowalski's comprehensive motion vocabulary: 43 rules across 7 categories for UI animation design and developer communication.

sources.why: Foundational cognitive theory: verbal and nonverbal processing channels. Picture superiority effect. Implications for visualization effectiveness.

sources.title: Visual Encoding and Graphical Perception – Healey & Enns
sources.why: Lecture on visual perception: encoding effectiveness, attention, visual memory, perception accuracy in graphs.

sources.title: Gestalt Principles in Data Visualization
sources.why: Application of Gestalt psychology (proximity, similarity, continuity, closure, connectedness) to data visualization design.

claims.rule: Place titles near their related charts; position legends close to charts they serve; position filters adjacent to charts they influence.
claims.quote: Titles should be placed near the charts they are related to. Color keys (legends) need to be located close to the charts they are used in. Filters/parameters (and other settings) should be positioned closer to the charts they influence.

claims.rule: Use color to group similar elements and direct attention, not as decoration without semantic meaning.
claims.quote: Use color efficiently to enhance navigation and perception of your visualizations. If the chart is merely colored without carrying any semantic meaning, it may be harder to interpret than if left without color altogether.

claims.rule: Sort and order chart elements for continuity: bars largest to smallest, time series past to future.
claims.quote: Bar charts are more comprehensible when arranged from larger to smaller, time charts from past to future, and so forth. This organization allows us to perceive them as one continuous whole.

sources.title: Gestalt Principles for Visual UI Design – Jakob Nielsen PhD
sources.why: Practical application of Gestalt principles to visual interface design: proximity, similarity, continuity for UI organization.

claims.rule: Users parse layouts in a fraction of a second before reading labels; ensure proximity, borders, alignment, color, and motion match content grouping.
claims.quote: Users parse a layout before they read its labels. Whitespace, borders, alignment, color, and motion determine what belongs together. When these cues fight the content, users attach the label, price, warning, status, or action to the wrong object.

claims.rule: Perceptual objects must match interaction objects: if a card looks selectable as one unit, all its contents should respond together.
claims.quote: Perceptual objects should match interaction objects. If a card looks like one selectable unit but only its title is clickable, the interface contradicts itself.

claims.rule: Reserve whitespace to separate visual chunks; dense layouts trigger grouping collapse where all elements cluster together.
claims.quote: Proximity also explains why cramming a dense form into a tight space backfires. Squeeze everything together and you trigger a grouping collapse: every element clusters with every other element, which is the same as no grouping at all. Whitespace isn't wasted space. It's the mortar that holds your visual chunks apart.

claims.rule: Use color similarity for buttons and interactive elements so users learn to treat matching visuals as interactive.
claims.quote: In a well-built interface, clickable buttons share the same color and shape. Users quickly learn to treat anything that looks that way as interactive.

claims.rule: Space form fields closer to their labels than to adjacent fields; equidistant gaps cause roughly 50% of users to pair them incorrectly.
claims.quote: when labels sit equidistant between two fields, they land in label limbo: users guess, and roughly half of them guess wrong

claims.rule: Test visual grouping at narrow breakpoints, maximum text sizes, longest content, and all error or loading states; ideal screenshots alone do not confirm correct grouping.
claims.quote: A layout that groups correctly only in the ideal screenshot is not correctly grouped

sources.title: Animation Performance 101: Browser Under the Hood – Viget
sources.why: Web animation performance: 60fps target, browser rendering pipeline, avoiding expensive CSS properties (layout/paint).

claims.rule: Aim for 60 frames per second to match device refresh rates; animations below this appear stuttered and erratic.
claims.quote: Good performance means hitting the ultimate goal of 60 frames per second (FPS). That's because most devices these days refresh their screen at a rate of 60 times a second. The browser needs to match this rate and paint a new frame on each refresh.

claims.rule: Animate only transform and opacity properties to avoid triggering layout or paint; all other property animations force expensive rendering work.
claims.quote: the most performant way to animate is with CSS keyframe animations or transitions on transform and opacity only

claims.rule: Apply will-change sparingly only to elements that animate often; overuse creates memory overhead that negates GPU benefits.
claims.quote: will-change is a powerful tool that should only be used sparingly. It is absolutely not recommended to put every element onto its own layer

sources.title: A Guide to Animation Performance on the Web – TutsPlus
sources.why: Web animation optimization: requestAnimationFrame, transform and opacity vs layout-triggering properties.

sources.title: CSS Easing with Cubic-Bezier – Flavio Copes
sources.why: Cubic-bezier easing curves: ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out definitions and use cases for entrance/exit animations.

claims.rule: Use ease-out for elements entering the screen; they arrive fast and settle gently, feeling responsive.
claims.quote: My advice: use ease-out for elements entering the screen. They arrive fast and settle gently, which feels responsive.

claims.rule: Use ease-in for elements leaving the screen and ease-in-out for elements moving between locations.
claims.quote: Use ease-in for elements leaving, and ease-in-out for elements that move from one place to another.

claims.rule: Reserve linear easing for genuinely mechanical elements: loading spinners, marquees, progress bars.
claims.quote: Reserve linear for things that genuinely are mechanical: loading spinners, marquees, progress bars.

sources.title: Automatic Colorblind Check – Datawrapper Academy
sources.why: Tool and guidance for testing visualizations against color vision deficiencies: protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia.

sources.title: Color Vision Deficiency Simulator – ArcGIS Pro
sources.why: Tool for simulating color blindness in visualizations: protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia, monochromacy.

claims.rule: Test interfaces in color vision deficiency modes to ensure distinguishability of red, green, and yellow hues.
claims.quote: In this mode, it is difficult to distinguish hues of green, red, and yellow from one another.

sources.title: Improve Your Designs With The Principles Of Similarity And Proximity – Smashing Magazine
sources.why: Gestalt principles applied to web/UI design: similarity and proximity for visual organization and hierarchy.

sources.why: Annual review of chart types: visualization examples and usage trends from Datawrapper Weekly Charts.

sources.why: Milestone article reflecting on 300 weekly visualization examples and trends in data visualization.

sources.why: Robert Kosara's blog on visualization, perception, cognition, and visual storytelling. Regular articles on visualization effectiveness.

sources.title: Optimize SVG Animations for Page Speed – SVGator
sources.why: SVG animation optimization: file size reduction, rendering performance, CSS vs JavaScript animation trade-offs.

claims.rule: Lazy load SVG animations to reduce First Contentful Paint and improve perceived page responsiveness.
claims.quote: Multiple SVG animations on a page can slow down First Contentful Paint (FCP) because the browser needs to evaluate all JavaScript before rendering.

claims.rule: Use CSS animations for simple hover or load effects because CSS rendering uses GPU and is faster than JavaScript animations.
claims.quote: CSS animations use the GPU for rendering, which makes them faster and more efficient.

claims.rule: Extract JavaScript from SVG files and load it only after page render completes to improve First Contentful Paint.
claims.quote: You can optimize this by not loading the JavaScript from SVGs until the page is fully loaded. To do this, extract the script tags from inside the SVG, place the JavaScript in an external file, and set it to load when a specific event triggers.

claims.rule: Load the SVG animation player from a CDN and cache it globally; reuse one cached player across multiple animations.
claims.quote: When multiple SVGs use the external player, it is downloaded only once and used by all animations. This is much faster than embedding the player in every SVG file.

claims.rule: Defer JavaScript execution from SVGs until after page render completes to improve First Contentful Paint.
claims.quote: extract the script tags from inside the SVG, place the JavaScript in an external file, and set it to load when a specific event triggers

claims.rule: Reduce SVG file size by 30% using SVGO optimization before animating to lower bandwidth and load time.
claims.quote: We've managed to reduce SVG file size by about 30% with this tool, though results vary depending on how well-formed the SVG already is.

claims.rule: Reserve space for lazy-loaded SVGs by setting width and height on the container to prevent layout shift.
claims.quote: Make sure to set the width and height of the object element to match the SVG dimensions. This way, the browser reserves the correct space for the SVG and prevents content from shifting when it renders.

sources.title: Modern SVG Animation Techniques – OpenReplay
sources.why: SVG animation approaches: CSS animations, SMIL, JavaScript libraries (GSAP, Anime.js) for interactive graphics.

claims.rule: Use CSS animations for simple, declarative effects requiring browser optimization and hardware acceleration.
claims.quote: CSS animations excel for simple, declarative animations that leverage browser optimization. They're ideal for hover effects, loading spinners, and basic state transitions.

claims.rule: Choose JavaScript libraries like GSAP for complex animations requiring timeline control, dynamic values, or physics-based effects.
claims.quote: Choose JavaScript libraries when CSS limitations become apparent—typically for timeline control, dynamic values, or physics-based animations.

claims.rule: Respect prefers-reduced-motion to ensure animations are accessible to users sensitive to motion.
claims.quote: Always check for reduced motion preferences: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)

claims.rule: Use SVG filters judiciously; they impact performance more than transforms or opacity changes.
claims.quote: Use filters judiciously—they impact performance more than transforms or opacity changes.

claims.rule: Respect prefers-reduced-motion media queries to disable animations for users sensitive to motion.
claims.quote: Always check for reduced motion preferences

sources.title: SVG Animations: Crisp, Scalable, High-Performance Web Animations – DEV Community
sources.why: SVG animation techniques: scaling, performance, responsive animation, comparison with raster graphics.

claims.rule: Use subtle animation that supports content rather than competing with it for a more professional experience.
claims.quote: Animation should support content—not compete with it. Subtle movement often creates a more professional experience than constant motion.

claims.rule: Respect the prefers-reduced-motion media feature to support users who prefer reduced motion in animations.
claims.quote: Support users who prefer reduced motion by respecting the prefers-reduced-motion media feature.

sources.title: Weekly Chart: Dot Pyramid – Datawrapper Blog
sources.why: Weekly chart showcase: dot pyramid visualization example and design principles.

claims.rule: Guide readers through non-standard chart types with annotations and clear axis labels explaining how to interact.
claims.quote: As these improvised scatter-type charts are a little different, we try to make sure we guide the reader through it as best we can: offering instruction to hover or select in the standfirst, where appropriate, and using annotations to explain how the axes work.
