sources.title: 2x Grid – IBM Carbon Design System
sources.why: Geometric foundation for typography, layouts, icons, and illustrations.

claims.rule: Divide space by two to create fluid grids; multiply fixed units by two to create fixed grids.
claims.quote: The core concept of the 2x Grid is to divide or multiply by two, forming a visual rhythm.

claims.rule: Always align type to the edge of box padding, never place type on the padding itself.
claims.quote: Always align type to the edge of box padding. Note, some design tools add padding to text boxes by default; check text box padding and remove it if necessary. Always place type against the padding. Never place type on the padding.

claims.rule: Use padding of 16 pixels at all standard breakpoints; margins at the outer edge are fixed per breakpoint.
claims.quote: Padding is always a fixed multiple of mini units: 16 pixels at all standard breakpoints.

claims.rule: Test designs and code at each standard breakpoint: 320px, 672px, 1056px, 1312px, and 1584px.
claims.quote: For best results, test designs and code at each of these standard breakpoints.

claims.rule: Scale column count by tiling fixed boxes if users want to see more items; scale box size with fixed column counts if users want to see more content per item.
claims.quote: If a user's goal is to see more items, scale column count by tiling fixed boxes. If a user wants to see more content within each item, scale boxes and use fixed column counts.

claims.rule: Test designs and code at five standard breakpoints: 320px, 672px, 1056px, 1312px, and 1584px to maintain layout integrity.
claims.quote: Use this set of standard breakpoints to maintain layout integrity across screen sizes. For best results, test designs and code at each of these standard breakpoints.

sources.title: Accessibility – IBM Carbon Design System
sources.why: Accessibility standards and WCAG compliance for Carbon components.

claims.rule: Translate visual information into text for screen reader users; test designs through a screen reader when possible.
claims.quote: Is visual information translated effectively into text? Can the image be understood through its metadata alone? When possible, test all designs through a screen reader.

claims.rule: Maximize readability and visual clarity for low-vision users; consider how proximity changes when magnified and follow keyboard guidelines.
claims.quote: Maximize the readability and visual clarity of content. Consider how the relative proximity of information changes when a page is magnified.

claims.rule: Avoid complex language, autoplaying animations, and flashing animations to reduce cognitive load for users with cognitive disabilities.
claims.quote: Designers should avoid complex language, autoplaying animations and videos, and flashing animations.

claims.rule: Transcribe and caption all videos and animations with meaningful audio; provide closed captioning for deaf and hard-of-hearing users.
claims.quote: Transcribe and caption all videos and animations that have meaningful audio.

sources.title: Color – IBM Carbon Design System
sources.why: Color palette, semantics, and accessible color contrast ratios.

claims.rule: Use token-based color names—not hex codes—so themes can scale and change without rewriting values.
claims.quote: Unlike hex codes, tokens apply universally across themes. For example, $layer , $border-subtle , $support-error .

claims.rule: In light themes, alternate layers between White and Gray 10; in dark themes, step lighter with each layer.
claims.quote: In the light themes, layers alternate between White and Gray 10 with each added layer. In the dark themes, layers become one step lighter with each added layer.

claims.rule: Do not apply components darker than the background unless using high-contrast mode.
claims.quote: Do not apply components that are darker than the background unless using high-contrast mode.

claims.rule: Avoid use of midtones in light themes to maintain clear layering and hierarchy.
claims.quote: Avoid use of midtones.

claims.rule: Use role-based color tokens in place of hex codes to enable themes and dark-mode support without code changes.
claims.quote: Tokens are a method of applying color in a consistent, reusable, and scalable way. They help us abstract how we use color from the values themselves.

claims.rule: Achieve 4.5:1 contrast for small text and 3:1 for large text (24px+) by stepping through color grades; consult the contrast table for minimum steps required.
claims.quote: small text is any size below 24px and requires a 4.5:1 contrast ratio. Large text is anything above 24px and requires a 3:1 contrast ratio.

sources.title: Icons – IBM Carbon Design System
sources.why: Icon system design, grid, and usage guidelines.

sources.title: Motion – IBM Carbon Design System
sources.why: Motion principles and animation guidelines for smooth user interactions.

claims.rule: Use productive motion for task-focused moments like button states and data rendering; reserve expressive motion for significant moments like opening a new page.
claims.quote: Productive motion is appropriate for moments when the user needs to focus on completing tasks. Microinteractions in Carbon such as button states, dropdowns, revealing additional information, or rendering data tables and visualizations were all designed with productive motion.

claims.rule: Speed up quickly and slow down smoothly using easing curves; avoid unnatural, distracting, or purely decorative easing.
claims.quote: Avoid easing curves that are unnatural, distracting, or purely decorative. IBM motion is essential and efficient, guiding users to value as quickly as possible.

claims.rule: Make motion duration dynamic based on distance or scale traveled; larger changes should take longer than micro-interactions.
claims.quote: Motion's duration should be dynamic based on the size of the animation; the larger the change in distance (traveled) or size (scaling) of the element, the longer the animation takes.

claims.rule: Use productive motion (fast, subtle) for task-focused microinteractions; reserve expressive motion (vibrant, slower) for significant moments like page opens or primary actions.
claims.quote: Reserve expressive motion for occasional, important moments, to better capture the user's attention and offer a rhythmic break to the productive experience.

claims.rule: Provide reduced-motion alternatives and simplified designs for mobile; ensure motion works across all screen sizes and accessibility settings.
claims.quote: Always provide alternatives for interface state transitions. Consider simplified or reduced motion designs for mobile and tablet. Make sure there is always a way to communicate similar messages statically.

sources.title: Spacing – IBM Carbon Design System
sources.why: Spacing scale for consistent visual rhythm and hierarchy.

claims.rule: Use the spacing scale with multiples of two, four, and eight; apply spacing tokens to margin and padding properties.
claims.quote: The Carbon spacing scale complements the 2x Grid and typography scale by using multiples of two, four, and eight.

claims.rule: Elements positioned near each other are perceived as related; increase space between elements to weaken their perceived relationship.
claims.quote: Elements in a design that are near each other are seen as being meaningfully related. As more space is added between elements, their perceived relationship weakens.

claims.rule: Give high-importance elements extra surrounding space to attract focus and prevent them from being overlooked.
claims.quote: Elements that have more spacing around them tend to be perceived as higher in importance than elements that have less space around them.

claims.rule: Use white space to break up sections and prevent cognitive overload; allow users' eyes to rest and process information.
claims.quote: White space helps with information processing; too much dense information can be disorienting or overwhelming for a user.

sources.title: Themes – IBM Carbon Design System
sources.why: Theming system and token customization for light and dark modes.

claims.rule: Use tokens to change styling system-wide by modifying one place instead of individual components.
claims.quote: With tokens, the code only needs to be changed in one place to see the effect system-wide.

claims.rule: Keep token roles constant across themes; only values change between themes.
claims.quote: Tokens are universal and never change across themes

sources.title: Typography – IBM Carbon Design System
sources.why: Type scale, font families, and typographic hierarchy.

claims.rule: Use productive type set for product spaces to maintain focus; use expressive set for editorial content.
claims.quote: The productive type set is primarily used within product spaces, where users benefit from a more condensed treatment of content to maintain focus on tasks.

claims.rule: Balance font weight and size carefully; larger lighter weight can rank higher than smaller bold weight.
claims.quote: A lighter weight font can rank hierarchically higher than a bold font if the lighter weight type size is significantly larger than the bold one.

claims.rule: Use semibold sparingly; reserve it for section headers, not long-form text.
claims.quote: The semibold weight is ideal for section headers, but should not be used for long text.

claims.rule: Keep body text color neutral; use primary blue only for actions and links.
claims.quote: Keep type color neutral in running text. Use primary blue for primary actions.

sources.title: Design Tokens – Microsoft Fluent 2
sources.why: Two-layer token system (global and alias) for semantic design values.

claims.rule: Use alias tokens to add semantic meaning and make function immediately recognizable without worrying about exact values.
claims.quote: Alias tokens are Fluent's second token layer and add semantic meaning to the stored values.

claims.rule: Name alias tokens so their function is immediately recognizable at a glance.
claims.quote: We name alias tokens so that their function is immediately recognizable. At a glance, you'll get an idea of where and how to apply consistent styles without worrying about the exact values.

sources.title: Typography – Adobe Spectrum
sources.why: Type scale using major second ratio (1.125) with Adobe typefaces.

sources.title: Foundations – Atlassian Design System
sources.why: Visual elements needed for engaging end-to-end user experiences.

sources.title: Typography – Atlassian Design System
sources.why: Applying typography at scale with contrast and token guidance.

claims.rule: Use responsive text with relative values (rem) for font size across different browser defaults.
claims.quote: Use responsive text, typography tokens, use relative values (rem) to determine font size on different browser default sizes.

claims.rule: Use correct heading levels and establish 2-4 size difference between heading levels for clear hierarchy.
claims.quote: Use between 2-4 heading size difference between levels.

claims.rule: Use minimum 16px font size for long-form text; avoid using 12px except for fine print.
claims.quote: The general guidance for comfortable reading is to use a minimum font size of 16px for long-form text such as blogs.

claims.rule: Apply body text in components with heavier font weight instead of heading text for greater contrast.
claims.quote: Don't use heading text in components, instead use body text with a heavier font weight to create greater contrast.

claims.rule: Limit line length to 60–80 characters per line for comfortable reading of body text.
claims.quote: For the English language, optimal line length is between 60 and 80 characters per line including spacing, or approximately 10-12 words.

claims.rule: Never truncate text; if truncation is unavoidable, provide a way for users to expand and read the full content.
claims.quote: Never truncate text. If you do use truncated text, for example if you are displaying user generated content of an unknown length, make sure that there's another option for people to expand and read the text.

claims.rule: Use metric style to emphasize short numbers and units in single-value tiles and chart visualizations.
claims.quote: Use metric style when you want to emphasize certain numbers. Numbers you can apply this style to include: metrics and standalone numbers (for example, 45%, 100)

sources.title: Color – Atlassian Design System
sources.why: Color system using design tokens with semantic meaning and accessibility compliance.

claims.rule: Apply color roles to convey semantic meaning: use brand for primary actions, warning for caution, danger for errors, success for favorable outcomes.
claims.quote: Color roles describe the intention behind the color. For example, color roles are applied to buttons to differentiate between primary, secondary, warning, or dangerous actions.

claims.rule: Use inverse tokens on bold backgrounds to maintain contrast and readability.
claims.quote: Inverse tokens are designed to show on bold backgrounds. There are inverse tokens for text, borders, and icons on bold backgrounds.

claims.rule: Pair selected colors with a visual cue like checkmark, underline, or border to avoid relying on color alone.
claims.quote: Pair selected colors with another visual cue, such as a checkmark, underline, border, or change in shape. This helps people identify selection without relying on color alone.

claims.rule: Layer hovered and pressed states onto the current state while keeping selected items recognizable during interaction.
claims.quote: Hovered and pressed states are temporary. Use the matching hovered or pressed token for the element's current state, and keep a selected item recognizable during interaction.

sources.title: Design Tokens – Atlassian Design System
sources.why: Name and value pairings representing design decisions (color, fonts, spacing, motion).

sources.why: W3C standards and industry best practices for accessible components.

claims.rule: Never use color as the sole means to provide information or request an action.
claims.quote: We never use color as the only means of providing information or requesting an action.

claims.rule: Maintain text-to-background color contrast of at least 4.5:1 for standard text and 3:1 for large text.
claims.quote: The combinations of text and their background colors do not fall below the WCAG recommended threshold ratio of 4.5:1 for standard or small text and 3:1 for larger text.

claims.rule: Use semantically correct markup and appropriate ARIA roles so assistive technologies identify components correctly.
claims.quote: The Design System enables accessible development by providing a set of semantically correct components, each with appropriate ARIA markup so they can be identified correctly to users of assistive technologies.

claims.rule: Provide text-based alternatives for all images, icons, and SVGs.
claims.quote: We provide a means of offering text-based alternatives for all images, icons and SVGs.

claims.rule: Mark all AI-generated content with a visible AI label to establish transparency.
claims.quote: Use the AI label and styling to mark any instances of AI usage

claims.rule: Display AI presence at every level where it occurs, from single words to entire pages.
claims.quote: Whether AI exists within a single word or across the entire page, users should clearly understand how pervasive an AI is implemented.

claims.rule: Use AI label styling only to identify AI instances, never as decoration.
claims.quote: Don't use the Carbon for AI styling as decoration

claims.rule: Use light-inspired effects (brightness, glow, gradients) to visually distinguish AI-generated content.
claims.quote: Carbon for AI uses light-inspired effects like brightness, glow, and gradients to emphasize AI instances across the experience.

claims.rule: Allow users to manually override AI-suggested content and revert to AI-generated content when needed.
claims.quote: These components can toggle between the AI variant and the default variant depending on the user's interaction. If the user manually overrides the AI-suggested content then the component will change from the AI variant to the default variant. Once edited, the user should still be able to switch back to the initially AI-generated content via a revert to AI button.

claims.rule: Use rem units for typography to support accessible browser zoom experiences.
claims.quote: Typography design tokens use rem units for a more accessible browser zoom experience.

claims.rule: Avoid using color as the primary method of emphasis in text hierarchy.

claims.rule: Left-align text with ragged right edges rather than justifying, centering, or right-aligning.

sources.title: Layout – GitHub Primer
sources.why: Standards for consistent, accessible, responsive experiences.

claims.rule: Organize layouts linearly to minimize friction, as humans parse shapes sequentially not in parallel.
claims.quote: Layouts are composed of shapes, and therefore parsed linearly. As a consequence, a layout should be organized aiming to create the least amount of friction for users.

claims.rule: Design layouts that leverage natural reading order and existing mental models from prior interactions.
claims.quote: People rely on their natural reading order (top-to-bottom, left-to-right in Latin script), and their acquired mental models from previous interactions to discover what they are looking for.

claims.rule: Never fix app header to viewport; let it scroll with page content.
claims.quote: App header is never fixed to the top of the viewport. It scrolls with the rest of the page.

claims.rule: Show only top-level context in context region; avoid full page paths.
claims.quote: Context region is not a full-path breadcrumb. Instead, it works alongside elements such as Local navigation and other in-page navigation components to give the user a full mental model of where they are located.

claims.rule: Limit page max-width to xlarge (1280px) to prevent paragraphs with excessive words per line.
claims.quote: Page layouts generally limit their maximum width to xlarge (1280px) so the content region doesn't render paragraphs with too many words per line.

claims.rule: Use three viewport ranges: narrow (<768px, 1 column), regular (≥768px, 2 columns), wide (≥1400px, 3 columns).
claims.quote: Viewport ranges target common scenarios when designing responsive layouts. They are based on the viewport width, and are opinionated about the number of layout columns that can fit in a given range.

claims.rule: Adjust content padding by breakpoint: 16px for xsmall–large, 24px for xlarge–xxlarge.
claims.quote: To provide more space for content on smaller screens, the padding should be adjusted according to the different breakpoints.

claims.rule: Never use right-aligned flushed panes; left-aligned panes prevent scrollbar conflicts.
claims.quote: The pane region of a split page layout is always flushed to the left. Don't use right-aligned flushed panes as their scrollbar may conflict with the page scrollbar.

sources.title: Responsive – GitHub Primer
sources.why: Responsive design patterns for all devices and preferences.

claims.rule: Support minimum viewport width of 320px and height of 256px for maximum device compatibility.
claims.quote: To guarantee maximum compatibility, pages should adapt to the browser's viewport size , without loss of information or functionality, starting at the following dimensions: Minimum viewport width : 320px Minimum viewport height : 256px

claims.rule: Ensure touch targets are at least 24px for AA accessibility, preferably 44px for AAA.
claims.quote: The AA accessibility standard GitHub strives for requires a minimum target size of 24px . However, it is recommended to aim for the AAA standard when possible.

claims.rule: Avoid pointing device media queries; design for multiple input types simultaneously.
claims.quote: Because of this, pointing device media queries such as coarse or fine are unreliable. Avoid relying on this type of query to conditionally modify parts of an interface.

claims.rule: Provide alternative access to hover-dependent features like tooltips for non-hovering devices.
claims.quote: Features that rely on hover such as tooltips or hovercards may not be available on these devices. Make sure the information presented is still accessible through other means, such as a direct link to a page with the information.

claims.rule: Respect user system preferences for color scheme, contrast, motion, and font size.
claims.quote: By default, GitHub must respect these preferences.

claims.rule: Use rem design tokens to respect browser default font size for low-vision accessibility.
claims.quote: Primer design tokens are designed to support rem units, which are relative to the browser's default font size. Use Primer-provided design tokens to ensure consistency across the system.

sources.title: Spacing – Atlassian Design System
sources.why: 8px base spacing system for consistent layout and hierarchy.

claims.rule: Build spacing systems on an 8-pixel base unit for visual consistency and responsive design.
claims.quote: Our spacing system is built around a base unit of 8 pixels. This base unit determines the spacing scale and ensures visual consistency across apps.

claims.rule: Use 0–8px spacing for small UI pieces like icon-text gaps and component padding.
claims.quote: Use the tokens from space.0 to space.100 (0px to 8px) for small and compact pieces of UI.

claims.rule: Group similar elements with consistent spacing to signal semantic relationships.
claims.quote: Using consistent spacing around elements lends them a visual similarity that helps the user understand their semantic relationship.

claims.rule: Place related elements closer together and unrelated elements farther apart to create meaning.
claims.quote: The distance between elements creates semantic meaning, elements that are placed close to one another are assumed to be related.

claims.rule: Use size and whitespace to establish visual hierarchy and rank elements by importance.
claims.quote: Varying the amount of whitespace around an element can be used to group elements together or separate them to impart greater importance.

claims.rule: Place related objects closer together and unrelated objects farther apart to signal semantic meaning.
claims.quote: The distance between elements creates semantic meaning, elements that are placed close to one another are assumed to be related. Use this principle to create meaning by placing more related objects closer together, and less related objects further apart.

claims.rule: Use spacing patterns to create visual rhythm; consistent spacing reinforces element similarity and importance.
claims.quote: Using a pattern of similar spacing between elements (such as in a table or list) creates a predictable rhythm for the user to follow. This consistent rhythm reinforces the similarity in importance of each of these elements.

sources.title: Iconography – Atlassian Design System
sources.why: Rounded icon system harmonious with typography and UI elements.

claims.rule: Use widely recognized symbols and established visual metaphors to ensure universal icon understanding.
claims.quote: Design icons that use widely recognized symbols and established visual metaphors. Ensure icons are easily understood by a diverse audience by avoiding specific cultural or language aspects.

claims.rule: Always pair icons with text labels to aid comprehension and avoid unnecessary icon clutter.
claims.quote: Use text labels to support icons wherever possible, and avoid using icons where they aren't necessary.

claims.rule: Design icons with simple shapes and minimum detail for quick recognition at small sizes.
claims.quote: Craft icons that are simple enough for quick recognition, yet detailed enough to convey meaning effectively, even at small sizes.

claims.rule: Use straight-on perspectives; avoid diagonal 3D shapes that confuse users at small icon sizes.
claims.quote: Shapes should appear straight on or from a full 90 degree profile. Don't use diagonal perspectives to create 3D shapes because these can be hard to discern at a glance, especially for people with some cognitive disabilities.

claims.rule: Use 16×16px medium icons as default; reserve 12px icons for chevrons and dense compact elements.
claims.quote: System icons are drawn within a 16 × 16px bounding box and are available in two sizes: Medium (16px) — use in most cases

claims.rule: Always pair icons with text labels to aid comprehension and avoid visual clutter.
claims.quote: Icons are powerful signifiers that can aid comprehension and help with navigation. They can also add clutter or confuse people when used poorly. Use text labels to support icons wherever possible, and avoid using icons where they aren't necessary.

sources.title: Button – IBM Carbon
sources.why: Button component usage and variants.

claims.rule: Use primary buttons only for the principal call to action; do not repeat on the same screen.
claims.quote: Primary buttons should only appear once per screen (not including the application header, modal dialog, or side panel).

claims.rule: Use danger buttons for destructive actions that could harm user data.
claims.quote: For actions that could have destructive effects on the user's data (for example, delete or remove).

claims.rule: Use links, not buttons, when the action navigates to a new page.
claims.quote: Do not use buttons as navigational elements. Instead, use links when the desired action is to take the user to a new page.

claims.rule: Do not mix different button sizes in button groups.
claims.quote: We do not recommend mixing different button sizes in button groups.

claims.rule: Do not use two high-emphasis buttons in a button group.
claims.quote: Do not use two high-emphasis buttons in a button group.

claims.rule: Make button labels wrap to a second line rather than truncate when space is insufficient.
claims.quote: When the button's label is too long to fit within the available space of the button, the label should overflow and wrap to the second line. We do not recommend truncating a button label.

claims.rule: Use the verb-plus-noun content formula for button labels except common actions like Done, Close, Cancel, Add, or Delete.
claims.quote: use the {verb} + {noun} content formula on buttons except in the case of common actions like "Done", "Close", "Cancel", "Add", or "Delete"

claims.rule: Left-align button labels, never center-align them even if the button is wide.
claims.quote: In a Carbon button, the label is always left-aligned, not center-aligned

claims.rule: Add a 1px border between all fluid buttons using the button-separator token for 3:1 distinction and accessibility.
claims.quote: There is a 1px border between all fluid buttons that use the $button-separator token for borders. This feature adds a 3:1 distinction between the two interactive UI elements. The border is a recommended feature to improve accessibility.

sources.title: Checkbox – IBM Carbon
sources.why: Checkbox component patterns.

claims.rule: Use radio buttons, not checkboxes, when only one option can be selected from a list.
claims.quote: If a user can select only one option from a list, radio buttons should be used instead of checkboxes.

claims.rule: Use the indeterminate state when a checkbox contains a sublist with some items selected and some unselected.
claims.quote: Use the indeterminate state when the checkbox contains a sublist of selections, some of which are selected, and some unselected.

claims.rule: Let wrapped text sit beneath the checkbox aligned at the top, never vertically centered with it.
claims.quote: Do let text wrap beneath the checkbox so the control and label are top aligned. Do not vertically center wrapped text with the checkbox.

claims.rule: Let wrapped checkbox label text sit beneath the control aligned at the top, never vertically center it.
claims.quote: Text should wrap beneath the checkbox so the control and label are top aligned

claims.rule: Keep checkbox labels to fewer than three words; reword or wrap rather than truncate.
claims.quote: We recommend checkbox labels being fewer than three words. If you are tight on space, consider rewording the label. Do not truncate checkbox label text with an ellipsis.

sources.title: Modal – IBM Carbon
sources.why: Modal dialog patterns and usage.

claims.rule: Never place labels or text in modal margins; only full-width components like tables may extend to edges.
claims.quote: Labels or text of any kind should never be in the modal margins.

claims.rule: Keep modal body text to 80% of modal width while allowing components to span 100%.
claims.quote: Ensure that the text is 80% of the modal's width. The components can span 100% of the width.

claims.rule: Set initial focus to the first input field in a form modal, or to the primary button if no form inputs exist.
claims.quote: set the initial focus to the first location that accepts user input. For example, if the modal contains a form then the focus should automatically be set to the first field when opened. If it is a transactional modal without form inputs in the body section then the first focus should be on the primary button.

claims.rule: Trap keyboard focus inside a modal until it is dismissed; Tab and Shift-Tab must not move focus outside.
claims.quote: Focus should then remain trapped in the dialog until it is closed. When navigating by keyboard, Tab and Shift-Tab do not move the focus outside of the modal.

sources.title: Dropdown – IBM Carbon
sources.why: Dropdown and select component patterns.

claims.rule: Do not use a dropdown when there are only two options; use radio buttons instead.
claims.quote: It is best practice not to use a dropdown if there are two options to choose from. In this case, use a radio button group instead.

claims.rule: Do not nest dropdowns or use them to display complex information; keep selections straightforward.
claims.quote: Do not nest dropdowns or use them to display overly complex information. Keep option selections as straight forward as possible.

claims.rule: Align default-style dropdown containers flush to grid columns so labels align with other page type.
claims.quote: Do align default style dropdown containers flush to the grid so the input label aligns with other type on the page.

claims.rule: Do not remove label text from dropdowns in favor of placeholder text; labels are always strongly encouraged.
claims.quote: Do not remove label text in favor of using placeholder text in the dropdown field. Labels are always strongly encouraged to be included when possible.

claims.rule: Open dropdown menus downward by default; open upward only if near screen edge to avoid cropping.
claims.quote: A dropdown can open up or down depending on its position on the screen. For example, if the dropdown appears at the bottom and close to the edge of the interface, the menu expands upward to avoid being cropped. By default, our dropdowns open downward.

claims.rule: Show 50% of the last option's height in menu overflow to signal more content; start scrolling at the sixth option.
claims.quote: we recommend showing 50% of the last option's container height to indicate there is more to see within the menu. We recommend starting a scroll at the sixth option in the menu list, but this may vary based on your specific use case.

claims.rule: Place vertical dividers only between two interactive elements in input fields; do not use between interactive and non-interactive elements.
claims.quote: Vertical dividers act as a visual separator between interactive elements in an input field. These vertical dividers are only present between two interactive elements, they should not be introduced between non-interactive elements like error states, other non-interactive icons, or buttons.

claims.rule: Present dropdown options in alphabetical order by default for easy scanning.
claims.quote: We recommend presenting the options in alphabetical order.

sources.title: Search – IBM Carbon
sources.why: Search input patterns and interactions.

claims.rule: Show a close icon after the user types to let them clear the search field.
claims.quote: Close icon: Appears after the user has actively typed into the search field. Acts as a function to clear the search field.

claims.rule: Use the magnifying glass icon to signify a search field universally.
claims.quote: Search icon: Signifies a search field. The magnifying glass icon is a universal way to indicate search.

claims.rule: Do not use search when data is small or information is easily found in one view.
claims.quote: Do not use when there is small or limited amounts of data. Do not use when the information is simple and can be found easily within one view.

claims.rule: Support both Enter key to submit and Escape key to clear in search fields.
claims.quote: Press Enter to submit text as a search term, or press Esc to clear the search field.

sources.title: Tabs – IBM Carbon
sources.why: Tabbed interface patterns.

claims.rule: Use tabs to group related content and reduce cognitive load by organizing into categories.
claims.quote: To help reduce cognitive load, use tabs to group related information into different categories.

claims.rule: Do not use tabs if users need to compare information across groups.
claims.quote: Tabs should not be used if the user needs to compare information in different groups, as this would result in the user having to click back and forth to complete a task.

claims.rule: Do not use tabs for filtering the same content; use a content switcher instead.
claims.quote: When toggling between different formats of the same content or filtering the same content, use content switcher instead.

claims.rule: Always select one tab by default in a tab group.
claims.quote: One tab is always selected by default.

claims.rule: Use auto-width alignment for line tabs; contained tabs may use grid-aware width.
claims.quote: Contained tabs can use either of these alignments, but line tabs must always use the auto-width alignment.

claims.rule: Use horizontal scrolling for tabs that exceed space; do not wrap tabs to multiple lines.
claims.quote: In responsive situations, horizontal tabs should not wrap to multiple lines or stack on top of each other; instead, they should scroll horizontally.

claims.rule: Keep tab labels to one or two words for quick scanning; stay concise to accommodate multiple languages.
claims.quote: Use short tab labels that are clear and specific. Labels should be one to two words, as these are easier to scan. Vertical tabs allow for more characters within a tab, but stay as concise as possible to avoid truncation and allow space for labels in various languages.

claims.rule: Set vertical tab height based on tab with most content to avoid excessive scrolling within tab panels.
claims.quote: The vertical tablist and panel height should be determined by the tab that has the most content. To avoid excessive scrolling within the tab panel, do not overload it with too much content.

claims.rule: Never apply skeleton states to toast notifications, overflow menus, dropdowns, modals, or loader components.
claims.quote: Never represent toast notifications, overflow menus, dropdown items, modals, and loaders with skeleton states.

claims.rule: Use full-screen loading indicators when the entire application is processing; use inline indicators for single-component processing.
claims.quote: Full-screen loading indicators tell a user the entire application is processing, while inline indicators show that a specific selection or action is processing.

claims.rule: Use progress indicators instead of loading indicators when a process will take more than a few seconds.
claims.quote: If a process will take more than a moment or two to complete, use a progress indicator instead.

claims.rule: Notify screen readers when an application is loading, busy, stuck, or fails.
claims.quote: A screen reader should notify a user if an application is loading, busy, gets stuck, or if a process fails.

claims.rule: Use proximity to signal which elements belong together and which are separate within a layout.

sources.title: Color – Adobe Spectrum
sources.why: Color palette and semantic color system.

claims.rule: Never use color alone to communicate meaning; always pair it with text labels or icons for clarity.
claims.quote: For every usage of color as a feedback method, there should be an accompanying label and/or icon to communicate meaning.

claims.rule: Use Spectrum's defined color palette exclusively to ensure consistency; never create custom colors.
claims.quote: Every part of the interface should use a color defined by Spectrum to ensure consistency across products.

claims.rule: Avoid placing colors with high hue contrast and near-equal saturation adjacent to prevent visual vibration and depth illusions.
claims.quote: Avoid placing colors directly on top of or adjacent to other colors that have a high degree of hue contrast with near-equal saturation or lightness.

sources.title: Color – Microsoft Fluent 2
sources.why: Fluent color system and theming.

claims.rule: Use lighter neutral colors on surfaces to highlight primary focus areas and establish visual hierarchy.
claims.quote: Use lighter neutrals on surfaces to highlight areas of primary focus and create a sense of hierarchy.

claims.rule: In dark mode, shift shared colors in saturation and brightness to reduce eye strain and accommodate visual accessibility.
claims.quote: In dark mode, the colors of the shared palette shift in saturation and brightness to reduce eye strain and accommodate visual accessibility needs.

claims.rule: Avoid overusing brand colors on large surfaces to preserve hierarchy and aid navigation clarity.
claims.quote: Avoid overusing brand colors or using them on large surfaces as they can dilute a hierarchy and make an experience difficult to navigate.

claims.rule: Use color tokens to guarantee consistent color usage across experiences and products without hunting hex codes.
claims.quote: The easiest way to guarantee uniform color usage is to use Fluent's design token system.

claims.rule: Use sentence case for all text; avoid all caps because it is difficult to read.
claims.quote: Use sentence case when writing, it fits most contexts. Don't use all caps to get a user's attention because it's difficult to read.

claims.rule: Use color on text to create emphasis or de-emphasis within visual hierarchy, not as sole indicator of importance.
claims.quote: Applying color can emphasize or de-emphasize text. Using a primary color on text will give it more visual prominence than the standard text color.

sources.title: Forms Pattern – IBM Carbon

claims.rule: Group related form tasks under section titles to help users scan and complete forms quickly.
claims.quote: Group related tasks under section titles to provide more context and make the interface easier to scan.

claims.rule: Arrange form fields in logical, predictable order such as first name before last name.
claims.quote: Follow a logical, predictable order—e.g first name first, last name second.

claims.rule: Keep users with a single interaction method throughout the form; minimize switching between keyboard and mouse.
claims.quote: Allow users to stay with a single interaction method for as long as possible (i.e. do not make users shift from keyboard to mouse numerous times in a single form).

claims.rule: Progressively disclose additional form inputs only when they become relevant to reduce cognitive load.
claims.quote: Progressively disclose additional inputs only as they become relevant

claims.rule: Use top-aligned labels for forms to enable quick completion and consistent left edge alignment.
claims.quote: Top-alignment enables quick completion. The label length has room to extend or vary, (e.g. other languages). When users are entering familiar content and are less likely to make data entry errors, top-alignment is ideal.

claims.rule: Keep form labels to one to three words only; labels are not helper text.
claims.quote: Labels are not helper text; be succinct. Use one to three words only.

claims.rule: Validate form fields on blur (when focus leaves) using client-side validation to catch errors immediately and show inline error messages.
claims.quote: real-time, inline validation (a.k.a. client-side validation) should happen as soon as the field loses focus

claims.rule: Do not disable primary action buttons in long forms because error messages and the submit button may not be visible simultaneously on screen.
claims.quote: For longer forms, do not disable primary action buttons because the error messages and the primary action button may not be visible on the screen simultaneously.

claims.rule: Ensure all visual information is also available as text for screen reader users.
claims.quote: Is visual information translated effectively into text? Can the image be understood through its metadata alone?

claims.rule: Design with high contrast to support low-vision users and those in poor lighting.
claims.quote: Vision worsens gradually starting around age 40, and good contrast helps this very large demographic use your interface.

claims.rule: Never convey information by color alone; use non-color indicators.

claims.rule: Provide captions and transcripts for all video and audio content.

claims.rule: Avoid flashing, autoplaying content, and complex language for cognitive accessibility.

claims.rule: Remember that 8% of men and 0.4% of women are color-blind; never use color alone to convey information.

sources.title: Accessibility – Microsoft Fluent 2
sources.why: Fluent accessibility standards and considerations.

claims.rule: Organize information in logical, predictable hierarchy to help users understand relationships.
claims.quote: Organize information in a logical and predictable way that helps people see relationships, make connections, and find their way around.

claims.rule: Create scannable section headings in large or bold text for efficient navigation.
claims.quote: Section headings with large or bold text can help visual users quickly scan and understand information for efficient navigation.

claims.rule: Manage focus visually and follow z-pattern (left to right, top to bottom) for keyboard users.
claims.quote: Focus should follow "z" pattern from left to right and top to bottom and not be "lost" after someone closes a temporary UI, like a dialog.

claims.rule: Maintain WCAG AA contrast: 4.5:1 for standard text, 3:1 for large text and interactive components.
claims.quote: Standard text must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 with the background. Large text (above 18.5 pixels Bold, or 24 pixels Regular) must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1.

claims.rule: Design layouts that reflow to 320px width and support 400% zoom without horizontal scrolling.
claims.quote: Design page layouts so that content reflows and can be presented without horizontal scrolling for zooms up to 400%. This means designing down to a 320 pixel breakpoint.

claims.rule: Provide descriptive alt text for images accessible to screen readers.
claims.quote: Provide descriptive alt text for visual media that is accessible to screen readers.

claims.rule: Use plain, concise, consistent language to support all readers and those learning English.
claims.quote: Steer clear of overly complicated or specific language. This makes skimming information easy and also helps people who may not have English as a first language.

sources.title: Motion Design Guide – IBM Carbon
sources.why: Motion principles and animation timings.

claims.rule: Use productive motion for task-focused moments; expressive motion for rare, significant moments.
claims.quote: Reserve expressive motion for occasional, important moments, to better capture the user's attention and offer a rhythmic break to the productive experience.

claims.rule: Speed up quickly and slow down smoothly with easing curves; avoid purely decorative motion.
claims.quote: Avoid easing curves that are unnatural, distracting, or purely decorative. IBM motion is essential and efficient, guiding users to value as quickly as possible.

claims.rule: Use exit easing when elements leave view; implies permanent departure or readiness to reappear.
claims.quote: Use exit-easing when removing elements from view, such as closing a modal or toaster. The element speeds up as it exits from view, implying that its departure from the screen is permanent.

claims.rule: Scale motion duration by the distance or size change; larger movements take longer.
claims.quote: Motion's duration should be dynamic based on the size of the animation; the larger the change in distance (traveled) or size (scaling) of the element, the longer the animation takes.

claims.rule: Use micro-interactions at 90–120 ms for immediate feedback on user input with ease-out easing.
claims.quote: Do micro-interactions use ease-out on user input? Do micro-interactions fall within a static duration ranging from 90–120 ms?

claims.rule: Provide static alternatives for motion; reduce or simplify motion on mobile and tablet screens.
claims.quote: Always provide alternatives for interface state transitions. Consider simplified or reduced motion designs for mobile and tablet.

sources.why: Apple motion and animation guidelines.

claims.quote: Use sentence-style capitalization for headings, titles, labels, banners, and similar elements, unless noted otherwise.

sources.title: Layout – Microsoft Fluent 2
sources.why: Fluent layout and spacing system.

claims.rule: Place closely-spaced elements to signal they belong together; increase space between groups to weaken perceived relationships.
claims.quote: Elements in a design that are in close proximity are seen as being meaningfully related. As more space is added between elements, their perceived relationship weakens.

claims.rule: Use spacing to create logical sections without lines or dividers; let white space help people process dense information.
claims.quote: Space is used to denote groups of associated information. Used correctly, spacing creates logical sections of content on a page without having to use lines or other graphical elements as a divider.

claims.rule: Give high-importance UI elements more surrounding space; elements close together may be overlooked individually.
claims.quote: UI elements that have more spacing around them draw more focus and tend to be perceived as higher in importance than elements that have less space around them. In fact, UI elements that are set close to each other might be overlooked.

claims.rule: Use a 4-pixel base unit spacing system consistently across all platforms for coherence and easy implementation.
claims.quote: The base unit is four pixels which allows a scale of supported sizes. A 4x system reduces confusion while being easy to implement.

claims.rule: Apply consistent spacing patterns to layouts, components, and patterns so people can navigate quickly and easily.
claims.quote: Consistent spacing in patterns is crucial to creating familiar visual rhythm and design cohesion across products so people can jump in quickly and easily.

claims.rule: Use a 12-column grid for layout flexibility and easy responsive adaptation across different screen sizes.
claims.quote: A 12 column framework is common for its flexibility and easy division. It's highly composite for layouts and can update responsively based on screen size.

claims.rule: Align baselines to a grid to establish vertical rhythm, making content easier for people to scan.
claims.quote: Aligning baselines to a specific absolute grid establishes a vertical rhythm — a pattern that's easier for the human brain to scan.

sources.title: Text Input – IBM Carbon
sources.why: Text input component patterns.

claims.rule: Use consistent field heights when pairing form components on the same page.
claims.quote: Be sure to use a consistent field height when pairing form components on the same page.

claims.rule: Avoid free-form text input when users can only select from predefined options; use dropdown, select, or radio buttons instead.
claims.quote: If a user can only enter an option from a predefined list then avoid using a free-form text input as it is likely to result in an error. Consider using a selection control such as a dropdown, select, or radio button group instead.

claims.rule: Match input field width to expected content length; avoid excessively wide fields that waste space.
claims.quote: The field widths of both text input and text area should reflect the intended length of the content while still aligning to the grid columns or mini unit grid.

claims.rule: Mark only the minority of fields as optional or required, depending on which are most common.
claims.quote: If the majority of the fields are required, mark only the optional field labels with (optional). If the majority of the fields are optional, mark only the required field labels with (required).

sources.title: Toggle – IBM Carbon
sources.why: Toggle switch component.

claims.rule: Use toggles only for immediate binary actions like on/off settings that apply instantly without confirmation.
claims.quote: Toggle is a control that is used to quickly switch between two possible states. Toggles are only used for these binary actions that occur immediately after the user flips the switch.

claims.rule: Avoid toggles for actions requiring feedback or confirmation, such as file deletion; use different components instead.
claims.quote: Avoid using toggles if the action requires immediate feedback or confirmation, such as deleting a file.

claims.rule: Use adjectives rather than verbs to describe toggle actions and affected object states in state text.
claims.quote: Use adjectives rather than verbs to describe actions and the state of the object affected.

claims.rule: Limit toggle state text to three words or less for clarity.
claims.quote: It must be three words or less and is displayed on the side of a toggle.

claims.rule: Make both the toggle switch and its label clickable to change state for improved usability.
claims.quote: The toggle component has two clickable areas: the toggle switch itself and the label associated with it. Users can click either area to change the toggle's state.

claims.rule: Display a checkmark in the on state for small toggles without visible label or state text to maintain accessibility.
claims.quote: Small toggle displays a checkmark tick in the on state to ensure the toggle is still accessible when label and state text are unavailable.

sources.title: Slider – IBM Carbon
sources.why: Range slider component.

claims.rule: Use sliders to let users select a single value or range of values from a predefined numeric range.
claims.quote: Use when selecting a single value or range of number values. Use sliders when there is a need to show a selection of a single value or range of values.

claims.rule: Do not use sliders for extremely large ranges (e.g., 1-1000) or very small ranges (e.g., 1-3).
claims.quote: Do not use for extremely large ranges, for example, 1-1000. Do not use ranges that are too small, for example, 1-3.

claims.rule: Do not use sliders for complex non-numeric input values.
claims.quote: Do not use complex inputted values that are not numbers.

claims.rule: Place slider labels above the slider so they remain visible when interacting with the handle.
claims.quote: Labels should be placed above the slider so the label does not become obscured when interacting with the handle.

claims.rule: Keep slider labels short and concise, limited to a single line of text.
claims.quote: Keep the label short and concise by limiting it to a single line of text.

claims.rule: Ensure min and max value text accurately reflect the user's selection via handles or number input.
claims.quote: Keep min and max value text should accurately reflect the user's selection using the handles or the number input.

claims.rule: Show tooltips on hover, focus, and active states if sliders lack number inputs to display selected values.
claims.quote: If the slider does not include number inputs to display the selected values, use a tooltip on hover, focus, and active to show the selected values.

sources.title: Tooltip – IBM Carbon
sources.why: Tooltip and contextual help patterns.

claims.rule: Do not include critical information in tooltips; use always-visible helper text for essential task information.
claims.quote: do not include pertinent information for the user to complete their task. Use helper text that is always visible

claims.rule: Never place interactive elements inside tooltips; use toggletips for buttons, links, or images instead.
claims.quote: Do not include interactive elements within a tooltip. Interactive elements in tooltips are inaccessible for some users

claims.rule: Show tooltip only on hover or focus, hiding it when the user moves away, for brief supplemental information.
claims.quote: A tooltip is exposed on hover or focus when you need to disclose brief, supplemental information that is not interactive.

claims.rule: Vertically center the caret tip with the trigger button to visually associate the tooltip with its source element.
claims.quote: The UI trigger button and caret tip should be vertically centered with each other to associate the tooltip and the trigger.

claims.rule: Position tooltips with auto-detection by default to avoid being cut off or covering essential content.
claims.quote: Tooltip directions, by default, are set to auto. Upon opening, tooltips can detect the edges of the browser to be placed in view

claims.rule: Use auto-positioning for tooltips by default to detect browser edges and avoid cutoff.
claims.quote: Tooltip directions, by default, are set to auto. Upon opening, tooltips can detect the edges of the browser to be placed in view so the container does not get cutoff.

sources.title: Breadcrumb – IBM Carbon
sources.why: Breadcrumb navigation component.

claims.rule: Reserve breadcrumbs for hierarchies with more than two levels; do not use them as a replacement for primary navigation.
claims.quote: Breadcrumbs are effective in products and experiences that have a large amount of content organized in a hierarchy of more than two levels.

claims.rule: Do not wrap breadcrumb trails across multiple lines; use an overflow menu to truncate when space is limited.
claims.quote: Breadcrumbs should never wrap onto a second line.

claims.rule: Keep the home breadcrumb visible as long as possible on smaller breakpoints before using overflow menus.
claims.quote: For most use cases at larger breakpoints, keep the first home breadcrumb link for as long as possible in breakpoints, even when an overflow might be present.

claims.rule: Make each breadcrumb link short and reflect its location clearly; never make the current page an interactive link.
claims.quote: Each page link should be short and clearly reflect the location or entity it links to.

claims.rule: Place breadcrumbs below the header and navigation but above the page title in the top left.
claims.quote: Breadcrumbs are placed in the top left portion of the page. They sit underneath the header and navigation, but above the page title.

sources.title: Discovering Dopamine's Role in Reward Prediction Error
sources.why: Dopamine neurons signal reward prediction error (gap between expected vs actual outcomes) which drives learning and behavior optimization.
sources.finding: Dopamine acts as teaching signal: fires for unexpected rewards, goes silent for predicted rewards, reducing below baseline for reward omissions

sources.title: Wanting vs. Liking: The Incentive Sensitization Theory
sources.why: Wanting (motivation to pursue) and liking (pleasure from reward) operate on separate neural systems, with dopamine driving wanting more than liking.
sources.finding: Wanting uses large robust dopamine systems; liking uses small fragile hedonic hotspots independent of dopamine

sources.title: Behavior Model and Tiny Habits
sources.why: Behavior = Motivation + Ability + Prompt. All three must converge at same moment for behavior to occur. Universal framework for behavior change.
sources.finding: Model referenced in 1900+ academic papers; Tiny Habits method has guided millions to behavior change through 6-step process

claims.rule: Ensure motivation, ability, and a prompt converge simultaneously for users to perform desired behaviors.
claims.quote: Behavior happens when Motivation, Ability, and a Prompt come together at the same time.

sources.title: Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience
sources.why: Flow occurs when challenge matches skill; achieves deep engagement and fulfillment. Balance between skill and challenge prevents boredom and anxiety.
sources.finding: Flow characterized by heightened focus, concentration, enjoyment, control and mastery; peak psychological satisfaction

sources.title: Improving the Streak
sources.why: Separating streak mechanic from daily goals increases retention and habit formation through lower barrier to consistency.
sources.finding: 3.3% increase in Day 14 retention; 1% increase in daily active learners; 10.5% boost in streak users in 20 days; learners with 7-day streak 2.4x more likely to use next day

claims.rule: Use streak mechanics to drive daily habit formation; users reaching 7-day streaks show significantly higher retention.
claims.quote: learners who reach a streak of 7 are 2.4 times more likely to continue using Duolingo the next day

sources.title: Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products
sources.why: Hook Model (Trigger, Action, Variable Reward, Investment) embeds habit loops into products to bring users back without paid marketing.
sources.finding: Four-step model reduces dependence on costly advertising; frequency of use and perceived utility are key factors in habit formation

sources.title: Wendy Wood
sources.why: 30 years research on habit mechanisms: context, repetition, and reward are the three bases for habit formation and change.
sources.finding: Habits operate in nonconscious mind; resistance to change depends on environment, repetition patterns, and reward association

sources.title: How Long to Form a Habit? 66 Days Average
sources.why: Measured the time required for habit automaticity across different behaviors, establishing benchmarks for habit formation tracking.
sources.finding: Median automaticity plateau 66 days; range 18-254 days depending on behavior complexity; 66-day figure is average of succeeders only

claims.rule: Expect automaticity timelines to vary widely by behavior type and individual; exercise habits take longer than eating or drinking habits.
claims.quote: The exercise median was 91 days, compared with 65 for eating and 59 for drinking.

claims.rule: Do not assume habit formation will reach completion within an observation period; exercise subgroup median exceeded the 84-day study window.
claims.quote: The observation period was 84 days, while the exercise median estimate was 91 days. More than half of those 13 selected exercise participants therefore had model-estimated times beyond the observation window.

claims.rule: Recognize that only 48% of participants with adequate data met full modeling criteria for habit formation in 84 days.
claims.quote: That left 39 participants, 48% of those with adequate data, for whom the asymptotic curve was a 'good fit.'

sources.title: Implementation Intentions: The Science of Turning Intention into Performance
sources.why: If-then plans (e.g., 'if situation X, then response Y') delegate goal pursuit to situational cues, increasing automaticity and success.
sources.finding: 2006 meta-analysis of 94 studies: medium-to-large effect size (d=0.65) on goal achievement across exercise, eating, recycling, voting

claims.rule: Use if-then plans to automate goal-directed responses by forming strong associations between situational cues and actions.
claims.quote: Implementation intentions are "if-then" plans that define in advance how a goal will be pursued when encountering critical situations.

sources.title: Self-Determination Theory: The Three Core Psychological Needs
sources.why: Autonomy, competence, and relatedness are three intrinsic needs that drive engagement; external rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation.
sources.finding: Intrinsic motivation superior to extrinsic in engagement and wellbeing; satisfying three needs drives self-initiated behavior

sources.title: Client Challenge
sources.why: Meta-analysis synthesizing gamification effectiveness across studies shows positive effects with variation by context.
sources.finding: Gamification is effective for instruction; factors for success not fully resolved, especially for cognitive learning outcomes

sources.title: How Duolingo Uses A/B Testing for Habit Formation
sources.why: Streak-saver notification at end of day alerts users to losing streak; separating mechanics increased early retention significantly.
sources.finding: Streak-saver notification paired with streak mechanic; requires strong justification and CEO approval for notification increases

sources.title: How the Brain Processes Social Media Rewards
sources.why: Brain's response to social rewards (likes) correlates with actual social media usage; ventromedial prefrontal cortex tracks social value.
sources.finding: Small brain activation = low social media use; large activation = high use; reputational gains trigger reward center activation

sources.title: Schedules of Reinforcement
sources.why: Variable-ratio schedules produce highest and most persistent response rates with no post-reinforcement pauses.
sources.finding: VR schedules unpredictable; result in high consistent frequency of responses; slot machines use VR (avg 1 in 100 coins wins)

claims.rule: Use variable-ratio reinforcement to create habit-forming behavior that persists even after rewards stop.
claims.quote: Variable-ratio is the most persistent: it is the most resistant schedule to extinction of all four, which helps explain the pull of gambling.

claims.rule: Reinforce behavior continuously during early learning; switch to partial reinforcement once the habit is established.
claims.quote: Due to the behavior being reinforced every time, the association is easy to make, and learning occurs quickly. However, this also means that extinction occurs quickly after reinforcement is no longer provided.

sources.title: Retention Causes Virality and Vice Versa
sources.why: Retention (users returning) enables virality; core product must solve recurring need; notifications cannot rescue weak retention curve.
sources.finding: 30x more visits if daily retention strong; retention set by core product not surface fixes; retention enables word-of-mouth

sources.title: Dark Patterns at Scale: Findings from Crawl of 11K Shopping Websites
sources.why: Taxonomy of dark patterns: Sneaking, Urgency, Misdirection. Found 1818 instances of deceptive UI across 11000 websites.
sources.finding: ML algorithm identified 53000 product pages on 11K sites; dark patterns defined as coercion steering and deception causing harm

sources.title: Dark Patterns as Anti-Patterns
sources.why: Taxonomy of 5 dark pattern categories: Nagging, Obstruction, Sneaking, Interface Interference, Forced Action.
sources.finding: Analyzed 118 practitioner-identified dark patterns; developed taxonomy connecting practitioner discourse with HCI ethics scholarship

claims.rule: Avoid artificially difficult processes; do not obstruct users from completing their task or accessing information.
claims.quote: obstruction (artificially difficult processes)

claims.rule: Disclose all relevant information before users commit to a purchase or transaction; never conceal or delay material facts.
claims.quote: sneaking (concealed relevant information)

sources.title: Deceptive Design Reference
sources.why: Living resource documenting dark pattern taxonomy, regulations (EU DSA, GDPR), and research on deceptive design practices.
sources.finding: Harmonized 10 taxonomies into 3-level ontology with 64 standardized dark pattern types; tracks regulatory status globally

claims.rule: Do not exploit psychological vulnerabilities through addictive design patterns that foster compulsive behavior; such practices face regulatory enforcement.
claims.quote: Addictive Design The user interacts with the product excessively, because its design exploits psychological vulnerabilities to foster compulsive behaviour.

sources.title: Digital Services Act: Article 25 Dark Patterns Ban
sources.why: DSA prohibits designing interfaces that deceive, manipulate, or distort users' free and informed decisions. In effect Feb 2024.
sources.finding: First express prohibition on dark patterns in EU law; Article 25 bans deception manipulation and distortion of choice

sources.title: Bringing Clarity to AI’s Decisive Inflection Point
sources.why: Organization led by Tristan Harris exposing dark patterns and deceptive design mechanics used to manipulate and addict users.
sources.finding: Identified mass deception infrastructure; documented manipulation mechanisms in product design; influenced tech industry accountability

sources.title: 7 Friends in 10 Days: The Aha Moment Threshold
sources.why: Users who connected 7+ friends in first 10 days became long-term active users; threshold where network effect clicked.
sources.finding: 7 friends = proxy for aha moment when feed becomes interesting; leads indicator for onboarding optimization

claims.rule: Compress time-to-first-value to under 5 minutes for elite products; industry median is 36 hours.
claims.quote: elite SaaS delivers first value in under 5 minutes; the industry median is roughly 36 hours

claims.rule: Identify activation as a specific in-product behavior threshold, not signup or onboarding completion.
claims.quote: An Aha moment is the in-product event where a user first experiences the core value of your product — the 'Now I get it' trigger that converts a trial user into a likely long-term customer. It is not signup, not onboarding completion, and not feature adoption.

claims.rule: Approximately 75% of users churn in the first week if they don't achieve activation.
claims.quote: ~75% of users churn in the first week if they don't hit activation

claims.rule: Segment activation thresholds by user type; B2B products often require both individual user activation and team-level activation.
claims.quote: Different user types may have different Aha moments. A B2B SaaS often has both a user Aha (individual finds value) and a team Aha (team workflow becomes embedded).

sources.title: How Peloton Builds Onboarding and Community Engagement
sources.why: Onboarding plus gamification and community features drive engagement; social engagement increases workout frequency.
sources.finding: Members engaging socially work out 15% more frequently; century club (100 rides) awards badge and tee; streak freezes boost retention

claims.rule: Build branching onboarding paths that tailor to user context and remove information barriers to reach activation quickly.
claims.quote: We have several branching paths that tailor the experience to the user and what information they may have, such as a subscription key or an existing Peloton account. This flexibility allows us to make sure there is always a path forward, so the user can start working out as quickly as possible.

claims.rule: Track which onboarding steps users skip to identify friction points that need redesign or clearer copy.
claims.quote: We can track how many members are skipping onboarding steps rather than engaging with them to see how valuable each step is.

sources.title: Strava: Gamification and Social Fitness Flywheel
sources.why: Leaderboards, segments, challenges, and kudos create social fitness flywheel that maintains industry-leading retention.
sources.finding: Convert 2 min app usage into 1 hour physical activity; 150M+ users; leaderboards drive competition and status motivation

sources.title: Lenny's Newsletter: Retention and Engagement Data
sources.why: Original survey research and benchmark data from hundreds of product operators on retention strategy and metrics.
sources.finding: 700K+ subscriber platform; publishes original survey research and benchmark data not commentary; 574K paid subscribers

sources.title: Reforge: Retention and Engagement Program
sources.why: Program for naming aha moment as measurable action with time window; every onboarding step judged against value delivery speed.
sources.finding: Guides reduced onboarding steps by 80%; 25% boost in satisfaction; teaches framework for measuring activation moment

sources.title: Appcues: Product Adoption and Onboarding Platform
sources.why: Drag-and-drop platform for creating in-app onboarding tours and checklists with personalization and flow triggers.
sources.finding: No-code solution for in-app guides (hotspots modals slideouts tooltips); targets flow activation on URL device type interaction

sources.title: Pendo: Product Usage and Adoption Platform
sources.why: In-app analytics combined with guided onboarding flows to monitor usage and drive feature discovery and adoption.
sources.finding: Layout templates for lightboxes banners tooltips; flow triggers based on URL device segment; 50+ integrations available

sources.title: Intercom: Unified Customer Communication Platform
sources.why: Consolidated support chat AI bots product tours and email campaigns for onboarding activation and retention messaging.
sources.finding: 40-60% of support queries resolve via Fin AI; CSMs message based on usage patterns (e.g. unused feature 30 days) to prevent churn

claims.rule: Train AI agents on existing knowledge and processes, then simulate conversations end-to-end before deployment.
claims.quote: Start with the knowledge you already have, then train Fin on your processes and policies. Use AI-driven Simulations to test fully simulated customer conversations from start to finish

claims.rule: Deploy AI agents across multiple channels so customers receive consistent responses wherever they contact you.
claims.quote: Deploy Fin across phone, email, chat, Slack, and more so every customer receives accurate, personalized responses, wherever they reach out

claims.rule: Centralize all support knowledge in one hub to measure content performance across every customer touchpoint.
claims.quote: Centralize, manage, and optimize all of the information that powers Fin, human, and self-serve support. See how your content is performing across every touchpoint including Fin, Copilot and on your Help Center with detailed reporting

sources.title: Linear: Speed as Core Feature and Philosophy
sources.why: Issue tracker built on speed and simplicity; keyboard-first interface makes issue creation as fast as Slack message.
sources.finding: Keyboard-first design enables issue creation in seconds (time parity with Slack); lightning-fast performance; minimalist design

claims.rule: Render UI before full data synchronization completes using minimum required state to prevent perceived application lag.
claims.quote: Render UI before vehicle_state sync when minimum required state is present, instead of blocking on full refresh

claims.rule: Show stale data indicators when background synchronization is in progress to maintain transparency.
claims.quote: Show a stale data banner while syncing

sources.title: Gartner Research: Enterprise User Experience
sources.why: Enterprise application leaders should build user journey maps voice of user programs and measure application effort vs ease.
sources.finding: B2B users expect B2C-level experiences; good UX makes compliance intuitive; team composition critical for superior outcomes

sources.title: The Eureka Factor: Aha! Moments and Insight in the Brain
sources.why: Insight moments involve burst of right hemisphere activity; different brain regions activate during insight than analytical thinking.
sources.finding: Right superior temporal gyrus shows high-frequency oscillations during insight; conceptual reorganization produces aha moment

sources.title: Not So Timely: Screen-On Push Notifications and User Engagement
sources.org: University of Copenhagen / MIT Media Lab
sources.why: Modest notification delay (1-6 min after screen-on) generates higher engagement than immediate delivery.
sources.finding: Immediate screen-on delivery reduces same-day logins by ~16%; peak engagement at 1-6 min delay; inverted-U relationship with timing

claims.rule: Delay push notifications by one to two minutes after screen-on detection to maximize user engagement.
claims.quote: slightly delayed screen-on pushes—arriving one to two minutes after users turn on their screens—generate significantly higher engagement than instantaneous pushes

claims.rule: Avoid delivering notifications with hyper-precise timing as excessive precision can reduce user receptivity and feel intrusive.
claims.quote: hyper-precise timing can backfire: messages delivered too immediately may feel intrusive, while modest delays enhance receptivity

sources.title: Pull to Refresh UI Pattern and User Engagement
sources.why: Pull-to-refresh gesture introduced by Loren Brichter in Tweetie; now ubiquitous pattern for data refresh with feedback.
sources.finding: Gesture confidence tied to visual feedback; refresh spinner should continue until data available; less intuitive than button

sources.title: Research
sources.why: Develops algorithms for spacing practice to optimize long-term retention through scientific spacing schedules.
