sources.title: Dark Pattern: Sneaking
sources.why: User drawn into transaction on false pretences through hidden or delayed information.

claims.rule: Never withhold or obscure information relevant to user decisions, especially costs or consequences of their actions.
claims.quote: Sneaking involves intentionally withholding or obscuring information that is relevant to the user (e.g. additional costs or unwanted consequences)

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Forced Action
sources.why: User required to perform undesirable action to access desired feature or service.

claims.rule: Never require users to complete undesired actions to access desired features; present optional actions clearly and separately.
claims.quote: Forced action involves a provider offering users something they want - but requiring them to do something in return.

claims.rule: Make rejection or skip options visually equal or more prominent than accept options; position them prominently, not hidden.
claims.quote: The 'skip this step' link was relatively small and hard to notice, positioned at the bottom right.

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Hard to Cancel
sources.why: Easy to subscribe but difficult to cancel; asymmetric friction in sign-up vs cancellation.

claims.rule: Expose cancellation prominently on the same interface where signup occurs; hiding it violates consumer protection law.
claims.quote: typically involves hiding the cancellation option, requiring users to call customer services to cancel

claims.rule: Complete subscription cancellation in seconds, not minutes; New York Times test showed 8 minutes of rep talk versus seconds for signup.
claims.quote: In one test it took roughly 8 minutes of conversation with a customer services rep to successfully cancel a subscription

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Preselection
sources.why: Default option pre-selected to influence decision-making in seller's favor.

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Obstruction
sources.why: Barriers and hurdles make it hard to complete tasks or access information.

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Hidden Subscription
sources.why: User unknowingly enrolled in recurring subscription without clear disclosure or explicit consent.

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Hidden Costs
sources.why: Low advertised price but unexpected fees revealed at checkout, violating user expectations.

claims.rule: Show all fees and total price before the user commits time or effort; reveal costs upfront, not at checkout.
claims.quote: Hidden costs involve obscuring or omitting additional fees, charges, or costs until the user is well into the purchasing or sign-up process

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Trick Wording
sources.why: Confusing or misleading language manipulates user action.

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Visual Interference
sources.why: Information hidden obscured or disguised contrary to user expectations through visual design.

claims.rule: Never hide critical information in small text, low contrast, or unexpected locations; use consistent hierarchy and prominence.
claims.quote: Hidden on the purchase screen was some small, low contrast text stating upgrades cannot be refunded. This text was the lowest contrast text on the page, and was difficult to see

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Fake Social Proof
sources.why: User misled into believing product more popular or credible than it really is.

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Fake Urgency
sources.why: User pressured with fake time limitation to complete action faster.

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Nagging
sources.why: Persistent interruptions with requests that may not be in user's best interests.

claims.rule: Recognize that repeated interruptions deplete attention as a tax, eventually forcing users to comply against their interests.
claims.quote: Every time an app or a website interrupts the user with a request to do something, this depletes the user's time and attention. This is like a tax that the provider imposes

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Fake Scarcity
sources.why: Pressure through fake indication of limited supply or popularity.

claims.rule: Never display false low-stock messages or fake demand indicators to pressure hasty purchase decisions.
claims.quote: displaying misleading messages about low stock levels or high demand

claims.rule: Do not exploit the scarcity cognitive bias by creating artificial urgency around limited supply or exclusivity.
claims.quote: By tapping into the scarcity cognitive bias, this deceptive pattern preys on users' natural tendency to assign more value to items that appear rare or exclusive

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Disguised Ads
sources.why: User mistakenly clicks interface element believing it to be functional but it's a disguised advertisement.

claims.rule: Visually distinguish advertisements from native content and interface elements with clear, persistent labeling.
claims.quote: These ads are often designed to look like interface elements, related articles, or other content that users might be interested in

claims.rule: Never make ad download buttons or calls-to-action resemble actual product download buttons or primary actions.
claims.quote: displaying advertisements with a prominent download button that closely resembles the actual download button for the desired software

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Confirmshaming
sources.why: Emotional manipulation through shaming labels to coerce desired action.

claims.rule: Never use derogatory, shaming, or guilt-inducing language in opt-out button labels or rejection options.
claims.quote: opt-out button labels that are worded in a derogatory or belittling manner, making users feel bad about choosing not to engage

claims.rule: Do not emotionally manipulate users by triggering guilt or shame to influence decisions they would not otherwise make.
claims.quote: Confirmshaming works by triggering uncomfortable emotions, such as guilt or shame, to influence users' decision-making

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Comparison Prevention
sources.why: Users unable to compare products due to complex presentation or hidden information.

claims.rule: Present price, taxes, fees, and key features consistently across all compared products on the same view.
claims.quote: Taxes and fees are included in two of the plan prices, but not included in the third. Since the taxes and fees are not shown for the third plan the user cannot deduce if it is better value or not

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Addictive Design
sources.why: Design exploits psychological vulnerabilities to foster compulsive behaviour.

claims.rule: Avoid infinite scroll, autoplay, pull-to-refresh, streaks, daily rewards, and variable rewards that exploit compulsive behaviour.
claims.quote: patterns such as variable reward schedules, loot boxes, infinite scroll, pull-to-refresh, autoplay, streaks, daily rewards, playing by appointment, and social validation loops

sources.title: Dark Pattern: Currency Confusion
sources.why: Real money converted to virtual currency to obscure true cost to user.

claims.rule: Display real currency equivalent alongside virtual currency prices to prevent spending confusion.
claims.quote: The real cost in fiat currency is not shown in the item purchasing experience.

claims.rule: Avoid decoupling payment from consumption to reduce users overspending.
claims.quote: when it is 'decoupled', people may overspend

sources.title: Microinteractions : How to Make UI Feedback Accessible
sources.why: Guide on making microinteractions and feedback accessible.

claims.rule: Use microinteractions to provide immediate feedback confirming user actions and reducing cognitive load.
claims.quote: Microinteractions improve usability by giving users immediate feedback on their actions, making the interface feel responsive and alive

claims.rule: Provide non-visual alternatives like sound, vibration, or text for color-only microinteraction feedback.
claims.quote: Adding alternative cues like sound, vibration, or text descriptions ensures that everyone receives the necessary feedback

claims.rule: Make focus states clear and easily identifiable for keyboard and assistive-device users.
claims.quote: Clear, easily identifiable focus indicators help these users track their progress through a webpage

claims.rule: Keep microinteractions simple, quick, and purpose-driven to avoid overwhelming or distracting users.
claims.quote: Microinteractions should be quick, subtle, and purpose-driven, not over-the-top or distracting

claims.rule: Pair all color-based feedback with non-visual cues like text, icons, or borders to ensure users with color blindness perceive microinteraction state changes.
claims.quote: combine color changes with other visual cues like text, icons, or borders to make actions clear

claims.rule: Ensure touch targets meet a minimum size of 44×44 pixels to accommodate users with limited dexterity across mobile and touchscreen devices.
claims.quote: typically aiming for a minimum size of 44px by 44px

claims.rule: Provide haptic and auditory feedback on mobile devices alongside visual feedback to serve users with visual impairments or limited sight.
claims.quote: haptic feedback (vibration) and auditory cues are essential for accessibility, especially for users with visual impairments or limited mobility

claims.rule: Respect prefers-reduced-motion system settings and ensure microinteraction functionality is preserved when motion is disabled.
claims.quote: Ensure that microinteractions are still functional and provide feedback when motion is reduced or disabled

claims.rule: Limit microinteraction complexity and frequency to avoid overwhelming users with cognitive disabilities or sensory sensitivities.
claims.quote: By designing clear and familiar interactions (e.g., progress indicators for loading times or error messages), users with cognitive challenges can more easily understand what's happening

sources.title: How to Make Motion Design Accessible: UX Choreography Part Two
sources.why: Guide on accessible motion and animation in UI design.

claims.rule: Use spatial motion to orient users about location, direction, and how to navigate back.
claims.quote: Spacial motion design applies our basic understanding of physical space and translates it into a digital system to help the user remember where they are, how they move forward, and how to get back

claims.rule: Ensure screen readers detect animated events, state changes, and overlays to prevent missing critical information.
claims.quote: Screen readers can miss events like partial page loads, temporary animated overlays (like toasts or banners), and animated state changes

claims.rule: Keep motion design moderate to prevent dizziness and disorientation in users with vestibular disorders.
claims.quote: People with vestibular disorders may experience motion design in an interface to be very unpleasant, nauseating, and/or disorienting to various degrees

claims.rule: Avoid drastic or fast motion that increases cognitive load by confusing object associations.
claims.quote: Motion design that is either too drastic, fast, or both can cause confusion and add to a user's cognitive load

claims.rule: Position animated notifications on-screen for low-vision users with screen magnification.
claims.quote: If animated events like a notification or toast come in and appear off screen, the user may not see it

claims.rule: Let users trigger motion through actions rather than auto-playing animations.
claims.quote: Motion design is best when it is subtle and happens after a user has taken an action. Motion design that auto-plays or is unexpected can be unpleasant for many people.

claims.rule: Keep animation at the point of focus to direct attention without distracting users.
claims.quote: Animation should be used to direct a user's attention to the most important thing on the screen that they may need to interact with.

claims.quote: Different fonts have different maximum heights (x-heights) even when they're the same size in points. So you need to be sure that when you change font, you check to see how your line spacing feels

sources.title: Website Forms Usability: Top 10 Recommendations
sources.why: NN/G research-based form design recommendations.

claims.rule: Remove unnecessary form fields to increase completion rates and submission accuracy.
claims.quote: Every time you cut a field or question from a form, you increase its conversion rate

claims.rule: Place labels immediately above or adjacent to their fields with minimal ambiguous spacing.
claims.quote: Labels should be close to the fields they describe (immediately above the field for mobile and shorter desktop forms, or next to the field for extremely long desktop forms). Avoid ambiguous spacing

claims.rule: List most-frequently-used values first in option lists.
claims.quote: for field values, also consider usage frequency, and list the most common values first when possible

claims.rule: Never use Reset or Clear buttons; they increase accidental data loss.
claims.quote: to avoid Reset buttons on web forms

claims.rule: Avoid placeholder text as labels; use explicit labels instead.
claims.quote: Avoid placeholder text

claims.rule: Forms with usability guidelines achieve 78% one-try error-free submissions versus 42% for non-compliant forms.
claims.quote: 78% one-try submissions in forms compliant with usability guidelines versus only 42% one-try submissions in forms violating them

claims.rule: Present form fields in a single column to maintain vertical momentum; avoid multi-column layouts that disrupt user flow.
claims.quote: Multiple columns interrupt the vertical momentum of moving down the form. Rather than requiring users to visually reorient themselves, keep them in the flow by sticking to a single column

claims.rule: Size text input fields to match expected input length, empirically: 19 characters fits 99.9% of city names.

sources.title: Skeleton loading screen design — How to improve perceived performance

claims.rule: Use skeleton screens for content loading to improve perceived performance over blank screens.
claims.quote: Unlike preloader animations and progress bars, skeleton loading screens improve perceived performance well since users can feel how data segments will appear on the screen even though they are not yet loaded.

claims.rule: Use animated skeleton loaders for content loading over one second to maintain user engagement.
claims.quote: Most designers choose animated skeleton loaders since they indicate the loading state effectively and keep the user engaged even if the loading time expands over about one second.

claims.rule: Match skeleton layout exactly to the final loaded screen so users immediately recognize content structure and section positions.
claims.quote: A skeleton screen should be consistent in layout and structure with the final loaded screen. This gives users an idea of what the final screen will look like, as well as where to potentially find the type of content they are looking for.

claims.rule: Exclude smaller UI elements like buttons, form fields, and labels from skeleton screens; use placeholders only for primary structural components.
claims.quote: Skeleton screens are more focused on structure and layout while excluding the smaller details, like icons or status indicators.

claims.rule: Use skeleton screens for container-based components like cards, tiles, grids, and data tables; avoid them for smaller components.
claims.quote: Skeleton screens primarily work best when loading container-based components, such as tiles, structured lists, grids, data tables, and card components.

claims.rule: Use distinguishable colors and clear but undistracted animations in skeleton screens to support accessibility and visibility.
claims.quote: Choosing distinguishable colors for skeleton screens' placeholders and implementing clear but undistracted animations is the best way to clearly indicate the loading state by prioritizing accessibility.

sources.title: Skeleton Screens vs Loading Spinners: When to Use Each

claims.rule: Use skeleton screens when fetching content and layout context matters, like feeds or dashboards.
claims.quote: Go for a skeleton screen when content is being fetched, and layout context matters, such as feeds, dashboards, search results, or product listings.

claims.rule: Use spinners for short, blocking actions like form submission or authentication, not content loading.
claims.quote: Use a spinner for short or blocking actions such as submitting a form, authentication, saving, processing, or payments.

claims.rule: Show visible loading feedback within 50 milliseconds to prevent users interpreting the interface as broken.
claims.quote: Research indicates that nearly 90% of users anticipate some form of interactive feedback — whether a hover response, visual state change, or loading indicator — within about 50 milliseconds of an action.

claims.rule: Display skeleton screens that mimic the final layout to help users recognize content structure immediately.
claims.quote: Because the placeholders match the final structure, users can scan the page instantly. They recognize a feed, a product listing, or a dashboard before the content arrives.

claims.rule: Use skeleton screens for content-heavy interfaces where layout context and content anticipation matter, such as feeds, dashboards, and product listings.
claims.quote: You can use a spinner for short or blocking actions such as submitting a form, authentication, saving, processing, or payments. But go for a skeleton screen when content is being fetched, and layout context matters, such as feeds, dashboards, search results, or product listings.

claims.rule: Implement progressive loading in skeleton screens so placeholders transform into real content, making users perceive the interface as faster.
claims.quote: A skeleton screen makes progress visible. As placeholders transform into real content, users experience continuous advancement. Even if both interfaces take the same number of seconds to load, the one with the skeleton screen is usually perceived as faster because users see incremental change rather than a single reveal.

claims.rule: Make modals visually distinct from background with strong border or shadow so users perceive the context shift.
claims.quote: Modals must be visually distinct from the background to help users understand the shift in context.

claims.rule: Ensure text contrast ratios are at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text in modal dialogs.
claims.quote: Text vs background contrast ratio ≥ 4.5:1 (normal text) or ≥ 3:1 (large text)

claims.rule: Trap keyboard focus inside modal so users cannot tab into background content while the modal is open.
claims.quote: A user should never be able to 'tab out' of the modal into the background content while it's open.

claims.rule: Return focus to the trigger button when modal closes so screen reader users do not lose navigation position.
claims.quote: When the modal closes, the focus must return to the button that opened it.

claims.rule: Close modals when users press Escape key to provide an expected and keyboard-friendly dismissal method.
claims.quote: Escape: Closes the modal and returns focus to the trigger button.

claims.rule: Make close button and action buttons at least 24px by 24px (44px on mobile) to accommodate limited dexterity.
claims.quote: Ensure the 'Close' button and any action buttons are at least 24px x 24px (preferably 44px on mobile) to accommodate users with limited dexterity.

claims.rule: Use aria-describedby to provide context for why the modal appeared, improving understanding for all users.
claims.quote: aria-describedby='ID': Points to the main description text of the modal. This provides immediate context for why the modal appeared.

claims.quote: Carousels are noticed, but often ignored as advertising or irrelevant content. The visual presence therefore does not automatically lead to interaction or understanding.

sources.why: Foundational dropdown design research with historical context and best practices.

sources.title: Autocomplete Beyond Search: Engaging Users with Next-Level UX
sources.why: Advanced autocomplete design patterns beyond basic search, with engagement strategies.

claims.rule: Return autocomplete results from the first keystroke to provide maximum responsiveness and user control.
claims.quote: Make sure results are returned from the first keystroke for maximum responsiveness and user control.

claims.rule: Include six to eight query suggestions in autocomplete menus to avoid overwhelming users with too many options.
claims.quote: Include 6 to 8 query suggestions.

claims.rule: Use inverted highlighting in autocomplete results, bolding untyped text to focus attention on what remains to be read.
claims.quote: Prefer "inverted" highlighting. This places in bold the pieces that weren't typed, focusing user attention on what remains to be read.

claims.rule: Make the search box full-width with a placeholder that tells users what to do, so it visually stands out on all devices.
claims.quote: The search box should visually stand out, be full-width and include a placeholder that tells users what to do.

claims.rule: Position search within natural thumb reach on mobile, avoiding top-center placement that requires stretching; center-bottom is ideal.
claims.quote: Put it where people can see it. The Uniqlo and Mad Kicks sites do an excellent job of placing it centrally at the bottom of the screen, within close reach of the thumb.

sources.title: Autocomplete Suggestions UX Best Practices
sources.why: Autocomplete suggestion design with research on user expectations and behavior.

claims.rule: Place the search box on every page at the top right or center of the screen where users expect to find it.
claims.quote: The search box should be available on every page of your website. Put it in a place users expect to see it. Research supports a search field that's integrated with your website's navigation, generally placed at the top right or center of the screen.

claims.rule: Ensure autocomplete hit areas are appropriately sized to prevent small targets that lead to mistakes or frustration.
claims.quote: Make sure you avoid small hit areas which can lead to mistakes or frustration. An appropriately sized hit area ensures that users can easily select the suggestion they want.

claims.rule: Keep autocomplete suggestion lists to around ten items on desktop and eight on mobile to prevent analysis paralysis.
claims.quote: When suggestions exceed around 10 items on desktop (and around eight on mobile), users either ignore suggestions or spend too much time reading through them.

sources.why: Research on searchable and sortable table functionality impact on user experience.

sources.why: Comprehensive data table best practices for usability and efficiency.

claims.rule: Set minimum button size to 42 pixels (9x9 mm) for accessibility and comfortable button size around 50 pixels (10x10 mm).
claims.quote: Minimum button size should be 42 px (9×9 mm) for accessibility. Comfortable button size is around 50 px (10×10 mm), matching the fingertip area.

claims.rule: Follow platform standards: Apple 44x44 points, Google 48x48 dp, or Microsoft 34x34 px plus spacing for touch-friendly buttons.
claims.quote: Apple (44×44 pt), Google (48×48 dp), Microsoft (34×34 px + spacing) set size rules.

claims.rule: Space buttons 12-48 pixels apart to prevent accidental taps and reduce user errors from too-close targets.
claims.quote: Spacing of 12-48 px between buttons prevents accidental taps and errors.

sources.title: System Buttons Actions

claims.rule: Use one primary button per screen to guide users toward the key task.
claims.quote: each screen should have only one primary button

claims.rule: Make primary action buttons filled with solid background color and high contrast from surrounding elements.
claims.quote: They need solid background color, high contrast with surrounding elements, and clear labels that describe the action

claims.rule: Position destructive buttons away from frequently used actions with enough padding to prevent accidental triggers.
claims.quote: They should be placed away from frequently used actions and include enough padding to prevent accidental triggers

claims.rule: Keep segmented controls between 2 and 5 options; more options become hard to read and tap.
claims.quote: Keep the number of segments between 2-5 — more options become hard to read and tap accurately

claims.rule: Use short, descriptive text labels in segmented controls that fit without truncation.
claims.quote: Text labels should be short and descriptive and fit without truncation

sources.title: Accessible Modals: Creation Guidelines
sources.why: Step-by-step guide to creating accessible modal dialogs with WCAG compliance.

claims.rule: Prefer native HTML <dialog> with showModal() for true modal behavior; use existing primitives only if they provide focus, inertness, containment, Escape, and focus restoration.
claims.quote: Prefer the native HTML <dialog> with showModal() for a true modal. It provides the modal behaviors required

claims.rule: Give dialogs an accessible name using a visible heading with aria-labelledby; avoid aria-label unless necessary.
claims.quote: Give the dialog an accessible name. Prefer a visible heading referenced with aria-labelledby

claims.rule: Move focus to the first useful control for short forms, a static heading with tabindex="-1" for long content, or the least destructive action for irreversible decisions.
claims.quote: Choose based on content: the first useful control for a short form, a static heading or introductory element with tabindex="-1" for long/structured content, or the least destructive action for an irreversible decision

claims.rule: Support Escape key to close modals; ensure only the topmost dialog closes when modals can stack.
claims.quote: Support Escape to close a modal, unless the product explicitly requires a different, documented behavior. Ensure only the topmost dialog closes when dialogs can stack

claims.rule: Provide a clearly named visible close or cancel control; do not make backdrop-click the only dismissal mechanism.
claims.quote: Provide a clearly named visible close/cancel control. Do not make backdrop-click the only dismissal mechanism

claims.rule: Restore focus to the opener when the modal closes; if the opener was removed, choose the next logical workflow target.
claims.quote: On close, restore focus to the opener when it still exists. If it was removed, choose the next logical workflow target and test that path

claims.rule: Make dialog content scrollable without trapping the close control; preserve focus indicators and avoid clipping essential actions at narrow widths.
claims.quote: Make the modal usable at narrow viewport widths: allow the dialog content to scroll without trapping the close control, preserve visible focus indicators, and avoid clipping essential actions

claims.rule: Do not close a dialog on accidental outside click when it would discard entered data or interrupt a critical task.
claims.quote: Do not close a dialog on an accidental outside click when it would discard entered data or interrupt a critical task without warning

sources.title: Modals 101: When and How to Use Them
sources.why: Modal dialog usage and implementation best practices.

claims.rule: Avoid automatically showing a modal when a user lands on a page unless genuinely critical for security or data loss prevention.
claims.quote: Arriving on a page is not considered user input. Avoid automatically showing a modal when a user lands on a page

claims.rule: Use role="dialog" or native <dialog> element; add aria-modal="true" and aria-labelledby or aria-label for accessibility.
claims.quote: Use role="dialog" or the native <dialog> element. Add aria-modal="true" so screen readers know the background is blocked. Use aria-labelledby or aria-label to provide the modal's name

claims.rule: For general dialogs, focus the first interactive element; for destructive actions, focus the least destructive option like Cancel.
claims.quote: For general dialogs, focus the first interactive element. For destructive actions, focus the least destructive option (e.g., the Cancel button)

claims.rule: Provide at least three ways to exit a modal: backdrop click, Escape key, and a footer button; include a close button if no Cancel button exists.
claims.quote: Provide users with at least three ways to exit the modal: Clicking outside the modal (backdrop click). Pressing the Escape key. Using a footer button (e.g., Cancel or Close)

claims.rule: Use specific button labels like "Delete File" instead of generic options; place primary action on the right, Cancel on the left in left-to-right languages.
claims.quote: Be specific: Use labels like "Delete File" instead of generic options like "OK". Place the primary action on the right and the Cancel action on the left

claims.rule: Maintain at least 40dp distance from left and right edges and 24dp from top and bottom; ensure content is 24dp from dialog edge.
claims.quote: Maintain a distance of at least 40dp from the left and right edges of the screen, and 24dp from the top and bottom. Ensure the dialog's content is 24dp from the dialog edge

claims.rule: On mobile, expand large modals to full width and use 75% screen width for small/medium modals; keep headers and footers fixed while allowing body to scroll.
claims.quote: Large modals: Expand to full width on mobile devices. Small/medium modals: Use 75% of the screen width on mobile. Keep headers and footers fixed while allowing only the body content to scroll

claims.rule: Avoid nested modals; use sequential modals, sidebars, drawers, tabs, or inline editing instead.
claims.quote: Nested modals create a poor user experience (UX) for several reasons: Users may lose their place within the workflow. Cognitive overload increases with multiple layers

claims.rule: Avoid vague error messages; use specific, helpful text like "Your session ended—please log in again" instead of "Error!".
claims.quote: Vague error messages (e.g., "Error!" vs. "Your session ended—please log in again")

claims.rule: Limit modal buttons to a maximum of three, including Cancel, to avoid overloading users.
claims.quote: Overloading modals with too many buttons (stick to three maximum, including Cancel)

sources.title: Accessible Modal Dialog Design: Focus, Escape, and Screen Reader Support
sources.why: Technical implementation of accessible modals with focus management and keyboard support.

claims.rule: When a dialog closes, return focus to the triggering element; if it no longer exists, move focus to a logical alternative to prevent keyboard users from losing their place.

claims.rule: Avoid nesting modals; if a secondary confirmation is needed, replace the current modal's content rather than layering a new dialog on top.
claims.quote: Opening a modal from within a modal creates layered focus traps that are extremely difficult to manage correctly. Avoid nesting modals

sources.title: Stanford Guidelines for Web Credibility
sources.why: Large study of web credibility assessment; 46.1% of participants rated design/look as primary credibility signal.
sources.finding: 46.1% of participants primarily assessed site credibility by overall design appearance; visual design is the dominant trust signal.

claims.rule: Provide citations and links to third-party sources to prove information accuracy.
claims.quote: You can build web site credibility by providing third-party support (citations, references, source material) for information you present, especially if you link to this evidence.

claims.rule: Show real people behind your organization; include employee bios with personal details.
claims.quote: Show there are real people behind the site and in the organization. Next, find a way to convey their trustworthiness through images or text. For example, some sites post employee bios that tell about family or hobbies.

claims.rule: Make contact information prominent: phone, address, and email.
claims.quote: Make it easy to contact you. A simple way to boost your site's credibility is by making your contact information clear: phone number, physical address, and email address.

claims.rule: Update content regularly and show recent review dates.

claims.rule: Limit ads and distinguish sponsored content clearly; avoid pop-ups.
claims.quote: Use restraint with any promotional content (e.g., ads, offers). If possible, avoid having ads on your site. If you must have ads, clearly distinguish the sponsored content from your own. Avoid pop-up ads, unless you don't mind annoying users and losing credibility.

claims.rule: Fix typos, broken links, and downtime immediately; errors severely damage credibility.
claims.quote: Avoid errors of all types, no matter how small they seem. Typographical errors and broken links hurt a site's credibility more than most people imagine. It's also important to keep your site up and running.

sources.why: Meta-analysis and review arguing working memory capacity is ~4 chunks for young adults, correcting Miller's 7±2 estimate.
sources.finding: Normal young adults retain 3-4 items in working memory when unable to form larger chunks; capacity ~4 (±1) not 7±2.

sources.title: When Choice is Demotivating: Can One Desire Too Much of a Good Thing?
sources.why: Jam display experiment: 24-flavor booth attracted 60% but only 3% purchased; 6-flavor booth attracted 40% but 30% purchased.
sources.finding: More options attracted more browsers (60% vs 40%) but reduced purchase rate (3% vs 30%); excess choice demotivates decisions.

sources.title: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk
sources.why: Foundational work on loss aversion and framing effects; people need 1.5-2.5x gain to accept fair-coin gamble.
sources.finding: Loss aversion coefficient ~2.25: losses psychologically weigh 1.5-2.5x more than equivalent gains; framing as loss makes people risk-seeking.

sources.title: Defaults and Donation Decisions
sources.why: Cross-European study: opt-out defaults yielded ~99% organ donation consent vs ~5% for opt-in; 60-point gap.
sources.finding: Organ donation consent: opt-out default 99% vs opt-in 5% across European countries; defaults had ~60-point effect with no overlap in distributions.

sources.title: Cognitive Load Theory, Learning Difficulty, and Instructional Design
sources.why: Foundational theory: working memory processes intrinsic (task) and extraneous (design) cognitive load; limited capacity ~7 items.
sources.finding: Working memory capacity ~7 items; intrinsic load (material difficulty) + extraneous load (design) cannot exceed capacity without learning failure.

sources.title: Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness
sources.org: University of Chicago & Harvard Law School
sources.why: Choice architecture framework: defaults, feedback, mapping, error handling, simplification, incentives shape decisions without restricting freedom.
sources.finding: No neutral defaults exist; choice architecture—defaults, feedback, structure—predictably nudges decisions in intended direction while preserving choice.

sources.title: The Fire AI Lab
sources.why: Before and after study: aesthetics correlated with both perceived and post-use perceived usability, but actual usability did not.
sources.finding: Pre-use perceived aesthetics correlated (r=0.70) with post-use perceived usability; actual usability had no effect on perception—halo effect confirmed.

sources.title: Social Proof in the User Experience
sources.why: Six principles: reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity; foundational for behavioral design.
sources.finding: Six universal influence principles (reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity) operate consistently across cultures and contexts.

sources.title: Excerpt: Yes! : NPR
sources.why: Hotel towel-reuse experiment: social-norm message (others reused) outperformed environmental message by ~25%.
sources.finding: Social-norm message ('others reused') increased towel reuse ~25% more than environmental message; similarity effect: room-specific norm > hotel-wide norm.

sources.title: Clinton, Obama, and the decoy effect!
sources.why: Economist subscription example: adding decoy (print-only at $125) to [digital $59, print $125] shifted choice from 68% digital to 84% bundle.
sources.finding: Adding inferior decoy option (print $125) redirected 84% to $125 bundle from 68% digital baseline; asymmetric dominance effect lifts revenue ~30%.

sources.title: The 'IKEA Effect': When Labor Leads to Love
sources.why: Four experiments (IKEA assembly, origami, Legos): effort alone increases valuation; effect disappears if task fails or is destroyed.
sources.finding: Effort increases product valuation even for low-quality output (IKEA assembly); effect requires successful completion—failure eliminates it.

sources.title: When More Pain Is Preferred to Less: Adding a Better End
sources.why: Cold water immersion: 60s in 14°C vs 60s+30s in 14°C then 15°C; subjects preferred longer trial despite more total pain.
sources.finding: Experience evaluation driven by peak pain (worst moment) and end state, not total duration; adding better ending increases repeat preference.

sources.title: Hick's law
sources.why: Reaction time increases logarithmically with choice count: RT = a + b·log₂(n); doubling choices doesn't double decision time.
sources.finding: Reaction time = constant + coefficient × log₂(number of choices); logarithmic growth means menu size moderately increases decision latency.

sources.title: Gorillas in Our Midst: Sustained Inattentional Blindness for Dynamic Events
sources.why: Basketball video: 50% of viewers failed to notice gorilla walking through the court; attention determines what we perceive.
sources.finding: 50% failed to notice unexpected gorilla during attentional task; change blindness reveals perception limited to attended objects, not complete scenes.

sources.title: Processing Fluency and Aesthetic Pleasure
sources.why: Ease of cognitive processing drives aesthetic preference; symmetric, simple, clear stimuli liked more than complex ones.
sources.finding: Processing fluency (mental ease) determines aesthetic preference; easy-to-process stimuli judged as more beautiful, truer, and preferred.

sources.title: Ego Depletion and Self-Regulatory Failure: A Resource Model of Self-Control
sources.why: Ego depletion: initial self-control task reduced persistence on second task; decision fatigue depletes mental resources.
sources.finding: Self-control acts as a muscle: initial restraint reduced subsequent persistence (puzzle-solving); important caveat: 2016 replication with 2,141 participants found no effect.

sources.title: Availability: A Heuristic for Judging Frequency and Probability
sources.why: People judge frequency by ease of recalling examples (availability); systematic bias because memorability ≠ actual frequency.
sources.finding: People estimate event frequency by mental ease of recall, not actual probability; creates systematic biases because visibility and frequency diverge.

sources.title: Effects of a Favor and Liking on Compliance
sources.why: Free Coke study: receiving unsolicited favor doubled raffle ticket purchases even among subjects who disliked the favor-giver.
sources.finding: Unsolicited favor (free Coke) doubled raffle ticket purchases; reciprocity norm obligates return favor regardless of liking or relationship.

sources.title: Robert Cialdini: Authority Matters if You Want to Pre-Suade Others
sources.why: Authority-wearing experimenter: 65% of subjects administered seemingly lethal shocks, showing authority overrides moral judgment.
sources.finding: 65% of subjects delivered maximum shocks when instructed by authority figure; authority principle overrides personal morality and conscience.

sources.title: Serial Position Effect (Primary & recency)
sources.why: Serial position effect: first items (primacy) and last items (recency) recalled better than middle items (forgetting curve).
sources.finding: Recall U-shaped by list position: primacy (first items stored in long-term memory) + recency (last items in working memory); middle items forgotten most.

sources.title: Über die Wirkung von Bereichsbildungen im Spurenfeld
sources.why: Distinctive (isolated) items in a list remembered far better; effect due to focused attention and deeper encoding.
sources.finding: Distinctive items recalled ~30% better; isolation captures attention, deepens encoding, and reduces interference from similar items.

sources.title: The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected: Purchase Acceleration, Illusionary Goal Progress, and Customer Retention
sources.why: Coffee-stamp study: participants accelerated purchases as rewards approached; illusory progress (head-start) increased engagement.
sources.finding: Customers accelerate purchase rate as goal approaches (goal-gradient effect); illusory progress via head-start increases retention and effort without real progress.

sources.title: The Endowed Progress Effect: How Artificial Advancement Increases Effort
sources.why: Pre-filled progress (2 of 10 stamps) compressed perceived distance to goal and boosted commitment dramatically.
sources.finding: Endowed progress (head-start of 2/10 stamps) increased completion rates by compressing psychological goal distance; effect activates goal-gradient acceleration.

sources.title: Using Eye Tracking to Understand Banner Blindness and Improve Website Design
sources.why: Eye-tracking reveals users systematically ignore banner ads; bright, flashing, irrelevant banners suffer worst blindness.
sources.finding: Users' eye gaze avoids banner ads systematically; irrelevant, bright, or flashing banners suffer worst blindness; text ads read ~2x more than display ads.

sources.title: When Product Assortment Leads to Choice Overload: A Conceptual Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.why: Meta-analysis of 99 observations (N=7,202): identified task difficulty, complexity, preference uncertainty, decision goal as choice-overload moderators.
sources.finding: Meta-analysis (99 conditions) found choice-overload effect significant when moderators present (difficulty, complexity, uncertainty); counters Scheibehenne zero-effect finding.

sources.title: The Psychology of Waiting Lines
sources.why: Foundational work: occupied time feels shorter; waits perceived differently by engagement, knowledge, fairness; applies to loading states, processing feedback.
sources.finding: Occupied time (active engagement) feels shorter than unoccupied time equally long; engaged waits feel 2x-3x shorter than empty waits.

sources.title: The Labor Illusion: How Operational Transparency Increases Perceived Value
sources.why: Flight-search study: users with visible progress accepted longer waits (preferred wait over instant result); perceived effort increases valuation.
sources.finding: Visible operational work (progress display) increased perceived value; users willing to wait longer when they see site 'working hard' on their behalf.

sources.title: Faster Progress Bars: Manipulating Perceived Duration with Visual Illusions
sources.why: Animated progress bars with visual illusions (ripple direction, acceleration phases) perceived as ~10% faster without changing actual speed.
sources.finding: Leftward ripples and progressive acceleration in progress bars reduce perceived wait time by ~10%; humans perceive nonlinear time passage.

claims.rule: Design progress bars to decelerate toward completion; users perceive faster completion when bars slow down at the end.
claims.quote: An understanding of which behaviors perceptually shorten or lengthen process duration can be used to engineer a progress bar that appears faster

claims.rule: Avoid linear progress bars; vary acceleration and deceleration to match human time perception rather than actual work completion.
claims.quote: humans do not perceive the passage of time in a linear way. This, coupled with the irregular behavior of progress bars, produces a highly variable perception

sources.title: Extraneous Factors in Judicial Decisions
sources.why: Analysis of 1,100+ parole decisions: early-day/post-break grants ~65%, late-day grants ~0%; tired judges rule in favor of status quo.
sources.finding: Parole grant rate 65% morning vs ~0% late-day; decision fatigue after repeated choices increases status quo bias; judges need cognitive rest.

sources.title: The Information Capacity of the Human Motor System in Controlling the Amplitude of Movement
sources.why: Movement time = a + b·log₂(distance/width); foundational for touch targets, button sizing, mouse control; logarithmic not linear relationship.
sources.finding: Reaction time MT = constant + coefficient × log₂(D/W); larger targets reduce selection time logarithmically; 2x distance ≠ 2x time.

sources.title: The Design of Everyday Things
sources.why: Introduced affordances concept: properties of objects that determine how they're used; feedback, mapping, constraints reduce cognitive load.
sources.finding: Affordances (perceived/actual properties) guide usage; good design uses feedback, mapping, constraints, and conceptual models to align user mental models.

sources.title: Festinger's Law
sources.why: Inconsistent beliefs produce psychological discomfort; people rationalize to reduce dissonance rather than changing behavior (especially after sacrifice).
sources.finding: Cognitive dissonance (conflicting beliefs) triggers rationalization not behavior change; effect strongest when past sacrifice was largest (not smallest).

sources.title: Treatise on Physiological Optics
sources.why: Visual perception is inference from fragmentary sensory data + stored knowledge; illusions reveal perception goes beyond data; perception ≠ sensation.
sources.finding: Visual perception = unconscious inference from sensory data + knowledge; illusions reveal perception involves unconscious logical reasoning, not just sensation.

sources.title: Distributed Practices in Verbal Recall Tasks: A Review and Quantitative Synthesis
sources.why: Meta-analysis: spaced practice superior to massed; optimal gap ~20-40% for 1-week test, 5-10% for 1-year test; too-short gaps worse than too-long.
sources.finding: Optimal review interval = 10-20% of retention period; too-short intervals more harmful than too-long; spaced review ~50% more effective than massed.

sources.title: Status Quo Bias in Decision Making
sources.why: Framing option as status quo increases choice rate vs neutral framing; pervasive bias in insurance, retirement, and health decisions.
sources.finding: Framing as status quo increases selection disproportionately; employees stick with default health insurance regardless of plan quality.

sources.title: Commitment and Consistency
sources.why: Small initial request (petition) led to 76% compliance with large later request vs 17% without foot-in-door; commitment shifts self-perception.
sources.finding: Small commitment (signing petition) increased large request compliance from 17% to 76%; consistency principle: prior commitment signals identity.

sources.title: Predicting Users' First Impressions of Website Aesthetics with a Quantification of Perceived Visual Complexity and Colorfulness
sources.why: 450 websites rated; visual complexity + colorfulness explain ~50% of aesthetic appeal variance at 500ms exposure; preferences vary by demographic.
sources.finding: Visual complexity + colorfulness predict 50% of aesthetic appeal variance in first 500ms; female users prefer more colorful sites than male users.

sources.title: Accountability Diffusion In Ai
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Assign a single, named decision owner accountable for each significant AI deployment's outcomes.
claims.quote: For every significant AI deployment, assign a clearly identified "decision owner" who is accountable for outcomes in that domain.

claims.rule: Map decision chains to expose where responsibility gaps exist in human-AI workflows.
claims.quote: To counter accountability diffusion, teams can map decision chains. Besio and colleagues' work suggests that such mapping helps reveal where responsibility currently stops and where it needs to be strengthened.

claims.rule: Design workflows where questioning AI output is expected and safe, not punished.
claims.quote: Designing workflows where questioning the system is expected and safe.

sources.title: Action Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Affect Heuristic
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Ai Literacy Gap
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Distinguish retrieved facts from generated predictions in AI interfaces; users infer accuracy from fluency and mistake output style for truth.
claims.quote: when the interface feels familiar and the writing sounds polished, it is easy to forget that the system is generating predictions rather than retrieving facts.

claims.rule: Train users on AI capabilities and limitations before deployment; institutions roll out AI tools on productivity expectations while investing little in education.
claims.quote: Organizations may roll out generative AI tools on the expectation that they will increase productivity, while investing little in education about limitations, bias, or verification.

claims.rule: Show confidence ranges and multiple candidate answers to help users form accurate expectations and reduce overreliance on single outputs.
claims.quote: Designers can show confidence ranges, highlight when a response is based on limited context, or present multiple candidate answers side by side.

claims.rule: Place verify buttons beside copy buttons and ask confirmation before sending; prompt users to double-check medical, financial, or legal content.
claims.quote: Small design choices such as placing a 'verify' button beside a 'copy' button, showing source links by default, or asking 'Does this look right?' before sending a message encourage reflection instead of automatic reuse.

claims.rule: Track user corrections, overrides, and questions as healthy signals of engagement, not failures; avoid optimizing only for usage volume and satisfaction.
claims.quote: Teams with higher AI literacy are more likely to track how often users correct, override, or question AI outputs and to treat those behaviors as healthy signals.

sources.title: Ambiguity Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Explain unfamiliar AI systems clearly to users; lack of clarity about how AI works increases hesitation to trust and adopt AI-assisted features.
claims.quote: A lack of clarity prompts unease on the part of the patient, making them hesitant to follow through with the doctor's treatment plan.

sources.title: Anchoring Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Avoid showing irrelevant numbers first; they become reference points that distort judgment of subsequent prices or values.
claims.quote: The initial price of the earrings became your anchor point for evaluating subsequent pricing information, shifting your perspective on what constitutes a good deal.

claims.rule: Ask users to generate counterarguments against initial anchor values during estimation or negotiation tasks to weaken anchoring effects.
claims.quote: Half of the experts were also asked to come up with arguments against the anchor price. These participants showed a weaker anchoring effect compared to those who hadn't come up with counterarguments.

sources.title: Attentional Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Design interfaces to help users broaden focus when facing emotionally charged information by prompting consideration of multiple options.
claims.quote: attentional bias shows up, however, we end up directing a much larger share of our focus toward a single option or stimulus, and this comes at the expense of others

claims.rule: Use visual hierarchy to de-emphasize threat-related or emotionally negative content; anxious users fixate on threatening cues even when irrelevant.
claims.quote: high-anxious individuals were slower to identify shapes, regardless of facial expression, suggesting that they were more fixated on facial cues, even if these cues were not necessarily threatening

sources.title: Authority Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Present evidence and reasoning separately from the messenger's credentials; users struggle to detach message content from the status of who delivers it.
claims.quote: The person's authority becomes the message itself. That is, we find it difficult to detach the content of the message from the status of the person delivering it.

claims.rule: Present expert credentials and evidence as separate elements; users struggle to detach message content from messenger authority, leading to uncritical acceptance.
claims.quote: we find it difficult to detach the content of the message from the status of the person delivering it

claims.rule: Use symbols of authority (titles, badges, certificates) cautiously; subtle authority cues influence trust disproportionately to actual credibility.
claims.quote: Subtle symbols of authority, such as a person's title (Dr, PhD, MD) or job title (CEO or Director), can immediately influence how we perceive the opinions and judgments of that individual

claims.rule: Surface dissenting expert opinions and alternative perspectives with equal visual prominence to majority positions; users default to high-authority voices.
claims.quote: Leaders or experts who are viewed as credible or high-status may have more influence on organizational decisions and strategies, potentially leading to important contributions from less authoritative employees being overlooked

sources.title: Automation Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Require human review of automated recommendations before action; users trust automated tools more than their own judgment, even when contradictory evidence appears.
claims.quote: You trusted the navigation system more than your own judgment, causing you to ignore what you saw with your own eyes.

claims.rule: Show contradictory signals prominently when automated tools conflict with user observation; users often ignore gut feelings and external warnings that contradict automation.
claims.quote: When we encounter contradictory information from another source or something feels off in our gut, we shouldn't ignore it.

claims.rule: Require explicit human review and sign-off before automated systems execute high-stakes decisions; users trust automation more than their own judgment.
claims.quote: Using a clinical decision support system increased prescribing errors by 56.9% when the system gave incorrect recommendations, compared to when clinicians relied on their own judgment without the tool

claims.rule: Limit automation to routine tasks only; apply human review to complex decisions involving multiple tradeoffs and uncertain outcomes.
claims.quote: While automation did a great job of taking over routine tasks, when it was applied to more complex problems involving human decision-making, people were more likely to make mistakes

sources.title: Availability Heuristic
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Bandwagon Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Use opinion polls and majority signals cautiously; they cause moderate-minded users to abandon minority views and conform to the perceived majority.
claims.quote: Opinion polls—regarding issues like climate change and gun control—caused ideologically moderate participants to abandon their minority opinions and conform to the majority, regardless of the topic.

claims.rule: Allow time between exposure to social signals and decision-making; delay decisions to reduce blind adoption of popular ideas.
claims.quote: allowing some time to pass between noticing social signals and making our final decision can allow for critical thinking

claims.rule: Foster psychological safety in teams by responding positively to dissent and experimentation; create space for minority opinions.
claims.quote: creating psychological safety in the workplace can help break cycles of conformity among teams

sources.title: Barnum Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Provide individual feedback to each employee rather than team-wide praise to ensure they internalize it accurately.
claims.quote: higher-ups may want to prioritize providing individual feedback to each employee to guarantee they will accurately relate the feedback back to themselves

claims.rule: Recognize and avoid vague statements in copy that could apply to any user; make claims specific and verifiable.
claims.quote: notice vague descriptions and generalized statements that could resonate with anyone

sources.title: Base Rate Fallacy
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Display aggregate statistics and base rates alongside individual reviews or testimonials in product recommendations.
claims.quote: we might ignore the product's two-star review on Amazon or the fact it had a sudden drop in sales quickly after its release

sources.title: Belief Perseverance
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Enable iterative testing and genuinely solicit feedback to prevent developers from persisting with flawed product concepts.
claims.quote: When developers or businesses cling to initial product concepts or marketing strategies without being receptive to feedback, they risk product failure.

sources.title: Benjamin Franklin Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Request direct feedback or contributions from users rather than using intermediaries to maximize brand likeability.
claims.quote: The results showed that the group who were asked to return their winnings directly by the researcher ended up liking him most. In other words, direct requests for a favor can increase likeability.

sources.title: Bikeshedding
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Prioritize meeting agendas by importance and complexity; allocate time proportionally to task significance, not ease.
claims.quote: you and your coworkers will likely find it much easier to talk about whether or not to get standing desks. As a result, everyone devotes a large portion of the scheduled meeting time to this more trivial matter

sources.title: Bottom Dollar Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Time promotions and special offers to coincide with payday and bonus periods when users have disposable income.
claims.quote: marketers can time their advertising to coincide with when most people have disposable income or are receiving a bonus. This may mean on a Friday, when most people get their paycheck

claims.rule: Time promotions to payday and bonus periods; satisfaction with purchases drops when spending depletes remaining budget.
claims.quote: marketers can time their advertising to coincide with when most people have disposable income or are receiving a bonus

claims.rule: Offer special incentives at end-of-period; discounts and deals reduce pain of payment when budget depletes.
claims.quote: marketers can also use these times as opportunities to use special incentives, like 2 for 1's or discounted rates

claims.rule: Align payment timing with consumption; delay payment methods amplify dissatisfaction when bills arrive during budget shortfalls.
claims.quote: when our bill comes, it is often at the end of the month which may coincide with the end of our budget

sources.title: Bounded Rationality
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Present information in digestible quantities; users cannot process all available data simultaneously due to cognitive limits.
claims.quote: our limited ability to consider all the choices available to us, our incomplete knowledge of all the potential outcomes of our behavior

claims.rule: Support satisficing decisions by highlighting the most relevant information; users optimize for good-enough choices, not perfect ones.
claims.quote: bounded rationality encourages us to make decisions that satisfy a particular criterion, such as being ethical, without making the most optimal choice

claims.rule: Place the most important information at eye level; users choose visible options over equally good hidden alternatives.
claims.quote: grocery stores can place the healthiest items at eye level to make us more likely to choose that option

claims.rule: Avoid vague product labels or claims; users satisfice with misleading information rather than investigate further.
claims.quote: Companies often label their products with enticing qualifiers with little-to-no meaning, such as the term 'cage-free' on a carton of eggs

sources.title: Bundling Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Show individual item prices clearly when offering bundles; bundling obscures per-item cost and reduces perceived waste.
claims.quote: bundling leads to a decoupling of transaction costs and benefits. What this means is that bundling items together makes the cost of each individual item less obvious

claims.rule: Physically separate bundled items at purchase and display, even if monetarily bundled, to make per-item costs visible.
claims.quote: physically separating the items can ensure consumers actually get the full value of their purchase

claims.rule: Require users to consciously calculate per-item cost before confirming bundle purchases to counteract bundling bias.
claims.quote: calculate the cost of each individual item, to see how much of the package we would have to use to make our purchase worth it

sources.title: Bye Now Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Cashless Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Show transaction friction for high-value purchases; digital payments reduce psychological pain and increase spending beyond intent.
claims.quote: physically parting with cash triggers a psychological response—where we feel the pain of spending significantly more. The absence of physical notes and coins disrupts the mental connection

claims.rule: Use friction to encourage intentional spending: require confirmation steps for digital transactions that users would reconsider with cash.
claims.quote: Credit card payments and digital payments are also much faster, reducing the amount of time we have to reconsider a purchase that might be over our budget

claims.rule: Add confirmation steps and friction for digital transactions to restore the psychological pain of payment and reduce impulsive overspending.
claims.quote: Credit card payments and digital payments are also much faster, reducing the amount of time we have to reconsider a purchase

sources.title: Category Size Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Choice Overload Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Limit product or option counts to reduce decision fatigue; more than 22 options significantly increases abandonment.
claims.quote: One study found that offering shoppers more than 22 options increased the likelihood that they would not make any choice

claims.rule: Highlight defaults early in multi-step decisions; users deplete decision-making capacity and revert to defaults later.
claims.quote: people buying cars chose more default features at the end of the buying process than at the beginning, suggesting that selecting among various options earlier in the process had depleted their decision-making capacity

claims.rule: Limit choice sets to 22 or fewer options to maintain purchase intent and reduce decision paralysis.
claims.quote: offering shoppers more than 22 options increased the likelihood that they would not make any choice

claims.rule: Separate browsing intent from purchase intent; allow users to explore options without commitment pressure to reduce cognitive load.
claims.quote: we are less likely to feel the effects of choice overload when we don't put any pressure on ourselves to commit to one option

claims.rule: Frame choices as final or nonreversible to reduce post-choice regret and rumination, even if returns are technically possible.
claims.quote: treating your choices as nonreversible (even if they technically are) can shut down this process before it gets started

claims.rule: Provide expert or domain-specific information to users with low knowledge to prevent paralysis when faced with many options.
claims.quote: when consumers are considered to be experts in a domain, the effect of choice overload is reversed

sources.title: Cognitive Dissonance
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Present information that aligns with users' existing beliefs to reduce psychological discomfort and resistance.
claims.quote: To create psychological consistency between his environmental beliefs and his not-so-environmental actions, John dismisses the lecture as misinformation

sources.title: Commitment Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Surface new information clearly when past commitments may no longer serve users' current goals.
claims.quote: We continue engaging in behaviors that may have made sense in the past but are no longer rational, given the information we have now.

sources.title: Confirmation Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Design for exploratory thought by prompting users to consider multiple viewpoints before deciding, not just rationalizing one belief.
claims.quote: exploratory thought, which takes into consideration many viewpoints before deciding where you stand

claims.rule: Encourage debate and interpersonal discussion in decision workflows to expose users to information they may have otherwise avoided.
claims.quote: Engaging in debate is a productive way to challenge our views and expose ourselves to information we may have otherwise avoided

sources.title: Decision Fatigue
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Schedule critical decisions and important meetings early in the day, before cognitive resources deplete.
claims.quote: we also make better decisions earlier in the day. To avoid decision fatigue, we can schedule work meetings and critical decision-making at the beginning of the day

claims.rule: Reduce the number of choices users must make per task; deploy AI or defaults to eliminate low-value decisions.
claims.quote: Reducing necessary choices or decisions is a common technique used to curb decision fatigue

claims.rule: Limit visible product or option counts to prevent choice overload; 74% of shoppers abandon carts when overwhelmed by options.
claims.quote: 74% of shoppers say they have abandoned their online shopping cart because they were too overwhelmed by all the options

claims.rule: Use decision-minimization tools to guide users through large option sets; tested approach reduced decisions by 39% while increasing satisfaction.
claims.quote: it decreased the number of decisions by 39% compared to heuristic strategies and by 20% relative to standard recommendation systems. Users were also found to be more satisfied

claims.rule: Ensure users eat or maintain blood glucose before decision-heavy workflows; glucose replenishment reverses ego depletion and improves choice quality.
claims.quote: supplying glucose helped individuals mitigate ego depletion and sometimes completely reversed it. The replenished willpower would enhance people's capacity for self-control and improve their decision-making abilities

sources.title: Declinism
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Decoy Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Price options clearly and objectively so users compare based on actual value, not relative positioning.
claims.quote: We tend to make decisions based less on which option best suits our purposes and more on what feels like the most advantageous choice.

sources.title: Delegation Creep
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Signal automation failures visibly; operators overlook problems the system does not flag.
claims.quote: decision makers miss problems the system does not flag and follow incorrect recommendations after good past performance

claims.rule: Design AI aids to preserve operator judgment; framing as accurate erodes critical review under pressure.
claims.quote: when tools are framed as accurate and efficient, people become more willing to lean on them and less inclined to question their recommendations, especially under time pressure

claims.rule: Limit scope creep of automated systems; gradual expansion into new uses increases harm without governance upgrades.
claims.quote: once in place, these systems are frequently expanded to new uses without a corresponding upgrade in governance or worker voice

claims.rule: Define which decisions AI may make alone, which require human review with criteria, and which must remain human-led.
claims.quote: Organizations can map tasks into tiers: low-stakes routine, medium-stakes judgment, and high-stakes critical decisions. For each tier, they can specify which tasks AI may perform alone, which require human review with clear criteria, and which must remain human-led.

claims.rule: Provide clear appeal processes and explanation mechanisms so affected people can contest AI-influenced decisions.
claims.quote: Clear appeal processes, explanation mechanisms, and support for contesting outcomes can help surface harms and boundary breaches early.

sources.title: Disposition Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Show investors their long-term portfolio performance, not individual stock gains or losses, to reduce emotional trading.
claims.quote: providing investors with a graph that showed their total portfolio performance helped shift their focus from individual stock gains/losses to overall wealth accumulation

sources.title: Distinction Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Separate option display to reduce overvaluing minor differences; joint comparison inflates perceived importance of trivial gaps.
claims.quote: when we directly compare our options, we become hypersensitive to any differences that exist between them. This makes the differences seem glaringly obvious

sources.title: Dunning Kruger Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Invite feedback from peers and experts on your work; overconfident people resist learning and share unvetted information.
claims.quote: overconfident individuals extremely resistant to being taught—since they believe they know the most—but they are also guilty of sharing the most information

claims.rule: Use 360-degree feedback systems so employees see their performance rated by multiple sources, not just their own self-assessment.
claims.quote: Implement 360-degree feedback systems to give employees a well-rounded view of their performance, helping them better understand their strengths and areas for improvement

claims.rule: Display objective performance metrics alongside self-ratings to align employee self-perception with measurable reality.
claims.quote: Use Objective Metrics: Rely on data-driven performance metrics to provide employees with a clear, accurate picture of their progress

sources.title: Einstellung Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Prompt exploration of multiple solution paths; familiar approaches block discovery of more efficient alternatives.
claims.quote: The Einstellung effect describes when we approach a problem with a mindset that worked for us in the past, even if a more efficient solution exists

sources.title: Empathy Gap
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Design for users in distress by incorporating lived-experience feedback, not assumptions from calm states.
claims.quote: A designer who hasn't got technical support from a professional psychologist may struggle to anticipate the needs, emotions, and decision-making processes of users who are experiencing distress, anxiety, or depression

sources.title: Endowment Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Avoid features that artificially increase perceived ownership; users will overvalue products they feel they own.
claims.quote: any tactic that makes us feel a sense of psychological ownership over a product can encourage us to spend more on it

claims.rule: Design free trials carefully: they create virtual ownership that leads users to pay for services they may not need.
claims.quote: Free trials give us a sense of virtual ownership, or the feeling that we already own a product before we do, which can make us feel emotionally attached to a product before we decide to buy it

sources.title: Extrinsic Incentive Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Design reward schemes assuming users value intrinsic rewards; do not rely only on monetary incentives.
claims.quote: you may incorporate some coupon codes to incentivize users. By neglecting the potential intrinsic rewards that may actually resonate more with a user than the extrinsic ones, you are failing to adequately optimize an incentive framework

sources.title: False Consensus Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: In team or collaborative tools, explicitly surface dissent and minority opinions to counter groupthink.
claims.quote: Groupthink occurs when groups strive to reach a consensus while minimizing conflicts, causing individuals to set aside their opinions in favor of the group majority

claims.rule: Seek real-world data and diverse user feedback rather than projecting your own preferences onto product design decisions.
claims.quote: Instead of assuming that others share your views or preferences, seek hard data to confirm or refute these assumptions

sources.title: Framing Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: When presenting pricing tiers, frame the middle option as the best value to discourage selection of the cheapest plan.
claims.quote: the middle tier is often framed as the best value option, discouraging users from opting for the cheapest plan

claims.rule: Frame new technology features as enhancing human ability and saving time, not as replacing human skills or invading privacy.
claims.quote: emphasizing how AI can enhance our human abilities, help us save time, or reduce our workloads rather than pointing out its potential to take our jobs

sources.title: Functional Fixedness
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Design interfaces to suggest multiple affordances for common objects; avoid implying single purposes.
claims.quote: Functional fixedness leads us to recognize only one affordance in an object when, in fact, there may be multiple

claims.rule: Present objects with multiple visual contexts or uses to help users recognize diverse affordances beyond conventional functions.
claims.quote: seeing pictures led participants to rely more on existing, top-down knowledge when generating unusual uses, resulting in less innovative responses than when they were exposed only to object names

sources.title: Fundamental Attribution Error
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Provide clear prompt guidance and examples to help users supply sufficient context, preventing them from blaming AI tools for poor outputs due to vague inputs.
claims.quote: Most will stress the importance of being detailed and specific, as well as providing clear context to the problem you wish to solve

sources.title: Gamblers Fallacy
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Google Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Information learned in context is recalled more accurately than information accessed via search.
claims.quote: information learned online is recalled less accurately than information learned from an encyclopedia

claims.rule: Encourage handwritten note-taking over passive reading to strengthen memory encoding.
claims.quote: Taking hand-written notes instead of just skimming also helps us actively store facts in our long-term memory

claims.rule: Provide frequent retrieval opportunities for learned material; memory strength depends on retrieval frequency.
claims.quote: the strength of memory is directly tied to how frequently memories are retrieved

claims.rule: Show information location explicitly when saving or storing; users remember access paths better than content.
claims.quote: participants better recalled which statements were saved than which were erased, suggesting that when we believe we will be able to access the information later, we remember how to access it rather than the information itself

sources.title: Halo Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Label products neutrally; health-related labeling inflates product ratings beyond actual quality.
claims.quote: when the same food products are labeled either 'organic' or 'conventional,' the 'organic' products receive higher ratings and consumers are willing to pay more for them

claims.rule: Use neutral product labels; health-related or premium labeling inflates perceived quality beyond actual product performance.
claims.quote: when the same food products are labeled either 'organic' or 'conventional,' the 'organic' products receive higher ratings and consumers are willing to pay more

sources.title: Hard Easy Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Show confidence calibration feedback; users overestimate ability on hard tasks and underestimate on easy ones.
