claims.quote: Our confidence usually doesn't match our actual ability, which can cause us to be ill-prepared when taking on hard tasks, and stress over easy tasks.

sources.title: Heuristics
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Reserve heuristic shortcuts for low-stakes decisions; require careful reasoning for high-impact choices.
claims.quote: The real problem occurs when we use heuristics for high-stakes decisions, where careful thought and objective rationality can help us avoid making serious errors.

claims.rule: Reserve System 1 thinking for low-stakes decisions; switch to System 2 deliberation for choices with significant consequences.
claims.quote: the goal is to use heuristics for decisions that don't require effortful, conscious thought—like deciding what to eat for breakfast—while switching to careful reasoning for high-stakes decisions, such as managing our finances or hiring employees.

claims.rule: In complex information contexts, actively seek diverse sources rather than relying on easily accessible or memorable examples.
claims.quote: heuristics can be avoided by making judgments more effortfully, but in doing so, we must actively seek diverse information and evidence instead of relying solely on information that is easily accessible and available.

sources.title: Hindsight Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Show decision-makers the uncertainty they faced at the time; reveal prior alternatives to prevent overconfidence.
claims.quote: Hindsight bias describes how we project this current knowledge onto the past, making it difficult to remember the uncertainty we initially faced

claims.rule: Ask users to log decisions and their predictions before outcomes are known to create an unalterable record and prevent memory distortion.
claims.quote: keep track of your past decisions and their associated predictions. This can be done in what's known as a 'decision journal'

sources.title: Hot Hand Fallacy
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Show users their full historical average alongside recent performance streaks to counter overconfidence in short-term trends.
claims.quote: The hot hand fallacy leads us to take a small pool of data—the opening minutes of one game—as a better indicator of future performance than an average save percentage calculated from seasons' worth of data.

claims.rule: In habit and progress trackers, warn users that recent success does not guarantee future performance and prepare them for inevitable plateaus and dips.
claims.quote: Learning skills are never linear. There will always be ups and downs in our curve towards success. But the hot hand fallacy may cause us to only anticipate the upward trends when using these apps, rather than preparing us for the dips yet to come.

claims.rule: Base AI system predictions on large historical datasets, not recent successful outputs, to prevent over-reliance when the algorithm shows a streak of quality.
claims.quote: when algorithms chug out numerous high-quality outputs in a row, we may expect the same level of quality for all future outputs. Statistically speaking, perfection is impossible

sources.title: Hyperbolic Discounting
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Prime users toward long-term thinking via words like 'future' and 'long-term' to reduce impulsive choices.
claims.quote: being exposed to words like 'future,' 'long-term,' and 'self-control' actually made participants more likely to think of themselves and their future

sources.title: Identifiable Victim Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Use specific named individuals with photos, not statistics, to drive donations and engagement.
claims.quote: statistics feel impersonal and cold whereas we can often visualize a particular individual in need

claims.rule: Show specific impact and outcomes tied to individual stories, not aggregate statistics.
claims.quote: charities can market their cause in a manner that is more likely to get them donations and help. Instead of relying on statistics, they may distribute materials that showcase a particular individual

claims.rule: Explicitly invite users to feel emotion; suppress default emotional regulation to increase help for multiple victims.
claims.quote: when prompted to allow ourselves to feel emotions, the identifiable victim effect can be reduced

sources.title: Ikea Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Ensure assembly or creation tasks are simple enough to succeed; failed completion destroys the effect.
claims.quote: when people failed to complete the box-building project or destroyed their Lego creations, the effect dissipated

claims.rule: Ask users for external feedback on self-made work to counteract overconfidence bias.
claims.quote: A simple strategy to deal with this is to make a habit of asking others for feedback

sources.title: Illusion Of Control
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Avoid designing interfaces that reward streak-based confidence; surface base rates and historical failure rates to counter false control beliefs.
claims.quote: a short streak of early wins—often called 'beginner's luck'—can dramatically inflate a person's perceived control over random outcomes

claims.rule: In uncertain systems, show users the limits of their influence and provide structured, systematic decision tools instead of relying on intuition.
claims.quote: those in charge often overestimated their ability to predict and manage the future through individual foresight practices, rather than relying on formal, systematic foresight methods

sources.title: Illusion Of Transparency
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Prompt explicit communication of intentions and feelings rather than relying on users to believe their state is obvious to others.
claims.quote: Individuals might refrain from expressing their true feelings or concerns due to the illusion that others can easily discern their emotions.

sources.title: Illusion Of Validity
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Recognize that confidence in predictions does not correlate with prediction accuracy; low information makes false certainty easier.
claims.quote: The less information we have, the easier it is to put together a satisfying story, which can lead us to believe that we know more than we actually do.

claims.rule: Surface base rates and objective statistics alongside individuating details in prediction or recommendation contexts; do not rely on pattern consistency alone.
claims.quote: we tend to ignore base rate information in favor of individuating information

claims.rule: Require critical analysis of missing information and alternative outcomes before committing to high-stakes decisions; prompt contingency planning.
claims.quote: Coming up with alternate predictions or developing contingency plans can help you prepare for different outcomes than the one you predicted

sources.title: Illusory Correlation
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Do not assume causation from repeated coincidence; use caution when rare events cluster by time or place.
claims.quote: We see that certain events consistently occur at the same time as, or just after, other events, leading us to conclude that they are somehow related.

claims.rule: Beware that authority figures spreading false correlations increase public acceptance; verify sources before accepting novel claims.
claims.quote: If the public learns about a flawed correlation between two events or factors from an individual with authority, they are more likely to accept it as truth.

sources.title: Illusory Truth Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Limit repetition of statements; even one second exposure increases perceived truth, with largest effect after second encounter.
claims.quote: all it takes is one repeated exposure of a given statement to increase our perception of truth

claims.rule: Present factual claims in statement form, not opinion form, to reduce illusory truth effects.
claims.quote: information presented as fact (e.g., "The diameter of the moon is 2,160 miles") is more likely to produce the illusory truth effect than information presented as opinion

claims.rule: Evaluate truthfulness of claims on first encounter; users who assess accuracy avoid illusory truth effects better than those who evaluate interestingness.
claims.quote: when participants had initially been asked to evaluate truthfulness instead of interestingness, they didn't show signs of the illusory truth effect

claims.rule: Warn users that familiar statements feel true even when false; awareness of processing fluency helps resist illusory truth.
claims.quote: ease of processing is our go-to tool to judge whether something is true, and it's only if that fails that we turn to our knowledge for help

sources.title: Impact Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Do not prioritize exciting features over usability; users adapt to environments slower than designers expect, so foundational reliability matters more.
claims.quote: designers often prioritize a product's most exciting features while overlooking features that users actually want

claims.rule: Help users broaden focus when predicting outcomes; narrowly focused predictions inflate expected emotional impact by 20–40 percent.
claims.quote: thinking about other future events or activities, rather than fixating on one, helps us acknowledge their collective influence on our future emotions. Studies show that people moderate their emotional forecasts when they think more broadly about their upcoming experiences

sources.title: In Group Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Incentivization
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Use external incentives cautiously; over-reliance on rewards reduces intrinsic motivation and engagement once incentives are removed.
claims.quote: relying on incentives can sap other intrinsic motivations to do things

claims.rule: Avoid rewarding high-effort tasks with external incentives; incentives reduce creativity and risk-taking by pushing users toward the easiest solution rather than the best one.
claims.quote: When people have been offered a reward to do something, they try to make the job as easy as possible, minimizing difficulty. This results in less creativity

sources.title: Just World Hypothesis
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: When marketing fair-trade or ethical products, emphasize concrete consumer agency and impact rather than highlighting injustice alone; frame choices as direct remedies, not distant moral obligations.
claims.quote: if they are shown that their purchases can actively help reduce injustice, they become more likely to buy fair-trade products

claims.rule: Design decision-support interfaces to prompt System 2 thinking (deliberate, slower analysis) by forcing users to review full context and alternative explanations before finalizing judgments about people or outcomes.
claims.quote: Slowing down the process by which we make our judgments and considering all of the information at hand allows us to make better decisions

sources.title: Lag Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Space repetitions of critical information over time rather than massing them together to improve long-term retention.
claims.quote: the longer the time between repetitions of information, the more likely we are to commit that information to memory

claims.rule: For retention beyond 7 days, space review sessions at least one day apart; for longer delays, extend spacing to 10 days or more.
claims.quote: the optimal length of time for teachers to repeat information to students is likely between one and ten days

sources.title: Law Of The Instrument
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Less Is Better Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Provide reference points and distribution information for attributes difficult to evaluate in isolation (e.g., horsepower, GPA, experience count).
claims.quote: when it's difficult to evaluate an object in isolation, people tend to think about other objects in the same category to use as a reference point

claims.rule: Minimize salience of negative attributes on superior options; ensure positive attributes are equally prominent across all choices.
claims.quote: people's impressions of the objectively superior option are often handicapped by a highly salient, negative feature

sources.title: Leveling And Sharpening
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Levels Of Processing Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Link new information to existing knowledge or imagery rather than relying on structural repetition alone for deeper encoding.
claims.quote: if we associate those terms with other information or imagery, it is encoded at a deep level and is easier to remember

claims.rule: Encode information semantically by relating it to meaning, emotion, or prior knowledge rather than structurally or phonemically.
claims.quote: A deep level of encoding occurs when we process information semantically, by associating it with emotion, idea or previous knowledge

claims.rule: Link new interface information to users' existing knowledge, emotions, or passions rather than relying on repetition alone.
claims.quote: if we associate new information with something meaningful, we are more likely to remember it

sources.title: Look Elsewhere Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Loss Aversion
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Frame options highlighting potential gains rather than risks to reduce loss-averse decision-making.
claims.quote: Phrasing a question as a loss may increase loss aversion, while phrasing that same question as a gain may reduce loss aversion, leading to a more calculated response.

claims.rule: Understand that loss intensity is roughly twice as powerful as equivalent gain in user motivation and decision-making.
claims.quote: losses are twice as powerful compared to their equivalent gains, a foundational concept of prospect theory.

sources.title: Mental Accounting
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Highlight sunk costs as non-recoverable to help users make forward-looking decisions rather than past-protecting ones.
claims.quote: the $100 is a sunk cost: it is spent, and no matter what you do, you will still be out $100

claims.rule: Segregate gains visually and in messaging; integrate losses to reduce perceived pain of larger purchases.
claims.quote: people are generally happiest when gains are segregated and losses are integrated. Even if the outcome is the same, we respond very differently depending on how things are presented.

claims.rule: Show sunk costs as already spent and non-recoverable; emphasize forward-looking value to prevent sunk-cost-fallacy decisions.
claims.quote: the $100 is a sunk cost: it is spent, and no matter what you do, you will still be out $100. If the costs of getting to the concert venue are greater than the pleasure you will get from seeing the show, then at the end of the day, going will result in a worse outcome than staying home.

sources.title: Mere Exposure Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Messenger Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Use credible messengers—trusted experts or authority figures—to present critical information or recommendations.
claims.quote: If we believe the messenger is credible, then we are more likely to accept the information at face value

claims.rule: When presenting opposing viewpoints or critical information, attribute them to highly credible sources to increase acceptance likelihood by 3x.
claims.quote: When readers were told that a credible author wrote the opposing viewpoint, they were three times more likely to change their opinion than those who thought the source was not credible.

claims.rule: Use pediatrician-created or endorsed health materials rather than generic content to increase parent adoption of self-care resources for minor childhood illnesses.
claims.quote: parents were more likely to use self-diagnosis charts and home treatment resources if pediatricians approved or created the material.

sources.title: Motivating Uncertainty Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Frame promotions as gamified chances to win rather than guaranteed discounts to increase engagement and resource investment.
claims.quote: a more effective means of garnering customer interest would be to hold a promotion such as 'win a chance at a free sweater when you spend 200.00$ or more!' The uncertain reward generates more excitement

claims.rule: Use variable reward schedules in reward programs rather than fixed rewards to sustain user engagement and reduce task abandonment.
claims.quote: Variable schedules are more unpredictable, which makes the behavior less prone to extinction. Behavioral extinction is when an organism ceases to engage in a certain learned behavior and it happens less quickly for randomized, rather than fixed schedules.

sources.title: Naive Allocation
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Present investment or resource-allocation options in a single unified list rather than separate category lists to reduce arbitrary equal distribution.
claims.quote: When the investment options are listed together, we view them as all fitting into the same category. When they are listed separately, we view them as distinct categories.

claims.rule: Use sequential rather than simultaneous choice presentation when decisions should reflect considered preference, not diversification bias.
claims.quote: Simultaneous choice is when we are given multiple decisions to make at the same time, whereas sequential choice is when we make multiple decisions one after the other.

sources.title: Naive Realism
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Test designs with users from multiple backgrounds, abilities, and cognitive styles to avoid assuming your perspective is universal.
claims.quote: When designers assume their perspective is universal, they might conclude that their designs are inherently intuitive, overlooking usability challenges for people with different abilities, cognitive styles, or cultural backgrounds.

claims.rule: Design interfaces assuming users have different mental models; test with diverse users to uncover perspective gaps.
claims.quote: Designers might not realize how much of their perspective is shaped by their experience and knowledge—and that most users don't possess the same understanding that they do.

claims.rule: Actively seek negative usability feedback; treat it as design truth, not user error.
claims.quote: designers might attribute negative responses to user error, missing key opportunities to improve the product for their intended users

sources.title: Negativity Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Balance error messages and critical feedback with equal-weight positive reinforcement in error and state-change copy to counteract negativity bias.
claims.quote: Negativity bias causes amplified emotional responses to negative events compared to positive events of equal magnitude.

claims.rule: Respond visibly to negative reviews in product interfaces; inaction amplifies negative perception.
claims.quote: Managing and responding to negative reviews in a constructive and public manner can help to mitigate these effects.

sources.title: Noble Edge Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Do not rely on halo effects from social responsibility to mask product quality gaps.
claims.quote: we are more likely to use the halo effect to form judgments regarding the quality of products sold at a store when we are unfamiliar with that type of product

sources.title: Normalcy Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Use premortem exercises to help teams imagine failure modes before launch; ask what could go wrong and why.
claims.quote: Make a premortem: humans are really good at revisiting and dissecting past negative events to try to understand the cause. While postmortems look backwards, premortems imagine potential disasters and explore their likely causes.

claims.rule: Make multiple forecasts (low, medium, high estimate) for outcomes instead of planning for a single scenario.
claims.quote: Make three estimates or forecasts for the future: when predicting a potential outcome, make a low, medium, and high estimate.

sources.title: Nostalgia Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: In marketing or persuasive copy, recognize that imagery evoking shared memories increases spending and social connectedness; use intentionally only for genuinely valuable offers.
claims.quote: Nostalgia elicits feelings of social connectedness, making us feel as though we have a social network in which we belong.

claims.rule: Recognize that nostalgic design increases perceived social connectedness, making money feel less important; this effect is specific to spending, not time.
claims.quote: participants who had recalled a nostalgic memory gave away more money, but not more time, than participants who had recalled a neutral memory

sources.title: Observer Expectancy Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Minimize researcher-participant communication and environmental cues that hint at study hypotheses to prevent biased responses.
claims.quote: demand characteristics are subtle cues from the experimenter that may give the participants some idea of what the study is about

claims.rule: Use double-blind study design where neither participants nor researchers know group assignment to prevent unconscious bias in treatment.
claims.quote: A double-blind research design can be effective in preventing the observer expectancy effect. In studies with this design, neither the participants nor the researchers know which participants are in the experimental group or which are in the control group.

claims.rule: Avoid leading questions and treat all study groups identically; even subtle verbal or non-verbal cues from researchers influence participant behavior.
claims.quote: researchers may ask participants leading questions, which prompt a specific response, or even treat participants in a way that elicits the desired behavior

sources.title: Omission Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Default to user benefit in bundled features; avoid pre-checked boxes that exploit omission bias to charge for unwanted extras.
claims.quote: When additional features are bundled with a product or service by default, such as checked luggage and seat selection on a plane fare, omission bias may make users less likely to opt-out

claims.rule: Store payment methods by default to reduce checkout friction and lower cart abandonment via omission bias.
claims.quote: shopping apps commonly have a default option to store credit card information for future purchases, making it less likely that a customer will abandon their shopping cart

sources.title: Optimism Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Surface concrete failure rates, base rates, and historical data prominently to counter optimism bias when users evaluate their own likelihood of success.
claims.quote: Tom exhibits the optimism bias because he refuses to take into consideration the past six businesses that failed before him as well as the environmental factors working against him

claims.rule: Surface base rates and historical failure data to ground user estimates in reality and counter optimism bias.
claims.quote: Look for statistics on how long it takes to complete the type of task on average. These are your base rates

claims.rule: Use premortem exercises: ask teams to imagine project failure and list causes before launch to surface blind spots.
claims.quote: Everyone on the team is instructed to imagine it is a year from the present and the project has failed. They are then instructed to write out what has gone wrong and why.

sources.title: Ostrich Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Break goals into specific, measurable milestones and display progress visibly to motivate monitoring and counter avoidance.
claims.quote: set clear, specific goals and break them into manageable steps so you can track your progress with objective measures

sources.title: Outcome Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Show users the decision process and reasoning behind recommendations, not only the final outcome, to prevent outcome bias from distorting future trust.
claims.quote: most postmortems are written as if the outcome was the only true measure of wisdom

claims.rule: Record decision reasoning, assumptions, and uncertainties before outcomes occur; compare afterward against actual information available.
claims.quote: Encourage decision-makers to record their reasoning before key choices: assumptions, data sources, alternative options, and known uncertainties.

claims.rule: Separate learning reviews (system behavior, weak signals) from accountability reviews; hold both conversations.
claims.quote: A learning review that focuses on system behavior, weak signals, tradeoffs, and how similar events can be prevented. A formal accountability review that applies clear standards to individual conduct.

sources.title: Overjustification Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Use positive feedback and verbal praise over tangible or monetary rewards; verbal reinforcement maintains intrinsic motivation longer.
claims.quote: Participants who received these verbal rewards maintained their motivation across puzzle-solving sessions—even after removing them—while control groups showed declining motivation.

sources.title: Parasocial Trust In Ai
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Design conversational AI with warmth, name-use, and memory of user details to build trust and engagement.
claims.quote: When an AI system speaks in a warm, conversational way, remembers details, and responds with empathy, people begin to feel a sense of relationship and safety.

claims.rule: Avoid framing AI as a supportive partner or confidant unless intentionally managing disclosure risk and consent clarity.
claims.quote: The more the relationship mimics that of a 'supportive partner,' behavioral recommendations may feel like relational obligations rather than optional suggestions.

claims.rule: Place transparent non-human disclosures at moments of high compliance (onboarding, first use, sensitive flows) with plain language.
claims.quote: Use clear, repeated disclosures in onboarding, first use, and sensitive flows, with plain language such as 'I am an AI system that predicts text based on patterns in data.'

claims.rule: Separate relational warmth (emotional processing) from high-stakes guidance (money, medicine, law) with distinct decision paths and human review.
claims.quote: Let the chatbot provide warmth for emotional processing, then route decisions about medication, money, or legal steps into a separate 'decision support' path with tighter framing, extra prompts, and human review.

claims.rule: Add deliberate friction before major decisions: offer step-back prompts showing alternatives people in similar situations consider.
claims.quote: Use step-back prompts before major decisions, such as 'Here are the alternatives people in your situation often consider.'

claims.rule: Let users control relational tone: offer settings to dial warmth up or down, choose context memory, and select proactive topics.
claims.quote: Systems can offer settings that let people dial the tone up or down, choose when the AI remembers context, and control what kinds of topics it can proactively raise.

sources.title: Peak End Rule
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: End user experiences with a positive moment or interaction to shape lasting memory of the entire experience.
claims.quote: The peak-end rule influences our evaluations of experiences and can impact human behavior, decision making, and perceptions in both positive and negative ways.

claims.rule: Highlight or create peaks during onboarding and key moments to anchor positive memory of the overall experience.
claims.quote: We tend to recall an event based primarily on its most emotionally intense moments (both good and bad) and how it ends, rather than the entire experience as a whole.

claims.rule: End product interactions on a high note, ensuring the final moment leaves a strong positive emotional impression.
claims.quote: by ending experiences on a high note, it's typical that they will be remembered in a more positive light

claims.rule: Create measurable peaks during critical moments in user flows to anchor positive recall of the entire experience.
claims.quote: we tend to recall an event based primarily on its most emotionally intense moments (both good and bad) and how it ends

claims.rule: End conversational AI interactions with warm, personalized closing statements to create positive memory of the entire exchange.
claims.quote: polite the bot is when your conversation comes to an end. It may leave you with a personalized, warm response such as "I'm glad I could help!

sources.title: Pessimism Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Planning Fallacy
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Display historical task duration or past project data to help users estimate timelines more realistically.
claims.quote: A hallmark of the planning fallacy is that we tend to maintain our optimism about how long a task will take despite historical evidence that contradicts it.

claims.rule: Break large projects into smaller subtasks for estimation; users estimate small task completion accurately but consistently underestimate large ones.
claims.quote: we are much better at planning for small ones: often, our estimates are remarkably accurate, and at worst, they are overestimates

claims.rule: Display historical completion data from similar past tasks to help users set realistic timelines for new projects.
claims.quote: If an organization or individual has completed similar projects in the past, they can use the outcomes of those previous experiences to set goals for new ones

sources.title: Pluralistic Ignorance
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Prompt round-table discussion where each member shares views individually to break assumed agreement and surface actual disagreement.
claims.quote: prompting a round-table discussion where each member shares their opinion can break the cycle of assumed agreement

sources.title: Present Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Primacy Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Present the most important information first in any sequence to maximize recall and decision influence.
claims.quote: The primacy effect plays a crucial role in human memory, recall of items, learning, and even first impressions

claims.rule: Place highest-rated or best-selling items at the top of lists to leverage positive first impressions on purchasing decisions.
claims.quote: Marketers understand this and often highlight the most positive feedback first or structure websites so their best-selling or highest-rated items appear at the top

claims.rule: In ballot, list, or choice interfaces, randomize order of equally valid options to prevent position bias from unfairly influencing selection.
claims.quote: In 71 of the 79 elections, candidates who were listed first garnered more votes when listed first than when placed in other positions

claims.rule: Place most critical content and highest-rated items at the start of sequences to maximize recall and positive framing.
claims.quote: students are more likely to remember information introduced at the beginning of a learning session, it makes sense to front-load the most critical content early

claims.rule: Vary sequence and repeat key points throughout content to reduce overreliance on first-presented information.
claims.quote: Try to vary the sequence or repeat key points throughout to reduce overreliance on what comes first

sources.title: Priming
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Use semantically related words and concepts near each other to prime users toward desired associations and faster recognition.
claims.quote: If you are first presented with the word 'doctor' a moment later, when presented with a list of unrelated words, you will recognize 'nurse' much faster than 'cat'

claims.rule: Introduce achievement-related language in interface copy and messaging to increase user effectiveness and engagement.
claims.quote: When a CEO primed his team with emails that contained achievement-related words (ex, prevail, accomplish, master), effectiveness rose by 15%, and efficiency rose by 35% over the workweek

claims.rule: Preview study materials before high-stakes tasks to reduce error rates and improve learning outcomes.
claims.quote: letting students preview a study list for an upcoming exam—can help reduce error rates and improve learning outcomes

sources.title: Projection Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: When presenting options, acknowledge that users' current emotional state may not reflect their future preferences and needs.
claims.quote: We project our current state of hunger into our predictions of how much we could eat later and as a result waste money and food

claims.rule: Avoid applying time-limited discounts or offers at moments of peak emotional engagement; defer decision points to a neutral emotional state.
claims.quote: A ski resort offering you a 10% discount on an annual pass when people return their equipment at the end of using a day pass. They are banking on the projection bias; that, in the moment, we will overestimate how many times we will come skiing that year

sources.title: Reactive Devaluation
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: In negotiation flows, present concession lists tied to prior user-stated preferences to reduce devaluation of offers.
claims.quote: the concessions she makes will be explicitly linked to the preferences he has stated. Consequently, when Jack receives this proposal there is less of a chance that he will say, 'Well.. if Jill is offering this up to me it must not have any value' and reject it

claims.rule: Offer users a menu of concession choices rather than a single proposal to maintain their sense of control and reduce rejection of fair offers.
claims.quote: creating 'concession menus', where we create a list of choices of concessions that the other party can pick from. This initiates a back-and-forth between the two parties and allows each side to maintain some level of control

sources.title: Recency Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Repeat key steps or information throughout a sequential process, not just at the beginning, to prevent users forgetting critical steps.
claims.quote: When presented with information in a sequential manner—that is, one after another—our brains are hardwired to remember the information that was most recently presented to us

claims.rule: Slow the presentation pace of sequential information and avoid verbal-only delivery to reduce recency effect strength.
claims.quote: the recency effect is stronger for longer lists of items and tends to occur more when the information is presented verbally rather than visually

claims.rule: Users recall the final 2–3 items in a sequence with double the accuracy of middle items; design accordingly.
claims.quote: the probability of recalling the first and last items on a list could be up to two times that of items in the middle of the list

sources.title: Regret Aversion
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Downward anticipated regret (fear of missing out) drives impulse buying more than upward regret (price drop); emphasize FOMO cautiously.
claims.quote: shoppers who experienced downward anticipated regret were more likely to engage in online impulsive buying. In contrast, the participants who experienced upward anticipated regret demonstrated less impulsive behavior

sources.title: Representativeness Heuristic
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Larger sample sizes override intuitive category matching; emphasize n-size when users judge probability from samples.
claims.quote: James drew a greater sample of balls than Sally, so he is in a better position to judge the contents of the jar

sources.title: Response Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Avoid leading questions that subtly prompt respondents toward a particular answer.
claims.quote: Leading questions can prompt survey-takers to respond in a certain way, even if it's not how they really feel. For example, in a customer-satisfaction survey a question like "Did you find our customer service satisfactory?" subtly leans towards a more favorable response, whereas asking the respondent to "Rate your customer service experience" is more neutral.

claims.rule: Emphasize survey anonymity to reduce social desirability bias in sensitive questions.
claims.quote: Emphasizing the anonymity of the survey can help reduce social desirability bias, as people feel more comfortable answering sensitive questions honestly when their names aren't attached to their answers.

claims.rule: Offer middle-ground response options to prevent acquiescence bias in survey scales.
claims.quote: acquiescence bias, which is the tendency to agree with all "Yes/No" or "Agree/Disagree" questions

claims.rule: Keep surveys brief to prevent extreme responding when respondents disengage from longer questionnaires.
claims.quote: it's important to factor in length when designing a survey or structured interview. If it's too long, participants may zone out and respond less carefully

sources.title: Restraint Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Design interfaces that acknowledge users' tendency to overestimate their self-control over impulses.
claims.quote: When we underestimate the power of our impulses, we overestimate our own control over them.

claims.rule: Smokers who believed they had high impulse control chose higher temptation levels and were significantly more likely to smoke.
claims.quote: smokers who received results for high-control of their impulses were more likely to choose a higher level of temptation than the low-control group

sources.title: Rosy Retrospection
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Account for users' tendency to recall positive aspects of past experiences more vividly when predicting future behavior.
claims.quote: Overestimating the enjoyable moments of a previous event, or the positive results of past decisions, can impact what we decide to do in the future. We might be overconfident when making similar future decisions or overlook challenges we've experienced in the past.

sources.title: Salience Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Highlight less visible but critical information to balance attention against emotionally striking details.
claims.quote: While quickly detecting what is important and deserving of attentional resources is an important survival and learning mechanism, our predisposition to focus on the most prominent and emotionally striking details leads us to ignore potentially vital pieces of information.

claims.rule: Display real-time feedback about consequences of user actions to counteract focus on vivid, immediate factors.
claims.quote: Studies have shown real-time feedback on a specific behavior can induce significant behavioral changes. When individuals are made aware of the consequences of their behavior as it occurs, they are more likely to adapt and make smarter choices.

claims.rule: Use bullet points and visual highlighting in AI-generated responses to make important information stand out.
claims.quote: Large language machines such as ChatGPT use the salience bias to present important information in a way that will stand out more to the user. Responses are often presented in bullet point form with salient information highlighted for ease of retrieval.

sources.title: Self Serving Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Design feedback mechanisms that encourage users to attribute failures to their own actions, not external factors.
claims.quote: If we do not attribute our failures to our own errors, we are unlikely to learn from them in the future. Furthermore, refusing to acknowledge our mistakes makes us susceptible to repeating them down the line.

claims.rule: Avoid defensive error messaging; frame product failures as opportunities for user improvement, not blame.
claims.quote: In the event that a customer is displeased with a product, a primary instinct may be to defend the project or pin the blame on the user for incorrect use. However, this can translate to further customer dissatisfaction and a missed opportunity for redemption.

sources.title: Serial Position Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Place task-critical information at the beginning or end of lists; users remember first and last items best.
claims.quote: presenting important information first or last on an interface guarantees users will store these items in their memory

claims.rule: Limit visible items per screen to reduce cognitive load; let users filter to view fewer options at once.
claims.quote: designers can allow users to activate filters so they only view a small number of clothing items instead of the entire stock

claims.rule: Integrate guiding tools to help users encode small chunks of information progressively.
claims.quote: Incorporating tools that guide users helps them encode small bits of information at a time

claims.rule: Avoid bullet-point lists in AI responses; varied formatting reduces serial position effect reinforcement.
claims.quote: language model AI often formats responses as bullet point lists to help enhance comprehensibility for users. However, this design feature may perpetuate the serial position effect even further

claims.rule: Vary the order of list items across multiple exposures so each item occupies different serial positions.
claims.quote: Instead of repeatedly studying the five facts in the same order, you might want to write them down in a different order the second time you go through them. That means that different items will be at the beginning, middle, and end of the series.

claims.rule: Avoid using bullet-point lists in AI responses; use varied formatting to reduce primacy and recency dominance.
claims.quote: The order in which machine learning generates outputs affects what pieces of information we encode and store in our memory. This is especially true since language model AI often formats responses as bullet point lists to help enhance comprehensibility for users. However, this design feature may perpetuate the serial position effect even further.

sources.title: Sexual Overperception Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Social Norms
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Use injunctive norms (show what others approve) alongside descriptive norms for behavior change.
claims.quote: Injunctive norms describe what people believe is approved or disapproved by others. That is, what society thinks you should do

sources.title: Source Confusion
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Display source attribution prominently; avoid widgets that hide where facts come from.
claims.quote: We don't encode the websites where we get our facts since we don't access the articles themselves. Instead, we merely browse through the search engine results page, which provides widgets containing exactly what we need to know

claims.rule: Use neutral, unbiased language in prompts and questions; avoid leading language that plants false memories.
claims.quote: if the officer had asked neutral questions—like 'How tall was the thief?' or 'What color was the thief wearing?'—Zachary would have been less likely to mistake her gender

claims.rule: Display source attribution directly on search results and information widgets; do not hide citations behind clicks.
claims.quote: We don't encode the websites where we get our facts since we don't access the articles themselves. Instead, we merely browse through the search engine results page, which provides widgets containing exactly what we need to know.

claims.rule: Citation systems in AI must display sources or acknowledge when sources are absent; do not provide detailed answers without indicating source provenance.
claims.quote: ChatGPT provides a lengthy response that distinguishes official languages from regional and even extinct ones. However, while Google directly links its answer to its source, ChatGPT does not cite a single one

claims.rule: Avoid leading questions in legal or high-stakes contexts; resist phrasing that suggests an answer or detail (e.g., "the gun" vs. "any weapon").
claims.quote: Did you see the gun, or did the officer tell you there was a gun? Did the cars smash into each other, or did the attorney simply suggest they did?

sources.title: Spacing Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Distribute training or onboarding content over multiple sessions rather than in one session.
claims.quote: By spacing out training sessions and incorporating well-placed follow-up content, organizations can improve employees' retention of important information

claims.rule: Limit single learning sessions to 30 minutes with breaks between to maintain retention.
claims.quote: A typical recommendation for learning sessions is 30 minutes long, with breaks to split up these sessions.

claims.rule: Use AI to predict and deliver content at each user's optimal review intervals based on their retention patterns.
claims.quote: AI systems to 'predict' the best time for each learner to review information, enhancing long-term retention and engagement

sources.title: Spotlight Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Assume users underestimate how little others notice their actions, appearance, or mistakes in interfaces.
claims.quote: people are less likely to notice our mistakes and shortcomings than we expect

sources.title: Status Quo Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Change default options to guide users toward optimal choices, not merely accept the existing norm.
claims.quote: the first group tended to choose the option framed as the default—even when the second group did not choose that option any more than the others

claims.rule: Reduce choice overload by limiting visible options to avoid users defaulting to status quo from decision paralysis.
claims.quote: the strength of the status quo bias is positively correlated with the number of options in a choice set

claims.rule: Automate beneficial changes to defaults so users benefit from optimal choices without active effort.
claims.quote: investors are rewarded by doing nothing, as the default option automatically shifts funds towards the optimal assets for their age group

sources.title: Suggestibility
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Present information in neutral, organized language; disorganized or unclear subject matter increases suggestibility.
claims.quote: lack of knowledge or flawed organization surrounding the subject matter being conveyed can also impact a person's level of suggestibility

sources.title: Survivorship Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Disclose full study parameters: sample size, dropout rates, and duration when presenting trial or product results.
claims.quote: What was the sample size? Did people drop out of the study? How long did they use the product for? All of these questions are important

sources.title: Take The Best Heuristic
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Highlight the most decisive differentiator when users choose between many similar options.
claims.quote: The one that we choose is usually the first one that we determine adequately differentiates between options and makes our choice easy

claims.rule: Offer 2–3 top criteria instead of all criteria when helping users compare alternatives; middle ground beats both extremes.
claims.quote: It might be best when making choices between alternatives, to use a decision-making process that falls somewhere in the middle. You might identify the top two or three criteria

sources.title: Telescoping Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Use explicit dates or references when collecting time-based data; do not rely on user memory of when events occurred.
claims.quote: it might be worthwhile to suggest referencing their email or credit card statement to increase the likelihood of getting accurate data

claims.rule: In surveys asking users to recall past events, provide reference aids like email or credit card statements to ground estimates in concrete data rather than memory.
claims.quote: it might be worthwhile to suggest referencing their email or credit card statement to increase the likelihood of getting accurate data from the respondent

sources.title: The Illusion Of Explanatory Depth
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Avoid strong-option UI for topics users understand poorly; users overestimate their knowledge and commit prematurely.
claims.quote: people far too often hold strong opinions about topics for which they have limited information

claims.rule: Require users to explain their understanding or reasoning before committing to high-consequence decisions; forced explanation reveals knowledge gaps and reduces overconfidence.
claims.quote: having to explain your knowledge brings you to realize how limited it is in reality

claims.rule: Break complex explanations into discrete, levelized steps; users confuse the ability to describe components or levels with true understanding of how systems work together.
claims.quote: being able to describe different levels of an item or concept inflates our perception of how much we know about it

sources.title: The Pygmalion Effect
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: Communicate high expectations to users through interface design; expectations influence behavior and performance.
claims.quote: others' expectations can greatly influence our performance. When someone thinks highly of us, we work hard to maintain that reputation.

claims.rule: Avoid messaging that activates negative stereotypes; even subtle cues about group identity can harm task performance.
claims.quote: Even subtle messaging that reminds people of the stereotypes about their social group can undermine people's performance.

claims.rule: Communicate high expectations to users through tone, design, and feedback; expectations influence task effort and actual performance outcomes.
claims.quote: others' expectations can greatly influence our performance. When someone thinks highly of us, we work hard to maintain that reputation

sources.title: The Sunk Cost Fallacy
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

sources.title: Zero Risk Bias
sources.why: Explainer of one cognitive bias with the original studies it rests on.

claims.rule: When risk is emphasized in the interface, users overspend and purchase unnecessary services; balance risk information carefully.
claims.quote: Zero risk bias is particularly strong in environments and situations where risk is emphasized, often leading to overspending and purchasing unnecessary services and items.

claims.rule: Most users prefer eliminating small risks entirely over reducing larger risks; prioritize risk reduction, not elimination.
claims.quote: if people are asked if they prefer the option to decrease a given risk from 5% to 0% or from 50% to 25%, most will opt for the former despite the drop from 50% to 25% being a far greater reduction in risk.

claims.rule: Offer free cancellation and no-contract options to eliminate switching costs and increase adoption.
claims.quote: no-contract plans and free cancellation policies for mobile phone services and internet packages can help eliminate the risk of being locked into a long-term commitment. If a customer knows they can opt out whenever they want without a penalty, they are more likely to sign up.

claims.rule: Hold AI tools to realistic error rates; users accept 11.3% error from humans but only 6.8% from AI, creating unfair standards.
claims.quote: people have significantly lower acceptable error rates for AI (6.8%) than humans (11.3%).

sources.title: Psychology of Design
sources.why: One-page catalogue of ~100 cognitive principles applied to product design, each with an example.

claims.rule: Reduce options to speed decisions; more options leads to harder choices and slower decision-making.
claims.quote: More options leads to harder decisions

claims.rule: Make targets large and close to the cursor; large and close elements are easier to interact with.
claims.quote: Large and close elements are easier to interact with

claims.rule: Avoid banner placement for important messages; users learn to ignore repeatedly exposed elements.
claims.quote: Users tune out the stuff they get repeatedly exposed to

claims.rule: Frame information positively or negatively based on desired action; presentation format affects user decisions.
claims.quote: The way information is presented affects how users make decisions

claims.rule: Show social proof to influence behavior; users adapt actions based on what others do.
claims.quote: Users adapt their behaviors based on what others do

claims.rule: Tap into curiosity by revealing missing information gradually; users want to seek out gaps.
claims.quote: Users have a desire to seek out missing information

claims.rule: Match interface patterns to users' preconceived mental models; interfaces should align with how people think tasks work.
claims.quote: Users have a preconceived opinion of how things work

claims.rule: Prefer familiar experiences; users adapt more easily to designs they recognize.
claims.quote: People prefer familiar experiences

claims.rule: Use real-world object metaphors to ease adoption; users adapt more readily to skeuomorphic designs.
claims.quote: Users adapt more easily to things that look like real-world objects

claims.rule: Offer something first to trigger reciprocity; people feel compelled to give back when they receive.
claims.quote: People feel the need to reciprocate when they receive something

claims.rule: Highlight individual people, not groups, to increase engagement; users care disproportionately about individuals.
claims.quote: Users care disproportionately about an individual as compared to a group

claims.rule: Surprise with variable rewards; unexpected rewards engage users more than predictable ones.
claims.quote: People especially enjoy unexpected rewards

claims.rule: Create an aha moment early; users need to quickly realize your product's value.
claims.quote: When new users first realize the value of your product

claims.rule: Show progress toward goals to boost motivation; motivation increases as users approach completion.
claims.quote: Motivation increases as users get closer to their goal

claims.rule: Favor simple solutions; complexity should only exist when necessary.
claims.quote: Simple solutions are often better than the more complex ones

claims.rule: Highlight social responsibility features; users prefer socially responsible companies.
claims.quote: Users tend to prefer socially responsible companies

claims.rule: Expose complex features progressively to reduce cognitive overwhelm during onboarding.
claims.quote: Users are less overwhelmed if they're exposed to complex features later

sources.title: Designing good government services: an introduction
sources.why: Foundational principles for designing government services with user-centered approach

claims.rule: Design services from end to end; include every step users take and supplier tasks outside government.
claims.quote: think about every single thing a user needs to do, including anything done by a supplier external to government

claims.rule: Minimize user actions; reduce steps and data entry to reach goals as seamlessly as possible.
claims.quote: Good services get a user to take the smallest number of steps possible to reach their goal.

claims.rule: Pre-fill known information; use postcode lookups or review prior entries instead of asking users to re-enter.
claims.quote: using a postcode lookup to help find an address, rather than asking the user to enter the address manually

claims.rule: Add confirmation screens for significant changes; show warnings before users alter personal data.
claims.quote: Where there is a risk a user will fail if they act too quickly, a good service slows them down. Like showing a warning screen before people make significant changes to their personal data.

claims.rule: Eliminate dead ends; lead every user to a clear outcome, even if ineligible.
claims.quote: Every user needs to be led to a clear outcome, even if they are not eligible for the service itself.

claims.rule: Make human help easy to access; provide obvious phone, email, online or face-to-face support.
claims.quote: a good service gives them an easy way to communicate with a human being. This might be over phone or email, face to face or online.

claims.rule: Hide internal structures from users; don't expose back-end systems or organizational boundaries.
claims.quote: A good service does not unnecessarily expose a user to internal structures behind it.

claims.rule: Test algorithms regularly; only use tools proven to work and verify them often in production.
claims.quote: Only use algorithms you know work properly and test them regularly once in use.

claims.rule: Update all views instantly when users change details; consistency across all parts builds trust.
claims.quote: When a user updates their details, they expect to see this change in all parts of a service straightaway.

sources.title: Understanding and meeting policy intent
sources.why: How to align service design with policy intent

sources.title: Designing with data: an introduction
sources.why: Using data insights to inform design decisions

claims.rule: Set hypotheses that specify the action, expected impact, and measurement before testing.

claims.rule: Use consistent formats and structures for data across your service so users and other services understand and reuse it.

claims.rule: Offer open file formats like ODT instead of proprietary types like XLS so users can open files with any software.

sources.title: Environmentally sustainable services

claims.rule: Compress and aggregate data; regularly delete data you do not need to reduce storage and bandwidth.

sources.title: Map and understand a user's whole problem

claims.rule: Map the entire user journey to spot breaks; ensure all parts of a multi-step task join up coherently.

sources.title: Structuring forms

claims.rule: Ask eligibility questions first so users learn early if they cannot use the service and do not waste time.
claims.quote: Start with questions that will let users know if they're not eligible for the service, so you do not waste people's time.

claims.rule: Use consistent question or statement format for page titles to help users focus on content, not presentation.

sources.title: Collecting personal information from users

claims.rule: Do not rely on users reading privacy notices for significant consequences; tell them in the main flow.

sources.title: Writing for user interfaces

claims.rule: Start with less text; add help only if user research shows it is needed.

claims.rule: Design the interface so users understand it without explanation; if explanation is needed, fix the interface.

claims.rule: Put important words first and drop unnecessary words to respect space constraints.
claims.quote: put the important words first and drop any unnecessary words.

claims.rule: Use direct language in error messages; avoid saying 'sorry' in validation errors.

claims.rule: Do not rely on shape, size, colour, or location alone to communicate information.

claims.rule: Use headings to break up long pages and make them easier to scan.
claims.quote: Break up long pages with headings. It's easier to scan and read.

claims.rule: Make link text clear and descriptive; avoid generic text like 'click here'.

claims.rule: Use sentence case for headings and labels, but do not add punctuation.

claims.rule: Minimize cognitive load by using clear language that matches users' own words.

claims.rule: Break complex questions into a series of simple questions, especially if parts are not relevant to all users.

claims.rule: Allow users to answer 'I'm not sure' or 'I do not know' when these are valid answers.

sources.title: Making your service more inclusive
sources.why: Inclusive design practices for government services

claims.rule: Recruit user research participants who represent the full range of people using your service.
claims.quote: recruit user research participants who represent the full range of people using your service

claims.rule: Provide a mix of channels that users need for each interaction; make it easy to move between channels.
claims.quote: Provide the mix of channels that users need for each interaction. Make it easy for users to move between channels.

claims.rule: Do not set inflexible deadlines; account for users who cannot respond quickly due to their circumstances.
claims.quote: Users cannot always act quickly, depending on their circumstances. Do not assume users will respond quickly just because you send an email or text, instead of a letter.

sources.title: Accordion
sources.why: Collapsible content container component

sources.title: Alert
sources.why: Notification and alert messaging component

claims.rule: Use alerts to keep users informed of important and time-sensitive changes or validation results.
claims.quote: An alert keeps users informed of important and sometimes time-sensitive changes.

sources.title: Button
sources.why: Primary interactive button component with states

claims.rule: Use buttons to draw attention to important actions with a large selectable surface area.
claims.quote: A button draws attention to important actions with a large selectable surface.

sources.title: Form
sources.why: Form structure and organization guidance

claims.rule: Display form controls in HTML order matching screen order, not rearranged by CSS.
claims.quote: Display form controls in the same order in the HTML as they appear on screen. Don't use CSS to rearrange the form controls.

claims.rule: Align validation messages visually with their input fields for screen magnifier users.
claims.quote: Visually align validation messages with the input fields so people using screen magnifiers can read them quickly.

claims.rule: Group related form controls in fieldset with legend labels.
claims.quote: Group each set of thematically related controls in a fieldset element. Use the legend element to offer a label within each one.

claims.rule: Use vertical form layouts for accessibility, especially for users with limited vision.
claims.quote: Keep your form blocks in a vertical pattern. This approach is ideal, from an accessibility standpoint, because of limited vision that makes it hard to scan from right to left.

claims.rule: Avoid disabled form states; use helper text and inline validation instead.
claims.quote: Avoid disabled states, especially for text inputs. Disabled states have low color contrast, do not offer meaningful feedback to screen reader users, and keyboard navigators can't focus on them.

claims.rule: Label optional fields explicitly with parenthetical 'optional' text.
claims.quote: Mark optional fields as "optional." Label optional fields with the word "optional" placed in parentheses.

sources.title: Table
sources.why: Data table component and display guidance

claims.rule: Use striped table rows with alternating background colors to improve readability.
claims.quote: A striped table can improve readability by visually grouping row content with alternating background colors.

sources.title: Header
sources.why: Page header and navigation region

claims.rule: List all important website sections as links in horizontal navigation.
claims.quote: List all important website sections as links in the horizontal navigation.

claims.rule: Use dropdown menus to preview lower-level content on large websites.
claims.quote: Dropdown menus help preview lower-level content. For large websites, use dropdown menus to help users preview lower-level content.

claims.rule: Use short, clear link labels without jargon.
claims.quote: Use short, clear link labels. Don't use jargon or unfamiliar terms.

claims.rule: Left-justify navigation link labels for scannability.
claims.quote: Left-justify. Left-justified link labels are more easily scannable.

claims.rule: Order navigation links by priority, highest-demand links on the left.
claims.quote: Present links in priority order. Higher-demand links should appear farther to the left, and lower-demand links should appear farther to the right.

claims.rule: Structure navigation by user tasks, not by organizational hierarchy.
claims.quote: Avoid org-structure navigation. Don't model your navigation after your agency's org structure. Instead, structure it according to the tasks and information your users most frequently need to access.

claims.rule: Highlight the current section in navigation to show user location.
claims.quote: Highlight the current section. Show users where they are within the site by highlighting the current section.

claims.rule: Add skip navigation link before header to bypass long navigation lists.
claims.quote: Add a skip navigation link before the header. Include skip navigation links to allow those using screen readers to bypass long navigation lists.

claims.rule: Support keyboard Tab navigation for all top-level navigation items.
claims.quote: Include tab focus for all top-level navigation navigation items. This feature will allow keyboard-reliant users to easily navigate interactive items.

claims.rule: Expand dropdowns on click or keyboard, not on hover.
claims.quote: Avoid using hover to expand dropdown lists. Hover is difficult for some users and won't work on touch screens. Dropdowns should expand on click or with keyboard navigation.

claims.rule: Use aria-label to distinguish multiple nav elements on a page.
claims.quote: Add context by labelling your nav element. If your page has more than one nav element, use the aria-label attribute to help assistive technology users understand the purpose of the navigation.

claims.rule: Use list elements for navigation links to assist screen readers.
claims.quote: Use list elements for your navigation links. This helps screen reader users navigate header content.

claims.rule: Add alt text to logo images for screen reader users.
claims.quote: Add alt text to your logo image. If you're using a logo that's an image rather than text, make sure you include alternative text for screen readers.

claims.rule: Use em, not H1, for text logos unless on homepage.
claims.quote: Don't use an H1 for your logo. If you're using a logo that's text, use an em , not an h1 , unless it's the homepage.

sources.title: Footer
sources.why: Page footer and sitemap component

sources.title: Modal
sources.why: Dialog and modal overlay patterns

claims.rule: Use modals sparingly to minimize unnecessary disruptions to workflow.
claims.quote: A modal prevents interaction with page content until the user completes an action or dismisses the modal. This intentionally interrupts the user's workflow. Use modals sparingly to minimize unnecessary disruptions.

claims.rule: Give modals simple, clear headlines explaining their purpose.
claims.quote: Modals should have a simple headline that explains its purpose. Use enough descriptive text to be clear what the user needs to do and why.

claims.rule: Avoid using modals for complex forms or large amounts of information.
claims.quote: Avoid using modals to display complex forms or large amounts of information.

sources.title: Pagination
sources.why: Multi-page navigation controls

claims.rule: Use pagination navigation for content split only by page size, not by meaningful categories.
claims.quote: Paginated content is any content split into multiple pages determined only by a specific amount of content per page, not split by any meaningful attribute, like feature or subject or step.

claims.rule: Allow users to jump to first and last pages in pagination.
claims.quote: Readers use the pagination component to move from page to page in paginated content, or directly to the first or last page of the paginated set.

sources.title: Combo box
sources.why: Searchable select component with autocomplete

sources.title: Date picker
sources.why: Calendar-based date selection component

claims.rule: Allow users to type dates manually instead of requiring calendar picker interaction.
claims.quote: Always allow a user to type in the date manually. Usability testing suggests some people prefer manually typing the date rather than using the calendar picker.

claims.rule: Provide a hint showing the expected date format to guide manual entry.
claims.quote: Provide a hint of mm/dd/yyyy to help users enter the proper date format if they opt not to use the date picker.

claims.rule: Never auto-submit forms when users select an option from interactive controls.
claims.quote: Avoid auto-submission. Don't use JavaScript to automatically submit the form (or do anything else) when an option is selected. Auto-submission disrupts screen readers because they select each option as they read them.

claims.rule: Disable only specific unavailable dates; disable the entire picker only when no dates are selectable.
claims.quote: Use date restrictions when only some dates are unavailable. Disable the entire picker only when users cannot enter any date, and explain how to make it available.

sources.title: Side navigation
sources.why: Secondary navigation sidebar

claims.rule: Indicate the current page in navigation using an active state to show user location.
claims.quote: Show the current page. Indicate where a user is within the navigational hierarchy. Use the "active" state to show users which page they have navigated to.

claims.rule: Keep navigation link text short, deriving them from page titles.
claims.quote: Keep the navigation links short. They can be shorter derivatives of page titles themselves.

claims.rule: Test navigation depth and breadth to balance usability and discoverability.
claims.quote: Always test your navigation. If the navigation hierarchy is too long, users may miss items at the bottom. If it's too deep, users may miss items that require too many clicks.

sources.title: Ask users for NHS numbers
sources.why: Pattern for capturing NHS identification numbers in forms

claims.rule: Use hint text to help users recognize the required format and know where to find the information.
claims.quote: help users recognise their NHS number and know the correct details to enter, for example with hint text

sources.title: Check answers
sources.why: Pattern for confirmation pages reviewing user-entered data

claims.rule: Group related data by category on check-answers pages to aid comprehension and review.
claims.quote: This pattern uses a summary list component for each group of answers on the page.

sources.title: Help users decide when and where to get care
sources.why: Care card component for healthcare guidance

claims.rule: Limit the number of care cards to avoid overwhelming users with alarming information.
claims.quote: Avoid having too many care cards on the page. We want to give essential information and reassure people, not to scare them.

sources.title: Confirmation page
sources.why: Pattern for successful transaction confirmation pages

claims.rule: Avoid too many different components on a confirmation page to prevent overwhelming users.
claims.quote: Avoid including too many different components on a confirmation page. Research suggests they can overwhelm people.

claims.rule: Include details about what will happen next and when on confirmation pages.
claims.quote: details about what will happen next and when

claims.rule: Use left-aligned heading text on confirmation pages for accessibility with screen readers.
claims.quote: The left-aligned heading text tested well with people who had visual impairments and used screen readers.

sources.title: Hub page
sources.why: Pattern for hub pages with multiple navigation options

claims.rule: Use cards to help users navigate to the content they need on hub pages.
claims.quote: Hub pages use cards to help users navigate to the content they need.

sources.title: Start page
sources.why: Pattern for service entry point pages

claims.rule: Use a start page at the beginning of a service where users input information to get something.
claims.quote: At the start of a service which involves the user inputting information in order to get something.

sources.title: Canada.ca Specifications
sources.why: Mandatory design elements and patterns for Canada.ca services

sources.title: Canada.ca Design Guidance
sources.why: Content design and web guidance for Canada.ca services

claims.rule: Write crisis communications in mobile-first, task-focused format with short sentences and bulleted lists.
claims.quote: Mobile-first, avoid duplication, add dates, write information as directions, use bulleted lists, keep sentences short

sources.title: Canada.ca Research Summaries
sources.why: Research findings supporting Canada.ca design decisions

sources.title: Focus Order (2.4.3)
sources.why: Understanding keyboard focus order requirements and best practices

claims.rule: Arrange focusable elements in an order that matches the logical meaning and operation of the page.
claims.quote: Focusable components receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability.

claims.rule: Ensure keyboard users can navigate through content sequentially without confusion about the interaction point.
claims.quote: When users navigate sequentially through content, they encounter information in an order that is consistent with the meaning of the content and can be operated from the keyboard.

claims.rule: Avoid nested focusable elements that cause a control to appear receiving focus multiple times.
claims.quote: It is a failure of Focus Order if items receive focus in an order that impedes the meaning or operation of content, or creates confusing or illogical focus orders — for example, a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements.

sources.title: Focus Visible (2.4.7)
sources.why: Visible focus indicators for keyboard navigation

claims.rule: Provide a visible indicator showing which element currently has keyboard focus.
claims.quote: Any keyboard operable user interface has a mode of operation where the keyboard focus indicator is visible.

claims.rule: Keep the focus indicator visible at all times while focus is maintained, without time limits.
claims.quote: The focus indicator must not be time limited: when the keyboard focus is shown, it must remain visible.

sources.title: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (2.4.11)
sources.why: Minimum visibility for keyboard focus indicators

claims.rule: Keep the focused component at least partially visible and not entirely hidden by author-created content.
claims.quote: When a user interface component receives keyboard focus, the component is not entirely hidden due to author-created content.

claims.rule: Use scroll padding or modal dialogs to prevent sticky headers, footers, and overlays from hiding focused elements.
claims.quote: Ways of passing include making the banner modal so the user has to dismiss the banner before navigating through the page, or using scroll padding so the banner does not overlap other content.

sources.title: Contrast (Minimum) (1.4.3)
sources.why: Minimum color contrast ratios for text and UI components

sources.title: Contrast (Enhanced) (1.4.11)
sources.why: Enhanced contrast requirements for accessibility

sources.title: Non-Text Contrast (1.4.11)
sources.why: Contrast requirements for UI components and graphical elements

sources.title: Target Size (Enhanced) (2.5.5)
