sources.why: Minimum clickable/touchable target sizes for interactive elements

claims.rule: Make interactive targets at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels to help users with limited dexterity.
claims.quote: The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels

claims.rule: Make frequently used or hard-to-reverse controls larger than 44×44 pixels to prevent mistakes.
claims.quote: larger sizes are used to reduce the possibility of unintentional actions. This is particularly relevant if any of the following are true: the control is used frequently; the result of the interaction cannot be easily undone

claims.rule: Use touch targets that account for finger size and obstructed vision on mobile screens.
claims.quote: A finger is larger than a mouse pointer, and generally obstructs the user's view of the precise location on the screen that is being touched/activated

sources.title: Reflow (1.4.10)
sources.why: Responsive layout requirements without horizontal scrolling

claims.rule: Design text to reflow within 320 CSS pixels width so users can read enlarged text without horizontal scrolling.
claims.quote: Content can be presented without loss of information or functionality, and without requiring scrolling in two dimensions for: Vertical scrolling content at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels

claims.rule: Stack content into single columns on narrow viewports to avoid multi-directional scrolling.
claims.quote: A common way for many article-driven web pages to meet the Reflow success criterion is to ensure that the presentation of a web page can adjust to a single column of content

sources.title: Text Spacing (1.4.12)
sources.why: Support for adjustable text spacing without loss of functionality

claims.rule: Ensure content adapts without loss when line height is set to 1.5×, paragraphs to 2×, letter spacing to 0.12×, and word spacing to 0.16× font size.
claims.quote: no loss of content or functionality occurs by setting all of the following and by changing no other style property: Line height (line spacing) to at least 1.5 times the font size; Spacing following paragraphs to at least 2 times the font size; Letter spacing (tracking) to at least 0.12 times the font size; Word spacing to at least 0.16 times the font size

claims.rule: Do not interfere with user overrides of text spacing to improve readability.
claims.quote: The author requirement is both to not interfere with a user's ability to override the author settings, and to ensure that content thus modified does not break content

sources.title: Content on Hover or Focus (1.4.13)
sources.why: Guidance for dismissible and persistent tooltips and transient UI

claims.rule: Let users dismiss popover content by pressing Escape without moving focus or hover.
claims.quote: A mechanism is available to dismiss the additional content without moving pointer hover or keyboard focus

claims.rule: Allow users to move the mouse pointer onto hover-triggered content without it disappearing.
claims.quote: If pointer hover can trigger the additional content, then the pointer can be moved over the additional content without the additional content disappearing

claims.rule: Keep popover content visible until the trigger is removed, dismissed by the user, or no longer valid.
claims.quote: The additional content remains visible until the hover or focus trigger is removed, the user dismisses it, or its information is no longer valid

sources.title: Accordion Pattern
sources.why: ARIA authoring practices for accordion/disclosure components

claims.rule: Use Enter or Space to expand collapsed accordion panels and collapse expanded ones.
claims.quote: Enter or Space : When focus is on the accordion header for a collapsed panel, expands the associated panel

claims.rule: Set aria-expanded true when an accordion panel is visible, false when hidden.
claims.quote: If the accordion panel associated with an accordion header is visible, the header button element has aria-expanded set to true . If the panel is not visible, aria-expanded is set to false

sources.title: Alert Pattern
sources.why: ARIA implementation for live alert announcements

claims.rule: Display alert messages that attract attention without interrupting focus or workflow.
claims.quote: An alert is an element that displays a brief, important message in a way that attracts the user's attention without interrupting the user's task

claims.rule: Use role alert on elements so screen readers announce them automatically when rendered.
claims.quote: Dynamically rendered alerts are automatically announced by most screen readers

claims.rule: Never use auto-disappearing alerts; they violate WCAG 2.2.3 timing requirements.
claims.quote: It is also important to avoid designing alerts that disappear automatically. An alert that disappears too quickly can lead to failure to meet WCAG 2.0 success criterion 2.2.3

claims.rule: Minimize alert frequency to protect users with visual and cognitive disabilities from interruption fatigue.
claims.quote: Another critical design consideration is the frequency of interruption caused by alerts. Frequent interruptions inhibit usability for people with visual and cognitive disabilities

sources.title: Button Pattern
sources.why: ARIA authoring for button semantics and interaction

claims.rule: Append ellipsis to button labels that launch dialogs to signal additional interface.
claims.quote: A common convention for informing users that a button launches a dialog is to append "…" (ellipsis) to the button label

claims.rule: Keep toggle button labels constant; do not change text when state changes.
claims.quote: Important: it is critical the label on a toggle does not change when its state changes.

claims.rule: Ensure button appearance and role match its actual function.
claims.quote: It is important that both the appearance and role of a widget match the function it provides.

claims.rule: Move focus into opened dialogs; return focus to opener after dialog closes.
claims.quote: If activating the button opens a dialog, the focus moves inside the dialog.

sources.title: Checkbox Pattern
sources.why: ARIA implementation for checkbox components

claims.rule: Use tri-state checkboxes to represent parent-child relationships in grouped options.
claims.quote: One common use of a tri-state checkbox can be found in software installers where a single tri-state checkbox is used to represent and control the state of an entire group of install options.

sources.title: Combobox Pattern
sources.why: ARIA patterns for select-with-autocomplete components

claims.rule: Support text input in comboboxes to let users filter and select values or input arbitrary text.
claims.quote: Some comboboxes allow users to type and edit text in the combobox and others do not.

claims.rule: Hide popups by default; display them only when triggered by focus, arrow key, or button.
claims.quote: The popup is hidden by default, i.e., the default state is collapsed.

sources.title: Dialog (Modal) Pattern
sources.why: ARIA authoring for modal dialog accessibility

claims.rule: Dim or obscure content behind active modal dialogs to signal inertness and prevent interaction.
claims.quote: Inert content outside an active dialog is typically visually obscured or dimmed so it is difficult to discern

claims.rule: Move focus into a dialog when it opens; set initial focus strategically by content size and task importance.
claims.quote: When a dialog opens, focus moves to an element inside the dialog.

claims.rule: Trap Tab and Shift+Tab focus within modal dialogs; do not allow escape without closing.
claims.quote: Like non-modal dialogs, modal dialogs contain their tab sequence. That is, Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus outside the dialog.

claims.rule: Include a visible close button in dialogs; allow Escape key to close.
claims.quote: It is strongly recommended that the tab sequence of all dialogs include a visible element with role button that closes the dialog, such as a close icon or cancel button.

claims.rule: For dialogs with destructive final steps, set initial focus to the safest action.
claims.quote: If a dialog contains the final step in a process that is not easily reversible, such as deleting data or completing a financial transaction, it may be advisable to set focus on the least destructive action

sources.title: Disclosure Pattern
sources.why: ARIA patterns for expandable content sections

claims.rule: Use right-pointing arrow or triangle to hint hidden content; point down when expanded.
claims.quote: When the controlled content is hidden, the button is often styled as a typical push button with a right-pointing arrow or triangle to hint that activating the button will display additional content. When the content is visible, the arrow or triangle typically points down.

sources.title: Listbox Pattern
sources.why: ARIA implementation for list selection components

claims.rule: Keep option names concise to aid screen reader users; avoid long strings spoken as single units.
claims.quote: Avoiding very long option names facilitates understandability and perceivability for screen reader users. The entire name of an option is spoken as a single unit of speech when the option is read.

claims.rule: Implement type-ahead search in listboxes, especially those with more than seven options.
claims.quote: Type-ahead is recommended for all listboxes, especially those with more than seven options

claims.rule: Support Space key to toggle selection state in multi-select listboxes without modifier keys.
claims.quote: Space : changes the selection state of the focused option.

sources.title: Menu and Menubar Pattern
sources.why: ARIA authoring for menu navigation patterns

claims.rule: Place keyboard focus on the first menu item when a menu opens or receives focus.
claims.quote: When a menu opens, or when a menubar receives focus, keyboard focus is placed on the first item.

claims.rule: Append an ellipsis (…) to menu item labels that launch dialog boxes.
claims.quote: A common convention for indicating that a menu item launches a dialog box is to append "…" (ellipsis) to the menu item label, e.g., "Save as …".

sources.title: Radio Group Pattern
sources.why: ARIA patterns for radio button groups

claims.rule: Set initial focus on the checked radio button when focus enters a radio group; if none are checked, focus the first button.
claims.quote: When focus moves into a radio group: If a radio button is checked, focus is set on the checked button. If none of the radio buttons are checked, focus is set on the first radio button in the group.

sources.title: Slider Pattern
sources.why: ARIA authoring for slider input controls

claims.rule: Place keyboard focus on the slider thumb, not the track, for mouse and keyboard users.
claims.quote: Focus is placed on the slider (the visual object that the mouse user would move, also known as the thumb.

claims.rule: Use aria-valuetext when the numeric slider value is not user-friendly; communicate the unit of measure or meaning.
claims.quote: If the value of aria-valuenow is not user-friendly, e.g., the day of the week is represented by a number, the aria-valuetext property is set to a string that makes the slider value understandable, e.g., "Monday".

sources.title: Switch Pattern
sources.why: ARIA patterns for toggle switches

claims.rule: Never change the switch label text when its state changes; label describes the switch purpose, not its state.
claims.quote: Important: it is critical the label on a switch does not change when its state changes.

sources.title: Table Pattern
sources.why: ARIA implementation for data tables

claims.rule: Use HTML table elements instead of WAI-ARIA table role; test thoroughly with assistive technology if using ARIA.
claims.quote: As with other WAI-ARIA roles that have a native host language equivalent, authors are strongly encouraged to use a native HTML table element whenever possible.

claims.rule: Replace tables with grids if they contain many interactive widgets to reduce the page tab sequence length.
claims.quote: If the number of widgets is large, replacing the table with a grid can dramatically reduce the length of the page tab sequence because a grid is a composite widget that can contain other widgets.

sources.title: Tabs Pattern
sources.why: ARIA authoring for tabbed interface components

claims.rule: Activate tabs automatically when they receive focus if panel content loads without noticeable latency; otherwise use manual activation.
claims.quote: It is recommended that tabs activate automatically when they receive focus as long as their associated tab panels are displayed without noticeable latency. This typically requires tab panel content to be preloaded.

sources.title: Tooltip Pattern
sources.why: ARIA patterns for accessible tooltip interactions

claims.rule: Dismiss tooltips when Escape is pressed or cursor leaves the trigger element and tooltip.
claims.quote: It typically appears after a small delay and disappears when Escape is pressed or on mouse out.

claims.rule: Keep focus on the triggering element while the tooltip displays.
claims.quote: Focus stays on the triggering element while the tooltip is displayed.

sources.title: Tree View Pattern
sources.why: ARIA implementation for hierarchical tree navigation

claims.rule: Visually distinguish between focused and selected items in trees.
claims.quote: It is important that the visual design distinguish between items that are selected and the item that has focus.

claims.rule: Show a visual keyboard indicator when an item receives focus in a tree.
claims.quote: When using a keyboard to navigate a tree, a visual keyboard indicator informs the user which item is focused.

claims.rule: Implement type-ahead for trees with more than 7 root nodes.
claims.quote: Type-ahead is recommended for all trees, especially for trees with more than 7 root nodes: Type a character: focus moves to the next node with a name that starts with the typed character.

sources.title: Page Structure
sources.why: Structuring web pages semantically for accessibility

claims.rule: Use heading hierarchy to allow screen reader users to skip to main content directly.
claims.quote: People using screen readers can skip to the main content directly and navigate to sections that are important to them.

claims.rule: Structure content logically so people with cognitive disabilities can find and prioritize information.
claims.quote: People with cognitive and learning disabilities can more easily find and prioritize content on the page.

sources.title: Page Regions
sources.why: Using landmarks to structure page regions

claims.rule: Use HTML5 header element or role=banner to mark site-wide header information.
claims.quote: HTML5 provides the <header> element, which can be used to define such a region.

claims.rule: Use HTML5 main element to identify the primary content region.
claims.quote: Use the HTML5 <main> element to identify the main content region of a web page or application.

claims.rule: Use HTML5 footer element or role=contentinfo to mark site-wide footer information.
claims.quote: HTML5 provides the <footer> element, which can be used to define such a region.

claims.rule: Use nav element with labels to identify navigation menus.
claims.quote: The HTML5 <nav> element can be used to identify a navigation menu. A web page can have any number of navigation menus. Use labels to identify each navigation menu.

claims.rule: Maintain consistent page region order across different screen sizes.
claims.quote: Components may be collapsed or even hidden on smaller screens, but components that show should appear in the same order for a particular view (set size and orientation).

sources.title: Headings
sources.why: Semantic heading structure for navigation and organization

claims.rule: Use the first h1 as the main page heading, not the site name.
claims.quote: The main heading is not the site name but the content heading, which is rank 1.

sources.title: Menus
sources.why: Creating accessible menu structures and interactions

claims.rule: Use markup that reflects menu structure and labels for screen reader users.
claims.quote: Screen reader and keyboard users benefit from keyboard interoperability and markup that allows them to operate menus in different ways.

claims.rule: Provide larger click targets in menus for users with fine motor difficulties.
claims.quote: Users with fine motor difficulties and touch screen users require larger targets to click or tap on.

claims.rule: Keep fly-out submenus visible briefly after mouse leaves the clickable area.
claims.quote: In fly-out menus, submenus should not disappear immediately after the mouse has left the clickable area.

claims.rule: Use distinct, easily identifiable menu states like current page indicators.
claims.quote: People with limited attention or short-term memory benefit from clear and distinct menus with easily identifiable states, such as the current page.

sources.title: Menu Structure
sources.why: Semantic markup for accessible menus

claims.rule: Use unordered lists for menus where item sequence is irrelevant.
claims.quote: Use an unordered list ( <ul> ) when the menu items are not in a specific order.

claims.rule: Use ordered lists for menus where sequence matters.
claims.quote: Use an ordered list ( <ol> ) when the sequence of the menu items is important.

claims.rule: Identify menus with the HTML5 nav element for direct user access.
claims.quote: Identify the menu, ideally using the HTML5 <nav> element to allow users access to the menu directly.

sources.title: Images
sources.why: Accessible image descriptions and alt text patterns

claims.rule: Provide text alternatives for all informative images.
claims.quote: Images must have text alternatives that describe the information or function represented by them.

claims.rule: Describe function, not appearance, for images used as buttons or links.
claims.quote: The text alternative of an image used as a link or as a button should describe the functionality of the link or button rather than the visual image.

claims.rule: Replicate text content exactly in alt text for images containing readable text.
claims.quote: If images of text are used, the text alternative should contain the same words as in the image.

sources.title: Informative Images
sources.why: Alt text guidance for images that convey information

claims.rule: Convey image meaning, not literal appearance, in alt text for informative images.
claims.quote: The text alternative should convey the meaning or content that is displayed visually, which typically isn't a literal description of the image.

sources.title: Complex Images
sources.why: Describing diagrams, charts and complex visual information

claims.rule: Make long descriptions available to everyone, not just screen reader users.
claims.quote: Make long descriptions available to everyone to reach a wider audience with your content. For example, show the description as part of the main content.

sources.title: Tables
sources.why: Creating accessible data tables with proper headers

claims.rule: Mark header cells with th and data cells with td elements.
claims.quote: Header cells must be marked up with <th> , and data cells with <td> to make tables accessible.

sources.title: Forms
sources.why: Designing accessible forms with labels and validation

claims.rule: Label every form control using the label element.
claims.quote: Use the <label> element, and, in specific cases, other mechanisms (e.g. WAI-ARIA, title attribute etc.), to identify each form control.

claims.rule: Group related form controls with fieldset and legend elements.
claims.quote: Use the <fieldset> and <legend> elements to group and associate related form controls.

claims.rule: Provide instructions for completing forms and individual controls.
claims.quote: Provide instructions to help users understand how to complete the form and individual form controls.

claims.rule: Split long forms into logical steps and inform users of progress.
claims.quote: Divide long forms into multiple smaller forms that constitute a series of logical steps or stages and inform users about their progress.

sources.title: Labeling Controls
sources.why: Form label association and naming conventions

claims.rule: Associate all form labels explicitly using the for attribute matched to the input id.
claims.quote: The for attribute of the label must exactly match the id of the form control.

claims.rule: Provide descriptive labels for every form control including text fields, checkboxes, radio buttons, and dropdowns.
claims.quote: Provide labels to identify all form controls, including text fields, checkboxes, radio buttons, and drop-down menus.

claims.rule: Hide visual labels using CSS that keeps them available to assistive technology, never with display:none.
claims.quote: The common approach used to hide information visually but keep them available to screen reader and other assistive technology users is to use CSS that will keep the information technically visible but practically hidden.

sources.title: Validating Input
sources.why: Accessible form validation and error messaging

claims.rule: Validate required input and clearly mark required form fields in labels and the UI.
claims.quote: Forms frequently include required input that needs to be clearly identified using labels. Also, the required attribute can be added to form controls, to programmatically indicate that they are required.

claims.rule: Perform validation on both client and server side; client-side alone does not ensure security.
claims.quote: Client-side validation alone does not ensure security; therefore data needs to be validated on the server-side as well.

sources.title: Carousels
sources.why: Accessible carousel/slideshow implementation

claims.rule: Allow users to pause carousel movement to prevent distraction and allow time to read content.
claims.quote: Users must be able to pause carousel movement because it can be too fast or distracting, making text hard to read.

claims.rule: Make all carousel functionality operable by keyboard, not mouse-only.
claims.quote: All functionality, including navigating between carousel items, must be operable by keyboard.

claims.rule: Announce carousel item changes to screen reader users and all users.
claims.quote: Changes to carousel items must be communicated to all users, including screen reader users.

claims.rule: Manage keyboard focus position in carousels in a reasonable and comprehensible fashion.
claims.quote: The keyboard position ("focus") is managed in a reasonable and comprehensible fashion.

sources.title: Tips for Designing
sources.why: Quick reference tips for accessible design practices

claims.rule: Provide sufficient contrast ratio between foreground text and background colors.
claims.quote: Foreground text needs to have sufficient contrast with background colors. This includes text on images, background gradients, buttons, and other elements.

claims.rule: Never use color alone to convey information; add symbols, numbers, labels, or other non-color cues.
claims.quote: Color should not be the only way information is conveyed. When using color to differentiate elements, also provide additional identification that does not rely on color perception.

claims.rule: Make interactive elements easily identifiable with distinct styles for hover, focus, and active states.
claims.quote: Provide distinct styles for interactive elements, such as links and buttons, to make them easy to identify. For example, change the appearance of links on mouse hover, keyboard focus, and touch-screen activation.

claims.rule: Ensure all interactive elements are reachable and show visible keyboard focus as users navigate.
claims.quote: It is important that users can reach all interactive elements using the keyboard, and that it is clear which element has focus.

claims.rule: Provide consistent naming, styling, and positioning of navigation across all pages.
claims.quote: Ensure that navigation across pages within a website has consistent naming, styling, and positioning.

claims.rule: Provide multiple navigation methods such as search or sitemap to help users find content.
claims.quote: Provide more than one method of website navigation, such as a site search or a site map.

claims.rule: Help users understand their location with orientation cues like breadcrumbs and clear headings.
claims.quote: Help users understand where they are in a website or page by providing orientation cues, such as breadcrumbs and clear headings.

claims.rule: Provide prominent, easily identifiable feedback for form submissions, errors, and page changes.
claims.quote: Provide feedback for interactions, such as confirming form submission, alerting the user when something goes wrong, or notifying the user of changes on the page. Instructions should be easy to identify.

sources.title: Tips for Developing
sources.why: Quick reference tips for accessible development

claims.rule: Use for attribute on labels linked to input id, or WAI-ARIA attributes, to associate labels with form controls.
claims.quote: Use a for attribute on the <label> element linked to the id attribute of the form element, or using WAI-ARIA attributes.

claims.rule: Include alternative text for all informational and functional images; use empty alt for decorative images.
claims.quote: Ensure that alternative text for images is added to all informational and functional images. Use empty alternative text, alt="" for decorative images, or include them in the CSS instead.

claims.rule: Declare the primary page language using lang attribute in html tag; mark language changes within content.
claims.quote: Indicate the primary language of every page by using the lang attribute in the html tag, for example <html lang="en"> . Use the lang attribute on specific elements when the language of the element differs from the rest of the page.

claims.rule: Use semantic markup for headings, lists, and tables to convey meaning and structure.
claims.quote: Use appropriate mark-up for headings, lists, tables, etc. HTML5 provides additional elements, such as <nav> and <aside> , to better structure your content.

claims.rule: Use WAI-ARIA roles to provide additional semantic meaning, such as role="search" for search functionality.
claims.quote: WAI-ARIA roles can provide additional meaning, for example, using role="search" to identify search functionality.

claims.rule: Match code order to the logical reading order; remove CSS and verify content order makes sense.
claims.quote: Ensure that the order of elements in the code matches the logical order of the information presented. One way to check this is to remove CSS styling and review that the order of the content makes sense.

sources.title: Inclusive Design Principles
sources.why: Seven core principles for inclusive design with visual posters

claims.rule: Ensure comparable experience quality and efficiency for all users regardless of ability or approach.
claims.quote: What the interface offers each user should be comparable in value, quality, and efficiency.

claims.rule: Use familiar, well-established design patterns applied consistently across functionality and presentation.
claims.quote: Familiar interfaces borrow from well-established patterns. These should be used consistently within the interface to reinforce their meaning and purpose.

claims.rule: Never suppress standard browser settings like zoom, orientation, font size, or contrast.
claims.quote: Do not suppress or disable the ability to change standard browser and platform settings such as orientation, font size, zoom, and contrast.

claims.rule: Allow users to control animations and auto-playing content; provide easy-to-find stop controls.
claims.quote: Where they play automatically, they should at least be easy to stop, by providing prominent playback controls.

claims.rule: Provide multiple ways to complete tasks, especially complex or non-standard ones, to suit user preferences.
claims.quote: Consider providing different ways for people to complete tasks, especially those that are complex or non standard.

claims.rule: Offer customizable alternatives like color-coded, repositionable captions for video to enhance experience.
claims.quote: Making them customizable, color coded, and repositionable provides a more comparable experience.

claims.rule: Use live regions to notify screen reader users proactively without requiring explicit user action.
claims.quote: A comparable experience for blind users, can be achieved by using a live region. The notification then requires no explicit action on the part of the user.

sources.title: Inclusive Design Tools and Guidance
sources.why: Toolkit for running inclusive design sprints and activities

sources.title: Inclusive Design Examples
sources.why: Real-world examples of products using inclusive design

sources.title: Styles
sources.why: Layout, typography, color and spacing guidance

claims.rule: Do not assign new meanings to colors; keep color usage consistent with existing GOV.UK conventions.
claims.quote: do not assign new meanings to colours

claims.rule: Do not change the style of buttons or adjust the thickness of borders on form inputs; maintain visual consistency.
claims.quote: do not change the style of buttons or adjust the thickness of borders on form inputs

sources.title: Components
sources.why: Reusable accessible components for forms and navigation

claims.rule: Use pre-built, core components to build consistent services and reduce duplication of effort.
claims.quote: Using pre-built, core elements allows government teams to build consistent services

claims.rule: Adapt individual components to different contexts and patterns rather than creating custom versions.
claims.quote: You can also use the individual components in different patterns and contexts

sources.title: Patterns
sources.why: Patterns for common tasks like entering names and addresses

claims.rule: Apply best practice design patterns for specific user tasks and page types to solve problems consistently.
claims.quote: Patterns are best practice design solutions for specific user-focused tasks and page types

sources.title: Non-Text Content (1.1.1)
sources.why: Alternative text for non-text content

claims.rule: Provide text alternatives for all non-text content so people with different abilities can access information.
claims.quote: All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose

claims.rule: Give controls and interactive elements a descriptive name that explains their purpose.
claims.quote: If non-text content is a control or accepts user input, then it has a name that describes its purpose

sources.title: Audio-only and Video-only (Prerecorded) (1.2.1)
sources.why: Media alternatives for audio and video

claims.rule: Provide text transcripts or audio tracks for audio-only and video-only prerecorded media.
claims.quote: An alternative for time-based media is provided that presents equivalent information for prerecorded audio-only content.

sources.title: Captions (Prerecorded) (1.2.2)
sources.why: Captions for prerecorded media

claims.rule: Include captions that identify speakers, capture dialogue verbatim, and describe meaningful sound effects and non-speech audio.
claims.quote: Captions not only include dialogue, but identify who is speaking and include non-speech information conveyed through sound, including meaningful sound effects.

claims.rule: Omit captions only when video merely restates information already presented as text on the page.
claims.quote: Captions are not needed when the synchronized media is, itself, an alternate presentation of information that is also presented via text on the web page.

sources.title: Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded) (1.2.3)
sources.why: Audio description for video content

claims.rule: Use pauses in dialogue to insert audio descriptions of actions, characters, scene changes, and on-screen text.
claims.quote: During existing pauses in dialogue, audio description provides information about actions, characters, scene changes, and on-screen text that are important and are not described or spoken in the main sound track.

sources.title: Captions (Live) (1.2.4)
sources.why: Live captions for synchronous media

claims.rule: Provide real-time captions for all live audio in synchronized media, identifying speakers and sound effects.
claims.quote: Captions not only include dialogue, but also identify who is speaking and notate sound effects and other significant audio.

sources.title: Audio Description (Prerecorded) (1.2.5)
sources.why: Enhanced audio description requirements

claims.rule: Avoid requiring audio description if all video information is already audibly conveyed in the main soundtrack.
claims.quote: If all of the important information in the video track is already conveyed in the audio track, no additional audio description is necessary.

sources.title: Sign Language (Prerecorded) (1.2.6)
sources.why: Sign language interpretation for deaf users

sources.title: Info and Relationships (1.3.1)
sources.why: Semantic information relationships in markup

claims.rule: Mark required form fields with both color and text, not color alone.
claims.quote: The labels for the required fields are displayed in red. In addition, at the end of each label is an asterisk character, *.

claims.rule: Associate form labels and icons programmatically so assistive tech can determine which fields are required.
claims.quote: Both the red text and the icon are programmatically associated with the appropriate form fields so that assistive technology users can determine the required fields.

claims.rule: Mark table headers programmatically so assistive tech can determine row and column associations.
claims.quote: The bus stop and bus cells are identified as headers for their corresponding row or column so that assistive technology can programmatically determine which bus and which bus stop are associated with the time in each cell.

sources.title: Meaningful Sequence (1.3.2)
sources.why: Reading order must match visual presentation

sources.title: Sensory Characteristics (1.3.3)
sources.why: Don't rely on shape, color or location alone

claims.rule: Label controls by name, not solely by shape, color, size, location, or sound.
claims.quote: Instructions provided for understanding and operating content do not rely solely on sensory characteristics of components such as shape, color, size, visual location, orientation, or sound.

sources.title: Orientation (1.3.4)
sources.why: Support portrait and landscape orientation

sources.title: Use of Color (1.4.1)
sources.why: Color alone must not convey information

claims.rule: Never use color alone to convey information; add shape, text, or pattern.
claims.quote: Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element.

sources.title: Audio Control (1.4.2)
sources.why: Control over background audio

claims.rule: If audio plays for more than 3 seconds, provide pause, stop, or independent volume control.
claims.quote: If any audio on a web page plays automatically for more than 3 seconds, either a mechanism is available to pause or stop the audio, or a mechanism is available to control audio volume independently from the overall system volume level.

sources.title: Images of Text (1.4.5)
sources.why: Avoid text rendered as images

claims.rule: Use text instead of images of text so users can adjust font size, color, and spacing.
claims.quote: Use text instead of pictures of text.

claims.rule: Only use images for text when the presentation is essential, such as logos, type samples, or diagrams conveying information visually.
claims.quote: A particular presentation of text is essential to the information being conveyed.

sources.title: Low or No Background Audio (1.4.7)
sources.why: Audio background requirements

claims.rule: Ensure background audio in speech content is at least 20 decibels lower than foreground speech, or let users turn it off.
claims.quote: The background sounds are at least 20 decibels lower than the foreground speech content, with the exception of occasional sounds that last for only one or two seconds.

sources.title: Keyboard (2.1.1)
sources.why: All functionality keyboard accessible

sources.title: No Keyboard Trap (2.1.2)
sources.why: Keyboard focus must not be trapped

claims.rule: Advise users how to escape focus traps if exit requires non-standard methods beyond arrow, Tab, or Esc keys.
claims.quote: If it requires more than unmodified arrow or tab keys or other standard exit methods, the user is advised of the method for moving focus away.

sources.title: Character Key Shortcuts (2.1.4)
sources.why: Single-character keyboard shortcuts guidelines

claims.rule: Avoid single-character keyboard shortcuts, especially for speech input users who risk accidental command triggers during dictation.
claims.quote: Single-key shortcuts are the exception. While using single letter keys as controls might be appropriate and efficient for many keyboard users, single-key shortcuts are disastrous for speech users.

sources.title: Bypass Blocks (2.4.1)
sources.why: Skip links and navigation bypass mechanisms

sources.title: Page Titled (2.4.2)
sources.why: Page titles identify purpose and content

claims.rule: Give each web page a descriptive title that identifies its topic or purpose.
claims.quote: Web pages have titles that describe topic or purpose.

claims.rule: In single-page applications, change the page title dynamically to match each distinct view or state.
claims.quote: In cases such as Single Page Applications (SPAs), where various distinct pages/views are all nominally served from the same URI and the content of the page is changed dynamically, the title of the page should also be changed dynamically to reflect the content or topic of the current view.

sources.title: Link Purpose (In Context) (2.4.4)
sources.why: Link text clearly describes link purpose

sources.title: Multiple Ways (2.4.5)
sources.why: Multiple navigation methods in web applications

sources.title: Headings and Labels (2.4.6)
sources.why: Headings and labels describe topic or purpose

claims.rule: Use descriptive headings and labels to help users understand page content organization.
claims.quote: Headings and labels describe topic or purpose.

claims.rule: A single word or character label suffices if it provides a clear navigational cue.
claims.quote: Labels and headings do not need to be lengthy. A word, or even a single character, may suffice if it provides an appropriate cue to finding and navigating content.

sources.title: Location (2.4.8)
sources.why: User location in site hierarchy visible

claims.rule: Show users where they are within a site structure using breadcrumbs, site maps, or location indicators.
claims.quote: Information about the user's location within a set of web pages is available.

sources.title: Link Purpose (Link Only) (2.4.9)
sources.why: Link text alone describes purpose

sources.title: Section Headings (2.4.10)
sources.why: Section headings organize content

claims.rule: Use section headings to organize page content into logical parts.
claims.quote: Section headings are used to organize the content.

claims.rule: Help users orient themselves and navigate content faster with heading structure.
claims.quote: People can orient themselves, especially those with cognitive or visual disabilities.

sources.title: Pointer Gestures (2.5.1)
sources.why: Multipoint and path-based gestures alternatives

sources.title: Pointer Cancellation (2.5.2)
sources.why: Down and up events cancelable or unexecuted

claims.rule: Activate controls on pointer release (up-event), not on press (down-event).
claims.quote: The down-event of the pointer is not used to execute any part of the function.

sources.title: Label in Name (2.5.3)
sources.why: Visible label matches accessible name

claims.rule: Place label text at the start of a control's programmatic name.
claims.quote: A best practice is to have the text of the label at the start of the name.

sources.title: Motion Actuation (2.5.4)
sources.why: Motion sensor triggers have alternatives

claims.rule: Allow users to disable motion-triggered functions to prevent accidental activation.
claims.quote: responding to the motion can be disabled to prevent accidental actuation

sources.title: Concurrent Input Mechanisms (2.5.6)
sources.why: Support multiple simultaneous input methods

sources.title: Dragging Movements (2.5.7)
sources.why: Drag actions have single pointer alternatives

claims.rule: Provide a single pointer alternative to any drag-based interaction.
claims.quote: All functionality that uses a dragging movement for operation can be achieved by a single pointer without dragging

claims.rule: Allow clicking anywhere on a slider track to move the thumb instead of requiring drag.
claims.quote: click/tap anywhere on the slider track to move the thumb to that position

claims.rule: Offer text input as an alternative to dragging for precise control.
claims.quote: an input beside a slider could allow any user to enter a precise value for the slider

sources.title: Language of Page (3.1.1)
sources.why: Page language declared in code

claims.rule: Programmatically indicate the default language of each web page.
claims.quote: The default human language of each web page can be programmatically determined

claims.rule: Screen readers load correct pronunciation rules when page language is specified.
claims.quote: Screen readers can load the correct pronunciation rules

sources.title: Language of Parts (3.1.2)
sources.why: Text in different languages marked

sources.title: On Focus (3.2.1)
sources.why: Focus alone must not cause unexpected context change

claims.rule: Do not change context when a component receives focus.
claims.quote: When any user interface component receives focus, it does not initiate a change of context

sources.title: On Input (3.2.2)
sources.why: User input alone must not cause unexpected context change

claims.rule: Warn users before input changes context unless behavior is already explained.
claims.quote: Changing the setting of any user interface component does not automatically cause a change of context unless the user has been advised of the behavior before using the component

sources.title: Consistent Navigation (3.2.3)
sources.why: Navigation patterns appear consistently across site

claims.rule: Repeat navigation in the same relative order across all pages.
claims.quote: Navigational mechanisms that are repeated on multiple web pages within a set of web pages occur in the same relative order each time they are repeated

sources.title: Consistent Identification (3.2.4)
sources.why: Components with same function identified consistently

claims.rule: Identify components with the same functionality consistently across pages so users recognize them.
claims.quote: Components that have the same functionality within a set of web pages are identified consistently.

claims.rule: Enable users to apply prior interaction knowledge to equivalent components on different pages.
claims.quote: Consistent identification allows users to apply knowledge gained from one page when interacting with another, reducing the effort required to locate and understand familiar functionality.

claims.rule: Help people with cognitive disabilities recognize repeated components without relearning functionality.
claims.quote: People with cognitive and learning disabilities benefit from consistent identification because it reduces the effort required to learn, recognize, and locate familiar functionality.

sources.title: Error Identification (3.3.1)
sources.why: Errors identified and described in text

claims.rule: Describe input errors in text so users know what is wrong and how to identify the problematic field.
claims.quote: If an input error is automatically detected, the item that is in error is identified and the error is described to the user in text.

claims.rule: Show all detected errors to users, not just the first one, to prevent repeated form resubmissions.
claims.quote: If several errors are present, only the first error message is exposed; once the user has provided an input that conforms to the type of field, and resubmits the form, the next error (if present) will be exposed.

sources.title: Labels or Instructions (3.3.2)
sources.why: Form labels and instructions provided

claims.rule: Provide labels or instructions for every form input so users know what data to enter.
claims.quote: Labels or instructions are provided when content requires user input.

claims.rule: Include data format instructions in labels, especially when formats differ from customary conventions.
claims.quote: Instructions or labels may also specify data formats for data entry fields, especially if they are out of the customary formats or if there are specific rules for correct input.

claims.rule: Label each option in radio buttons, checkboxes, and similar controls so users understand what they select.
claims.quote: In the case of radio buttons, checkboxes, comboboxes, or similar controls that provide users with options, each option must have an appropriate label so that users know what they are actually selecting.

claims.rule: Balance form clarity by providing essential instructions without cluttering the page with unnecessary information.
claims.quote: The intent of this success criterion is not to clutter the page with unnecessary information but to provide important cues and instructions that will benefit people with disabilities.

sources.title: Error Suggestion (3.3.3)
sources.why: Error correction suggestions provided

claims.rule: Suggest known corrections when input errors are detected, unless it jeopardizes security.
claims.quote: If an input error is automatically detected and suggestions for correction are known, then the suggestions are provided to the user, unless it would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.

claims.rule: Provide correction suggestions to help users with cognitive disabilities fill forms successfully.
claims.quote: Providing information about how to correct input errors allows users who have learning disabilities to fill in a form successfully.

sources.title: Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data) (3.3.4)
sources.why: Prevention and recovery for critical transactions

claims.rule: For high-consequence transactions, allow users to review, confirm, and correct information before finalizing.
claims.quote: A mechanism is available for reviewing, confirming, and correcting information before finalizing the submission.

claims.rule: Check user input for errors and let users correct them before submission on important transactions.
claims.quote: Data entered by the user is checked for input errors and the user is provided an opportunity to correct them.

claims.rule: Recognize that users with disabilities are more likely to make mistakes and require safeguards.
claims.quote: Users with disabilities may be more likely to make mistakes. People with reading disabilities may transpose numbers and letters, and those with motor disabilities may hit keys by mistake.

sources.title: Help (3.3.5)
sources.why: Context-sensitive help available

claims.rule: Provide context-sensitive help that is obvious and accessible when users need it during a task.
claims.quote: The existence of context-sensitive help should be obvious to the user and they should be able to obtain it whenever they require it.

claims.rule: Offer context-sensitive help to prevent mistakes without interrupting the user's workflow.
claims.quote: Using context-sensitive help, users find out how to perform an operation without losing track of what they are doing.

sources.title: Error Prevention (All) (3.3.6)
sources.why: Error prevention for all user input submission

claims.rule: Provide users with ability to reverse, check, or confirm submissions before finalizing.
claims.quote: Reversible Submissions are reversible. Checked Data entered by the user is checked for input errors and the user is provided an opportunity to correct them. Confirmed A mechanism is available for reviewing, confirming, and correcting information before finalizing the submission.

claims.rule: Help users with disabilities avoid mistakes by allowing them to detect errors before submission.
claims.quote: Providing the ability to review and correct information gives the user an opportunity to detect a mistake before taking an action.

sources.title: Parsing (4.1.1)
sources.why: Valid markup and no duplicate IDs

sources.title: Name, Role, Value (4.1.2)
sources.why: Component name, role, and state programmatically exposed

sources.title: Status Messages (4.1.3)
sources.why: Status messages announced to screen readers

claims.rule: Assign roles to status messages so assistive technology can announce them without interrupting focus.
claims.quote: status messages can be programmatically determined through role or properties such that they can be presented to the user by assistive technologies without receiving focus.

sources.title: Accordion
sources.why: Collapsible content component

sources.title: Back link
sources.why: Navigation back to previous page

claims.rule: Place back links before main content so users can skip all navigation links if needed.
claims.quote: Always place back links at the top of a page, before the <main> element. Placing them here means that the 'Skip to main content' link allows the user to skip all navigation links, including the back link.

claims.rule: For complex journeys, use descriptive link text like 'Go back to [page]' instead of just 'Back'.
claims.quote: For more complex user journeys, consider using different link text, like 'Go back to [page]'. For example, in an admin system with many different areas. In this case, if you used 'Back', it might not be clear to users what they are going back to.

sources.title: Breadcrumbs
sources.why: Navigation breadcrumb trail

claims.rule: Place breadcrumbs at the top of a page, before the main element.
claims.quote: Always place breadcrumbs at the top of a page, before the <main> element.

claims.rule: Start breadcrumbs with home and end with the parent section of the current page.
claims.quote: The breadcrumbs should start with your 'home' page and end with the parent section of the current page.

claims.rule: Collapse breadcrumbs on mobile to show only first and last items when they are long.
claims.quote: If you have long breadcrumbs you can configure the component to only show the first and last items on mobile devices.

claims.rule: Ensure breadcrumb contrast ratio is at least 4.5:1 with background on dark surfaces.
claims.quote: the background colour must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 with white to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum), level AA

sources.title: Button
sources.why: Interactive button component with variants

claims.rule: Write button text in sentence case describing the action it performs.
claims.quote: Write button text in sentence case, describing the action it performs.

claims.rule: Use only one default button per page for the main call to action.
claims.quote: Avoid using multiple default buttons on a single page. Having more than one main call to action reduces their impact, and makes it harder for users to know what to do next.

claims.rule: Align primary action button to the left edge of the form.
claims.quote: Align the primary action button to the left edge of your form.

claims.rule: Use warning buttons only for destructive actions that cannot be undone.
claims.quote: Only use warning buttons for actions with serious destructive consequences that cannot be easily undone by a user.

claims.rule: Confirm destructive actions with a second step; do not rely on color alone.
claims.quote: Do not only rely on the red colour of a warning button to communicate the serious nature of the action. This is because not all users will be able to see the colour or will understand what it signifies.

claims.rule: Ensure button contrast ratio is at least 4.5:1 with background on dark surfaces.
claims.quote: the white button and background colour must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum), level AA

sources.title: Character count
sources.why: Character limit indicator for text inputs

claims.rule: Only use character count when there is a legal or technical reason for the limit.
claims.quote: Only use the character count component when there is a good reason for limiting the number of characters users can enter.

claims.rule: Allow users to exceed the limit; show they have entered too many characters.
claims.quote: This component does not restrict the user from entering information. The user can enter more than the character limit, but are told they've entered too many characters.

sources.title: Checkboxes
sources.why: Multiple selection checkbox component

claims.rule: Position checkboxes to the left of their labels for findability.
claims.quote: Always position checkboxes to the left of their labels. This makes them easier to find, especially for users of screen magnifiers.

claims.rule: Order checkbox options alphabetically by default or by frequency.
claims.quote: Order checkbox options alphabetically by default. In some cases, it can be helpful to order them from most-to-least common options.

claims.rule: Add hint text like 'Select all that apply' if users may not know multiple selection is possible.
claims.quote: Do not assume that users will know how many options they can select based on the visual difference between radios and checkboxes alone. If needed, add a hint explaining this, for example, 'Select all that apply'.

claims.rule: Group checkboxes in a fieldset with a legend describing them.
claims.quote: Group checkboxes together in a <fieldset> with a <legend> that describes them, as shown in the examples on this page.

sources.title: Cookie banner
sources.why: Cookie consent notification

sources.title: Date input
sources.why: Date entry with day, month, year fields

claims.rule: Use date input when users know or can easily look up the date without a calendar.
claims.quote: Use the date input component when you're asking users for a date they'll already know, or can look up without using a calendar.

claims.rule: Accept month names written in full or abbreviated form in date fields.
claims.quote: Accept month names written out in full or abbreviated form (for example, 'january' or 'jan') as some users may enter months in this way.

claims.rule: Do not automatically tab between date input fields as it may confuse users.
claims.quote: Never automatically tab users between the fields of the date input because this can be confusing and may clash with normal keyboard controls.

sources.title: Details
sources.why: Expandable details/disclosure element

claims.rule: Use details component to reveal optional information only when users need it, not essential information.
claims.quote: Make a page easier to scan by letting users reveal more detailed information only if they need it.

claims.rule: Write short, descriptive link text so users quickly determine whether to click.
claims.quote: Make the link text short and descriptive so users can quickly work out if they need to click on it.

claims.rule: Never use details component for information the majority of users need.
claims.quote: Do not use the details component to hide information that the majority of your users will need.

claims.rule: Use details instead of tabs or accordions only when displaying a single section of content.
claims.quote: Use the details component instead of tabs or an accordion if you only have 1 section of content.

sources.title: Error message
sources.why: Error messaging and validation feedback

claims.rule: Always place error messages in red after the question text and hint text, with red border connecting message to question.
claims.quote: put the message in red after the question text and hint text use a red border to visually connect the message and the question it belongs to

claims.rule: Never clear form fields when showing error messages; keep both passing and failing answers.
claims.quote: Do not clear any form fields when showing the Error message component. Keep both passing and failing answers.

claims.rule: Explain what went wrong and how to fix it in every error message.
claims.quote: show an error message when there is a validation error. In the error message explain what went wrong and how to fix it.

sources.title: Error summary
sources.why: Summary of all form errors at page top

claims.rule: Always show an error summary at the top of page for any validation error, even if there is only one.
claims.quote: Always show an error summary when there is a validation error, even if there's only one.

claims.rule: Link each error in the error summary to the field or first field containing the error.
claims.quote: You must link the errors in the error summary to the answer they relate to.

sources.title: Exit this page
sources.why: Emergency page exit button (ESC key)

claims.rule: Use shift key triple-press as accessible discreet activation method for keyboard-only users.
claims.quote: The keyboard option, where the user can press shift 3 times, gives users a discreet way to activate the component, particularly keyboard-only users.

sources.title: File upload
sources.why: File input component

claims.rule: Only ask users to upload files if it is critical to service delivery.
claims.quote: You should only ask users to upload something if it's critical to the delivery of your service.

claims.rule: Allow users to reuse previously uploaded files within a journey unless security or privacy prevents it.
claims.quote: Make sure users can easily reuse a previously uploaded file within a single journey, unless doing so would be a major security or privacy concern.

claims.rule: Use specific error messages for each file upload error condition.
claims.quote: Make sure errors follow the guidance in the Error message component and have specific error messages for specific error states.

sources.title: Fieldset
sources.why: Form field grouping semantic element

claims.rule: Use fieldset component to group related form inputs and show their relationship.
claims.quote: Use the fieldset component to group related form inputs.

sources.title: GOV.UK header
sources.why: Page header with branding and navigation

claims.rule: Place the GOV.UK logo and header at the top of every page to maintain user trust across GOV.UK.
claims.quote: You must use the GOV.UK header component at the top of every page. This is to maintain user trust as they move around the GOV.UK website and other government websites and services.

claims.rule: Show only the GOV.UK logo and GOV.UK-wide links in the default header; do not add service-specific branding.
claims.quote: It should only show the GOV.UK logo and any GOV.UK-wide links and tools to help your users. Do not

sources.title: GOV.UK footer
sources.why: Page footer with links and information

claims.rule: Include a copyright notice in the footer to clarify who owns the copyright.
claims.quote: Add a copyright notice to the footer to clarify who owns the copyright.

sources.title: Inset text
sources.why: Highlighted text callout

claims.rule: Use inset text sparingly to differentiate blocks like quotes, examples, or additional information from surrounding content.
claims.quote: Use inset text very sparingly - it's less effective if it's overused.

claims.rule: Do not use inset text for very important information; use Warning text component instead for legal or critical content.
claims.quote: Some users do not notice inset text if it's used on complex pages or near to other visually prominent elements. For this reason, avoid using inset text as a way of highlighting very important information that users need to see. If you need to draw attention to very important content, like legal information, use the Warning text component instead.

sources.title: Notification banner
sources.why: Notification and alert banner

claims.rule: Use notification banners only for information not directly relevant to the current page task; put task-relevant info in main content.
claims.quote: If the information is directly relevant to the thing the user is doing on that page, put the information in the main page content instead.

claims.rule: Show at most one notification banner per page; combine messages or show only the highest priority banner.
claims.quote: Avoid showing more than one notification banner on the same page. Instead, combine the messages in a single notification banner. If the messages are too different to combine, only show the highest priority notification banner.

sources.title: Pagination
sources.why: Multi-page navigation control

claims.rule: Break content across pages only if it improves performance or usability; avoid infinite scroll for keyboard users.
claims.quote: Only break up content onto separate pages if it improves the performance or usability of your service. Avoid using the 'infinite scroll' technique to automatically load content when the user approaches the bottom of the page. This causes problems for keyboard users.

claims.rule: Do not use pagination for linear journeys like forms; use Button and Back link components instead.
claims.quote: Do not use this Pagination component for linear journeys – for example, where you're asking the user to complete a form. Instead, use the Button component (usually a 'Continue' button) to let the user move to the next page – and a Back link component to let them move to the previous page.

claims.rule: Stack pagination links vertically for related content pages to aid screen magnifier users.
claims.quote: Stack the links vertically, so they're more obvious to screen magnifier users when they're zoomed in.

sources.title: Panel
sources.why: Success message or important content panel

claims.rule: Use Panel component only to highlight important content on confirmation or interruption pages; never for other information.
claims.quote: Never use the Panel component to highlight any other information.

claims.rule: Keep panel text brief as a high-level explanation; use short words to prevent wrapping on zoom.
claims.quote: Keep your panel text brief, as it's only meant for a high-level explanation of what has happened. Aim to use short words and phrases to make sure highlighted information is easy to read at different screen sizes.

sources.title: Password input
sources.why: Password field with show/hide toggle

claims.rule: Allow users to show passwords as plain text to verify entries before submission.
claims.quote: This allows users to visually check their password before they submit it, which helps them reduce errors and choose passwords that are more unique and secure.

claims.rule: Hide passwords by default; only show on user request via toggle button.
claims.quote: Hide passwords by default until the user chooses to show it using the 'show' button. Users might not be in a private space when entering or creating a password, so you should hide passwords by default.

claims.rule: Never reveal whether username or password was wrong in login errors.
claims.quote: If the user enters their account details incorrectly, do not reveal whether they got the username or password wrong.

claims.rule: Allow copy and paste in password fields for password manager compatibility.
claims.quote: Always allow users to copy and paste in password fields. People may have very good reasons why they want to do this, for example if they're using a password manager.

sources.title: Radios
sources.why: Single selection radio button component

claims.rule: Position radio buttons to the left of their labels for discoverability.
claims.quote: Always position radios to the left of their labels. This makes them easier to find, especially for users of screen magnifiers.

claims.rule: Provide escape option like 'None of the above' if users cannot deselect once chosen.
claims.quote: Users cannot go back to having no option selected once they have selected one, without refreshing their browser window. Therefore, you should include 'None of the above' or 'I do not know' if they are valid options.

claims.rule: Group radios in a fieldset with legend describing the question.
claims.quote: Group radios together in a <fieldset> with a <legend> that describes them, as shown in the examples on this page. This is usually a question, like 'Where do you live?'.

sources.title: Select
sources.why: Dropdown select component

claims.rule: Avoid select dropdowns in public services; use radios or ask narrowing questions instead.
claims.quote: The select component should only be used as a last resort in public-facing services because research shows that some users find selects very difficult to use.

claims.rule: Do not pre-select options in question contexts to avoid biasing user answers.
claims.quote: If you use the component for questions, you should not pre-select any of the options in case it influences users' answers.

claims.rule: Keep hint text to one short sentence without full stops or links.
claims.quote: Keep hint text to a single short sentence, without any full stops. Do not use links in hint text.

sources.title: Skip link
sources.why: Keyboard skip to main content link

claims.rule: Include skip link on all pages to let keyboard users jump to main content.
claims.quote: All GOV.UK pages must include a skip link. Usually, you should place the skip link immediately after the opening <body> tag.

claims.rule: Visually hide skip link until keyboard activation to avoid screen clutter.
claims.quote: The skip link component is visually hidden until a keyboard press activates it.

sources.title: Summary list
sources.why: Definition list for key-value pairs

claims.rule: Use description list element to pair labels with values in summary contexts.
claims.quote: The summary list uses the description list ( <dl> ) HTML element, so only use it to present information that has a key and at least one value.

sources.title: Table
sources.why: Data table component with responsive design

claims.rule: Use table captions like headings to help users find, navigate, and understand tables.
claims.quote: Use the <caption> element to describe a table in the same way you would use a heading. A caption helps users find, navigate and understand tables.

claims.rule: Use scope attribute on headers to distinguish row and column headers for assistive tech.
claims.quote: Use table headers to tell users what the rows and columns represent. Use the scope attribute to help users of assistive technology distinguish between row and column headers.

claims.rule: Right-align numbers in table cells to make comparison easier.
claims.quote: When comparing columns of numbers, align the numbers to the right in table cells.

sources.title: Tabs
sources.why: Tabbed interface component

claims.rule: Display one section of content at a time using tabs for related information.
claims.quote: The tabs component lets users navigate between related sections of content, displaying one section at a time.

sources.title: Tag
sources.why: Status label/badge component

claims.rule: Use adjectives, not verbs, for tag text to prevent users thinking tags are interactive.
claims.quote: Use adjectives (descriptive words) and not verbs (action words) for the names of your tags. Using a verb might make a user think that clicking on them will do something.

claims.rule: Do not make tags interactive as users unlikely to identify them as clickable elements.
claims.quote: Do not use tags to create links, buttons or other interactive elements, as users: are unlikely to identify the tags as something they're meant to interact with

claims.rule: Limit the number of tag statuses shown to help users remember them.
claims.quote: Tags should be helpful to users. The more you add, the harder it is for users to remember them. So start with the smallest number of statuses

sources.title: Task list
sources.why: Multi-task progress tracker

claims.rule: Do not use task lists for services requiring specific completion order.
claims.quote: Do not use the task list for a long service that needs to be completed in a specific order.

sources.title: Text input
sources.why: Text field input component

claims.rule: Always provide visible labels above text inputs, not placeholder text.
claims.quote: All text inputs must have labels, and in most cases the label should be visible.

claims.rule: Match text input width to expected content length to set user expectations.
claims.quote: Help users understand what they should enter by making text inputs the right size for the content they're intended for.

claims.rule: Use fixed-width inputs for content with specific, known length like postcodes or phone numbers.
claims.quote: Use fixed width inputs for content that has a specific, known length. Postcode inputs should be postcode-sized, phone number inputs should be phone number-sized.

sources.title: Textarea
sources.why: Multi-line text input component

claims.rule: Always provide visible labels above textareas, not placeholder text.
claims.quote: You must label textareas. Placeholder text is not a suitable substitute for a label, as it disappears when users click inside the textarea.

claims.rule: Set textarea height proportional to expected text amount using rows attribute.
claims.quote: Make the height of a textarea proportional to the amount of text you expect users to enter. You can set the height of a textarea by specifying the rows attribute.

claims.rule: Never disable copy and paste in textareas as users often need this functionality.
claims.quote: Users will often need to copy and paste information into a textarea, so do not stop them from doing this.

sources.title: Warning text
sources.why: Warning callout text component

claims.rule: Use warning text component for important messages about legal consequences or critical actions.
claims.quote: Use the warning text component when you need to warn users about something important, such as legal consequences of an action, or lack of action, that they might take.

sources.title: Ask users for addresses
sources.why: Address entry pattern

claims.rule: Use address lookup with UPRN identifiers to reduce data errors and eliminate manual address matching.
claims.quote: Using UPRN identifiers helps users enter addresses accurately. This helps your service by making address data more consistent and easier to handle, which reduces errors and removes the need for manual address matching in the future.

claims.rule: Provide manual address entry option for users with international or unlisted UK addresses.
claims.quote: provide a manual option for people with international addresses or addresses that are missing or not properly listed in the address lookup

sources.title: Ask users for bank details
sources.why: Bank account information entry

claims.rule: Use one sort code input field instead of multiple fields to reduce user effort and improve completion speed.
claims.quote: Use one input for the sort code. It allows users to enter their sort code more quickly, and avoids them needing to read and understand multiple input labels.

claims.rule: Let users choose alternative payment methods instead of assuming bank account availability.
claims.quote: Not everyone has a bank account or wants to share their account details online. Let users choose to get paid by an alternative method.

claims.rule: Accept sort codes with flexible formatting including spaces, hyphens, and dashes.
claims.quote: Let users enter their sort code in whatever format is familiar to them. Allow additional spaces, hyphens and dashes.

sources.title: Ask users for dates
sources.why: Date input pattern guidance

claims.rule: Match date input field format to the format shown on source documents like passports or credit cards.
claims.quote: When asking for a date exactly as it's shown on a passport, credit card or other document, make the fields match the format of the original.

claims.rule: Allow users to enter approximate dates when exact dates are difficult to remember.
claims.quote: Allow users to enter an approximate date when you are asking them for information they may not know or may struggle to remember.

claims.rule: Never require JavaScript as the only input method for calendar controls; provide text input alternative.
claims.quote: Never make a calendar control that depends on JavaScript as the only input option. Allow users to enter the date into a text input as well as use the control.

sources.title: Ask users for email addresses
sources.why: Email input pattern

claims.rule: Make email input fields wide enough to display at least 30 characters of the entered address.
claims.quote: The field should be wide enough for most users to see their entire email address once they have entered it. A good rule of thumb is to make sure you can see at least 30 characters at once.

claims.rule: Warn users of common misspellings in email providers but allow them to proceed.
claims.quote: You can check for common misspellings of popular email providers, for example 'homtail.com' instead of 'hotmail.com'. Warn users if you detect one, but allow them to proceed in case it's a genuine email address.

sources.title: Ask users for names
sources.why: Name input pattern guidance

claims.rule: Only request names when genuinely needed to deliver the service.
claims.quote: Only ask for people's names if you need that information to deliver a service.

claims.rule: Use single name field to accommodate diverse name formats; multiple fields risk mismatches.
claims.quote: A single name field can accommodate the broadest range of name types, but means you cannot reliably extract parts of a name.

claims.rule: Allow users to change their name to respect identity and prevent service abandonment.
claims.quote: Allowing users to change their name helps your service respect their personal identity. It also means they can continue using your service without having to start over.

sources.title: Ask users for phone numbers
sources.why: Phone number input pattern

claims.rule: Only collect phone numbers when genuinely needed; offer alternative contact methods.
claims.quote: Only collect phone numbers from people if you genuinely need them. Not everyone has or can use a phone, so make sure you give users a choice about how they can be contacted.

claims.rule: Accept phone numbers in flexible formats with spaces, hyphens, dashes, brackets, and country codes.
claims.quote: Let users enter phone numbers in whatever format is familiar to them. Allow for additional spaces, hyphens, dashes and brackets, and be able to accommodate country and area codes.

sources.title: Check answers
sources.why: Review submitted answers pattern

claims.rule: Provide inline change links alongside each answer so users can edit without leaving the page.
claims.quote: < a class = "govuk-link" href = "#" > Change < span class = "govuk-visually-hidden" > name </ span > </ a >

claims.rule: Use visually hidden text to clarify what each change link modifies for screen reader users.
claims.quote: < span class = "govuk-visually-hidden" > name </ span >

sources.title: Complete multiple tasks
sources.why: Multi-step task workflow pattern

claims.rule: Help users understand the order tasks must be completed in and which ones are done.
claims.quote: Help users understand: the tasks involved in completing a transaction the order they should complete tasks in when they've completed tasks

claims.rule: Only use a task list page for longer transactions spanning multiple sessions.
claims.quote: Only use a complete multiple tasks page for longer transactions involving multiple tasks that users may need to complete over a number of sessions.

sources.title: Confirmation page
sources.why: Transaction confirmation page pattern

claims.rule: Show a reference number prominently so users can track their application.
claims.quote: Your reference number < br > < strong > HDJ2123F </ strong >

claims.rule: Explain what happens next and when so users know what to expect after submission.
claims.quote: Your confirmation page must include: a reference number, if there is one details of what happens next and when

claims.rule: Allow users to save or bookmark confirmation pages as receipts.
claims.quote: Some users will bookmark the confirmation page as a form of receipt. You should allow them to return to the page, whenever possible.

claims.rule: Include links to information users are likely to need next after completing a transaction.
claims.quote: links to information or services that users are likely to need next

sources.title: Question page
sources.why: Single question form page pattern

claims.rule: Ask only one question per page to help users focus and understand what is being asked.
claims.quote: Start by asking one question per page Asking just one question per question page helps users understand what you're asking them to do

claims.rule: Include a back link at the top of question pages so users can change previous answers without trusting the browser back button.
claims.quote: Some users do not trust browser back buttons when they're entering data. Always include a Back link component at the top of question pages

claims.rule: Never mark mandatory fields with asterisks; use (optional) for optional fields instead.
claims.quote: Never mark mandatory fields with asterisks.

claims.rule: Pre-populate fields or show carried-forward responses to avoid asking users to re-enter known information.
claims.quote: If the same type of information is needed more than once, make it easier to reuse previously entered answers through one of these methods: pre-populating the relevant fields showing carried-forward responses

claims.rule: Make the reason for asking each question clear to users.
claims.quote: On every question page you should: make sure it's clear to users why you're asking each question

sources.title: Start page
sources.why: Service entry point page pattern

claims.rule: Use action-focused button text like Start now or Sign in rather than generic labels.
claims.quote: include a 'button' linking into the service, with text that's consistent with the action you're asking users to take – for example, 'Start now', 'Sign in'

claims.rule: List documents and information users will need before starting the service.
claims.quote: You'll also need to list any documents or information the user will need to help them complete the service

claims.rule: Ask eligibility questions inside the service rather than blocking users at the start page.
claims.quote: Avoid using the start point to provide complex eligibility information. Instead, ask questions inside the service to find out whether the user is eligible.

sources.title: Interruption page
sources.why: Interim alert or notice page

claims.rule: Use interruption pages sparingly and only when users might make a costly or irreversible mistake.
claims.quote: Use Interruption pages to warn the user before they: do something unusual that's probably a mistake do something that cannot be undone

claims.rule: Keep interruption panel content short and do not include form elements inside the panel.
claims.quote: Keep information within the panel short. Do not place any other components or form elements inside the panel.

claims.rule: Only use interruption pages when there is clear evidence of need and no other way to prevent the error.
