claims.quote: Do not use Interruption pages unless you're confident that both: there's evidence of a clear need to pause the user journey it's the only way to give the user information

sources.title: Page not found
sources.why: 404 error page pattern

sources.title: Design Principles
sources.why: Core USWDS design principles

claims.rule: Document and share research findings with team members, managers, and the public when appropriate.
claims.quote: Share your findings. Document and share your research findings with team members, managers, and the public whenever practical.

sources.title: Landing page
sources.why: Landing page template

sources.title: Documentation page
sources.why: Documentation page template

sources.title: 404 page
sources.why: Error page template

claims.rule: Use straightforward plain language on 404 pages; structure includes heading, explanation, fixes, actions, and support channels.
claims.quote: This kind of error can be frustrating or confusing. Straightforward plain language can help. Use a 404 page to explain the error and instruct the user what to do next.

sources.title: Authentication pages
sources.why: Login and authentication page templates

claims.rule: Provide context explaining why account creation is needed; remove unnecessary distractions from the page.
claims.quote: The best way to help is to provide context about why they're creating an account and to remove unnecessary distractions from the page.

claims.rule: Use a shared authentication service where possible to ensure consistency across government websites.
claims.quote: You should use a shared service or the authentication page templates to create a more consistent experience across sites and services.

sources.title: Form templates
sources.why: Common form layout templates

claims.rule: Display form controls in HTML order matching screen order; do not use CSS to rearrange them.
claims.quote: Display form controls in the same order in the HTML as they appear on screen. Don't use CSS to rearrange the form controls.

claims.rule: Align validation messages visually with their input fields for screen magnifier users.
claims.quote: Visually align validation messages with the input fields so people using screen magnifiers can read them quickly.

claims.rule: Group related form controls in fieldset elements with legend labels for screen reader users.
claims.quote: Group each set of thematically related controls in a fieldset element. Use the legend element to offer a label within each one.

claims.rule: Use simple vertical layouts for forms to aid users with limited vision who scan left-to-right.
claims.quote: Keep your form blocks in a vertical pattern. This approach is ideal, from an accessibility standpoint, because of limited vision that makes it hard to scan from right to left.

claims.rule: Avoid disabled form states; use helper text, tooltips and inline validation instead.
claims.quote: Avoid disabled states, especially for text inputs. Disabled states have low color contrast, do not offer meaningful feedback to screen reader users, and keyboard navigators can't focus on them.

claims.rule: Use aria-disabled and JavaScript to disable elements when necessary, not the disabled HTML attribute.
claims.quote: Support screen reader users and keyboard navigators by using aria-disabled=true instead of the disabled attribute to indicate the presence of a disabled element

claims.rule: Add the required HTML attribute to form inputs to enforce field validation before submission.
claims.quote: Add the required attribute to your form elements to indicate that a field must be filled out before submitting the form.

claims.rule: Label optional fields with the word optional in parentheses.
claims.quote: Mark optional fields as "optional." Label optional fields with the word "optional" placed in parentheses.

sources.title: Buttons
sources.why: Button component variations

claims.rule: Align primary action buttons to the left edge of forms.
claims.quote: Align the primary action button to the left edge of your form.

claims.rule: Make buttons stretch full width on mobile for easier pressing with one hand.
claims.quote: On smaller screens, such as on mobile, buttons stretch across the screen's width. This makes them easier to press for users holding a phone in their right hand.

claims.rule: Use only one primary button per page to avoid reducing its impact and user clarity.
claims.quote: Use only 1 primary button on a page. Having more than 1 reduces their impact and makes it harder for users to know what to do next.

claims.rule: Ensure button contrast ratio of at least 3:1 with dark backgrounds to meet WCAG 2.2 AA.
claims.quote: The background colour must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 with white to meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, level AA

sources.title: Card
sources.why: Card content container

claims.rule: Use cards to visually group related content and actions so users complete tasks more quickly.
claims.quote: Use a card to visually group related content and actions to help users do what they need to more quickly.

claims.rule: Avoid wrapping entire clickable cards in anchor tags due to poor screen reader experience.
claims.quote: For clickable cards, avoid wrapping the entire card in an anchor tag as this can be a difficult experience for screen reader users.

claims.rule: Keep card content short so users can scan for relevant and actionable information quickly.
claims.quote: Keep the card short so it is easy to scan for relevant and actionable information.

sources.title: Checkboxes
sources.why: Checkbox form control

claims.rule: Use checkboxes to let users select one or more options from a set on a form.
claims.quote: Use checkboxes to let users select 1 or more options on a form.

sources.title: Date input
sources.why: Date field component

claims.rule: Use date input to help users enter dates like appointment dates with separate day, month, year fields.
claims.quote: Use date input to help users enter a date, like an appointment date.

sources.title: Details
sources.why: Expandable details element

claims.rule: Use details component to let users reveal information only when needed, making pages easier to scan.
claims.quote: Make a page easier to scan by letting users reveal more detailed information only if they need it.

claims.rule: Make details link text short and descriptive so users quickly decide if they need to click.
claims.quote: Make the link text short and descriptive so users can quickly work out if they need to click on it.

claims.rule: Avoid using details in transactional forms; users may mistake blue text for a navigation link.
claims.quote: users being reluctant to expand the details component in user testing sessions for transactional services (forms). When asked why they wouldn't click, they explained that they thought the link text (blue underlined text) would take them to a new page

sources.title: Error message
sources.why: Error message component

claims.rule: Explain what went wrong and how to fix it in every error message.
claims.quote: Explain what went wrong and how to fix it.

claims.rule: Use red borders to visually connect error messages to their corresponding form fields.
claims.quote: use a red border to visually connect the message and the question it belongs to

sources.title: Error summary
sources.why: Error summary component

claims.rule: Always show an error summary at the top of the page, even if only one mistake exists.
claims.quote: Always show an error summary when there is a validation error, even if there's only 1 mistake.

claims.rule: Move keyboard focus to the error summary when the page loads so screen readers announce it immediately.
claims.quote: move the keyboard focus to the error summary

claims.rule: Link each error in the summary to the corresponding form field for easy navigation.
claims.quote: link to each of the answers that have validation errors

sources.title: Expander
sources.why: Expandable content container

claims.rule: Do not use expanders on pages with other interactive elements like buttons or text inputs to avoid distraction.
claims.quote: on pages with other interactive elements, such as buttons or text input – there's a risk that expanders will distract users

sources.title: Fieldset
sources.why: Form field grouping

claims.rule: Place the legend as the first element in a fieldset to describe the group of inputs.
claims.quote: The 1st element in a fieldset must be a <legend> which describes the group of inputs.

sources.title: File upload
sources.why: File input component

claims.rule: Support drag-and-drop file uploads alongside the traditional file picker button.
claims.quote: or drop file

sources.title: Footer
sources.why: Page footer

sources.title: Header
sources.why: Page header

claims.rule: Place an organization logo or service name at the top of every page to confirm the user's location.
claims.quote: Use the appropriate header at the top of every page to show users they are on an NHS service

claims.rule: Include a search function in the header to help users find content quickly.
claims.quote: help them get started in finding what they need

sources.title: Pagination
sources.why: Page navigation control

claims.rule: Show the current page and surround it with adjacent page numbers to help users understand their position.
claims.quote: Use pagination to help users navigate forwards and backwards through a series of pages

sources.title: Radios
sources.why: Radio button component

claims.rule: Use radio buttons when users must select exactly one option from a mutually exclusive list.
claims.quote: Use radios when you want users to select only 1 option from a list

sources.title: Select
sources.why: Dropdown select component

claims.rule: Use select dropdowns only as a last resort for long option lists; prefer radios or checkboxes when possible.
claims.quote: Use select to let users choose an option from a long list but only use it as a last resort

sources.title: Summary list
sources.why: Key-value pair list

claims.rule: Display a summary list at the end of a form to let users review and edit their responses before submission.
claims.quote: Use the summary list to summarise information, for example, a user's responses at the end of a form

sources.title: Table
sources.why: Data table component

claims.rule: Consider alternatives to tables (summaries, lists, expanders, tabs) for complex data to reduce cognitive overload.
claims.quote: In staff services, complex data tables can lead to cognitive overload, a poor user experience and performance issues

claims.rule: Avoid using tables to lay out page content; use a grid system instead.
claims.quote: Do not use a table to lay out content on a page. Use the grid system instead

sources.title: Tabs
sources.why: Tabbed interface

sources.title: Tag
sources.why: Status/label tag component

claims.rule: Use adjectives rather than verbs for tag labels to avoid users thinking they are clickable.
claims.quote: Use adjectives rather than verbs for the names of your tags. Using a verb might make a user think that clicking on them will do something.

claims.rule: Limit tag statuses to the minimum needed; add more only if user research confirms necessity.
claims.quote: The more you add, the harder it is for users to remember them. So start with the smallest number of statuses you think might work, then add more if your user research shows there's a need for them.

sources.title: Task list
sources.why: Multi-task progress list

claims.rule: Display task completion status and hints alongside task names to help users identify what they have done and still need to do.
claims.quote: The task list component displays all the tasks a user needs to do, and allows users to easily identify which ones are done and which they still need to do.

sources.why: Text input field

sources.title: Textarea
sources.why: Multi-line text input

sources.title: Analyzing Good Designs: Ritual.com
sources.why: Analysis of visual design excellence and real-world application of design principles.

sources.title: AI-Generated Images Can Perform as Well as Stock Photography
sources.why: Empirical evidence on AI image performance compared to stock photography in UI design.

claims.rule: Use AI-generated images without declaring them; users perceive them as trustworthy without knowing their origin.
claims.quote: When users didn't know whether an image was AI-generated, the images we tested did not create any perception penalty compared to stock photos.

claims.rule: Show diverse teams and collaboration in hero images; users trust companies that depict teamwork over hierarchy.
claims.quote: Webpages using both AI-generated images and real images received many positive open-ended comments indicating that they were trustworthy, largely due to depictions of collaboration and teamwork in the images.

claims.rule: Screen AI-generated images for diversity, representation, and authentic collaboration before use; inspect hands, text, reflections, and background details.
claims.quote: Review representation: Who is shown, who is missing, and how are people portrayed? Assess authenticity: Do the people, setting, and interactions feel believable? Inspect for AI errors: Check text, hands, screens, glass reflections, and background details.

sources.title: Handmade Designs: The New Trust Signal
sources.why: Evidence that hand-crafted visual design elements increase user trust and engagement.

claims.rule: Use handmade-looking designs with visible imperfections to signal authenticity and human effort in an AI-fatigued world.
claims.quote: Now, many people are tired of overly polished, gauzy, AI-generated visuals that look good from afar but fall apart in the details. When anyone can generate a sleek image in minutes, polish stops being a quality signal.

claims.rule: Credit the human artist behind handmade designs; authorship matters now more than ever as a trust signal.
claims.quote: That emphasis on authorship matters now more than ever. With the right prompting, an AI tool could theoretically replicate this style. What it cannot replicate is the human story behind the work.

claims.rule: Include variable line weights, incomplete paths, visible brushstrokes, hand-lettered type, misalignment, and organic shapes in handmade designs.
claims.quote: These visual styles share certain traits: line weights that vary, shapes that don't quite close, visible brushstrokes, handwritten typefaces, and various textures. Nothing is perfectly centered. Nothing is perfectly smooth.

claims.rule: Pair handmade visuals with human-sounding UX copy to reinforce authenticity and build trust.
claims.quote: Voice is part of the aesthetic too. UX writing that sounds like a real person gives the same impression as handmade visuals. Pair handmade visuals with human-sounding copy.

claims.rule: Credit the human artist by name in all promotions of handmade designs; authorship is a trust signal that distinguishes human work from AI.
claims.quote: That emphasis on authorship matters now more than ever. With the right prompting, an AI tool could theoretically replicate this style. What it cannot replicate is the human story behind the work. That story is what gives the final result its value and makes it irreplaceable.

claims.rule: Don't use warmth and handmade aesthetics to conceal product shortcomings; misaligned visual messaging undermines trust when product cannot deliver on promises.
claims.quote: When the brand feels welcoming and secure, but the associated tool fails standards of security or accuracy, users will feel misled. Warmth that conceals the true attributes of a product undermines trust.

sources.title: Good Visual Design, Explained
sources.why: Fundamental principles and rules for effective visual design in user interfaces.

claims.rule: Use a grid with columns and gutters; vary gutter size by purpose to organize layouts consistently across pages.
claims.quote: Grids are made up of columns with gutters between them. While there is no ideal gutter size, different gutter sizes are suited to different purposes.

claims.rule: Limit designs to three type sizes to establish strong hierarchy without overwhelming the user.
claims.quote: As a rule of thumb, limiting your designs to 3 type sizes will establish a strong hierarchy without overwhelming the design or user.

claims.rule: Increase leading and shorten line lengths to make dense text blocks easier to read and avoid user overwhelm.
claims.quote: Consider slightly increasing the default leading if you have a lot of text (either several paragraphs or longer paragraphs), as walls of text can feel overwhelming.

claims.rule: Use monochromatic color palettes to create polished, accessible designs that emphasize content without color expertise.
claims.quote: Monochromatic palettes are the easiest to work with and create, and are the most accessible to novice visual designers.

claims.rule: Limit color palette to two main colors for visual balance and hierarchy; reserve extended color experimentation for designers with significant color expertise.
claims.quote: In your own designs, limiting your color palette to just two colors will create balance and enforce visual hierarchy. Only if you have extensive color experience should you experiment with more complex color harmonies.

claims.rule: Avoid neon colors; they distract users and reduce overall design effectiveness.
claims.quote: Exercise caution with neon colors (such as highlighter yellow), as they may distract users and affect the overall effectiveness of the design.

sources.title: Button States 101
sources.why: Guidelines for designing button states to communicate interaction affordances.

sources.title: Anatomy of Good Icons
sources.why: Research-backed principles for designing clear, recognizable icons in interfaces.

sources.title: Preference Testing for Assessing Visual Design
sources.why: Methods for validating visual design choices through preference testing research.

sources.title: Grids 101
sources.why: Fundamental principles of grid systems in layout design.

claims.rule: Use grid systems with columns, gutters, and margins to structure content consistently across layouts.
claims.quote: Page grids use columns, gutters, and margins to structure content—boosting layout consistency, readability, and visual flow.

claims.rule: Ensure grids adapt to various screen sizes and orientations for consistency across platforms.
claims.quote: A good grid adapts to various screen sizes and orientations, ensuring consistency across platforms.

sources.title: Visual Design Principles in Action
sources.why: Real-world application and demonstration of core visual design principles.

claims.rule: Apply five key visual design principles—scale, hierarchy, balance, contrast, and Gestalt—to critique and improve designs.
claims.quote: Use the 5 key visual design principles—scale, hierarchy, balance, contrast, and Gestalt principles—to objectively critique and improve designs.

sources.title: Button States: Communicate Interaction
sources.why: Guidelines for using button states to signal affordances and feedback.

claims.rule: Communicate five button states—enabled, disabled, hover, focus, pressed—with distinct visual cues so users know what is clickable.
claims.quote: Minor visual changes help users distinguish between 5 different button states: enabled, disabled, hovered, focused, pressed.

claims.rule: Use high contrast between enabled buttons and the rest of the design to catch users' attention for primary actions.
claims.quote: High contrast between the button and the rest of the design

claims.rule: Add 150–200ms delay to hover state to prevent accidental color changes from mouse movement.
claims.quote: a slight delay (around 150–200ms) should be added to this state

claims.rule: Show focus state within 100–150ms and use a stroke or outline, not color alone, to meet accessibility standards.
claims.quote: The focus state should appear pretty quickly (around 100-150ms) after the user uses the keyboard.

claims.rule: Display disabled buttons with reduced contrast and desaturated colors to signal they are not clickable.
claims.quote: A light gray or otherwise desaturated color or a more muted version of its abled state to signal it isn't clickable or tappable

claims.rule: Display focus state within 100–150ms using a stroke or outline, never color alone, to meet accessibility standards.
claims.quote: focus state should appear pretty quickly (around 100-150ms) after the user uses the keyboard

claims.rule: Show pressed state feedback within 100–150ms so users perceive the action as instantaneous.
claims.quote: pressed state should appear within 100–150ms for the user to register that the pressing action is instantaneous

claims.rule: Use stroke or outline for keyboard focus state, not color change alone, to accommodate users with vision impairments.
claims.quote: stick to the stroke or outline to indicate focus, as opposed to relying on color change alone

claims.rule: Add ARIA-disabled attribute to disabled buttons so screen readers announce their inactive state.
claims.quote: Disabled button states should also have the ARIA-disabled: true attribute added to the code

sources.title: Card View vs. List View
sources.why: Comparative analysis of card vs. list layouts for content presentation.

claims.rule: Use list view for easy sorting and space efficiency; use card view for visual engagement and effective grouping.
claims.quote: List view allows for easy sorting and is space efficient, while card view is visually engaging and creates effective groupings.

sources.title: Neobrutalism: Definition and Best Practices
sources.why: Design style patterns and usability implications of neobrutalism in interfaces.

claims.rule: Use high contrast and bold, primary colors in neobrutalist designs to emphasize key functions and enhance visual impact.
claims.quote: Neobrutalist designs use bold, primary colors and high-contrast combinations to emphasize key functions and UI elements.

claims.rule: Employ thick borders, angular forms, and solid lines to create structure without gradients or shadows in neobrutalist designs.
claims.quote: This style does not shy away from using thick borders, angular forms, and solid lines that create structure without relying on gradients or shadows.

claims.rule: Use bold, solid drop shadows offset by approximately 4px instead of soft, layered shadows to maintain raw aesthetics.
claims.quote: It incorporates solid, single-color shadows (e.g., a black drop shadow offset by 4px) to add depth while maintaining the raw aesthetic.

claims.rule: Carefully balance neobrutalism's distinctive look with usability to avoid overwhelming or confusing interfaces.
claims.quote: designers must carefully balance its distinctive look with usability to avoid ending up with an overwhelming or confusing interface.

claims.rule: Restrict neobrutalist color palettes to 2–3 bold high-contrast colors to avoid overwhelming users.
claims.quote: Restrict your palette to 2–3 bold, high-contrast colors (e.g., black, neon green, electric blue) to avoid overwhelming users

claims.rule: Use generous padding of 24–32px margins in neobrutalist layouts to create breathing room and focus attention.
claims.quote: offset dense geometric shapes and thick borders with generous padding (e.g., 24–32px margins) to create breathing room

claims.rule: Pair bold, chunky headlines with clean, neutral body fonts like Roboto or Inter to maintain readability.
claims.quote: Pair bold, unconventional headlines (e.g., a chunky sans-serif font) with clean, neutral body fonts like Roboto or Inter

claims.rule: Use solid drop shadows offset by 4px instead of soft layered shadows to maintain neobrutalist raw aesthetics.
claims.quote: a black drop shadow offset by 4px

sources.title: Testing Visual Design: A Comprehensive Guide
sources.why: Methods for validating visual design effectiveness through user testing.

claims.rule: Use attitudinal testing methods to evaluate brand alignment and first impressions of visual design choices.
claims.quote: Attitudinal methods help explore how users feel about a design's aesthetics, tone, and style. These methods are ideal when your goal is to evaluate brand alignment or assess users' first impressions.

claims.rule: Use first-click tests to determine if users can locate their goal quickly on a page with specific tasks in mind.
claims.quote: First-click tests are ideal for interfaces where users are likely to have a specific goal in mind when they visit your site.

claims.rule: Conduct 5-second tests to capture users' initial visual impressions before they process details or read copy.
claims.quote: Five seconds of viewing time is too short for reading copy or noticing details like specific fonts, but it is enough to formulate an impression of the visual style

claims.rule: Avoid warning participants in 5-second tests that designs will be shown briefly, to capture authentic reactions.
claims.quote: avoid warning participants that the design will be shown for only five seconds. This helps capture participants' authentic initial reactions

claims.rule: Use first-click tests to verify users can locate information within seconds using task-specific goals.
claims.quote: First-click tests tell you if users can accurately find what they need on your website

claims.rule: Make design variations in preference testing significantly different enough for nondesigners to detect immediately.
claims.quote: the differences must be significant enough to be immediately detectable to a nondesigner

claims.rule: Counterbalance or randomize the order of design variations to prevent first-version bias in preference testing.
claims.quote: counterbalance or randomize the order in which you present design variations to your participants

claims.rule: Present behavioral tasks before aesthetic questions in combined usability and visual-design tests to avoid biasing task results.
claims.quote: It's important to present behavioral tasks first and aesthetic assessments afterward

claims.rule: Keep numerical rating questionnaires short; longer surveys increase likelihood of random or unmotivated responses.
claims.quote: Short and easy questionnaires are ideal. The longer the questionnaire, the higher the chance of random answers

claims.rule: Use closed word-choice testing to verify users perceive target brand attributes from design elements.
claims.quote: Providing users with a limited set of words allows you to focus on whether participants pick up the target brand attributes

sources.title: Glassmorphism: Definition and Best Practices
sources.why: Design pattern analysis and usability considerations for glassmorphism effects.

claims.rule: Ensure text and graphical elements in translucent components meet WCAG contrast requirements for readability.
claims.quote: Ensure that text and graphical elements meet contrast requirements. Since glassmorphic components are translucent, textual elements can fall over multiple colors, which can affect readability.

claims.rule: Use opacity and background blur to establish visual hierarchy and depth in glassmorphic elements.
claims.quote: Glassmorphism is a visual-design style that utilizes different levels of translucency to create depth and contrast between foreground and background elements

claims.rule: Apply more background blur to glassmorphic components when backgrounds are complex or intricate; less blur risks distracting users and harming text readability.
claims.quote: More background blur is better, especially with intricate backgrounds (e.g., video, photography, animations).

claims.rule: Use simple or single-color backgrounds behind glassmorphic components when you control the background; this reduces the need for extreme blur.
claims.quote: If you have control of what appears behind a translucent component, opt for simple or single-color backgrounds.

claims.rule: Check glassmorphic text contrast against multiple background colors using tools; text may have sufficient contrast only over certain areas of complex backgrounds.
claims.quote: If you are designing a card component over a busy background, your text might only have enough contrast over certain areas and be challenging to read.

sources.title: Design Systems vs. Style Guides
sources.why: Distinction and relationship between design systems and style guides.

claims.rule: Establish a dedicated team to maintain design systems continuously; without oversight, systems become outdated and lose utility.
claims.quote: Design systems require continuous maintenance and oversight to ensure they do not become outdated, so a team is needed to manage it.

sources.title: The Hamburger-Menu Icon Today: Is it Recognizable?
sources.why: Empirical evidence on recognizability of hamburger menu icons in modern interfaces.

claims.rule: Place hamburger icons in the top-left corner to improve user recognition and interpretation.
claims.quote: Users generally understand the icon to mean categories hidden here as long as it appears in the expected spot: the top-left corner of the screen.

claims.rule: Maintain standard hamburger styling with three stacked lines of equal length for maximum recognizability.
claims.quote: participants correctly identified the hamburger icon as the main menu or top-level site categories, especially when it appeared in expected locations and with standard styling (3 stacked lines of equal length).

claims.rule: Avoid embellishments to familiar hamburger icons; position familiarity matters more than stylistic variations.
claims.quote: such embellishments are unnecessary: Altering a familiar form can introduce

claims.rule: Use subtle motion or transitions when the hamburger menu opens to reinforce the interaction and guide user expectations.
claims.quote: Use subtle animation or transitions: If tapping the icon reveals a navigation panel, subtle motion cues can reinforce the interaction and guide user expectations.

claims.rule: Scale the hamburger icon appropriately for screen size; a smartphone-sized icon becomes invisible on large desktop screens.
claims.quote: Scale the hamburger icon appropriately: A hamburger icon sized for a smartphone can become nearly invisible on a large desktop screen.

claims.rule: Provide additional navigation methods alongside the hamburger menu: inline links, related links lists, visible search, and footer links reduce interaction cost.
claims.quote: Provide additional navigation methods: Support the hamburger with in-line links, lists of related links, a highly visible search function, and footer links.

claims.rule: Add visual padding around the hamburger icon to increase visibility; crowding it near headers or other elements reduces discoverability.
claims.quote: Add visual padding around the icon: Crowding the icon near headers or other UI elements reduces visibility.

sources.title: Tabs, Used Right
sources.why: Guidelines for proper use of tabs in information architecture and navigation.

sources.title: Menu-Design Checklist: 17 UX Guidelines
sources.why: Research-backed 17-point checklist for effective menu design and navigation.

claims.rule: Display navigation menus on larger screens; use hamburger menus only when space constraints require it.
claims.quote: The hamburger menu is a necessary evil on smaller screens, where we must balance content and navigation with limited screen real estate. Menus shouldn't be hidden when you have plenty of space to display them.

claims.rule: Avoid cascading multilevel dropdown menus; use mega menus or landing pages instead.
claims.quote: A simple dropdown menu works well for one-tier navigation but becomes frustrating with two tiers. It is highly inadvisable for more than two tiers, as it increases the risk of accidentally selecting the wrong subcategory or of closing the menu altogether.

sources.title: Card Sorting vs. Tree Testing
sources.why: Comparison of card sorting and tree testing methods for information architecture validation.

claims.rule: Use card sorting as a discovery method early in design to uncover user mental models for content organization.
claims.quote: Card sorting is typically conducted early in the design process to help designers generate ideas for possible navigation structures that align with users' expectations.

claims.rule: Use tree testing to validate an existing or proposed navigation structure by testing content findability.
claims.quote: Tree testing is used to validate a proposed or existing navigation structure by testing the findability of content.

sources.title: Tree Testing Part 2: Interpreting the Results
sources.why: Methods for analyzing tree testing data to improve information architecture.

claims.rule: Consider task criticality when setting success-rate targets; mission-critical or revenue-generating tasks should achieve over 90% success.
claims.quote: a mission-critical or revenue-generating task should have a very high success rate (ideally >90%)

claims.rule: Use 62% median success rate as baseline; score tasks as Poor (<40%), Fair (41–60%), Good (61–80%), Very Good (80–90%), or Excellent (>90%).
claims.quote: median success rate for tasks was 62%, with the interquartile range from 37% – 83%. Their suggested rubric for task success scores in a tree testing study is: Poor : <40% Fair : 41% – 60% Good : 61% – 80% Very Good : 80% – 90% Excellent : >90%

claims.rule: Investigate time spent on tasks in detail; users spending long times may have completed tasks but experienced mentally taxing processes.
claims.quote: Time spent is also worth investigating in detail, as it adds additional understanding of the mental effort involved in finding a resource.

claims.rule: Mark multiple correct answers when testing polyhierarchy; review detailed destination data to see which correct answers users actually selected.
claims.quote: you can mark multiple correct answers for the same task, and then review what proportion of your participants selected each of the correct answers

claims.rule: Use polyhierarchy (cross-listing) only when data shows a substantial portion of users will look for an item in multiple parent categories.
claims.quote: use polyhierarchy only if your data indicates that a substantial portion of your users will look for an item in multiple parent categories

claims.rule: Compare task success rates within similar hierarchy depths, not across different depths; use own historical data as frame of reference.
claims.quote: it would be more realistic to compare either: The success rate for the food-stamps task to that of another task which also targets content that is 6 levels down

claims.rule: Use 50+ participants per tree for quantitative tree testing to achieve reasonably narrow confidence intervals and detect statistically significant differences.
claims.quote: Typically, 50+ participants per tree are needed for a quantitative study to achieve reasonably narrow confidence intervals and find a statistically significant difference

sources.title: Information Architecture vs. Sitemaps
sources.why: Distinction between information architecture practices and sitemap documents.

claims.rule: Build information architecture as an ongoing process, not a single deliverable; involve content inventory, audit, taxonomy, research, and structural planning.
claims.quote: An IA is not a single deliverable : there is no single document that you "finish" and check off your list. It's an ongoing website-management process

claims.rule: Establish IA structure first, then create sitemaps to visualize it; IA is the foundation that defines organization and content relationships.
claims.quote: The IA comes first, the sitemap follows. IA is the foundation that defines the overall structure and organization of content.

sources.title: Tree Testing: Evaluate Menu Labels and Categories
sources.why: Tree testing methodology for validating information architecture and navigation labels.

claims.rule: Define tree hierarchy down to the lowest subcategory level that contains resources users will search for, not just top-level categories.
claims.quote: Go beyond creating just the top-level navigation categories — define your tree down to the lowest level of subcategories that will contain the resources you will ask study participants to find.

claims.rule: Conduct moderated pilot sessions before quantitative tree testing to verify task wording is understandable and catch nuances missed in quantitative data.
claims.quote: We recommend beginning a quantitative tree test with a small qualitative study for two reasons: To pilot your study design and ensure that your tasks are understandable and do not bias participants. To obtain insights about why users chose the answers they did

sources.title: 3 Common IA Mistakes (that Are All Due to Low Information Scent)
sources.why: Common information architecture mistakes and their relationship to information scent.

claims.rule: Use navigation labels with strong information scent; avoid vague verbs like Explore, Discover, Learn, or Partner in category names.
claims.quote: Vague verbs (such as Explore, Discover, Learn, Partner , etc.) are not effective category names — they offer too little differentiation and do not help users make an effective, informed choice. Don't use them for your navigation categories .

claims.rule: Use task-based verbs in navigation only when specific and clear; Explore or Learn are too vague but Go Paperless & Auto Pay is effective.
claims.quote: Task-based categories can be successfully labeled with specific verbs that describe what the user is about to do (such as Go Paperless & Auto Pay for a utility site, for example).

sources.title: The UX of Phone-Tree Systems: 16 Usability Guidelines
sources.why: Research-backed guidelines for designing usable phone tree navigation systems.

claims.rule: Recognize that 60% of users who seek help online choose phone contact; phone trees are critical for omnichannel experience even in digital-first products.
claims.quote: users trying to complete tasks online reached out for help in 64% of cases . Of those who reached out for help, 60% decided to do so over the phone

claims.rule: Present language options before any other audio content so callers can select their language immediately.
claims.quote: If callers have the option to select their language, they should be given this choice immediately. Don't force callers to listen through lengthy messages in a language they don't understand

claims.rule: Warn callers and give them time to prepare before presenting detailed information like phone numbers, emails, or web addresses.
claims.quote: Warn callers with phrases such as We would like to provide you with some other resources such as contact emails, phone numbers, and websites. You might want to grab a pen

claims.rule: Speak technical information at half normal speed and offer options to repeat it or receive it via text.
claims.quote: Present technical information twice as slowly as a normal speaking rate. Callers trying to remember or capture information such as a phone number will be very grateful.

claims.rule: Use consistent keypad controls throughout the phone tree: same keys for undo, repeat, and other functions across all menus.
claims.quote: The same keypad options should perform these two functions throughout the entire phone tree and the labels used for these functions should also be consistent throughout the design

claims.rule: Always provide keypad selection as an alternative to voice-based natural language input in phone trees.
claims.quote: Always provide an alternative navigation method — such as listening to menu options and making a selection. The difference between these methods is comparable to the value of providing meaningful navigation items in addition to the search bar on a website.

claims.rule: Provide useful information outside operating hours: hours, FAQ pages, and emergency contact details.
claims.quote: For organizations who have long periods without anyone answering the phones (such as overnight), there should still be useful information provided in a recording for callers

claims.rule: Remove promotional statements and keep phone-tree messages concise; avoid lengthy advertisements or irrelevant details.
claims.quote: Trapped callers do not want to listen to advertisements, promotions, or wordy messages that ramble on about things that are irrelevant and prevent them from accomplishing their current task

claims.rule: Provide brief auditory confirmation when callers make a selection to show the system registered their choice.
claims.quote: Provide brief feedback confirming callers' actions. When callers make a selection in a phone tree, they need clear feedback confirming that they made the choice they meant to or that their choice was registered by the system.

claims.rule: Only share web addresses that directly relate to the caller's selected topic, not the homepage.
claims.quote: A web address is helpful only if the corresponding page directly relates to a topic the caller has indicated is relevant. However, be cautious of long URLs that will be difficult to remember or write down.

sources.title: Taxonomy 101: Definition, Best Practices, and How It Complements Other IA Work
sources.why: Fundamentals of taxonomy design for organizing and classifying content.

claims.rule: Choose user-friendly preferred terms for taxonomy concepts and link internal business jargon as nonpreferred synonyms.
claims.quote: The best practice is to choose a user-friendly term as your preferred term and link internal business jargon or more technical language as nonpreferred synonyms.

sources.title: Information Architecture: Study Guide
sources.why: Comprehensive study guide covering information architecture principles and practices.

claims.rule: Use clear, specific link labels that signal where users will go and what they'll find.
claims.quote: Better Labels for Website Links: the 4 Ss for Encouraging Clicks

claims.rule: Avoid vague link text like 'Learn More'; use descriptive labels that explain the destination or action.
claims.quote: "Learn More" Links: You Can Do Better

claims.rule: Organize content in multiple categories when items fit ambiguously; use polyhierarchy to improve findability.
claims.quote: Polyhierarchies Improve Findability for Ambiguous IA Categories

sources.title: Quantity Yields Quality in UX: Iterative vs. Parallel vs. Competitive Design
sources.why: Research on design iteration approaches and their impact on outcome quality.

sources.title: Why So Many Info Tips Are Bad (and How to Make Them Better)
sources.why: Research on effective design of information tips and tooltips in interfaces.

claims.rule: Do not use info tips for obvious, redundant, or marketing content; they waste user time and erode trust.
claims.quote: Redundant or obvious tips waste users' time and undermine trust.

claims.rule: Use the lowercase i icon for optional, nice-to-know information that supplements understanding.
claims.quote: The encircled lowercase i icon is broadly understood to indicate optional, helpful information.

claims.rule: Keep info tips brief and task-focused; assume most users will never see them and design for those who are stuck.
claims.quote: Assume that most users will never see the info tip.

claims.rule: Assume most users will never see an info tip; design it for those confused or stuck, needing clear, immediate task guidance.
claims.quote: assume that most users will never see the info tip. Those who do have extra motivation for seeking them out are confused, stuck, or need clarification or reassurance.

claims.rule: Never hide form constraints, character limits, or legal disclaimers in info tips; display them at the primary level of the interface.
claims.quote: any constraints, rules, or limitations for inputs should be displayed on the primary level.

claims.rule: Keep info-tip content inline or adjacent to the element it supports; avoid modals, overlays, or new pages that disconnect users from their workflow.
claims.quote: When possible, ensure that info tips are displayed inline or adjacent to the relevant element. Obscuring the current step or view of the interface makes it harder for users to connect the guidance with the task at hand.

sources.title: Web UX: Study Guide
sources.why: Comprehensive guide to web user experience design principles and practices.

claims.rule: Design for scanning, not reading; users scan web pages word by word reading is rare.
claims.quote: Users scan web pages instead of reading word by word

claims.rule: Use clear, descriptive link text starting with keywords; avoid vague labels like 'Get Started' or generic phrases that confuse user intent.
claims.quote: Guidelines for writing link text

claims.rule: Place different colors on visited and unvisited links to help users understand which content they have already explored.
claims.quote: Change the Color of Visited Links

sources.title: Explainable AI in Chat Interfaces
sources.why: Guidelines for designing AI explanations in conversational interfaces.

claims.rule: Do not rely on source citations alone to build user trust; users rarely click links to verify information.
claims.quote: People rarely click citation links

claims.rule: Make citations visible and prominent; do not bury them in the response body to encourage verification.
claims.quote: Style citations differently from the main output response. Do not bury citations in the body of the answer.

claims.rule: Place sources next to the specific claim they support so users can verify information in context.
claims.quote: Place sources directly next to the specific claim or sentence they support.

claims.rule: Use factual, neutral language in AI explanations; avoid first-person phrasing that anthropomorphizes the model's reasoning.
claims.quote: Instead, use factual, neutral language (e.g., This answer is based on the following source: [link].)

claims.rule: Avoid step-by-step explanations that imply certainty; provide sources and clarify limitations instead until true explainability improves.
claims.quote: Given that step-by-step reasoning is often unreliable, designers should avoid using step-by-step explanations that imply certainty or transparency.

sources.title: Prompt to Design Interfaces: Why Vague Prompts Fail and How to Fix Them
sources.why: Research on prompt effectiveness for AI-assisted design and prototyping.

claims.rule: Provide mock data in realistic format to guide AI-generated layouts; AI designs improve when working with actual content rather than placeholder abstractions.
claims.quote: Providing sample content or data guides the AI to generate better designs.

sources.title: Designing Effective Contextual Menus: 10 Guidelines
sources.why: Research-backed 10-point guideline set for designing context menus.

claims.rule: Place contextual menu icons near the content they affect to aid spatial interpretation.
claims.quote: The location of the contextual-menu icon should clearly indicate

claims.rule: Use contextual menus only for secondary, noncritical actions, not essential task flows.
claims.quote: Contextual menus are not appropriate for actions users rely on frequently. They are best used for secondary or low-priority options

claims.rule: Recognize kebab and meatball icons signal hidden options when used consistently.
claims.quote: both kebab (⋮) and meatball (⋯) icons were generally recognized to mean 'more options' or 'other actions,' as long as the icon followed the guidelines

sources.title: Tesler's Law: Shift Complexity to Simplify UX
sources.why: Explanation and application of Tesler's Law for complexity reduction in interfaces.

sources.title: Good from Afar, But Far from Good: AI Prototyping in Real Design Contexts
sources.why: Research on limitations and best practices for AI-assisted prototyping.

claims.rule: Provide specific, detailed text prompts with explicit design requirements for AI tools.
claims.quote: longer prompts with clear, detailed design requirements consistently yield better results — particularly with AI tools that generate code-based prototypes

claims.rule: Include visual design references and Figma links in prompts to AI tools; high-fidelity artifacts yield more accurate translations.
claims.quote: An image is worth a thousand words proves remarkably accurate here. When AI tools can examine existing patterns, spatial relationships, hierarchy, and aesthetic treatments through the artifacts you provide, they can produce more consistent and accurate designs that match your vision.

claims.rule: Use specific, detailed text prompts with explicit design requirements; avoid vague language that forces AI to make assumptions.
claims.quote: Longer prompts with clear, detailed design requirements consistently yield better results — particularly with AI tools that generate code-based prototypes, which can produce outputs that resemble the work of a human designer.

claims.rule: Disambiguate design vocabulary in prompts; define whether terms like 'profile page' refer to social, personal, or enterprise contexts.
claims.quote: When working with AI, designers need to disambiguate the language of their prompts as much as possible , so that they can precisely communicate the exact situation they need to design for.

claims.rule: Use AI prototyping for ideation, early exploration, and proof-of-concept demos, not final production designs.
claims.quote: AI's limited grasp of design nuances and inconsistent output make it best suited for ideation, concept exploration, and early-phase prototype testing, rather than later stages.

sources.title: The Edge Cases that Break Hearts (And Products)
sources.why: Importance of handling edge cases in user experience design.

claims.rule: Make user names editable and update them everywhere in the product, including URLs.
claims.quote: Make names editable and reflect those changes everywhere in the product – even in URLs.

claims.rule: Provide multiple account-recovery options that do not depend on the same device.
claims.quote: Have multiple account-recovery options that don't all depend on the same device.

claims.rule: Make support contact information accessible to users who are not logged in.
claims.quote: Make your support-contact information findable and usable when someone isn't logged in.

claims.rule: Allow easy account switching without requiring repeated logout and login.
claims.quote: Account switching should be trivial. Don't make people log out and back in every single time they want to change.

claims.rule: Offer user profiles on shared devices to separate viewing histories and recommendations.
claims.quote: If your product is likely to be used on a shared device like a television or an iPad, give users profiles and let them decide who the user really is.

claims.rule: Allow users to update their name everywhere in the product, including URLs and search indexes, without losing discoverability.
claims.quote: Make names editable and reflect those changes everywhere in the product – even in URLs. Plan for gradual rollouts where both names work, at least temporarily, by default.

claims.rule: Support easy account switching without forcing repeated logout and login cycles.
claims.quote: Account switching should be trivial. Don't make people log out and back in every single time they want to change. In some cases, you can let people sign in once and then create multiple subaccounts or just associate multiple accounts with the same login information.

claims.rule: Provide multiple recovery options for locked-out users that do not depend on the same device or method.
claims.quote: Have multiple account-recovery options that don't all depend on the same device. Make your support-contact information findable and usable when someone isn't logged in.

claims.rule: Design collaborative features to handle slow connections, real-time conflicts, and asynchronous editing with clear conflict resolution.
claims.quote: Design for both asynchronous and real-time collaboration. Show clear conflict resolution. Make it obvious when someone's changes aren't saving.

claims.rule: Cache data intelligently and provide offline-mode fallbacks for users with spotty internet connections.
claims.quote: Offline-first design isn't just for developing countries. Cache intelligently, and, whenever possible, provide some sort of off-line mode. Show clear indicators of sync status.

claims.rule: Build safety features, blocking, and reporting mechanisms from the ground up, not as reactive afterthoughts.
claims.quote: Build safety features from the ground up, not only as a response to problems. Make blocking and reporting easy and effective.

sources.title: Few Guesses, More Success: 4 Principles to Reduce Cognitive Load in Forms
sources.why: Four principles for minimizing cognitive load in form design.

claims.rule: Group related form fields together to help users retrieve information from memory.
claims.quote: Grouping related questions helps users retrieve information from memory more easily.

claims.rule: Use clear section headings in forms to establish context and reduce cognitive load.
claims.quote: adding clear, descriptive headings to each section provides users with a helpful preview of the upcoming topic. These signposts reduce cognitive load by establishing context

claims.rule: Use containers or visual dividers to reinforce form field groupings.
claims.quote: If spacing doesn't provide enough clarity on how elements are related, reinforce groupings with containers, subtle divider lines, or colored backgrounds.

claims.rule: Use branching logic to show only relevant form fields based on user input.
claims.quote: Forms with branching logic work the same way. This approach — often referred to as a 'wizard' — dynamically displays relevant fields based on users' prior input. Wizards not only minimize the physical effort required to fill out the form but also save users from spending attentional resources to scan and filter irrelevant questions.

claims.rule: Use clear, descriptive section headings in forms to establish context and reduce cognitive load.
claims.quote: Adding clear, descriptive headings to each section provides users with a helpful preview of the upcoming topic. These signposts reduce cognitive load by establishing context before users encounter specific fields.

claims.rule: Use containers, divider lines, or colored backgrounds to reinforce visual groupings of form fields.
claims.quote: If spacing doesn't provide enough clarity on how elements are related, reinforce groupings with containers, subtle divider lines, or colored backgrounds. This is the Gestalt principle of common region in action: visual boundaries help users quickly see which parts of the form belong together.

claims.rule: Use single-column form layouts to provide a clear, predictable vertical path and improve accessibility.
claims.quote: Research consistently shows that single-column layouts outperform multicolumn designs for form-completion rates. A single column provides a clear, vertical path that's easy to follow and scale across devices.

claims.rule: Distinguish required fields from optional fields using both asterisks and explicit optional labels.
claims.quote: If you decide to include optional questions, clearly distinguish them from required ones . In addition to using an asterisk to mark required fields, explicitly mark optional fields. This practice reassures users that they can skip nonessential questions and lightens their cognitive load.

claims.rule: Display progress indicators on multipage forms to show completion status and motivate users to finish.
claims.quote: Progress indicators give users a visual representation of how much they've filled and how much remains, helping them gauge the effort required to complete the form. This sense of progression also fosters a feeling of accomplishment, which in turn motivates users to continue until the end.

claims.rule: Write form labels and instructions at the 6th to 8th-grade reading level; avoid jargon and internal terminology.
claims.quote: We usually recommend writing at the 6th to 8th-grade reading level for general audiences — users shouldn't need to understand specialized vocabulary to fill your form. The most effective forms use language that mirrors how users naturally think and speak about the information being requested.

claims.rule: Use positive, opt-in wording for checkboxes instead of negative statements that require mental reversal.
claims.quote: Negative wording complicates how users interpret questions, as it forces them to mentally reverse statements. It increases cognitive effort and the risk of errors. This is especially relevant for standalone checkboxes — opt-in statements should use language that matches the intended outcome.

claims.rule: Ask one question at a time in forms and surveys; avoid double-barreled questions.
claims.quote: Double-barreled questions are questions that ask about two things at once ; they are a common survey pitfall. They introduce ambiguity as users might agree with one part but disagree with another.

claims.rule: Use standard form element styles and behaviors; avoid novel interactions for checkboxes, radio buttons, and other controls.
claims.quote: Users develop mental models about how form elements should look and behave based on their experiences across websites . Using consistent, familiar patterns allows users to apply existing knowledge and focus on the task at hand, rather than figuring out how the interface works.

claims.rule: Match input field length to expected content length; short fields signal brief responses, long fields suggest detailed input.
claims.quote: The size of an input field provides a visual cue about the expected length of the answer. A short field suggests a brief response , ideal for concise data like ZIP codes or age. A longer field implies that more detailed input is needed , such as an address, description, or comment.

claims.rule: Place labels and help text outside input fields; never use placeholders as the sole instruction method.
claims.quote: While placeholders — the text inside input fields that disappears when users tap into the field — may seem like a space-efficient way to provide guidance at first glance, they cause significant usability problems : They disappear when users start typing, forcing them to remember instructions using short-term memory .

claims.rule: Use input constraints (e.g., character limits, amount caps) to prevent invalid data before users see error messages.
claims.quote: In cases where clear rules define acceptable options, constraints become beneficial as they prevent users from making costly or time-consuming mistakes. Rather than letting users input invalid data and then showing an error message later, proactive constraints catch errors before they occur.

sources.title: Less Effort, More Completion: The EAS Framework for Simplifying Forms
sources.why: Framework for reducing effort and complexity in form design.

claims.rule: Remove nonessential form questions to lower perceived effort and improve completion.
claims.quote: The fewer fields they see upfront, the lower the perceived effort. Forms should only ask for essential information

claims.rule: Justify each form question to users, especially sensitive or unexpected ones.
claims.quote: A simple, clear explanation reassures users, builds trust, and helps them understand the rationale behind each question. Users will be more likely to complete the form when they understand how their data will be used.

claims.rule: Defer nonurgent form questions until after establishing trust with the user.
claims.quote: Not every question needs to be asked immediately. Before adding additional questions to your form, ask yourself, 'Do we need this information now?' If it can wait, postpone it.

claims.rule: Allow guest checkout and defer account creation to after purchase completion.
claims.quote: A better implementation is to allow the user to check out as a guest and postpone password creation to the confirmation page, after they placed the order.

claims.rule: Use conditional logic to avoid asking irrelevant questions based on user context.
claims.quote: Avoid asking users questions that don't apply to them. Use conditional logic to guide users down different paths based on their answers and keep each path as short as possible.

claims.rule: Ask for only essential information; eliminate nonessential, nonurgent, or irrelevant questions from forms.
claims.quote: Forms should only ask for essential information — if a question isn't critical or relevant, eliminate it.

claims.rule: Justify form questions to users, especially unexpected or sensitive ones, to build trust.
claims.quote: A simple, clear explanation reassures users, builds trust, and helps them understand the rationale behind each question.

claims.rule: Prefill form fields with existing data rather than asking users to re-enter information.
claims.quote: If your organization has access to existing data — either from integrations or prior user submissions — use it to prefill form fields and allow users to verify or update the information as needed.

claims.rule: Infer data from user input instead of asking separately; derive city and state from ZIP code, age from birthdate.
claims.quote: Instead of asking users to provide information that can be easily inferred, use automation to streamline the process. For example, derive the city and state from a ZIP code or calculate age based on a birthdate.

claims.rule: Use input masks to auto-format phone numbers, dates, and other structured data as users type.
claims.quote: Input masks help users understand the correct format, prevent errors, and make it easier to doublecheck their input.

sources.title: Checkboxes: Design Guidelines
sources.why: Design guidelines for checkbox component in forms and interfaces.

claims.rule: Use square checkboxes with checkmarks, never circles, to avoid confusion with radio buttons.
claims.quote: Users expect checkboxes to look like checkboxes: squares (with or without rounded corners), with a checkmark to communicate selection.

claims.rule: Make checkbox labels clickable and enlarge the target area to at least 1 cm × 1 cm for adequate touch targets.
claims.quote: Make the label clickable to allow for adequate touch-target size (at least 1 cm x 1 cm).

claims.rule: Use nested checkboxes with an indeterminate state when users are expected to select all items in a list frequently.
claims.quote: Nested checkboxes are useful when you expect many users to select all the checkboxes in a list.

claims.rule: Make checkbox labels and surrounding area clickable with a minimum 1 cm × 1 cm touch target.
claims.quote: Include a perimeter around the checkbox and make the label clickable to allow for adequate touch-target size (at least 1 cm x 1 cm).

claims.rule: Word checkbox labels positively to avoid double negatives that confuse users.
claims.quote: Ensure that all your label statements are worded positively. Negatively worded statements force users to contemplate double negatives, leading to errors.

claims.rule: Display checkbox lists vertically, never horizontally, to preserve scannability and label alignment.
claims.quote: Display your list vertically. Vertical checkbox lists are easier to scan than horizontal ones.

claims.rule: State minimum or maximum selection requirements explicitly and provide real-time visual feedback.
claims.quote: Clearly state any requirements in the instructions and provide real-time visual feedback when the requirements have been satisfied or violated.

sources.title: 10 Survey Challenges and How to Avoid Them
sources.why: Common challenges in survey design and methods to address them.

claims.rule: Distribute surveys immediately after an event while memory is fresh to reduce recall bias.
claims.quote: Distribute a survey to participants as soon as possible following the event related to your research. For example, if your survey asks why a user subscribed to a particular service, have the subscription act as a trigger for the survey, while their rationale for subscribing is as fresh as possible.

claims.rule: Use ranges for sensitive data (age, income) rather than asking for exact numbers to reduce prestige bias.
claims.quote: Providing age or income ranges will avoid requiring respondents to directly input their age or salary and will be less likely to result in a distortion.

claims.rule: Use semantic-differential scales instead of Likert scales to reduce acquiescence bias in surveys.
claims.quote: Use a semantic-differential scale rather than a Likert scale. A semantic-differential scale still asks participants to provide a rating but provides a continuum of response options specific to the nature of the question.

sources.title: Marking Required Fields in Forms
sources.why: Guidelines for clearly indicating required form fields to users.

claims.rule: Use an asterisk before or at the beginning of field labels in red to aid visual scanning on longer forms.
claims.quote: Showing it at the beginning in a different color makes it slightly easier to identify the required fields, which may prove useful when the form is longer.

claims.rule: Place the required-field asterisk at the label's beginning in red to let users scan left edge quickly on longer forms.
claims.quote: put it just before the field description is to help the eyes easily locate which fields are required by scanning just the left-most character of the label.

sources.title: Date-Input Form Fields: UX Design Guidelines
sources.why: Guidelines for designing effective date input fields in forms.

claims.rule: Accept flexible date formats (dashes, slashes, spaces, dots) without requiring leading zeros; parse user input.
claims.quote: Do not require users to enter special characters to format dates. Whatever format users chose for entering the date (dashes, spaces, slashes, dots between the month, day, and year components), their input should be recognized.

claims.rule: Do not use split date fields with drop-downs for month, day, and year; they increase interaction cost.
claims.quote: Split date fields with drop-downs for month, day, and year require a lot of unnecessary steps. This method increases interaction cost by adding additional clicks and scrolling. We advise against using this pattern.

claims.rule: Use calendar pickers only for dates within one year; for dates far in past or future, allow direct typing.
claims.quote: Calendar pickers should be used for events close to the present time — within less than a year. However, they can be frustrating for users who choose dates far in advance because they require too much navigation

claims.rule: Accept dates without leading zeros and in varied formats; parse user input as 9-3-17, 09/08/17, or 9/3/17 equivalently.
claims.quote: Whatever format users chose for entering the date (dashes, spaces, slashes, dots between the month, day, and year components), their input should be recognized. Moreover, leftmost zeros should not affect the date.

claims.rule: Disable and gray out illogical date pairs (return before departure, past dates) to prevent user error.
claims.quote: Users should be prevented from entering a return date that takes place before the departure date or that is in the past. Make the choices clear by disabling and graying out options that are not available

sources.title: Let Loyal Shoppers Edit Saved Credit Cards
sources.why: UX research on simplifying payment method management for loyal customers.

claims.rule: Display enough card information (last four digits and type) to let users identify the saved card without fully revealing the number.
claims.quote: The credit card number itself should not be fully revealed, but enough information should be visible to allow the user to easily identify the card.

sources.title: When to Hide Content Behind Forms and When to Give Content Away
sources.why: Research on optimal form gate placement for content acquisition.

claims.rule: Keep early-stage awareness and educational content ungated to avoid distrust and establish thought leadership.
claims.quote: Content such as articles and blog posts should not be gated if your main goal is to establish stronger thought leadership, increase site traffic, and improve SEO.

claims.rule: Gate only high-value, unique content (research, webinars, trials) when purchase intent is high and users cannot find it elsewhere.
claims.quote: People are more willing to risk offering their personal information when they perceive your content as valuable and unique. Sometimes it's appropriate to gate high-value content in resources such as research papers, webinars, and training videos.

claims.rule: Use progressive profiling to collect user data over time instead of demanding one long form upfront; customize questions to the buyer's intent.
claims.quote: Rather than asking people to complete a long and tedious profile form, collect information about each prospect over time, by asking different questions that are customized to the situation and buyer's intent.

sources.title: Slider Design: Rules of Thumb
sources.why: Guidelines for designing usable slider controls in interfaces.

claims.rule: Place slider labels above or beside the control, not below, so users can see them while dragging on touch devices.
claims.quote: any labels describing the slider or its currently selected value must appear beside or above both thumbs involved

claims.rule: Use sliders only when approximate values satisfy the user's goal, not when precision matters.
claims.quote: Sliders work best when the specific value does not matter to the user, but an approximate value is good enough.

claims.rule: Avoid sliders when users need to select a precise value; use them only for approximate ranges that satisfy the task.
claims.quote: Sliders work best when the specific value does not matter to the user, but an approximate value is good enough. Thus, Kayak may get away with using sliders for duration and arrival and departure hours, as most users will be fine with a departure time that is, say, midday, and won't care to specify the exact moment of the departure.

claims.rule: Place slider labels above or beside the control, never below, so they remain visible when the user's finger obscures the track.
claims.quote: In order to remain visible during use, any labels describing the slider or its currently selected value must appear beside or above both thumbs involved: the thumb of the user, and the thumb of the slider (also known as the knob or elevator).

sources.title: Preventing User Errors: Avoiding Unconscious Slips
sources.why: Strategies for designing forms and interfaces that prevent user slips and mistakes.

claims.rule: Redesign systems to prevent slips rather than asking users to be more careful or blaming them for errors.
claims.quote: The designer is at fault for making it too easy for the user to commit the error. Therefore, the solution to user errors is not to scold users, to ask them to try harder, or to give them more extensive training. The answer is to redesign the system to be less error prone.

claims.rule: Offer contextual suggestions and autocomplete to prevent typos and reduce errors during text input.
claims.quote: you can preempt typos from turning into problems by offering contextual suggestions while the user types

claims.rule: Use helpful constraints to force users toward valid options; prevent backward-stepping errors like selecting a return date before departure.
claims.quote: If users aren't limited in the dates they can choose, they may slip and accidentally select a set of dates for their flight that don't follow the rules. A helpful constraint here will force users to pick a date range that fits.

claims.rule: Offer contextual autocomplete and search suggestions to prevent typos from breaking user goals, especially on touchscreens without haptic feedback.
claims.quote: While you cannot prevent a user from making typos (which are slip-type errors), you can preempt typos from turning into problems by offering contextual suggestions while the user types.

claims.rule: Offer sensible default values (e.g., reminders set to tomorrow) to prevent errors in repetitive tasks and teach users about reasonable choices.
claims.quote: Especially when users have to perform repetitive actions, or in situations where they need to use precision, start by offering reasonable defaults that are likely to fit their real-world goals, and then allow them to refine their choices.

sources.title: Don't Force Users to Register Before They Can Buy
sources.why: Research on registration friction and its impact on e-commerce conversion.

claims.rule: Highlight user-focused registration benefits like order tracking, not company benefits like newsletters.
claims.quote: Briefly highlight the benefits of registration from the users' perspective and not the company's perspective when asking users to register.

claims.rule: Allow guest checkout without mandatory account creation; offer registration only as an optional password field during purchase.
claims.quote: Rather than forcing users to register before checking out, provide the option to register within the checkout process by presenting optional fields for the user to enter a password.

sources.title: Dark Mode: How Users Think About It and Issues to Avoid
sources.why: Research on user preferences and usability issues related to dark mode design.

claims.rule: Achieve WCAG 2 minimum contrast ratio (4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text) with desaturated colors on dark backgrounds, avoiding highly saturated hues.
claims.quote: Highly saturated colors on dark backgrounds have poor visibility and do not comply with accessibility guidelines, such as the WCAG 2 requirement of a minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text.

claims.rule: Use one font color at varying opacity levels to maintain readability across different dark-mode background colors.
claims.quote: When choosing the color of fonts in dark mode, use one color with different levels of opacity. This allows you to accommodate different background colors throughout the interface.

sources.title: Foldable Smartphones: New Devices, New Opportunities
sources.why: Design considerations and opportunities for foldable device interfaces.

claims.rule: Design for two viewport sizes on fold-out phones: smartphone screen when closed and tablet-sized screen when unfolded.
claims.quote: Fold-out phones blur the lines between smartphones and tablets. When unfolded, the full-sized screen offers significant advantages for tasks requiring a larger viewport or a combination of multiple apps.

sources.title: 13 QR-Code Usability Guidelines
sources.why: Research-backed 13-point guideline set for QR code design and placement.

claims.rule: Tell users what a QR code does and where it leads with a label or short URL visible near the code.
claims.quote: Designers must provide enough contextual information about the code to convince the user to scan it. Without contextual information, QR codes are not trustworthy or enticing.

claims.rule: QR codes should link to mobile-friendly pages, not generic homepages; assume users will scan and visit on mobile devices.
claims.quote: You can assume that users scanning a QR code will visit the associated site on a mobile device. QR codes should lead to mobile-dedicated or responsive sites.

claims.rule: Deep-link QR codes to specific pages or actions relevant to the code's context, not to generic homepages.
claims.quote: Users expect a QR code to link to information directly related to the context of the code rather than to a generic homepage.

sources.title: Should You Build a Smartwatch App?
sources.why: Decision framework and research for designing smartwatch applications.

claims.rule: Build smartwatch apps only when they enable microinteractions users already attempt on mobile, away from their phones.
claims.quote: What microinteractions do people already attempt in our mobile application? Could a smartwatch app support these interactions when users are away from their phones?

claims.rule: Do not build smartwatch apps for complex interactions like reading, writing, or video; users prefer pulling out their phone.
claims.quote: A smartwatch application that offers a rudimentary ability to complete complex interactions, such as reading, writing, or watching a video, is unlikely to offer much value.

claims.rule: Prioritize native smartwatch apps over third-party ones; 80% of smartwatch interactions occur in native applications.
claims.quote: From over 200 submitted interactions, over 80% were in applications native to the device, such as messages, activity trackers, and timers.

sources.title: 6 Types of Useful Smartwatch Interactions
sources.why: Six interaction patterns designed specifically for smartwatch constraints.

claims.rule: Time smartwatch suggestions precisely to context; poorly timed suggestions are useless even if contextually relevant.
claims.quote: Suggestions are extremely powerful when the timing and context are right because they will seem personalized, responsive, and aware of the user's current needs and activities. However, they are practically useless if their timing is off.

sources.title: The Negative Impact of Mobile-First Web Design on Desktop
sources.why: Research showing problems when desktop experience is compromised for mobile-first design.

claims.rule: Limit full-width images on desktop; multiple large images fragment text content across the page, reducing information density.
claims.quote: A few large images on a desktop page can work well. However, if the page has too many big images, the text-based content that is displayed inline or in between images becomes dispersed and fragmented across the page.

claims.rule: Keep related content together on the same viewport to reduce cognitive load and back-and-forth scrolling.
claims.quote: Keep critical, related content grouped together in the same viewport. Consider which information is most relevant to understanding the offering and choose designs that keep this content together to reduce back-and-forth scrolling.

claims.rule: Avoid accordions on desktop; they fragment content and increase interaction cost compared to expanded layouts.
claims.quote: Accordions can contribute to content fragmentation and significantly increase the interaction cost of finding crucial information, without the benefit they bring on mobile.

claims.rule: Add scrolling cues at viewport edges to prevent illusion of completeness and signal more content below.
claims.quote: If no scrolling cues exist to indicate that there is more content to discover, users are likely to miss this content.

sources.title: Passwordless Accounts: One-Time Passwords (OTPs) and Passkeys
sources.why: UX design for passwordless authentication methods on mobile devices.

sources.title: Bottom Sheets: Definition and UX Guidelines
sources.why: Guidelines and best practices for mobile bottom sheet component design.

claims.rule: Do not stack multiple bottom sheets; overlapping sheets confuse users about interaction patterns and dismissal methods.
claims.quote: Stacking several bottom sheets on top of each other

claims.rule: Support the Back button or gesture to dismiss bottom sheets to maintain expected navigation patterns.
claims.quote: You can prevent this issue by supporting the use of Back for dismissing the bottom sheet, thus allowing the users to seamlessly return to the previous view.

sources.title: Neurodivergence: What is it and Why Does it Matter
