sources.why: Understanding neurodivergence and its implications for accessible interface design.

claims.rule: Design for simplicity, clarity, control, and support to help neurodivergent users manage executive-function and sensory challenges.
claims.quote: Neurodivergent users face executive-function, communication, and sensory challenges. Neuroinclusive design helps all users by focusing on simplicity, clarity, control, support, and co-creation.

sources.title: Why Disabled Buttons Hurt UX (and How to Fix Them)
sources.why: Research on accessibility issues with disabled button states and alternatives.

claims.rule: Avoid disabled buttons; if necessary, explain why the button is disabled and when it becomes enabled.
claims.quote: Disabled buttons often confuse users by appearing clickable but providing no response or feedback.

sources.title: Direct Access vs. Sequential Access: Why Direct Is Better
sources.why: Evidence for favoring direct access over sequential navigation for accessibility.

claims.rule: Favor direct access to users' preferred items instead of forcing sequential navigation through content.
claims.quote: favor direct access to the user's preferred item instead of forcing users to go through your content in a serial order

sources.title: Accessible Solutions Benefit Everyone: Here's How
sources.why: Research showing how accessible design improves experience for all users.

claims.rule: Design for accessibility needs; accessible solutions benefit all users by making products easier to use overall.
claims.quote: Designing for specific needs, like accessibility, ends up benefiting everyone by making products easier to use for all.

sources.title: Alt Text: Avoid Redundancy to Improve Usability
sources.why: Guidelines for writing effective alt text that improves accessibility without redundancy.

sources.title: Alt Text: What to Write
sources.why: Best practices and examples for writing descriptive alt text.

claims.rule: Keep alt text under 150 characters; screen-reader users cannot pause mid-text and have limited working memory.
claims.quote: Alt text shouldn't be much longer than around 150 characters. Users can't pause and resume the screen reader in the middle of alt text without going back to the beginning.

claims.rule: Frontload alt text with the most important words so users can decide quickly whether to listen to the rest.
claims.quote: Frontload alt text with the most important words, to help users make a quick and informed decision about whether it's worth listening to the rest of the alt text before moving on.

claims.rule: Skip alt text for decorative images; empty alt attributes prevent screen readers from announcing file names.
claims.quote: Decorative images create a specific look and feel for sighted users but don't convey information relevant for any tasks. Because of this, they're superfluous and don't merit screen-reader users' time or attention, so the alt-text attribute should be empty so that the screen reader skips right over them.

claims.rule: End alt text with a period to signal screen readers to pause, even for fragments.
claims.quote: End alt text with a period, even if it isn't a full sentence. The period ensures that the screen reader pauses after reading the alt text.

claims.rule: Avoid technical jargon and abbreviations in alt text unless users will certainly understand them.
claims.quote: Avoid technical jargon and abbreviations unless users are certain to understand them.

claims.rule: Never reuse alt text for the same image across different contexts; reanalyze the context each time.
claims.quote: Never reuse alt text for the same image without reanalyzing the context in which the image is placed.

claims.rule: Mention people's identity only if race, ethnicity, gender, religion, or culture is relevant to the image's purpose.
claims.quote: Mention identity only if it's relevant. If the race, ethnicity, gender, religion, or cultural identifiers of the people pictured aren't part of the reason the image was included, don't mention them.

claims.rule: For complex informative images, edit page copy to state the message as a list or table, making alt text unnecessary.
claims.quote: Make complex informative images more accessible by altering the page copy surrounding the image. Editing the page copy to communicate the image's message often makes the visual itself redundant. In many cases, this could be as simple as including a list or table within the HTML of the page.

claims.rule: Use long descriptions (structured text, lists, or tables) for complex images when page copy cannot be edited.
claims.quote: Long descriptions house more detailed information than is reasonable to stuff into traditional alt text. They can include longer paragraphs of text, lists, or tables.

sources.title: Alt Text: Not Always Needed
sources.why: Research on when alt text is necessary and when it can be omitted.

claims.rule: Screen-reader users prioritize task information over visual description; focus alt text on purpose, not appearance.
claims.quote: Most of the time, screen-reader users don't wonder what images look like. Instead, they want to know their purpose.

claims.rule: Prioritize large-font captions and informative page copy over alt text for users with low vision.
claims.quote: These users benefit more from meaningful, large-font image captions and informative page copy than from alt text.

sources.title: Usability Testing With Older Adults
sources.why: Methods and considerations for testing usability with older adult participants.

claims.rule: Accommodate visual impairments including nearsightedness, farsightedness, astigmatism, presbyopia, and cataracts when testing interfaces.
claims.quote: common visual impairments include nearsightedness, farsightedness, astigmatism, presbyopia, and cataracts. These impairments may affect your participant's ability to view content on a screen.

claims.rule: Accommodate hearing loss ranging from mild to profound; over 5% of the world's population experiences hearing loss requiring treatment.
claims.quote: over 5% of the world's population experiences hearing loss that requires treatment. Hearing loss can range from mild to profound.

claims.rule: Design for motor impairments common in aging: reduced range of motion, diminished coordination, and illnesses like stroke and Parkinson's disease.
claims.quote: Motor impairments, like a reduced range of motion and diminished coordination, are typical parts of aging. Illnesses like stroke and Parkinson's disease also affect older adults more than any other demographic.

claims.rule: Use clear instructions and short, realistic tasks to accommodate cognitive changes in aging affecting memory, problem solving, attention, and comprehension.
claims.quote: Aging can affect many aspects of cognitive function including memory, problem solving, attention, visual comprehension, and linguistic comprehension. Clear instructions and short, realistic tasks will help your older user-test participants.

claims.rule: Alternate physically demanding tasks with stationary ones to avoid exerting older participants excessively during usability tests.
claims.quote: The research team alternated more physically demanding tasks with stationary ones to avoid exerting older participants too much during the study.

sources.title: Accessibility Widgets Are Not Enough for Screen-Reader Users
sources.why: Research showing limitations of accessibility widgets for true screen reader support.

claims.rule: Do not rely on accessibility widgets alone; design products so screen-reader users can sequentially and directly access content.
claims.quote: Screen-reader users do not consider accessibility menus helpful.

sources.title: Accessibility vs. Inclusive Design
sources.why: Distinction between accessibility compliance and inclusive design practices.

sources.title: Accessibility and Inclusivity: Study Guide
sources.why: Comprehensive study guide on accessibility and inclusive design principles.

claims.rule: Recognize that 15–20% of the world's population lives with a disability and 15–20% is neurodiverse; exclude these users at business risk.
claims.quote: An estimated 15-20% of the world's population live with a disability of some kind, and an estimated 15-20% of the world is neurodiverse. We cannot afford to exclude these users from our target markets.

claims.rule: Treat accessibility and inclusivity as mindsets, not checklists or procedures; they are branches of usability.
claims.quote: Accessibility and inclusivity are branches of usability. They are mindsets rather than collections of procedures, regulations, or checklists.

claims.rule: Design visual treatments that help both sighted and vision-impaired users find, see, and understand information.
claims.quote: Accessibility efforts must go beyond simply adding ALT text to images — they must help sighted users too. Mindful visual treatments help users find, see, and understand the information on web pages.

claims.rule: Screen-reader users experience a linear, one-dimensional interface; design products to make sense sequentially, not with widgets alone.
claims.quote: Users with low or no vision may rely on screen readers to access the web. Screen readers create a linear, one-dimensional experience that is much different from how sighted users interact with designs.

sources.title: Visual Treatments that Improve Accessibility
sources.why: Visual design techniques that enhance accessibility for users with disabilities.

claims.rule: Account for color contrast, don't rely on color alone, and make interactive elements easy to identify in accessible visuals.
claims.quote: To design accessible visuals, account for color contrast, don't rely on color alone, make interactive elements easy to identify, provide useful alternative text for images, and test your visuals with real users.

sources.title: The 10 Best Intranets of 2023: Trends in Design and Process
sources.why: Trends and best practices in intranet design based on top implementations.

claims.rule: Frame intranets around fostering connection, collaboration, and authentic employee engagement to improve productivity, creativity, and teamwork.
claims.quote: using the intranet to connect employees can improve productivity, creativity, innovation, and teamwork while addressing intrinsic needs for social interaction and culture

sources.title: GenAI for Complex Questions, Search for Critical Facts
sources.why: Research on appropriate use cases for generative AI vs. search in information seeking.

claims.rule: Design AI tools to handle multiple simultaneous constraints better than traditional search.
claims.quote: ChatGPT seems to be able to handle three or four constraints better than Google can.

sources.title: How AI Succeeds (and Fails) to Help People Find Information
sources.why: Analysis of AI system performance in supporting user information-seeking tasks.

sources.title: How AI Is Changing Search Behaviors
sources.why: Empirical research on how AI availability is shifting user search behavior patterns.

sources.title: 12 Design Recommendations for Calculator and Quiz Tools
sources.why: Research-backed guidelines for designing calculators and interactive quiz tools.

claims.rule: Embed calculators directly in relevant webpages rather than popups or separate pages.
claims.quote: Users prefer tools that are readily accessible and embedded on relevant pages rather than in popups or on dedicated pages.

claims.rule: Never require registration or email to view calculator results; show results immediately on-page.
claims.quote: Users do not like signing up for an account or waiting for an email to see their results because, when they are using a calculator, they are just exploring, not committing.

claims.rule: Dynamically update results as users input information so they see cause-and-effect.
claims.quote: Users especially like it when the output is dynamically calculated as they input their information, so they can see how different inputs affect the outputs.

sources.title: 3 Types of Online Calculator and Quiz Tools
sources.why: Taxonomy of calculator and quiz tool types with design implications.

claims.rule: Frame conversion-calculator outputs in meaningful ways that match the user's task.
claims.quote: Frame the outputs of a conversion calculator in ways that make sense to the user. The tasks users try to accomplish with the calculator should inform how the outputs are presented.

claims.rule: Use predictive calculators only if users trust the source, as they rarely question complex algorithms.
claims.quote: Users do not generally question the accuracy of the predictions if they trust the website providing the calculator.

sources.title: Calculators and Quizzes: User Expectations
sources.why: Research on user expectations and mental models for calculator interfaces.

claims.rule: Assume more detailed inputs will produce more personalized and narrow outputs.
claims.quote: The more information users feed a tool, the more personalized they expect the outputs will be.

claims.rule: Ensure tools actually utilize all detailed inputs provided; generic outputs frustrate users.
claims.quote: Tools that accept many details but only offer general information are considered equally useless because they don't seem capable of personalization.

sources.title: Enriched Site-Search Suggestions: Rarely Used
sources.why: Empirical data on low adoption of enriched search suggestions despite implementation efforts.

claims.rule: Display search suggestions quickly; images delay results past user submission.
claims.quote: enriched search results, especially those containing images, are delayed or may not load at all because users are finished typing and submitting their query before they can be displayed

claims.rule: Align suggestions to search intent, not exploration; avoid unrelated trending items.
claims.quote: Users are unlikely to abandon their known-item search to explore other new items — or even notice them — during search tasks. In fact, irrelevant enriched search results are often interpreted as an annoyance and an unwanted distraction.

claims.rule: Keep enriched search suggestions in a fixed layout; do not shift content types based on query.
claims.quote: Maintain dedicated spaces for various content types (as opposed to shifting the location of specific types of enriched site-search suggestions based on queries).

claims.rule: Label all enriched suggestion types explicitly to prevent users from interpreting them as promotional content.
claims.quote: Clearly label the enriched suggestion types (e.g., top sellers, recommended products, recent searches) so that users do not have to guess what they're seeing or why it's being displayed.

claims.rule: Preserve simple text autocomplete suggestions even when offering enriched search results.
claims.quote: Do not eliminate simple text autosuggestions. Users heavily utilize these basic site-search suggestions even when enriched search suggestions are present.

claims.rule: Limit graphical content in search suggestions to reduce loading delay and banner blindness.
claims.quote: Limit the amount of graphical and dynamic content, which can cause slower loading times and contribute to banner blindness.

sources.title: Intranet-Search Essentials
sources.why: Best practices for search functionality in internal intranet systems.

claims.rule: Expose the search box always; do not hide it behind a magnifying-glass icon.
claims.quote: Use a search box, not just a search icon. Place it in the upper right corner of the global navigation menu.

claims.rule: Placeholder text must appear and disappear only when user types; remain on focus.
claims.quote: The placeholder text should remain in the field when users focus their cursor in it, and only when the user starts typing the keyword, should it disappear.

sources.title: The Search Before the Search: Keyword Foraging
sources.why: Research on user cognitive processes when formulating search queries.

claims.rule: Avoid inventing new terminology; users will not search for branded or unfamiliar terms.
claims.quote: avoid inventing new terminology whenever possible, particularly branded terminology. If you invent a new term, your users will definitely not know it.

claims.rule: Use plain language and common terms in content; accept imperfect search queries from users unfamiliar with domain terminology.
claims.quote: focus on anticipating what language people might use to search for your products or content if they didn't know the correct term

claims.rule: Deploy faceted filters to help users discover and learn specialized vocabulary in complex domains like car parts, skin care, and home improvement.
claims.quote: Faceted systems can sometimes be helpful for formulating queries in unfamiliar domains

claims.rule: When using branded terminology, include plain language alternatives alongside it for SEO and user education.
claims.quote: If you do use branded terms, make sure you include the plain language alternative alongside it on the site

sources.title: The Love-at-First-Sight Gaze Pattern on Search-Results Pages
sources.why: Eyetracking study on how users scan search result pages.

claims.rule: In 20% of search queries, users look at only one result and rely on search engine ranking; trust in top placement drives this behavior.
claims.quote: in 20% of the 377 search instances, people looked at only one result on the SERP

claims.rule: Position critical answers in distinctive SERP features (featured snippets, tables, panels) to attract immediate attention and satisfy search intent.
claims.quote: SERP features like the featured snippet always look distinct compared to organic search results and guide the eyes

claims.rule: Tailor content to address users' precise questions to increase likelihood of being featured in prominent SERP positions where users focus their gaze.
claims.quote: They should understand their users' needs and questions and tailor their content so that it addresses those questions precisely

sources.title: How Search Engines Shape Gaze Patterns During Information Seeking: Google vs. Baidu
sources.why: Comparative eyetracking study of search result page scanning across different engines.

claims.rule: Place task-relevant content in primary areas; users ignore sidebars with irrelevant promotions or ads.
claims.quote: the right rail had a fair-to-high concentration of irrelevant content, users were likely to quickly abandon it even if they happened to glance at it

claims.rule: Promote internal products only when directly relevant to the user's current search query.
claims.quote: it's okay to promote your content on the SERP, as long as it is relevant to the user's task

sources.title: Three Key SERP Features: Featured Snippets, People Also Ask, and Knowledge Panels
sources.why: Analysis of impact and usability of key search engine result page features.

claims.rule: Featured snippets, People Also Ask, and knowledge panels direct attention and modify search queries.
claims.quote: These features are heavily used, and they can strongly influence the search process. They can direct attention on the results page, help users modify their queries, influence their information needs, and even end tasks on the SERP itself.

claims.rule: Use SERP features as visual signposts to verify result relevance quickly.
claims.quote: SERP features — particularly the ones with images and video thumbnails — can take on the role that logos play on a webpage: they act as signposts that enable users to quickly verify that the results are indeed for the entity they are interested in.

claims.rule: Include images or visual elements in search results to act as quick signposts that verify result relevance.
claims.quote: SERP features — particularly the ones with images and video thumbnails — can take on the role that logos play on a webpage: they act as signposts that enable users to quickly verify that the results are indeed for the entity they are interested in

claims.rule: Design featured snippets to mimic natural language query expansion; show related questions without requiring users to reformulate.
claims.quote: most users are terrible at generating alternate search strategies. But through SERP features, Google can present several expanded interpretations of the query in natural language and allow the user to explore those alternatives without leaving the page

claims.rule: Use 'People Also Ask' accordions to redirect user tasks; loaded questions should relate to the clicked question.
claims.quote: When one accordion is opened, Google loads more questions into the feature, usually related to the question that was clicked

sources.title: Good Abandonment on Search Results Pages
sources.why: Research distinguishing unsuccessful search from satisfied user abandonment.

claims.rule: Recognize when users find complete answers on results pages without clicking through.
claims.quote: Good abandonment is when the user's information need is successfully and entirely addressed by the search-results page, with no need to click on a result or reformulate the query.

claims.rule: Present facts in scannable, consistent formats to answer simple queries without requiring clicks.
claims.quote: Google can scan a website for that information and present it to them in a consistent, easily scannable format.

claims.rule: Present simple facts (addresses, phone numbers, definitions, dates) in consistent, scannable formats on results pages.
claims.quote: When people are searching for simple facts (statistics, dates, deadlines, addresses, phone numbers, etc.), they don't need to click on a search result anymore: Google can scan a website for that information and present it to them in a consistent, easily scannable format

sources.title: Complex Search-Results Pages Change Search Behavior: The Pinball Pattern
sources.why: Eyetracking research on scanning patterns for complex search result layouts.

claims.rule: Expect SERP features to dominate attention; account for high visibility in interaction design.
claims.quote: When SERP features (like featured snippets) were present on a SERP in our study, we found that they received looks in 74% of cases (with a 95% confidence interval of 66–81%).

claims.rule: Use consistent SERP layouts across queries so users don't reassess the page structure with each result.
claims.quote: if you're designing SERPs for your in-site search, it's a better bet to use a consistent layout that doesn't change radically from query to query

claims.rule: For research tasks, place critical information below the fold; 20% of selections occur there vs. 5% for fact-finding.
claims.quote: 20% of selections in research tasks were below the fold. Both scenarios confirm the disproportionately high importance of information above the fold on web pages

claims.rule: Embed site-specific search boxes in top results; display the search query syntax to teach advanced search operators.
claims.quote: Displaying the command in the search box is a good method to raise awareness of advanced search commands, which are virtually never used by the general web audience

claims.rule: Limit SERP decision time; users spend 5.7 seconds on average before selecting the first result.
claims.quote: users spent an average of 5.7 seconds considering results before they made their first selection (with a 95% confidence interval from 4.9 to 6.5 seconds)

sources.title: How Information-Seeking Behavior Has Changed in 22 Years
sources.why: Longitudinal research on shifts in user information-seeking strategies and behaviors.

claims.rule: Recognize that passive, accidental learning through browsing is now a major mode of information acquisition.
claims.quote: A fair amount of information was acquired in a passive way, without looking for it, during browsing.

claims.rule: Design for understanding topics, not just finding specific facts; users increasingly seek depth, not quick answers.
claims.quote: A larger proportion of current critical internet activities involved finding answers and gathering information in order to better understand a topic.

claims.rule: Account for passive browsing; 14% of critical incidents in 2019 involve accidental discovery vs. 4% in 1997.
claims.quote: a larger proportion of the reported instances in the new study involved passive information acquisition (14% versus only 4% in 1997 — the difference was statistically significant, p < 0.05)

claims.rule: Support smartphone use as primary; 42% of critical incidents occur on smartphones vs. desktop.
claims.quote: we found that most of the critical incidents (42%) occurred when people were using their smartphones — critical smartphone use was higher than critical desktop use

claims.rule: Enable social inquiry in purchase flows; 67% of Product Info & Purchase social interactions are inquiries to companies.
claims.quote: for Product Info & Purchase decisions, though only 20% of instances had accompanying social-interaction behavior, 67% of their social interaction was Inquire

sources.title: Search Box vs. Navigation
sources.why: Research on tradeoffs between search and navigation for information access.

claims.rule: Provide both search and navigation; search alone forces users to invest cognitive effort in query construction.
claims.quote: When websites prioritize search over navigation, users must invest cognitive effort to create queries and to deal with the weak implementations of site search.

sources.title: Progress Indicators Make a Slow System Less Insufferable
sources.why: Research on effectiveness of progress indicators in mitigating perceived wait times.

claims.rule: Show feedback immediately when the system requires more than one second; reduce user uncertainty during waits.
claims.quote: Progress indicators tell users (a) that the system needs more time to process the last user action (for instance, to load a file, or to install a new update), and (b) approximately how much time remains.

claims.rule: Display time estimates for waits longer than 10 seconds; otherwise users will abandon the task.
claims.quote: If the result will take more than 10 seconds to appear, you should also show users an estimate of when the computer will be finished. Otherwise, the user will go out for lunch.

claims.rule: Use progress indicators to reduce perceived wait time by engaging cognitive attention on the indicator itself.
claims.quote: They can reduce users' perception of time: Users devote some cognitive resources to the feedback itself, and they pay less attention to the wait itself.

claims.rule: Show immediate visual feedback for all actions; users assume unacknowledged clicks failed and try again.
claims.quote: Without any visual change from the system, most users will assume the action was not registered and they will try again

claims.rule: Use looped spinners only for 2–10 second delays; avoid for sub-1-second or longer waits.
claims.quote: This indicator should be reserved for actions that take between 2-10 seconds. For anything that takes less than 1 second to load, it is distracting to use a looped animation

claims.rule: Use percent-done bars for waits ≥10 seconds; users grow impatient with indefinite spinners.
claims.quote: we don't recommend looped animation for actions that take longer than 10 seconds, because users quickly grow impatient if they feel like they aren't making progress

claims.rule: Animate progress bars slower at start, faster toward end to avoid disappointment and sustain satisfaction.
claims.quote: Start the progressive animation slower and allow it to move faster as it approaches the end. This way you don't risk establishing a faster expectation than the system can maintain. Exceeding customer expectations always creates more satisfaction than disappointing customers

claims.rule: Progress indicators triple wait tolerance; users wait 3× longer with feedback than without.
claims.quote: the people who saw the moving feedback bar experienced higher satisfaction and were willing to wait on average 3 times longer than those who did not see any progress indicators

claims.rule: Allow users to cancel long processes; don't hijack system control during waits ≥10 seconds.
claims.quote: For actions that take a little while, give users the option to stop the process, in case they decide they cannot wait. Otherwise, your design may be hijacking control of the system

sources.title: The Need for Speed, 23 Years Later
sources.why: Updated research on performance thresholds and user experience impact after 23 years.

claims.rule: Detect delays as short as 100 milliseconds; anything longer breaks the sense of directness and control.
claims.quote: People can detect delays as short as 1/10th of a second, so anything that takes longer doesn't feel 'instant.'

claims.rule: Keep mobile page load times under three seconds; longer waits cause 53% of visits to end.
claims.quote: Google found 53% of mobile visits ended if a page took longer than 3 seconds to load.

claims.rule: Target pages that load in under two seconds on desktop; load times beyond this drop conversion 50% or more.
claims.quote: Conversion rates were highest for pages that loaded in less than 2 seconds; longer load times correlated with 50% drops in conversion rates and increased bounce rates, especially for mobile visitors.

claims.rule: Target subsecond load times as the ideal; prioritize each incremental speed gain over settling for average.
claims.quote: Subsecond load times would be ideal; realistically, this target is incredibly difficult to achieve while also delivering rich and engaging content.

sources.title: The 3 Response Time Limits in Interaction Design
sources.why: Three critical time limits for system response established through UX research.

sources.title: Variable Fonts and Wide-Screen Layouts: Adopting Data-Driven Progressive Enhancements
sources.why: Research on progressive enhancement strategies for responsive typography.

sources.title: Timing Guidelines for Exposing Hidden Content
sources.why: Guidelines for optimal timing of revealing progressively loaded content.

claims.rule: Delay hover-triggered content 0.3–0.5 seconds to confirm intent before exposing large disruptive overlays.
claims.quote: after the mouse cursor paused movement and remained in the target area for around 0.3–0.5 seconds, at which time the hidden content can safely be animated onto the page.

claims.rule: Wait 0.5 seconds after cursor leaves a hover target before collapsing exposed content to tolerate minor mouse drift.
claims.quote: Only if the user has clicked or tapped outside of the target area, or the mouse cursor has left the target area and exposed content for longer than 0.5 seconds, can the intent to collapse the exposed content be determined.

sources.title: When the UI Is Too Fast
sources.why: Research on negative effects of excessively fast UI transitions on comprehension.

claims.rule: Signal changes far from the user's current focus with stronger visual cues than simple replacement.
claims.quote: Changes outside the user's field of vision might be overlooked and require stronger signaling than simply replacing the old information with something new

claims.rule: Allow extra time for users with language barriers or disabilities to process rapidly changing screens.
claims.quote: This is particularly problematic for slower users, such as international customers who don't read your language well or old or disabled users

sources.title: Website Response Times
sources.why: Research on acceptable and optimal response time limits for web systems.

claims.rule: Achieve 0.1-second response to direct user actions to create the illusion of direct manipulation.
claims.quote: 0.1 seconds gives the feeling of instantaneous response — that is, the outcome feels like it was caused by the user, not the computer

claims.rule: Respond within 10 seconds maximum or users will abandon the task and lose focus.
claims.quote: After 10 seconds, they start thinking about other things, making it harder to get their brains back on track once the computer finally does respond

claims.rule: Reduce response time by even 0.1 seconds to lift conversion rates measurably.
claims.quote: When sites shave as little as 0.1 seconds off response time, the outcome is a juicy lift in conversion rates

claims.rule: Replace heavy server processing and complex widgets with simpler, faster alternatives.
claims.quote: today's big response-time sinners are typically overly complex data processing on the server or overly fancy widgets on the page

sources.title: Powers of 10: Time Scales in User Experience
sources.why: Framework of distinct time scales in UX and their psychological implications.

claims.rule: Deliver visual impressions in under 50 milliseconds; users form rough design judgments in this window.
claims.quote: people can make rough decisions about a web page's visual appeal after being exposed to it for as little as 50 ms

claims.rule: Limit videos to 1–2 minutes because passive viewing bores web users in active mode.
claims.quote: most internet videos should last no more than 1–2 minutes because people don't like passively watching something for much longer than that while they're in the active frame of mind induced by web surfing

claims.rule: Support revisitation by tracking user progress across multiple visits spanning days or weeks.
claims.quote: sites must support revisitation behaviors, for example by keeping track of what users have done in previous visits

sources.title: Nielsen's Law of Internet Bandwidth
sources.why: Historical research on predictable growth patterns in internet bandwidth and implications.

claims.rule: Design for low-end users lagging 2–3 years behind high-end bandwidth; avoid bloated designs even as speeds increase.
claims.quote: The vast masses of users are low-end and will lag 2–3 years behind the high-end users.

claims.rule: Optimize for download speed as the dominant design criterion until bandwidth reaches 1.5 Mbps; minimize design complexity.
claims.quote: For the next 5 years, the web will be dominated by users with such slow connections that any reasonable web page will take much longer to download than the response time limits indicated by human factors research. Thus, the dominant design criterion will be download speed in all web projects until about the Year 2003. Minimalist design rules.

sources.title: Response Times: The 3 Important Limits
sources.why: Foundational research establishing three critical response time thresholds in UX.

claims.rule: Deliver response feedback within 0.1 seconds for users to perceive instant system reaction.
claims.quote: 0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously

claims.rule: Keep response under 1 second to preserve uninterrupted user thought flow without special feedback.
claims.quote: 1.0 second is about the limit for the user's flow of thought to stay uninterrupted

claims.rule: Show progress indicators for operations exceeding 10 seconds to reassure users and allow other tasks.
claims.quote: percent-done progress indicators should be used for operations taking more than about 10 seconds

claims.rule: Time UI animations to a real-time clock, not computation speed, so usability persists across hardware upgrades.
claims.quote: animations, to be timed according to a real-time clock rather than being timed as an indirect effect

sources.title: Comparison Tables: 5 Scenarios When Not to Use Them
sources.why: Research on limitations of comparison tables and scenarios where alternatives work better.

sources.title: Bulk Actions: 3 Design Guidelines
sources.why: Guidelines for designing bulk action interfaces in data-heavy tables.

sources.title: Leverage AI for Mock Tables and Charts When Testing Prototypes
sources.why: Techniques for using AI-generated data in prototype testing of data-heavy interfaces.

claims.rule: Users scrutinize unfamiliar data for outliers and inconsistencies; use realistic mock data in prototypes.
claims.quote: when participants were given unfamiliar data, they spent more time looking for outliers and inconsistencies

claims.rule: Use realistic mock data in prototypes because users scrutinize unfamiliar tables and charts for outliers and inconsistencies.
claims.quote: Research in data sensemaking by Laura Koesten and colleagues found that when participants were given unfamiliar data, they spent more time looking for outliers and inconsistencies than when they worked with familiar data.

claims.rule: Contextualize mock table data to audience size, industry, geography, and market to avoid unrealistic values.
claims.quote: Your table will be less helpful if your AI is modeling data for a large enterprise when your app targets mall businesses. For example, business size, industry or market, geography, or time periods can all influence the table's data.

claims.rule: Account for full dataset size when generating subset rows so values remain plausible relative to the whole.
claims.quote: The dataset may be much larger. Describe the size of the larger dataset, if known, so the AI can account for these additional records when calculating values.

claims.rule: Request SVG format for AI-generated charts to preserve editability of elements in design tools.
claims.quote: Generating charts in SVG format makes them easy to import and edit in design tools like Figma.

sources.title: Data Tables: Four Major User Tasks
sources.why: Research on primary user tasks with data tables and design implications.

claims.rule: Order table columns by user importance and group related columns adjacent to minimize eye movement.
claims.quote: The default order of the columns should reflect the importance of the data to the user and related columns should be adjacent

claims.rule: Ensure users always know what data cell belongs to which record in large tables.
claims.quote: it can be complicated to understand what each cell stands for and to which record it belongs

sources.title: Compensatory vs Noncompensatory: 2 Decision-Making Strategies
sources.why: Cognitive decision-making patterns and their implications for comparison table design.

claims.rule: Provide filter controls to help users eliminate options quickly when facing many alternatives.
claims.quote: Filters and faceted navigation on product-listing pages are the most common tools that support this noncompensatory criteria selection, allowing users to quickly eliminate options that don't possess those chosen traits.

claims.rule: Filter attributes must match the characteristics users care most about, or omit the filter entirely.
claims.quote: the filter attributes must be relevant to users and match the characteristics that they care the most about. Presenting a filter that only includes one or a few irrelevant attributes is almost more maddening than not presenting a filter at all.

claims.rule: Limit compare tools to show no more than 5 products side by side; do not require users to compare more alternatives than working memory can handle.
claims.quote: Compare tools that allow users to select a few products and directly compare them are also helpful. Remember that there is no need to support more than about 5 products in each of these tools

claims.rule: Show both positive and negative attributes for each alternative so users can determine whether benefits outweigh drawbacks.
claims.quote: Even when evaluating a single item, people must see both the pros and cons to determine whether there are enough benefits to outweigh any negative aspects

claims.rule: Implement multiword search that filters results to items matching every word in the query, not items matching any word separately.
claims.quote: a user searching a site for 'wooden box' would expect to receive a list including only boxes that were made of wood — not all items on the site that are wooden plus all items that are boxes

sources.title: Mobile Tables: Comparisons and Other Data Tables
sources.why: Strategies for displaying complex data tables on mobile devices.

claims.rule: Lock column headers in place when tables scroll vertically beyond one screen.
claims.quote: For any table that fills more than a single vertical screen, sticky column headers help users know what they are looking at. Without sticky headers, it is easy to lose the context of what the table is displaying.

claims.rule: Lock the left column in place when users must scroll horizontally to see all table data.
claims.quote: If users must scroll horizontally to see all the data, the leftmost column, which is typically a column of row headers, should be locked in place, so users can see the necessary labels at all times.

sources.title: 4 Tips for Bulleted Lists in Digital Content
sources.why: Eyetracking-informed best practices for presenting bulleted lists.

sources.title: Love at First Sight in Eyetracking
sources.why: Eyetracking research on initial gaze patterns and visual prominence.

sources.title: The Lawn Mower Eyetracking Pattern for Scanning Comparison Tables
sources.why: Eyetracking study identifying lawn mower scanning pattern for comparison tables.

claims.rule: Lay out comparison tables to match the lawn-mower eye pattern: rows and columns aligned, labels close to data.
claims.quote: Users are likely to methodically scan comparison tables row by row, from right to left and back again.

claims.rule: Keep column labels close to rows to avoid forcing users to search upward when comparing entries.
claims.quote: Because the column labels were so far from some of the rows, the participant had to leave his scanning pattern, travel far up to page to read the labels, and then return to refind the same row — adding time and cognitive strain to his comparison task.

claims.rule: Use fixed column headers so users never lose column identity while scanning comparison tables downward.
claims.quote: use fixed table headers, so that column titles are always visible. This prevents users from having to look all the way back at the top of page, potentially losing their place in the table.

claims.rule: Let users hide irrelevant products in multi-column tables to preserve the lawn-mower scanning pattern.
claims.quote: Allow them to hide products or services that they are not interested in, if your table has more than 2 columns.

claims.rule: Group Yes/No and checkmark rows together to avoid disrupting the lawn-mower pattern.
claims.quote: Group Yes/No Features Together

claims.rule: Move empty or placeholder rows to the end of the table, never in the middle of active scanning content.
claims.quote: When users scan the table in a lawn mower pattern, it's likely that they will accidentally scan the placeholder content, which provides no information.

sources.title: How People Read Online: New and Old Findings
sources.why: Updated eyetracking research on online reading patterns and behaviors.

claims.rule: Use clear noticeable headings to break content into scannable sections.
claims.quote: Using clear, noticeable headings and subheadings to break up content and label sections so that people can scan to find only what they're most interested in

claims.rule: Place important information up front in content structure, subheadings, and links.
claims.quote: Placing information up front (in other words, "front-loading") in the structure of our content, as well as in subheadings and links, to allow people to understand the message quickly while scanning

claims.rule: Use bulleted lists and bold text to focus the eye on the most important information.
claims.quote: Employing formatting techniques like bulleted lists and bold text to allow the eye to focus on the most important information

claims.rule: Keep online content concise and use plain language for clarity.
claims.quote: Using plain language to keep content concise and clear

claims.rule: Avoid pull quotes and inline ads mid-article; they disrupt scanning and cause attention dropout.
claims.quote: they tended to disrupt reading. Several participants in our study began reading articles nearly linearly and completely until they hit a pull quote or inline ad. After reaching one of those elements, the participants abandoned their reading and fell into light scanning.

sources.title: The Pinball Pattern of Scanning Search Results Pages
sources.why: Eyetracking visualization of non-linear scanning patterns on search results.

claims.rule: Recognize that modern search results force non-sequential scanning; design for variable attention distribution, not linear flow.
claims.quote: users don't always process search results sequentially. They distribute their attention more variably across the page than in the past.

sources.title: Change Blindness in User Interfaces
sources.why: Research on user inability to notice interface changes and design implications.

claims.rule: Mark significant UI changes with strong visual cues to overcome change blindness; subtle changes go unnoticed.
claims.quote: Significant changes in a web page can remain unnoticed when they lack strong cues, due to the limitations of human attention.

sources.title: Text Scanning Patterns: Eyetracking Evidence
sources.why: Eyetracking evidence of how users scan text content on screens.

claims.rule: Structure text with headings and subheadings; absent these, users revert to inefficient F-pattern scanning.
claims.quote: In the absence of subheadings and bullets, users tend to fixate on the words toward the beginning of lines and toward the top of the page.

claims.rule: Bold, color, or link important words to trigger spotted-pattern scanning over inefficient F-pattern.
claims.quote: They visually stand out in the text because they are styled differently (e.g., links, differently colored words, bolded words, bulleted lists).

claims.rule: Use meaningful headings and subheadings; the layer-cake pattern with headings is far more effective than F-pattern scanning.
claims.quote: Aside from reading almost every word, the layer-cake pattern is by far the most effective way in which users can scan pages.

claims.rule: Chunk content with subheadings and call-out points even for motivated readers seeking deep comprehension.
claims.quote: even for the commitment pattern, text comprehension is improved when the content is chunked and calls out its main points in subheadings.

sources.title: Setup of an Eyetracking Study
sources.why: Practical guide for designing and conducting eyetracking research studies.

claims.rule: Use at least 39 eyetracking participants per task to generate reliable aggregate heatmap data.
claims.quote: To get this type of visualization, we recommend having at least 39 participants perform the same task on the same page.

sources.title: The Layer-Cake Pattern of Scanning Content on the Web
sources.why: Eyetracking research on hierarchical scanning patterns for web content.

claims.rule: Make subheadings visually stand out and descriptive so users engage in efficient layer-cake scanning.
claims.quote: When headings and subheadings visually stand out on the page and are descriptive, users engage in an efficient scanning pattern that allows them to quickly find the information that they need.

claims.rule: Avoid making subheadings so bright or large they resemble ads; users will ignore them.
claims.quote: Be careful to not make the subheadings so absurdly brighter or larger than the body text that they look like promotions or ads instead of page content and cause users to ignore them.

claims.rule: Use consistent visual treatment (typeface, color, size, or weight) to signal hierarchy between body text and subheadings without making subheadings resemble promotions.
claims.quote: Marking subheadings so they visually stand out relative to the rest of the text in a consistent, predictable manner

sources.title: Banner Blindness Revisited: Users Dodge Ads on Mobile and Desktop
sources.why: Updated eyetracking research on banner blindness across devices.

claims.rule: Avoid placing legitimate content in traditional ad locations (top banner, right rail) where users habitually ignore ads.
claims.quote: Because desktop ads typically appear at the top of the page or in the right rail, web users sometimes ignore the content placed there.

claims.rule: Do not style content with colors, backgrounds, or formatting that distinguish it from surrounding elements, as users mistake visually distinct items for ads.
claims.quote: Anything that stands out from immediate surrounding context is likely to be considered an ad, although its presentation may be consistent with other elements on the page that are not visible at the time.

claims.rule: On mobile, avoid inline ads within scrollable content; they occupy too much screen proportion for users to avert their gaze and interrupt reading flow.
claims.quote: A mobile inline ad is so large in proportion to the screen size that users cannot avert their eyes from it as they swipe down.

sources.title: Scrolling and Attention
sources.why: Eyetracking research on how scrolling affects user attention and focus.

claims.rule: Place critical content in the top 20% of the page; 42% of viewing time concentrates there.
claims.quote: more than 42% of the viewing time fell within the top 20% of the page

claims.rule: Expect sharp attention drop below the fold; users spend 57% of time above it, 17% in second screenful.
claims.quote: the pattern of a sharp decrease in attention following the fold remains the same in 2018 as in 2010

claims.rule: Within the first screenful, concentrate 65% or more of content in the top half of the viewport.
claims.quote: More than 65% of the viewing time above the fold was concentrated in the top half of the viewport

claims.rule: Structure pages well so users understand layout quickly; they scan efficiently after orientation.
claims.quote: they need to understand how the page is organized. Once they do so, they tend to focus very efficiently only on the information relevant to the task

claims.rule: Use visual styling like headers and bold text to signal importance and help users locate new content sections.
claims.quote: Users rely on elements like headers and bolded text to identify when information is important, and to locate new segments of content.

claims.rule: Include visual signifiers such as cut-off text to show users that scrollable content exists below the fold.
claims.quote: Include signifiers (such as cut-off text) to tell people that there is content below the fold.

sources.title: Banner Blindness: Ad-Like Elements Divert Attention
sources.why: Eyetracking visualization of banner blindness phenomenon in web design.

claims.rule: Avoid design elements that resemble ads; users ignore content that signals advertising.
claims.quote: People tend to ignore design elements that signal advertisements

sources.title: Attention Leans Left on Websites
sources.why: Eyetracking evidence of leftward bias in horizontal attention distribution.

claims.rule: Place primary content on the left; users spend 80% of viewing time on the left half of the page.
claims.quote: Web users spend 80% of their time viewing the left half of the page and 20% viewing the right half

sources.title: Eyetracking Shows How Task Scenarios Influence Where People Look
sources.why: Research showing impact of task context on gaze patterns and attention.

claims.rule: Design layouts and hierarchy to guide attention; users' focus follows their task goals and page structure.
claims.quote: How users attend to information on a page depends on their tasks and goals, as confirmed by new eyetracking research. Good design promotes efficient scanning

sources.title: F-Shaped Pattern of Reading on the Web: Misunderstood, But Still Relevant (Even on Mobile)
sources.why: Updated analysis of F-pattern reading behavior and its continued relevance.

claims.rule: Prioritize the first line of content; it receives more gazes than subsequent lines.
claims.quote: First lines of text on a page receive more gazes than subsequent lines of text on the same page

claims.rule: Emphasize first few words on the left of each line; they receive more fixations than words to the right.
claims.quote: First few words on the left of each line of text receive more fixations than subsequent words on the same line

claims.rule: Use scannable structure with headings and subheadings to break up text blocks.
claims.quote: Layer-cake pattern occurs when the eyes scan headings and subheadings and skip the normal text below

claims.rule: Design to prevent the F-shaped pattern; good design can break users' habit of scanning only top and left.
claims.quote: Good design can prevent F-shape scanning

claims.rule: Place the most important points in the first two paragraphs to align with users' natural scanning focus.
claims.quote: Include the most important points in the first two paragraphs on the page.

sources.title: Exhaustive Review or "I Can't Believe It's Not There" Phenomenon: Evidence from Eyetracking
sources.why: Eyetracking evidence of user search failures and overlooked content.

claims.rule: Follow established web-design patterns; violating them causes users to re-scan the page repeatedly.
claims.quote: Common web-design patterns and how most other websites are designed set user expectations for where UI elements and content will appear

claims.rule: Avoid layouts that create confusion; repeated scanning indicates users' expectations were not met.
claims.quote: Exhaustive review happens when people are confused because the page content or the page UI violates users' expectations

claims.rule: Follow established web-design conventions for element placement; only deviate if usability research proves dramatic improvement.
claims.quote: If you're considering a design that deviates from web conventions, test it thoroughly and use it only if all your usability research indicates that it is dramatically better than the norm.

sources.title: Horizontal Attention Leans Left
sources.why: Research on left-leaning horizontal scanning bias in Western users.

claims.rule: Place primary content on the left half of the page; users fixate there 80% of the time.
claims.quote: 80% of their time viewing the left half of the page and 20% viewing the right half

claims.rule: Reserve the leftmost 10% of screen for navigation, not content, as users scan past it quickly once learned.
claims.quote: users have become quite good at recognizing navigation and don't have to spend time viewing it until they need it

claims.rule: Use conventional top or left navigation formats to maximize alignment with users' established viewing patterns.
claims.quote: Utilize conventional top navigation or left navigation formats

claims.rule: Place secondary and lower-priority content on the right side of the page, as it receives significantly less attention.
claims.quote: the right side of the page garners a lot less attention than the left, and that the very leftmost area should be reserved for navigation. Keep secondary content to the right

sources.title: UX Writing: FAQs from Practitioners
sources.why: Practitioner insights on common questions and best practices in UX writing.

claims.rule: Write at a 6th–8th grade reading level for general audiences to maximize comprehension across all literacy levels.
claims.quote: Aim for a 6th – 8th grade reading level for general audiences

claims.rule: Use plain language and jargon only when user research confirms your audience understands and prefers technical terms.
claims.quote: Use jargon only when your audience expects and uses it. Before including a word that could be unclear to some users, make sure you have evidence from user research

claims.rule: Document both stable voice attributes and tone-shift guidance in your style guide for different contexts and channels.
claims.quote: Your content standards or style guide should document both stable voice attributes and tone-shift guidance across contexts and channels

claims.rule: Adapt tone to the user's emotional state: empathetic in errors, encouraging in onboarding, neutral in reference content.
claims.quote: more empathetic in an error message, more encouraging in onboarding, more neutral on a policy page

claims.rule: Adapt tone to user emotion: empathetic in errors, encouraging in onboarding, neutral on reference content.
claims.quote: Your tone will shift depending on context: more empathetic in an error message, more encouraging in onboarding, more neutral on a policy page.

claims.rule: Use jargon only when user research confirms your audience understands and prefers technical terms.
claims.quote: Use jargon only when your audience expects and uses it. Before including a word that could be unclear to some users, make sure you have evidence from user research, survey data, or site-search logs that your audience understands and prefers a technical term.

claims.rule: Use descriptive link text that communicates destination, not generic labels like "Learn More" or "Click Here".
claims.quote: Learn More is a lazy link or button label. It tells users nothing about what they'll learn or where they'll go after clicking. It's also a significant accessibility failure: screen readers will announce Learn More, Learn More, Learn More, across a page with no way to distinguish among them.

sources.title: Search Bar UI: Definition & UX Design Inspiration
sources.why: Best practice examples and design patterns for search bar implementations.

claims.rule: Make the search field prominent and always visible in the header to signal that search-led browsing is supported.
claims.quote: A persistent search bar signals immediately to the user that the site supports and encourages search-led browsing

claims.rule: Provide a clear button (X) to let users clear the search field and start a new search without leaving results.
claims.quote: Clear button (X): Appears once the user has typed, allowing them to clear the field without backspacing character by character

claims.rule: Offer autocomplete and predictive suggestions for keywords, categories, and products to guide user search refinement.
claims.quote: Guide shoppers with autocomplete and predictive keyword, category, and product suggestions

claims.rule: Persist search queries in the input field to allow users to easily refine and adjust searches without retyping.
claims.quote: Persist queries in the input field for easy refinement

claims.rule: Use icon-triggered or collapsed search cautiously; reduced prominence may cause users to miss the search feature entirely.
claims.quote: its reduced prominence can mean some users miss it altogether

claims.rule: Use icon-triggered search cautiously; reduced prominence causes users to miss the feature entirely.
claims.quote: However, use this with caution, as its reduced prominence can mean some users miss it altogether.

sources.title: What is a Product Spec Sheet? Examples & UX Design Inspiration
sources.why: Analysis of product specification sheet design patterns and best practices.

claims.rule: Use a single-column layout with left-aligned labels and key specs first to make technical data scannable.
claims.quote: a single-column layout works best here (with clear attribute labels to the left of the table). Group related specs under clear subheadings, display key details first

claims.rule: Use row styling with alternating backgrounds or subtle borders to help users match labels to values easily.
claims.quote: Use alternating backgrounds or subtle borders within the table to connect labels directly to their values

claims.rule: Define jargon and technical terms with tooltips or inline microcopy to help all users, not just domain experts.
claims.quote: ensure you define any key jargon or terminology by using tooltips or inline microcopy

claims.rule: Standardize spec sheet labels, ordering, and units of measure across all products of the same type for reliable comparison.
claims.quote: display spec sheets so that the same attribute always appears with the same name, in the same format, with the same unit conventions across products of the same type

claims.rule: Always append units of measure to numerical values to prevent user confusion with metric versus imperial measurements.
claims.quote: Always append the unit of measure to numerical values

claims.rule: Use collapsible sections or truncation on mobile instead of dense compression to avoid excessive scrolling.
claims.quote: consider using vertically collapsible sections or truncation rather than compressing the layout

claims.rule: Display key specifications first, before less critical attributes, to prioritize user decision-making information.
claims.quote: display key details first, and use row styling so users can easily match labels to values

claims.rule: Use alternating row backgrounds or subtle borders in spec tables to help users track labels across to their values.
claims.quote: Use alternating backgrounds or subtle borders within the table to connect labels directly to their values and make it easier for users to scan

claims.rule: Measure and track spec sheet UX performance; 64% of ecommerce sites have poor or mediocre spec sheet design.
claims.quote: almost two-thirds (64%) of ecommerce sites' spec sheets are poor or mediocre

claims.rule: Ensure identical attribute labels, ordering, and units across all products of the same type; 30% of sites fail this.
claims.quote: 30% of sites have severe issues with specs across products of the same type

sources.title: What is a UI Badge? Definition & Ecommerce Best Practice Examples
sources.why: Best practice patterns and design guidance for badge components in e-commerce.

claims.rule: Keep badge copy brief—1–2 words for text, numbers for counts—to communicate meaning at a glance.
claims.quote: Label or count: The text or number inside the container. Should be as short as possible (1–2 words for text badges, a number for notification badges)

claims.rule: Avoid using badges for universal, obvious, vague, or low-value information to prevent visual clutter and preserve signal value.
claims.quote: Avoid using badges when the information is universal, obvious, vague, or of low value

claims.rule: Limit badges per product to retain their highlight function; overuse dilutes value and causes users to ignore them.
claims.quote: If most items carry a badge, it stops functioning as a highlight and can even have the opposite effect, as users become blind to them

claims.rule: Use red for sale and urgency, green for stock and new labels, and grey for neutral information.
claims.quote: Typical badge colors are red for sale/urgency messages, green for in stock/new labels, and grey for neutral/informational content

claims.rule: Reserve badges for information that genuinely influences purchase decisions; omit universal, obvious, or low-value attributes.
claims.quote: A badge should only appear when the information it communicates would genuinely influence a user's decision to click through or purchase

claims.rule: Write badge copy as 1–2 words maximum using plain language; avoid internal campaign names or vague promotional wording.
claims.quote: Badge labels need to be short, concrete, and self-explanatory, because they're consumed during rapid scanning. Avoid brand-specific phrases, internal campaign names, or vague promotional wording

sources.title: Building a UX Research Practice: Team Structure & Tools
sources.why: Framework for establishing and scaling UX research practice in organizations.

claims.rule: Use session behavior tools to validate audit findings at scale and measure the proportion of users affected.
claims.quote: Session data can confirm what proportion of mobile users never interact with the filter control

sources.title: How to Present UX Research Findings to Get Buy-In From Stakeholders
sources.why: Strategies for effectively communicating research findings to stakeholders.

claims.rule: Translate UX findings into business outcomes—revenue, conversion, risk, or cost—that match each stakeholder's priorities.
claims.quote: My biggest takeaway from working with different stakeholders — from business to finance to legal — is framing whatever your UX findings are in the lens of what that specific stakeholder cares about.

claims.rule: Frame usability issues using loss aversion: present data showing what users will lose, not what they gain.
claims.quote: stakeholders were much more likely to act on suggested changes when the data was presented with a negative frame. It aligns directly with game theory and loss aversion: the pain of a potential loss is psychologically far more powerful than the pleasure of a gain.

sources.title: How to Use Heuristic Evaluation to Find UX Issues Fast
sources.why: Practical guide to applying heuristic evaluation methodology for UX assessment.

claims.rule: Scope heuristic evaluations to a single flow—checkout, product page, search—and evaluate desktop and mobile in separate sessions.
claims.quote: Evaluate on desktop and mobile separately, not in the same session. Mobile-specific issues are often underrepresented in evaluations that treat mobile as an afterthought to a desktop UX review.

claims.rule: Run evaluations with three to five independent reviewers and brief them separately to reduce missed issues and prevent cross-contamination.
claims.quote: Evaluations with three to five independent evaluators find significantly more issues than single-evaluator reviews.

claims.rule: Prioritize usability issues by user impact, not by fix difficulty.
claims.quote: Prioritize issues by user impact rather than fix difficulty, making sure to evaluate mobile experiences in dedicated sessions

claims.rule: Rate usability issue severity by user impact, not by fix difficulty or your personal preference.
claims.quote: Rate based on likely user impact, not your personal reaction to the issue, and not how easy the fix would be.

claims.rule: Conduct mobile heuristic evaluations in a separate dedicated session, not as a spot-check at the end of desktop review.
claims.quote: Conduct a separate mobile evaluation pass for each flow and treat it as a distinct evaluation, not a quick spot-check at the end of a desktop session.

claims.rule: Test error states and edge cases deliberately during heuristic evaluation, not only the successful path.
claims.quote: Many heuristic violations occur in error states, edge cases, and recovery paths.

sources.title: E-cigarette & Vaping UX Benchmark: 3,600+ Performance Scores and 2,500+ Best Practice Examples
sources.why: Large-scale e-commerce UX benchmark study with performance data and best practices.

sources.title: B2B Electronic Components & Machinery UX Benchmark: 2,600+ Performance Scores and 2,000+ Best Practice Examples
sources.why: B2B e-commerce UX benchmark with performance metrics and design examples.

sources.title: New Event Ticketing UX Research: 3 Key Takeaways
sources.why: Findings from event ticketing UX research across leading platforms.

sources.title: B2B Medical & Pharma UX Benchmark: 3,400+ Performance Scores and 2,600+ Best Practice Examples
sources.why: B2B pharmaceutical e-commerce UX benchmark with extensive best practice database.

sources.title: Using AI To Find Usability Problems: Examining Task Failure
sources.why: Research on effectiveness of AI in identifying real usability issues.

claims.rule: When AI analyzes usability videos, expect 35–60% false alarms and occasional hallucinations; use it as an assistant, not a replacement.
claims.quote: Most metrics comparing the overlap of usability problems were within ten percentage points of each other (e.g., 40% vs. 45% of human-identified problems found by AI). The one real divergence was in the type of AI-only errors: the PetSmart video had more false alarms (60% vs. 35%) but zero hallucinations (compared to three in the OpenTable case study).

sources.title: ChatGPT vs Humans for Coding Open-Ended Responses, Three Years Later
sources.why: Longitudinal comparison of AI vs. human coding of qualitative research data.

claims.rule: Use AI to code open-ended survey comments; consistency and agreement with human coders has improved significantly since 2023.
claims.quote: In short, we found that ChatGPT-5.6 not only matched human levels of interrater agreement and achieved near-perfect self-consistency, but has also evolved into a far more granular analyst, subdividing core themes into small subcategories.

claims.rule: Use AI to code open-ended survey responses; it now matches human coder agreement and exceeds prior model consistency.
claims.quote: human-to-ChatGPT-5.6 agreement (0.749) was statistically indistinguishable from human-to-human agreement (0.704, p = .475)

claims.rule: Prompt explicitly for edge-case handling; ambiguous responses caused variance in AI coding (e.g. 'Na', 'Not sure') across runs.
claims.quote: Subtle shifts in classification like this could lead to lower agreement. Fortunately, this type of model variance can likely be mitigated with a more explicit prompt instruction regarding edge-case handling.

sources.title: How Well Do Digital Twins Predict SUS Scores?
sources.why: Research on synthetic user generation accuracy for predicting usability metrics.

sources.title: Do Participants Say Less to AI Than to Human Moderators?
sources.why: Research on AI moderation effectiveness and impact on participant responses.

claims.rule: AI moderators scored significantly worse than humans on context-aware follow-up and trust-building, even with equal procedural adherence.
claims.quote: The AI moderator also scored significantly worse than the human moderator on context-aware follow-up and on building trust, even though the two were indistinguishable on procedural adherence.

claims.rule: AI moderators will dominate conversation; in in-depth interviews, plan for AI to speak 80% more than human moderators despite identical scripts.
claims.quote: Human moderators spoke on average 55 WPM compared to AI moderators' 99 WPM. That is, on average, AI moderators were speaking 80% more than human moderators.

sources.title: Effectiveness of AI Moderators: A Literature Review
sources.why: Comprehensive literature review of AI moderator effectiveness in UX research.

claims.rule: Use AI moderators for structured, high-volume data collection; reserve human moderators for discovery and studies requiring judgment about when and how to probe.
claims.quote: For structured, high-volume, consistency-driven data collection, an AI moderator seems like a reasonable tool today. For discovery, emotional nuance, and studies where the whole point is to find what you didn't know to ask about, the human moderator isn't going anywhere yet.

sources.title: Nine Design Fixes for Your UX Research Reports
sources.why: Design best practices for presenting UX research findings effectively.

claims.rule: Use generous whitespace in margins and between components to prevent visual clutter and focus attention.
claims.quote: Generous whitespace prevents visual clutter and focuses the reader's attention on the most important content, making the overall presentation cleaner and less overwhelming.

claims.rule: Left-align text instead of center-aligning to create predictable reading patterns and reduce cognitive load.
claims.quote: Left-aligned text is easier to read than centered text. Consistent left alignment creates a predictable reading pattern, reducing cognitive load and helping the reader process information more efficiently.

claims.rule: Use two or three colors in information hierarchy instead of many, as excessive colors diminish visual hierarchy and reduce effectiveness.
claims.quote: Color helps highlight specific information, but do so sparingly, as too many colors make it harder to discern the hierarchy, diminishing their purpose.

sources.title: Five Ways to Use Rapport When Moderating
sources.why: Techniques for building rapport with research participants during moderation.

claims.rule: Stay neutral about outcomes; avoid encouraging language that teaches participants to perform for approval.
claims.quote: Stay neutral, not encouraging. "Great job!" feels supportive, but it teaches the participant to perform for you instead of reacting honestly to the product.

claims.rule: In remote sessions, look at the camera lens rather than the participant's video feed to register as eye contact on their screen.
claims.quote: On camera, look at the lens, not the face. In a remote session, eye contact with the participant's video feed doesn't register as eye contact on their end. Looking at the camera does.

sources.title: Streamlined Measurement of the UX of AI
sources.why: Framework for efficiently measuring user experience with AI systems.

claims.rule: Select two to three items per construct to measure AI UX attitudes, targeting scale reliability of at least 0.70.
claims.quote: Our typical target for measuring a construct at this stage of questionnaire development is to select two to three items per construct with the goal of achieving scale reliability (measured with coefficient alpha) of at least 0.70 for each construct.

claims.rule: Measure AI UX across six core constructs: Productivity, Trust, Dependency, Anxiety, Personification, and Early Adoption.
claims.quote: We identified 34 candidate items across six constructs (AI Productivity, AI Trust, AI Dependency, AI Anxiety, AI Personification, and Early Adoption)

sources.title: Using AI To Find Usability Problems: A Replication
sources.why: Replication study on AI effectiveness for identifying usability problems.

sources.title: Can We Trust AI to Moderate UX Interviews?
sources.why: Evaluation of AI moderation reliability and trustworthiness in UX research.

sources.title: Measuring the UX of AI
sources.why: Methodologies for measuring and evaluating user experience with AI products.

claims.rule: Use standardized metrics like UX-Lite to assess usefulness and usability of AI products.
claims.quote: For attitudes, we've found that standardized metrics like the UX-Lite ® provide a good measure of overall attitudes toward a product's usefulness (capabilities/features) and usability (ease of use).

claims.rule: Measure AI productivity gains; a 2026 Anthropic survey found 86% of users reported work speed improvements.
claims.quote: Results from an Anthropic survey indicated 86% of respondents reported improvements in the speed of their work.

sources.title: UX and NPS Benchmarks of Health Insurance Websites (2026)
sources.why: Benchmark study of UX and customer satisfaction metrics for health insurance sites.

sources.title: Assessing the Validity of Your Research
sources.why: Framework for evaluating research validity in UX studies.

claims.rule: Establish content validity by consulting experts to confirm survey items represent relevant content.
claims.quote: To establish content validity, you consult experts in the field and look for a consensus of judgment.

sources.title: Sample Sizes for Rating Scale Confidence Intervals
sources.why: Statistical guidance on determining adequate sample sizes for rating scale studies.

claims.rule: Use rating scale standard deviations of 20–28% of maximum range instead of 50% for binary data to reduce sample size needs substantially.
claims.quote: All else being equal, sample size requirements based on these estimates (from 20–28%) will be substantially lower than estimates based on the standard deviation of binomial metrics (which is 50% of the range of the scale when p = .5).

claims.rule: For ±2-point margin of error on a 0–100 rating scale at 95% confidence, use n=603 with typical standard deviation instead of n=2,398 for binary metrics.
claims.quote: At a margin of error of ±2 points, you'd need 2,398 participants using a binary metric. You would need just a quarter of that (603) using the typical rating scale's standard deviation of 25% of the maximum range.

claims.rule: For multi-item questionnaires, use standard deviation of 20% of scale range to estimate sample size when no historical data exists.
claims.quote: If your primary analyses will be multi-item questionnaires, it's reasonable to use the 's = 20' column.

sources.title: Measuring Usability with the System Usability Scale (SUS)
sources.why: Comprehensive guide to administering and interpreting the SUS metric.

claims.rule: Use SUS on very small sample sizes (two or more users) for reliable usability perception data.
claims.quote: SUS can be used on very small sample sizes (as few as two users) and still generate reliable results.

sources.title: Changing the Net Promoter Scale: How Much Does It Matter?

claims.rule: Use 11-point NPS scales consistently; switching to 10 or 5-point scales introduces 4% average scoring error.
claims.quote: The average absolute difference when changing scales is around 4 percentage points

claims.rule: Avoid 10-point NPS scales; they reduce detractors by 8% without reducing promoters, inflating loyalty scores.

sources.title: UX and NPS Benchmarks of Clothing Websites (2026)

sources.title: How Much Does a Usability Test Cost?

claims.rule: Budget $7–$10 per general consumer participant for unmoderated online panel recruitment; $40–$100 for specialized profiles.
claims.quote: the lowest cost per participant will range from between $7 and $10 (general consumer profile) and go up substantially to $40 to $100 (specialized profiles

claims.rule: Budget $100–$300 per qualified participant for external moderated recruitment, plus $12K–$15K for 20 participants with qualifications.

sources.title: Context Libraries: How AI Power Users Manage Context Engineering
sources.why: Research on context management strategies for AI power users.

claims.rule: Update context files when work processes shift, don't leave them static for months.
claims.quote: A context file was often written once but used for months, and much of what participants had written no longer matched how they worked.

claims.rule: Ask the AI to audit context against recent ambient sources like meeting transcripts to surface stale instructions.

claims.rule: Give the AI explicit feedback when your working style drifts from established routines; don't silently ignore broken automations.

claims.rule: Structure context so it is discoverable and usable for models, not just stored; apply information architecture principles to context itself.

claims.rule: Keep context files short, under a few hundred lines; anything longer probably contains material that doesn't need to load every time.

sources.title: Context Architecture
sources.why: Framework for designing context in AI-powered systems.

claims.rule: Structure context so it is discoverable and usable for models, not just stored; apply information architecture principles to context itself.
claims.quote: LLMs need the same foundations. The challenge is not only the access to information. It is making that information meaningful, structured, and usable for both humans and machines.

claims.rule: Use context as your primary lever to shape AI behavior when you cannot control the training data or foundation model.

claims.rule: Load only essential context; excess context makes the model less able to attend to relevant information, harming results.
