sources.title: Explicit Decisions: Help Your Users Choose Correctly
sources.why: Guidelines for supporting user decision-making through explicit design.

sources.title: Organize Information with LATCH
sources.why: Framework for organizing information using Location, Alphabet, Time, Category, Hierarchy.

claims.rule: Organize information using one of five methods: Location, Alphabet, Time, Category, or Hierarchy (LATCH) to improve findability and navigation.
claims.quote: The LATCH framework organizes information based on location, alphabet, time, category, and hierarchy.

sources.title: Explicitly State the Difference Between Options

claims.rule: Use comparison tables or move differentiating features to the top when options differ on only a few attributes.

claims.quote: Before investigating how users interact with a particular system, step back and understand the broader domain in which that system operates.

claims.rule: Triangulate insights across multiple research methods and roles to reveal how work moves across people, tools, and organizational boundaries.
claims.quote: Effective research in these domains requires triangulating insight across methods (e.g., interviews, workflow mapping, observations) and roles (e.g., frontline users, supervisors, adjacent teams).

claims.rule: Observe expert users working in their actual environment, not in labs, to discover contextual factors that shape system use.
claims.quote: Real-world conditions — such as environmental constraints, interruptions, shared equipment, or cross-team coordination — shape how systems are actually used.

claims.rule: Use scenario-based interviews and discussion with domain experts to assess reasoning, not just task completion accuracy.
claims.quote: ask them to walk through how they would interpret and act on the data presented. Rather than focusing on whether users complete a task correctly, the team observes how the users reason through the decision

claims.rule: Prototype at low fidelity—sketches, storyboards, wireframes—to test workflow logic early without committing resources to full builds.
claims.quote: low-fidelity mockups can be used to simulate alert-escalation paths or triage workflows, allowing domain experts to walk through hypothetical scenarios

sources.title: Wireflows 101
sources.why: Introduction to wireflow diagrams for mapping user interactions.

sources.title: Supporting 'Power Users' Isn't Enough: 3 Complex-App User Types
sources.why: User types in complex applications and design implications.

claims.rule: Design for Legacy users by avoiding sudden UI changes and offering safe, low-risk ways to explore improvements.
claims.quote: Supporting legacy users means recognizing that familiarity doesn't always equal mastery, and that productivity, not resistance, is often at the heart of their hesitation.

claims.rule: Provide meaningful error messages that include actionable next steps, not just descriptions of what went wrong.
claims.quote: Provide meaningful error messages that include actionable next steps

sources.title: How to Increase the Visibility of Error Messages
sources.why: Techniques for making error messages more visible and noticeable.

sources.title: Power Law of Learning: How to Launch New Designs Successfully
sources.why: Research on learning curves and design change management.

claims.rule: When launching new designs, expect temporary productivity loss as users unlearn practiced behaviors on old interfaces.
claims.quote: Time on task decreases with the number of times the task has been performed in the past. As a result, a new version of an app translates into a temporary productivity loss for its users.

sources.title: Indicators, Validations, and Notifications: Pick the Correct Communication Option
sources.why: Guidelines for choosing appropriate feedback mechanisms in applications.

claims.rule: Use indicators—visual cues like icons, color, or animation—to highlight dynamic content or UI elements that require attention.
claims.quote: Indicators are visual cues intended to attract users' attention to a particular piece of content or UI element that is dynamic in nature.

claims.rule: Use validation messages to tell users how to fix an error, not just that a problem exists.
claims.quote: Validation messages should follow the guidelines for error messages rather than simply identifying the problem, they should tell users how to fix it.

claims.rule: Place validation error messages near the problematic field and pair with an icon indicator to signal which input needs correction.
claims.quote: Since validation is contextual, it can be helpful to use an icon indicator along with the validation message to help communicate which input(s) are missing or need corrected

sources.title: AI Summaries of Reviews
sources.why: Research on AI-generated review summaries and their effectiveness.

claims.rule: Present AI-generated review summaries as a paragraph with formatting that supports scanning, not unformatted text blocks.
claims.quote: Most AI summaries were (unfortunately) presented as blocky, unformatted chunks of text. Lack of formatting made them a bit difficult to scan

claims.rule: Do not let AI summaries block access to individual reviews; users need both summary and original reviews.
claims.quote: Note that AI summaries don't eliminate users' desire to explore the actual individual reviews.

claims.rule: Include disclaimers explaining that AI summaries are unverified by the company to manage legal risk and user trust.
claims.quote: Disclaimer: A small note or tooltip explaining that the content is AI-generated and unverified by the company

claims.rule: Supplement AI summaries with traditional review features like rating averages, histograms, and filters.
claims.quote: Supplemented, but did not replace, traditional review-summarization UI elements such as review average ratings, histograms, or filters

claims.rule: Include themed keywords from reviews alongside the summary so users can identify topics matching their questions.
claims.quote: Themes: A collection of the most-mentioned themes across all reviews

sources.title: Livestream Ecommerce: 7 Tips for Good UX
sources.why: Seven tips for designing effective livestream shopping experiences.

sources.title: Is Livestream Selling Right for Your Business?
sources.why: Decision framework for adopting livestream e-commerce.

sources.title: Transactional Notification 101
sources.why: Fundamentals of transactional notification design.

sources.title: 4 Ways to Support International Purchasers
sources.why: Strategies for serving international e-commerce customers.

claims.rule: Offer at least two support channels—live chat, email, telephone, or social media—for international purchasers.
claims.quote: Choose at least two of the following: live chat, email, telephone, and social media

sources.title: 6 Tips for Improving Language Switchers on Ecommerce Sites
sources.why: Best practices for language selection in international e-commerce.

claims.rule: Place language switchers in top corners on desktop and above the fold on mobile for discoverability.
claims.quote: language-switching feature on ecommerce sites should be placed in the top corners on desktop sites and above the fold on mobile

claims.rule: Language switchers must show enough detail and flexibility to satisfy international user needs for language and region.
claims.quote: with enough details and flexibility to satisfy user needs

sources.title: How to Create a Successful Livestream-Ecommerce Experience
sources.why: Comprehensive guidelines for successful livestream shopping.

claims.rule: Use livestream for complex, personal products that benefit from real-time Q&A rather than commodity items.
claims.quote: The products or services are highly personal and complicated and benefit from Q&As

claims.rule: Integrate livestream into ecommerce apps for informative, detail-oriented sessions; embed livestreams in social-media platforms when entertainment and celebrity influence drive revenue.
claims.quote: If you want your sessions to be informative and detail-oriented, integrate them into ecommerce apps, to supplement your product pages. But if a large portion of your revenue comes from targeted ads on social media or if celebrities play an essential role in promoting your products, embedding livestreams in social-media platforms may be better.

sources.title: Livestream Ecommerce Supports Both Goal-Oriented and Impulsive Shoppers
sources.why: Research on how livestream formats serve different shopper types.

claims.rule: Show products in real-life context during livestream, not polished studio settings, to appear more tangible and build confidence.
claims.quote: Products in livestream sessions, which were shown in a real-life context, seemed more tangible

claims.rule: Display livestream indicators on product listings and allow picture-in-picture viewing of livestream while browsing product details.
claims.quote: a livestreaming indicator appears on the product-listing page for those items with an ongoing livestream

claims.rule: Segment livestream recommendations by user behavior frequency and interests; show livestreams every 1–2 videos to heavy users and every several minutes to users who dislike livestreams.
claims.quote: The frequency of promoted livestream sessions varied across participants; on average, a livestream session showed up every 3 videos people browsed. But those who enjoy watching livestreams to kill time are shown a livestream promotion for every 1 or 2 videos; in contrast, users who dislike livestreams might browse videos for several minutes without encountering any livestream session.

sources.title: Community Ecommerce
sources.why: Design patterns for building community in e-commerce platforms.

sources.title: Transactional Notifications: Their Characteristics and When to Use Them
sources.why: Guide to transactional notification design and implementation.

claims.rule: Write concise, easy-to-digest transactional messages; verbose content damages user trust in your brand.
claims.quote: A concise message conveys the message that the customers' time is valued and, thus, helps increase trust in your brand

claims.rule: Frontload key information in the first few words of SMS; users read only the first several words when scanning.
claims.quote: Failing to frontload the key information can cause critical details to be overlooked, as people read only the first several words when scanning a message.

sources.title: Translate User-Generated Content for Global Audiences
sources.why: Strategies for managing multilingual user-generated content.

claims.rule: Show individual 'Translate' links only for reviews in languages other than the user's default setting; omit buttons for same-language content.
claims.quote: When sites opt to provide individual translation links like Etsy did, the Translate button should be provided only when the reviews are written in a language other than the default browser setting. In other words, they should not be included on every review.

sources.title: Models Matter: A Case for Using Diverse Models on Ecommerce Websites
sources.why: Research on representation and diversity in e-commerce imagery.

claims.rule: Display diverse models across ecommerce site photography to help shoppers see themselves represented in products.
claims.quote: When models were diverse, shoppers noticed. Many study participants were happy to see models of different sizes, ages, and races on ecommerce sites

claims.rule: Allow shoppers to select models by size or height to visualize product fit on bodies similar to their own.
claims.quote: Several of these sites went beyond just showing diverse models in site photography — they allowed shoppers to choose the model on which to view the products

claims.rule: Allow shoppers to select models by size, height, or skin tone on both product-listing and product-detail pages.
claims.quote: A user shopping for jeans on GoodAmerican.com noticed that she could choose her preferred model early in the shopping journey, on the product-listing page, and again on the product-detail pages.

claims.rule: Persist model selection across all products within a category to reduce interaction cost; do not force users to reselect for each item.
claims.quote: Features that prompt shoppers to select a specific model should persist this selection across all other products within the product category to avoid the interaction cost associated with selecting a model for every product.

claims.rule: Place model-selection buttons or icons in high-contrast, highly visible locations on both category and product pages for discoverability.
claims.quote: Because model-selection features are so valuable to shoppers, they must be easily discoverable and implemented through high-contrast buttons or icons placed in highly visible places on both the category page and the product page.

claims.rule: Consistent application of products and poses across models prevents confusion; ensure the same product shade or fit is clearly applied identically.
claims.quote: Although the page allowed users to view the same shade on different models, the variability in the model poses and in the application of the product, in conjunction with the low visibility of the selected color, made it hard for one shopper to realize what she was viewing.

sources.title: Applying Luxury Principles to Ecommerce Design
sources.why: Design principles specific to luxury e-commerce markets.

claims.rule: Provide detailed product information even when items cannot be purchased online to maintain customer interest.
claims.quote: regardless of how much luxury brands want to sell online, they must provide better product details

claims.rule: Support in-person visits by providing rich online product information even for items sold offline, because luxury shoppers research before purchasing in stores.
claims.quote: even brands who don't want to allow online purchases still need ecommerce sites — just ones that lack a checkout process. This is because luxury shoppers often want to research products online, even when they intend to purchase them in person

claims.rule: Provide critical product details like material, size, and dimensions without jargon; avoid unexplained measurements expecting users to calculate or convert.
claims.quote: At the very least, provide critical product details such as material, size, and heel height.

claims.rule: Show price ranges when exact prices cannot be displayed; all but the wealthiest customers have rough price points in mind.
claims.quote: Consider providing at least a price range when specific prices can't be shown. Remember that all but the wealthiest of customers will have at least a rough price point in mind.

claims.rule: Reserve visual design experimentation for ornamental sections; prioritize readability and function in navigation, filters, descriptions, and payment areas.
claims.quote: perfect places to experiment and let visual design shine without frustrating customers.

claims.rule: Invest in professional copyediting, quality assurance, and translation; typos and bugs damage luxury brand perception more severely than in mainstream ecommerce.
claims.quote: Such sloppy mistakes chipped away at participants' perception of those brands — a disastrous outcome for luxury, where brand reputation is everything.

claims.rule: Include brand history, leadership, and values throughout the site, not only in About Us sections, to foster emotional connections luxury customers seek.
claims.quote: It's a good idea to include interesting company-identity information throughout the site, not just in an About Us section.

sources.title: Luxury Shopping User Groups and Journeys
sources.why: User segmentation and journey mapping for luxury e-commerce.

claims.rule: Design for the consideration phase of the luxury shopping journey, where brands often fail their customers.
claims.quote: Luxury brands often fail their customers during the "consider" phase of their journey

claims.rule: During the consideration phase, provide product organization and information architecture that helps users find specific items and categories without friction.
claims.quote: Poor organization and information architecture: Participants struggled to find specific products as well as general product categories.

claims.rule: Explain product names, attributes, and terminology; do not assume luxury shoppers know all brand jargon even if they know the brand well.
claims.quote: Confusing product names, attributes, and terminology: Several sites failed to explain and clarify the different products and their attributes.

claims.rule: Design recommendation systems for digital channels; luxury brand sites often provide no recommendations, unlike in-store where salespeople guide customers.
claims.quote: Bad product recommendations: Unlike the in-store experience, most of these sites provided unhelpful recommendations if at all.

claims.rule: Support generous return policies and address shipping concerns explicitly; anxiety about returns increases with item cost and emotional investment.
claims.quote: Several luxury shoppers also reported feeling anxious about returns.

sources.title: The New Siri's Biggest Strength Is Not Intelligence
sources.why: Analysis of what makes AI assistants effective beyond intelligence.

claims.rule: Show users which sources were searched and explain gaps when an AI agent cannot find information across multiple apps.
claims.quote: An agentic experience must show the user which sources were searched and explain relevant gaps

claims.rule: Design AI assistants to access and use relevant personal context already stored on users' devices without requiring manual data entry.
claims.quote: An AI agent should answer questions about information that is already on the user's phone without making them find it and paste it into the conversation

claims.rule: Explain why a source was searched when its relevance is unclear; show where answers came from, especially when searches span unexpected domains.
claims.quote: When a source's relevance is unclear, explain it, and show where the answer came from.

sources.title: The New Big Ball of Mud: Why Agentic AI Systems Turn Fragile
sources.why: Architecture and design challenges in agentic AI systems.

claims.rule: Plan AI system architecture for long-term durability and maintainability, not just short-term functionality.
claims.quote: A big ball of mud is a system scraped together for short-term functionality, not architected for long-term durability

claims.rule: Prioritize rebuilding and refactoring context and workflows instead of allowing throwaway code to accumulate and block future improvements.
claims.quote: These throwaway pieces are rarely useless, so they stay. Participants seemed to have two reasons for not having the AI rebuild them: a lack of time and fear of breaking the existing value

claims.rule: Audit global context in a single sitting; if too long to review at once, move non-universal instructions to local context.
claims.quote: Audit the global context from start to finish once in a while. This context type affects everything the system does, so it should be short enough to review in one sitting.

claims.rule: Name the context type when directing AI to make system changes; retain understanding of impact instead of delegating change comprehension to the AI.
claims.quote: Name the context type when directing a change. Even if users don't know exactly where each file lives or every word inside it, knowing what's happening in each context type allows them to tell the AI, "go update XYZ in the global context" rather than "go fix this wherever you think it matters"

sources.title: How AI Works and How Users Think About It: Study Guide
sources.why: Comprehensive guide to user mental models of AI systems.

sources.title: When Should You Disclose AI Use? The PACED Framework
sources.why: Framework for deciding when and how to disclose AI use to users.

claims.rule: Disclose the specific role AI played and the extent of AI involvement, not just that AI was used, because audience reactions depend on both factors.
claims.quote: audiences' reactions depend on knowing not only whether the AI was used, but also on knowing what role it played and how much AI contributed to the content

claims.rule: Emphasize human judgment and accountability in AI disclosures, especially when human oversight is expected by the audience.
claims.quote: readers had more negative reactions when the disclosure suggested that AI had produced the content autonomously, without clear human involvement and accountability

sources.title: Designing AI Products and Features: Study Guide
sources.why: Comprehensive guide to designing with and for AI systems.

claims.rule: Lead with user value, not AI capability. Demonstrate how AI solves real problems before mentioning the technology.
claims.quote: Companies should lead with the value that AI implementations offer rather than counting on AI to create value.

claims.rule: Narrow the scope of AI features to increase user understanding and adoption.
claims.quote: Narrowly scoped AI features are easier to understand and have better user adoption.

claims.rule: Support users in writing effective prompts through hybrid interfaces combining text input with graphical controls.
claims.quote: UIs that combine prompt-based inputs with a graphical user interface (GUI) can improve the usability of image-generation tools.

claims.rule: Use contextually relevant, personalized, task-specific prompt suggestions matching user experience level.
claims.quote: Prompt suggestions must be contextually relevant, personalized, and specific both to the task and to the user's level of experience.

sources.title: The 3 Roles of Context for AI Agents
sources.why: Three critical roles context plays in AI agent performance.

claims.rule: Store global and local context in separate, dedicated files or databases; keep ambient context in its raw form with API or MCP connections.
claims.quote: Participants generally kept information playing the three roles in separate places. Global and local context lived in distinct files or databases

claims.rule: Enable agents to read and update task-specific context files (local) themselves; document change logs and task lists for the agent to maintain.
claims.quote: Some of it (task lists, change logs, decision logs) is written and kept current by Claude itself, not just read.

claims.rule: Curate global context carefully to relieve users of repeating details across conversations; include best practices, governance rules, brand guidelines, and clarification instructions.
claims.quote: Global context can be powerful because it relieves the user of having to specify these details in each new conversation.

sources.title: AI Can Help Write an Article, but It Can't Stand Behind It
sources.why: Editorial and liability considerations for AI-assisted content.

claims.rule: Use AI to enhance clarity and meet format constraints, but retain human editorial judgment for all substantive decisions.
claims.quote: AI may contribute words and even some ideas to our articles, but humans remain responsible for editorial judgment.

claims.rule: Have humans verify claims flagged by AI; AI identifies potential issues but never certifies correctness.
claims.quote: AI never certifies that the claim is correct. When it flags an issue, it's the editor's or the author's job to go back to the source, double-check the claim, and correct the error if they find one.

claims.rule: Never delegate editorial judgment or factual verification to AI; humans must always verify flagged claims by returning to original sources.
claims.quote: AI never certifies that the claim is correct. When it flags an issue, it's the editor's or the author's job to go back to the source, double-check the claim

claims.rule: Use AI to identify logical contradictions and structural weaknesses in arguments, but maintain human responsibility for weighing and accepting or rejecting suggestions.
claims.quote: I weigh its suggestions rather than accept them as answers. I keep those that strengthen the argument and that I believe to be applicable, and I discard the rest.

sources.title: Test Complex Interactions Earlier with AI Prototyping
sources.why: Using AI for early-stage interaction testing and prototyping.

claims.rule: Build interactive AI prototypes with realistic data and multiple states early to surface edge cases before deployment.
claims.quote: AI tools make it feasible to build fully interactive prototypes of complex interfaces so you can test them with users earlier in the design process.

claims.rule: Test conversational AI with open-ended user input, not predetermined paths, to discover how agents handle unexpected requests.
claims.quote: Study participants could input anything they'd like, rather than having to follow a predetermined path. As a result, the researchers could see how the agent handled unexpected requests.

claims.rule: Test filter interactions with real data and user clicks, not static mockups, to discover how the system responds to filtering actions.
claims.quote: a key aspect of filter design is how the system responds when users interact with it (for example, by applying or removing it). To thoroughly test filters, users should be able to click through and use the system as they would with the real product.

claims.rule: Provide AI prototyping tools with detailed prompts describing layout, interactions, edge cases, empty states, and error states to produce high-fidelity results.
claims.quote: Craft a detailed, specific prompt to guide the AI tool in building a high-quality interface. The prompt should describe the interface you want (the layout, the interactions, the edge cases) and include a file containing your data.

claims.rule: Review AI-generated prototypes for design flaws before production: wrong patterns, confusing hierarchy, and unnecessary repetition hide beneath polished appearance.
claims.quote: AI-generated prototypes may look complete while introducing all sorts of assumptions and inaccuracies, such as using the wrong design pattern for the situation, creating a confusing hierarchy, or unnecessarily repeating elements.

sources.title: Using AI for UX Work: Study Guide
sources.why: Guide to leveraging AI tools in UX design and research work.

claims.rule: Focus design strategy on defining user needs and intent rather than pixel-pushing; curate meaningful context for AI.
claims.quote: The core skills valuable today are moving more toward the pure UX work of defining user needs, specifying user intent, and overseeing the creation of excellent journeys — not the UI design of pushing pixels around in a design tool.

sources.title: AI Can't Replace Real Research in Empathy Mapping
sources.why: Limitations of AI for empathy mapping and user understanding.

claims.rule: Use AI only to organize and synthesize research you've already collected; never ask AI to generate user quotes or fill research gaps.
claims.quote: AI can help you organize research you've already collected, but it can't create research evidence about the specific, messy experience of real users.

claims.rule: Use AI only to organize and summarize research data you've already collected, not to generate user quotes, behaviors, or fill research gaps.
claims.quote: Even though AI should not be used for generating user content in empathy maps, it can be helpful for synthesizing data produced from real-user research.

sources.title: The Custodial Era of UX: Cleaning Up After AI
sources.why: Technical debt and design issues created by AI-generated outputs.

claims.rule: Evaluate AI output rigorously before shipping; production speed must not outpace UX evaluation.
claims.quote: Production has become cheaper than UX evaluation. It can now take less time to create an experience than to decide whether that experience is useful, usable, trustworthy, or coherent.

claims.rule: Identify and fix AI-generated content that is awkward, generic, or obviously artificial before launch.
claims.quote: Copy, graphics, and audio that are so obviously AI-generated that they become awkward distractions (and reputation killers)

claims.rule: Remove AI features that add complexity without solving real user problems.
claims.quote: Products overloaded with "smart" functionality that adds complexity but solves few real problems

claims.rule: Triage AI-generated features with cost-benefit analysis before refinement; decide what to keep, simplify, integrate, postpone, or remove.
claims.quote: don't start right away by polishing it. Triage it first and do a cost–benefit analysis.

claims.rule: Match evidence rigor to risk level; low-risk features warrant quick tests, high-stakes workflows need rigorous methods.
claims.quote: Match the evidence to the risk involved: a low-risk feature may warrant quick user tests, a new high-stakes workflow may warrant more rigorous (and time-consuming) methods.

claims.rule: Build shared team judgment by explaining triage decisions transparently so teams learn to distinguish buildable from useful features.
claims.quote: Explain why the feature works or doesn't, so the rest of the team learns how to apply the same UX criteria to the next idea.

claims.rule: Capture organizational UX knowledge in context files and design systems to guide AI-generated work and reduce predictable problems.
claims.quote: capture the design and UX knowledge within your organization and use it to inform AI-generated work

claims.rule: Edit AI-generated content ruthlessly to remove messages that obscure core value, redundant controls, and duplicated workflows.
claims.quote: Messages that obscure the core value? Redundant controls? Duplicated workflows? All of these should be removed rather than improved.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence: Glossary
sources.why: Glossary of AI terminology relevant to UX professionals.

claims.rule: Use automation bias safeguards: introduce friction at high-stakes moments and provide easy verification or override methods.
claims.quote: Introducing friction at high-stakes moments and providing easy ways for users to verify or override a result help prevent automation bias.

claims.rule: Ensure human-in-the-loop oversight only works when reviewers have information, time, expertise, and authority to intervene.
claims.quote: it counts as oversight only when the reviewer has the information, time, expertise, and authority to intervene.

sources.title: One AI Output Is an Example, Not an Evaluation
sources.why: Methodology for evaluating AI system outputs in user research.

claims.rule: Never evaluate an AI system from a single output; test with multiple representative inputs and repeated runs.
claims.quote: One good output demonstrates that a system can perform a task. It does not show how often or how reliably the system will do so.

claims.rule: Test AI systems with multiple representative inputs run repeatedly; report average performance and confidence intervals, not single outputs.
claims.quote: test multiple representative inputs, run each input repeatedly, and summarize the resulting distribution of scores

claims.rule: Measure both test-input variability and run-to-run variability; identical overall scores can mask different failure patterns.
claims.quote: two customer-service systems are each tested on 10 questions, with 5 runs per question. They both produce acceptable answers on 80% of the 50 runs

claims.rule: Document all system details before evaluation: model version, prompts, settings, tools, context, and date; repeat evaluation if any change.
claims.quote: carefully document all the details: record the model and version, prompts or instructions, settings, tools, context, and evaluation date.

sources.title: Dogfooding vs. QA vs. User Research
sources.why: Comparison of testing approaches for AI and complex systems.

claims.rule: Do not substitute employee usage for user research; employees know too much to represent real users.
claims.quote: They're insiders performing use, not real users encountering it fresh.

sources.title: How to Decide When an AI Tool Is Worth Keeping
sources.why: Framework for evaluating the value of AI tools and features.

claims.rule: Match the AI tool to your recurring task first; do not adopt based on demo performance alone.
claims.quote: Before you spend money, change a workflow, or ask colleagues to adopt anything, define the task first: what would this tool help you do?

claims.rule: Measure total time to complete work, not just AI generation time, to evaluate true velocity gains.
claims.quote: Velocity: Measure Total Time, Not Generation Time

claims.rule: Define the recurring task before evaluating an AI tool; match the tool's capabilities to that task, not vice versa.
claims.quote: Start with a recurring task that takes meaningful time or effort, then ask whether the tool's capabilities match that task.

claims.rule: Verify that the tool and its data handling comply with your organization's security and privacy policies before use.
claims.quote: Before spending hours testing a tool, make sure it's appropriate for the data you plan to give it. Is the tool approved by your organization?

claims.rule: Benchmark AI output against your own real work samples, not demo results, to assess whether quality is fit for the actual task and its stakes.
claims.quote: Pick an actual example of your own work and ask: is the tool's version better than, as good as, or good enough compared with what you already produce?

claims.rule: Count all time spent on setup, prompting, review, correction, and reformatting when measuring velocity; generation time alone does not predict total time saved.
claims.quote: Compare the total time required with and without the tool: setup, prompting, reviewing, correcting errors, reformatting, and moving material between systems.

claims.rule: Separate one-time friction (setup, learning) from recurring friction (workflow steps, handoffs) when assessing tool fit for ongoing tasks.
claims.quote: It's reasonable for a new tool to require setup and practice, but it's less reasonable for it to lead to an awkward, error-prone workflow forever.

sources.title: UX-Context Design: Using UX Knowledge to Inform AI-Generated Design
sources.why: Applying UX expertise to improve AI-generated design outputs.

claims.rule: Encode research findings and design standards as machine-readable context so any tool or person generates consistent output.
claims.quote: Context enables you to avoid middle-of-the-road output.

claims.rule: Curate raw research data and distill reasoning into AI-ready formats; traditional design documents do not serve AI models.
claims.quote: A persona has a stock photo and a first name with the intention of helping a human to empathize and remember. However, a model does not need persuading, it needs the underlying reasoning.

claims.rule: Store research synthesis and design standards in machine-readable formats (e.g., DESIGN.md, UX.md) that AI tools can read when generating anything.
claims.quote: The output of research and design work is, primarily, context that anyone in the organization can include when using AI to generate anything from slides to prototypes to working software.

claims.rule: Keep UX context alongside product code, update it as the product changes, and let AI tools read it on every generation; do not hand it off and leave it behind.
claims.quote: It lives with the product's code, changes when the product changes, and is read by every AI tool in the organization each time something gets generated.

sources.title: Don't Outsource the Learning: Why Human-Led Research Still Matters in the Age of AI
sources.why: Importance of human-led research despite AI advancement.

claims.rule: Include your team in user research sessions so they experience stories firsthand, not secondhand through reports.
claims.quote: Teams that observe user research are more likely to build a shared understanding and empathy for their users and the problem space.

claims.rule: Present research findings as stories about user experiences, not just data themes, because stories engage memory and emotion more powerfully.
claims.quote: Personal narratives engage brain regions associated with emotion, memory, and social reasoning more strongly than nonnarrative text.

claims.rule: Protect research phases where learning occurs: moderate sessions live, observe together, debrief as a team, and do interpretive work yourself.
claims.quote: The parts of the process to protect are the ones where the learning lives: moderating sessions, observing them live, debriefing together, and doing the interpretive work of deciding what the data means.

claims.rule: Personal stories trigger wider brain networks than technical content, engaging regions for emotion, memory, and social reasoning more strongly.
claims.quote: Personal narratives triggered a widespread network of activity across listeners, including regions involved in social reasoning, emotional processing, and memory.

claims.rule: Reading a comprehensive report creates an illusion of learning; actual retention mirrors students rereading notes without active engagement.
claims.quote: Reading a comprehensive, coherent report can create an 'illusion of learning,' where you feel informed but retain very little afterward.

sources.title: The 5 Qualities of Site-Specific AI Chatbots
sources.why: Five key dimensions for effective chatbot design.

claims.rule: Allow users to escalate immediately to a human agent when they explicitly request it, without gatekeeping or additional explanations.
claims.quote: Never gatekeep when the user explicitly asks to be connected to a human. If a customer asks for a human agent, the bot should immediately honor that request.

claims.rule: Design chatbots to handle questions adjacent to their trained domain, not just exact FAQs, so users feel the bot understands their real goals.
claims.quote: A bot that's too narrow is rigid and misses questions adjacent to the user's goal; a bot that's too broad answers off-domain and drifts beyond what the company authorized. The target is the middle — appropriately scoped: flexible enough to handle adjacent questions, disciplined enough to redirect what's genuinely out of scope.

claims.rule: Offer chatbot escalation to humans when the bot cannot answer effectively or detects user frustration or repeated rephrasing.
claims.quote: Beyond explicit requests, chatbots should offer to escalate when they can no longer answer effectively or when the user shows signs of frustration or extra effort (e.g., repeatedly rephrasing the same question).

claims.rule: Present suggested next steps as easily scannable, clickable buttons rather than buried in lengthy explanations.
claims.quote: Suggested next steps should be easily scannable and self-contained (ideally presented as clickable buttons), rather than buried in lengthy explanations that require careful reading.

claims.rule: Suggest follow-up actions only after the user's primary goal is resolved, not during active task completion.
claims.quote: When a user is working toward a goal, the bot should not distract them with unrelated suggestions. Suggest possible follow-up questions or related topics only after a resolution has been achieved or the primary goal has been addressed.

claims.rule: Close the gap between information and action by linking directly to products, resources, and actions rather than naming them.
claims.quote: Rather than simply naming a product or resource or telling people where to find it, they should link to it directly, including visuals and quick links (e.g., Add to cart , Save to favorites, Compare, Return policy ).

claims.rule: Acknowledge the situation plainly without claiming feelings the bot cannot have; say what happened, not how you feel about it.
claims.quote: When acknowledging users' emotions, a chatbot should not express feelings it cannot have; for example, saying I'm sincerely sorry about the delay can come across as performative. The better approach is to acknowledge the situation — for example, Two weeks is a long time to wait. Let me see what I can do to fix this .

claims.rule: Describe the situation itself, not the user's inner emotional state; avoid claims like 'I understand your disappointment.'
claims.quote: While it's appropriate to describe the situation itself (for example, That's a stressful situation ), chatbots should not make claims about the user's inner state (for example , I understand your disappointment ).

claims.rule: Surface bot capabilities contextually when most relevant, not as an exhaustive opening list that users will forget.
claims.quote: You can outline the bot's scope in its opening message, but don't show an exhaustive list of everything it can do. Users may find that overwhelming and forget it as the conversation moves forward. Instead, surface capabilities contextually , when they are most relevant.

claims.rule: Explain why a limitation exists and what the next step is, not just that you cannot help.
claims.quote: Compare I can't help with that , which is vague, with I don't have access to your purchase history, but I can connect you to someone who does . The second response explains the limitation and the next step.

sources.title: Ecommerce UX Audit: How to Find What's Hurting Your Conversion
sources.why: Framework for conducting comprehensive e-commerce UX audits.

claims.rule: Make main navigation product hierarchy immediately obvious; hiding catalog behind generic entries like 'Shop' adds friction.
claims.quote: Shoppers should be able to glance at your navigation menu and immediately digest the site's top-level structure

claims.rule: Expose product categories at first navigation level on mobile; hiding them behind generic entry points adds friction.
claims.quote: Hiding your entire catalog behind generic entry points like 'Shop' or 'Products' adds unnecessary friction, especially on mobile where product categories need to be exposed right at the first level

claims.rule: Make size, color, availability, and customization logic immediately clear; users should never decode configuration options.
claims.quote: Users should never have to decode size, color, availability, or customization logic just to figure out if the specific version they want is actually available

claims.rule: Show full order total including shipping, taxes, and fees before checkout; users abandon when costs aren't transparent.
claims.quote: If users can't see a clear order total (including shipping, taxes, and other fees), many will hesitate or abandon rather than start checkout half-informed

claims.rule: Support both increment/decrement buttons and direct text input for quantity; 61% of sites use only one method, creating friction.
claims.quote: 61% of sites in our ecommerce UX benchmark make it unnecessarily difficult for users to update the quantity of cart products, by using either only an open text field or a drop-down, rather than both together

claims.rule: Offer prominent guest checkout option; 18% of shoppers abandon when forced to create an account.
claims.quote: If users are pushed to sign in or create an account before they can proceed, many interpret it as friction; 18% of shoppers have abandoned a purchase because they were forced to create an account

claims.rule: Design payment fields for typing accuracy with clear validation and alternative payment methods if card isn't standard.
claims.quote: Users need payment fields that support typing accuracy, clear validation, and sensible alternatives if their preferred method isn't standard card entry

claims.rule: Include a review step in multistep checkout so users verify addresses, shipping, payment, and totals before submission.
claims.quote: In multistep checkouts especially, the review step is where users verify addresses, shipping choices, payment details, and totals without having to backtrack through the whole flow

claims.rule: Preserve filter states and cart contents when users move between mobile pages; loss of progress causes context loss.
claims.quote: Users should be able to move back and forth between pages without losing filter states or cart contents

claims.rule: Group mobile page content into collapsed sections to avoid endless scrolling; allow filter refining without excessive tapping.
claims.quote: Users should be able to refine large lists and evaluate product details without opening endless overlays, jumping through tabs, or scrolling through bloated pages

claims.rule: Surface cost, delivery, returns, and stock information early and repeatedly in mobile checkout to prevent late surprises.
claims.quote: Key cost, delivery, returns, and stock information should appear early and repeatedly during the checkout process to help build and maintain purchase confidence

sources.why: Benefits and value proposition of comprehensive UX audits.

claims.rule: Test checkout design changes systematically; research shows large sites gain up to 35% conversion uplift from checkout redesign.
claims.quote: the average large-sized ecommerce site can gain as much as a 35% increase in conversion rate just by making design changes to their checkout process

claims.rule: Evaluate designs against external standards to remove internal bias from objective assessment.
claims.quote: An audit conducted against an external standard removes that bias.

claims.rule: Benchmark mobile checkout against industry median and top quartile sites to calibrate competitiveness.
claims.quote: how far below the median it sits, and what the top quartile of sites in your category looks like

claims.rule: Audit designs before launch to reduce total cost of UX fixes, including development, testing, and redesign cycles.
claims.quote: UX problems caught early — before a site redesign ships, a new checkout flow goes live, or mobile experience is revamped — are significantly cheaper to fix

claims.rule: Conduct pre-launch audits of new flows at design stage, not after shipping; fixes cost less and avoid full sprint rework.
claims.quote: A pre-launch audit of a new checkout flow, conducted before development begins, surfaces these issues when they're still design decisions — not engineering changes. The same issue that takes a developer an afternoon to fix in a wireframe can take an entire sprint to fix after it's shipped

claims.rule: Evaluate against external standards to remove internal bias; familiarity blinds teams to first-time user friction.
claims.quote: Familiarity with the website also creates genuine blind spots: interactions that feel intuitive to a team that built them may be confusing to a first-time user

claims.rule: Use research-backed audit standards so findings map to documented failure patterns, not subjective reviewer preference.
claims.quote: A finding isn't rated severe because one reviewer found it annoying. It's rated severe because it maps to a pattern that usability testing has documented as a consistent cause of abandonment or failure

claims.rule: Give mobile UX dedicated audit attention; mobile accounts for ~75% of retail visits but gets late, shallow testing.
claims.quote: Mobile accounts for the majority of ecommerce traffic on most sites, generating around three quarters of retail store visits. Mobile UX is often worse than desktop, and mobile-specific issues are sometimes underrepresented in routine design reviews
